children.name: Agaricomycetes
children.commonName: Mushrooms, Bracket Fungi, Puffballs, and Allies

children.name: Agaricales
Cortinariaceae
Cortinarius
children.description: Webcaps are a massive genus of mushrooms that form partnerships with tree roots, helping forests thrive while producing their own fruiting bodies above ground. These fungi are known for the cobweb-like partial veil that covers young mushrooms, which gives them their common name. They come in an amazing array of colors from deep violets and brilliant oranges to earthy browns and yellows.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Webcaps are distinguished by their characteristic cortina - a silky, cobweb-like veil that protects the gills when young and often leaves rusty brown spore deposits on the stem as the mushroom matures. Unlike many other mushroom groups, they always form mycorrhizal relationships with trees.
children.funFact: Cortinarius is the largest genus of mushrooms in the world, with an estimated 2,000+ species globally, and New England alone hosts over 100 different webcap species in its diverse forests.

children.name: Thaxterogaster
children.description: Thaxterogaster is a genus of mushrooms that were formerly classified as webcaps (Cortinarius) but have been reclassified based on genetic studies. These fungi form partnerships with tree roots and are characterized by their often colorful caps and the tendency of many species to bruise or change color when damaged.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true webcaps, Thaxterogaster species have distinct genetic markers and often show more pronounced color changes when bruised or cut. Many species in this genus display vibrant purples, greens, and other striking colors.
children.funFact: The bruising webcap lives up to its name by turning bright blue or purple when its flesh is damaged, creating a dramatic color-changing display that helps with identification.

children.name: Phlegmacium
children.description: Phlegmacium is a genus of mushrooms commonly known as webcaps, characterized by their distinctive web-like partial veil that covers the gills when young. These fungi form important partnerships with tree roots, helping forests absorb nutrients from the soil. Many species in this group display beautiful colors ranging from browns and purples to blues and yellows.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other webcap relatives, Phlegmacium species typically have more robust, fleshy caps and stems, and their web-like veils are often more prominent and persistent than in related genera.
children.funFact: The blushing webcap gets its name because its flesh turns pink or reddish when cut or bruised, like a mushroom that's embarrassed!

children.name: Aureonarius
children.description: Aureonarius is a genus of medium-sized mushrooms that are part of the webcap family, known for their golden to orange-brown colors and connection to tree roots. These mushrooms form beneficial partnerships with trees, helping them absorb nutrients from the soil in exchange for sugars from the tree.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished from other webcaps by their warm golden to tawny orange coloration and specific microscopic spore characteristics. They typically have a more robust appearance than many of their webcap relatives.
children.funFact: The name 'Aureonarius' comes from the Latin word 'aureus' meaning golden, referring to the beautiful golden hues that make these mushrooms stand out in the forest.

children.name: Cystinarius
children.description: Cystinarius is a genus of mushrooms commonly known as webcaps, named for the web-like partial veil that covers young mushroom caps. These fungi are mycorrhizal partners with trees, forming beneficial relationships with forest roots while producing distinctive rusty-brown spore prints.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Webcaps in this genus are distinguished by their robust, stocky appearance and the characteristic web-like cortina that stretches between the cap and stem in young specimens. They typically have thick, sturdy stems and caps that range from reddish to brown tones.
children.funFact: The name 'webcap' comes from the delicate, spider web-like veil called a cortina that protects the developing gills, which eventually breaks apart as the mushroom matures, sometimes leaving silk-like remnants on the stem.

children.name: Calonarius
children.description: Chalkland Webcaps are a small group of mushrooms that belong to the larger webcap family, known for their distinctive spore-bearing structures and ecological relationships with trees. These fungi form beneficial partnerships with tree roots, helping forests exchange nutrients through underground networks. They get their common name from their preference for chalky, limestone-rich soils.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Chalkland Webcaps are distinguished from other webcap mushrooms by their specific habitat requirements, particularly their preference for alkaline, chalky soils. They typically have a more restricted geographic distribution compared to their more common webcap relatives.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'Chalkland' Webcaps, New England's single species in this genus, Atkinson's Fungus, demonstrates how these specialized soil-loving mushrooms can adapt to the varied geological conditions of our region's diverse landscapes.

children.description: Webcaps are a diverse family of mushrooms that get their name from the cobweb-like partial veil that covers young mushroom caps, leaving behind rusty brown spores on the gills. These fungi form important partnerships with tree roots, helping forests absorb nutrients while receiving sugars in return. They're among the most common mushrooms you'll encounter in New England's woodlands, though many species can be tricky to tell apart.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The signature cobweb-like veil and rusty brown spore prints make webcaps distinctive from other mushroom families. Unlike many other fungi, they form essential mycorrhizal relationships with trees and typically have gills that change color as spores mature.
children.funFact: Webcaps are considered one of the most challenging mushroom groups for identification - even experts often need microscopic examination to distinguish between the hundreds of similar-looking species!

children.name: Hygrophoraceae
Hygrocybe
children.description: Waxcaps are colorful mushrooms known for their bright, waxy-looking caps that feel smooth and often slightly slippery to the touch. These eye-catching fungi come in brilliant shades of red, orange, yellow, and purple, making them some of the most vibrant mushrooms you'll encounter in New England's forests and grasslands. They typically have thick, waxy gills that match or complement their cap colors.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other mushrooms, waxcaps have distinctively thick, waxy gills and caps with a characteristic smooth, almost greasy texture. Their unusually bright colors and the waxy feel of their surfaces make them easy to distinguish from other mushroom groups.
children.funFact: Many waxcap species are considered indicators of healthy, undisturbed grassland ecosystems - some require soil that hasn't been fertilized for decades to thrive!

children.name: Hygrophorus
children.description: Woodwaxes are a group of mushrooms known for their distinctively waxy or greasy-feeling caps and gills that feel slippery to the touch. These fungi typically have thick, widely-spaced gills and often display beautiful colors ranging from pure white to golden yellow, pink, or purple. They form beneficial partnerships with tree roots, particularly conifers, helping forests exchange nutrients.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other mushroom groups, woodwaxes have gills that feel noticeably waxy or greasy when rubbed between your fingers, and their gills are typically much thicker and more widely spaced than most other mushrooms.
children.funFact: The Herald of Winter gets its dramatic name because it's one of the few mushrooms that continues fruiting well into late fall and early winter, often appearing after the first frosts when most other fungi have disappeared for the season.

children.name: Cuphophyllus
children.description: Waxcaps in the genus Cuphophyllus are small to medium-sized mushrooms with waxy, often translucent caps that feel smooth and slightly greasy to the touch. These mushrooms typically have white spores and grow in grassy areas like meadows, lawns, and forest clearings. They come in subtle colors ranging from white and gray to pale orange and violet hues.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other waxcap genera, Cuphophyllus species have relatively thick, waxy gills that are often widely spaced and tend to be white or pale colored. Their caps typically have a matte or slightly translucent appearance rather than the bright, vibrant colors seen in other waxcap groups.
children.funFact: Many waxcaps, including Cuphophyllus species, are considered indicator species of healthy grassland ecosystems - their presence suggests that the soil has not been heavily fertilized or chemically treated.

children.name: Humidicutis
children.description: Humidicutis is a genus of small, delicate mushrooms known as waxcaps that love moist environments. These fungi have distinctively waxy or greasy-feeling caps and gills, and they typically grow in moss, decaying wood, or other damp organic matter in forests.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other waxcaps that grow in grassy areas, Humidicutis species prefer humid forest environments and often have more subdued colors. Their caps and gills have a characteristic waxy texture that feels almost slippery to the touch.
children.funFact: The genus name Humidicutis literally means 'moist skin,' perfectly describing both their preferred damp habitats and their distinctive waxy appearance.

children.name: Gliophorus
children.description: Waxcaps in the genus Gliophorus are small to medium-sized mushrooms known for their waxy, slippery caps that often display brilliant colors. These fungi typically grow in grassy areas, meadows, and heathlands, where they play an important ecological role in nutrient cycling. All members of this genus have a distinctly waxy or greasy texture to their caps when fresh.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Gliophorus waxcaps are distinguished from other waxcap genera by their particularly slimy or viscid (sticky) cap surfaces and their preference for acidic, nutrient-poor soils. They also tend to have more translucent flesh and thinner stems compared to their close relatives.
children.funFact: The Parrot Mushroom gets its name from its amazing ability to change colors as it ages, starting bright green like a parrot's feathers and gradually fading to yellow and orange!

children.name: Arrhenia
children.description: Arrhenia is a genus of small, delicate mushrooms that typically grow on moss, decaying wood, or other organic matter in moist environments. These fungi produce thin, often cup-shaped or oyster-like fruiting bodies that are usually brown, gray, or whitish in color. They play an important ecological role as decomposers, helping to break down organic material in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Arrhenia mushrooms are distinguished by their small size, thin flesh, and preference for growing directly on moss or in very moist habitats where other mushrooms rarely thrive. Their spores are typically smooth and white, and many species have gills that run down the stem.
children.funFact: Despite their tiny size, Arrhenia mushrooms are tough survivors that can fruit even in the coldest months when most other fungi have gone dormant for the winter.

children.name: Lichenomphalia
children.description: Lichenomphalia is a fascinating genus that represents a unique partnership between fungi and algae, forming what are known as lichenized mushrooms. These organisms combine the typical mushroom structure of cap and stem with the symbiotic relationship found in lichens, where the fungus provides structure and protection while the algae produce food through photosynthesis.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike typical mushrooms that decompose organic matter, or regular lichens that form crusts or leafy structures, Lichenomphalia species produce actual mushroom fruiting bodies while maintaining a lichen partnership with green algae.
children.funFact: Lichenomphalia species are among the very few organisms on Earth that blur the line between mushrooms and lichens, making them living examples of how nature doesn't always fit into neat categories.

children.name: Gloioxanthomyces
children.description: Gloioxanthomyces is a small genus of waxy cap mushrooms known for their distinctively shiny, slippery caps that glisten when moist. These mushrooms typically have a waxy texture and produce white spores, growing in grassy areas and open woodlands.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished from other waxcaps by their exceptionally glossy, almost greasy-looking caps that maintain their shine even when dry. They also tend to have a more robust, stocky appearance compared to their more delicate waxcap relatives.
children.funFact: The name 'Gloioxanthomyces' literally means 'slimy yellow fungus,' referring to the characteristically slippery, often yellowish caps that feel almost soap-like to the touch.

children.name: Cantharellula
children.description: Cantharellula is a small genus of mushrooms that produces distinctive funnel-shaped fruiting bodies with a characteristic hump or bump in the center of the cap. These fungi are decomposers that help break down organic matter in forest ecosystems. The genus contains only a few species worldwide, with just one species found in New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true chanterelles, Cantharellula mushrooms have true gills rather than ridges on the underside of their caps, and they feature a distinctive central bump or umbo that gives them their 'humpback' appearance.
children.funFact: The name Cantharellula means 'little chanterelle' because these mushrooms were once thought to be closely related to chanterelles, but genetic studies have shown they belong to a completely different fungal family.

children.name: Ampulloclitocybe
children.description: Ampulloclitocybe is a small genus of mushrooms that includes fungi with distinctive club-shaped or swollen stem bases. These mushrooms are typically found growing on decaying wood in forests, where they help break down dead organic matter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their notably enlarged, bulbous stem bases that give them a distinctive club-like appearance, which is reflected in the common name of the single New England species.
children.funFact: The genus name Ampulloclitocybe literally means 'flask-shaped Clitocybe,' referring to the characteristic swollen stem base that looks like a small bottle or flask.

children.name: Chromosera
children.description: Chromosera is a small genus of rare aquatic plants that grow in freshwater habitats like ponds and slow-moving streams. These delicate plants are known for their distinctive lilac-colored foliage that gives them their common name. They are part of a specialized group of aquatic flowering plants adapted to life underwater and at water's edge.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Chromosera stands out from other aquatic plants due to its unique purple-lilac colored leaves, which is unusual among freshwater vegetation. The plants also have a distinctive growth pattern with leaves arranged in opposite pairs along the stem.
children.funFact: Chromosera lilacifolia gets its purple coloration from specialized pigments that may help protect the plant from intense sunlight filtering through shallow water.

children.name: Pseudoarmillariella
children.description: Pseudoarmillariella is a small genus of mushrooms that were once classified with the honey mushrooms (Armillaria) but have since been recognized as a distinct group. These fungi are characterized by their pale, streaked caps and their ability to decompose dead wood in forest environments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true honey mushrooms, Pseudoarmillariella species lack the distinctive ring around the stem and have a different spore print color. They also have a more delicate appearance with distinctive streaked patterns on their caps.
children.funFact: The name Pseudoarmillariella literally means 'false little Armillaria,' reflecting how these mushrooms were originally mistaken for small honey mushrooms until genetic studies revealed they belonged to their own separate lineage.

children.name: Chrysomphalina
children.description: Chrysomphalina is a small genus of delicate mushrooms that grow on decaying wood in forests. These tiny fungi have thin, translucent caps and slender stems, creating an almost fairy-like appearance on fallen logs and branches.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their small size, golden-yellow coloration, and preference for growing on well-rotted hardwood. They have widely spaced gills and produce white spores.
children.funFact: Despite their delicate appearance, Chrysomphalina mushrooms are important decomposers that help break down dead wood and return nutrients to the forest ecosystem.

children.name: Porpolomopsis
children.description: Porpolomopsis is a small genus of delicate mushrooms known as waxcaps, characterized by their waxy, translucent appearance and bright colors. These fungi are typically found in grasslands and meadows, where they help decompose organic matter in the soil. In New England, this genus is represented by just one species - the beautiful Pink Waxcap.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Porpolomopsis are distinguished from other waxcaps by their distinctive cap shape that resembles a small hood or bonnet, and their particularly waxy, almost greasy texture when fresh.
children.funFact: The Pink Waxcap's scientific name 'calyptriformis' means 'hood-shaped,' referring to its distinctive cap that looks like a tiny pink bonnet sitting in the grass.

children.name: Neohygrocybe
children.description: Neohygrocybe is a small genus of waxy cap mushrooms that are characterized by their smooth, waxy-textured caps and stems. These fungi are typically found in grasslands and meadows, where they help decompose organic matter in the soil.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other waxcap genera, Neohygrocybe species have a distinctive nitrous odor (like bleach or swimming pool chemicals) and typically display pale yellow to whitish coloration.
children.funFact: The single New England species, the Nitrous Waxcap, gets its name from its strong chemical smell that can be detected from several feet away when the mushroom is fresh.

children.description: Waxcaps and their allies are a diverse family of mushrooms best known for their distinctive waxy or greasy-feeling caps and gills. Many species display brilliant colors including bright yellows, oranges, reds, and even blues, making them some of the most eye-catching fungi in New England forests and grasslands. This family includes not only the classic waxcaps but also some species that form partnerships with algae to create lichen-like organisms.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The waxy or greasy texture of their caps and gills is the most reliable identifying feature, often accompanied by thick, widely-spaced gills. Unlike many mushroom families, waxcaps typically have white spore prints and their gills often appear to be made of wax.
children.funFact: Some members of this family, like Lichenomphalia, are actually part fungus and part algae, forming colorful lichen partnerships that blur the line between the fungal and plant kingdoms.

children.name: Amanitaceae
Amanita
children.description: Amanita mushrooms are a large and diverse genus of fungi known for their distinctive appearance, featuring a cap, stem, and often a cup-like structure called a volva at the base. Many species also have a ring around the stem and may display patches or scales on their caps. This group includes some of the most beautiful mushrooms in New England forests, but also some of the most dangerous.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Amanitas are distinguished from other mushrooms by their white spore prints and the presence of a volva (cup or bulbous base) where the stem meets the ground. Many also have a ring on the stem and white gills that remain free from the stem.
children.funFact: This genus contains both the world's most deadly mushrooms (like the Destroying Angel and Death Cap) and some prized edible species, making proper identification absolutely critical for mushroom foragers.

children.name: Zhuliangomyces
children.description: Zhuliangomyces is a small genus of fungi that produces distinctive mushrooms with slimy, gelatinous caps. These fungi are saprobic, meaning they feed on decaying organic matter and help break down dead plant material in forest ecosystems. They belong to a group of fungi known for their unique jelly-like textures.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their notably slimy, mucilaginous cap surface that gives them a distinctly wet, dripping appearance even in dry conditions.
children.funFact: This genus was only recently described by scientists and is named after Chinese mycologist Zhu-Liang Yang, highlighting how much we still have to discover about fungal diversity.

children.description: The Amanitaceae family includes some of the most recognizable mushrooms in New England forests, characterized by their distinctive white gills and often prominent ring around the stem. These fungi typically emerge from the ground with a cup-like structure called a volva at the base, which may be buried or visible. Most species in this family form beneficial partnerships with tree roots, helping forests thrive.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their white spore prints, free gills that don't attach to the stem, and the presence of both a ring (annulus) and basal cup (volva) in many species. The volva at the stem base is particularly diagnostic, setting them apart from other white-gilled mushrooms.
children.funFact: This family contains both some of the most deadly poisonous mushrooms in the world (like the destroying angel) and some prized edible species, making proper identification absolutely critical for foragers.

children.name: Entolomataceae
Entoloma
children.description: Pinkgills are a diverse group of mushrooms that get their name from their distinctive pink spores, which give the gills a rosy hue as the mushroom matures. These fungi are typically small to medium-sized with caps that can range from colorful to drab, and they're found growing on wood, soil, or sometimes even parasitizing other mushrooms. With 48 species found in New England alone, pinkgills represent one of the more species-rich mushroom groups in our region.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The pink spores and resulting pink-tinted gills are the key identifying feature that separates pinkgills from other mushroom groups. Unlike mushrooms with white, brown, or black spores, the salmon to rose-colored spore print is diagnostic for this genus.
children.funFact: The Aborted Entoloma has a fascinating relationship with honey mushrooms - when it parasitizes them, it transforms the honey mushrooms into bizarre, cauliflower-like blobs that are actually considered a gourmet edible!

children.name: Clitopilus
children.description: Clitopilus is a genus of small to medium-sized mushrooms that are saprophytic, meaning they feed on decaying organic matter in forest soils and leaf litter. These mushrooms are characterized by their pink spore prints and gills that run down the stem (called decurrent gills). They typically have white to grayish caps and are found growing on the ground in woodlands throughout New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The pink spore print is the key identifying feature that separates Clitopilus from other white-gilled mushrooms. Their strongly decurrent gills and terrestrial habitat also help distinguish them from similar-looking oyster mushrooms that grow on wood.
children.funFact: The Sweetbread Mushroom (Clitopilus prunulus) gets its name from its distinctive smell, which resembles fresh bread dough or flour, making it one of the few mushrooms you can identify by scent alone!

children.name: Lulesia
children.description: Lulesia is a small genus of moths in the family Geometridae, commonly known as geometer moths or inchworms. These moths are characterized by their delicate wings and the caterpillars' distinctive looping movement as they crawl.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Lulesia moths can be distinguished from other geometrid moths by their specific wing patterns and coloration, though detailed examination is often needed for proper identification.
children.funFact: The caterpillars of Lulesia moths move by arching their bodies into loops, earning geometrid moths the nickname 'inchworms' or 'loopers.'

children.name: Rhodocybe
children.description: Rhodocybe is a small genus of mushrooms known for their distinctive pink-colored spores and gills. These mushrooms typically have pale, tan-colored caps and grow on decaying organic matter in forests. They are part of the larger group of fungi that help decompose dead plant material in woodland ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The pink-colored spores and gills that develop a pinkish tinge as the mushroom matures set Rhodocybe apart from other similar-looking brown mushrooms. Their spore color is particularly distinctive when viewed in spore prints.
children.funFact: The name 'Rhodocybe' literally means 'pink head' in Greek, referring to the rosy-colored spores that give these mushrooms their characteristic appearance.

children.description: The Entolomataceae are a diverse family of mushrooms known for their distinctive pink spores, which create pink spore prints when the mushroom cap is placed gill-side down on paper. These fungi typically have gills that are attached to the stem and angular spores when viewed under a microscope. They include both saprophytic species that decompose organic matter and some that form beneficial relationships with plant roots.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their pink spore prints and uniquely angular, multi-sided spores that look geometric under magnification. Unlike many other pink-spored mushrooms, most Entolomataceae have gills that are attached to or run down the stem rather than being free from it.
children.funFact: The genus name 'Entoloma' literally means 'inrolled fringe,' referring to how the edges of young mushroom caps are typically rolled inward before they expand and flatten out.

children.name: Hymenogastraceae
Gymnopilus
children.description: Rustgills are a group of medium to large mushrooms that get their name from their distinctive rusty orange-brown spore prints and gills that often develop rust-colored stains as they age. These fungi are typically found growing on decaying wood, logs, and stumps throughout New England's forests. Most species in this group have golden-yellow to orange-brown caps and produce bitter-tasting flesh.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Rustgills are distinguished from other mushrooms by their characteristic rusty orange-brown spore prints and their preference for growing on wood rather than soil. Many species also have a partial veil that leaves a ring on the stem and distinctive bitter or acrid taste.
children.funFact: The Spectacular Rustgill lives up to its name as one of the largest mushrooms in this group, with caps that can reach over 8 inches across and create impressive golden clusters on dead hardwood trees.

children.name: Galerina
children.description: Moss Bells are small, delicate mushrooms that typically grow in wet, mossy environments like bogs, marshes, and forest floors. These little brown fungi have thin stems and small, bell-shaped caps that often have a distinctive rusty-brown spore print. Most species in this group prefer damp, acidic conditions and can be found growing among mosses and other low vegetation.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Moss Bells are distinguished from other small brown mushrooms by their rusty-brown spore prints and their preference for growing in wet, mossy habitats. They typically have thin, fragile stems and small caps that are often hygrophanous, meaning they change color as they dry out.
children.funFact: Some Moss Bell species, particularly the Funeral Bell, contain deadly toxins similar to those found in Death Cap mushrooms, making proper identification crucial for mushroom foragers.

children.name: Psilocybe
children.description: Psilocybe mushrooms are a group of small to medium-sized fungi that typically grow on decaying wood, wood chips, or in grassy areas. These mushrooms are characterized by their dark spore prints and their ability to produce certain psychoactive compounds. They often have slender stems and caps that range from bell-shaped to conical.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their dark purple-brown to black spore prints and the tendency for some species to bruise blue when damaged. Unlike many other small brown mushrooms, Psilocybe species typically have a partial veil when young that may leave a ring on the stem.
children.funFact: The name 'Psilocybe' comes from Greek words meaning 'bald head,' referring to the smooth, often hairless caps that many species in this genus display.

children.name: Agrocybe
children.description: Agrocybe is a genus of small to medium-sized mushrooms commonly known as fieldcaps, typically found growing in grassy areas, mulch, and disturbed soils. These mushrooms are characterized by their brown to tan caps, sturdy stems with distinctive rings, and their preference for nutrient-rich environments. Most species in this genus are saprophytic, meaning they decompose organic matter and play an important role in soil health.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Fieldcaps are distinguished from other brown mushrooms by their prominent stem rings and their tendency to grow in open, grassy habitats rather than in deep woods. Their spores are typically brown to dark brown, and many species have a distinctive mealy or flour-like odor.
children.funFact: The Spring Fieldcap (Agrocybe praecox) is one of the earliest mushrooms to appear each year, often fruiting when the ground is still cool from winter, earning it the nickname 'the early bird of the mushroom world.'

children.name: Hebeloma
children.description: Poisonpies are a group of medium-sized mushrooms that grow from the soil, often appearing in disturbed areas like roadsides, gardens, and forest edges. These fungi have brownish caps and pale gills, and they play an important role as decomposers in forest ecosystems. Despite their ominous name, they're called 'poisonpies' because of their bitter, unpleasant taste rather than being deadly toxic.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Poisonpies can be recognized by their radish-like odor, brownish caps that often have a darker center, and gills that start pale but develop rusty-brown spores as they mature. Unlike many similar mushrooms, they typically have a distinctive bitter taste and often show tears or droplets on their gill edges when young.
children.funFact: The scientific name Hebeloma literally means 'youth edge' in Greek, referring to the droplets that often appear along the edges of young mushroom gills - a key identification feature for this genus.

children.name: Kuehneromyces
children.description: Kuehneromyces is a small genus of wood-decomposing mushrooms that are commonly found growing on dead hardwood logs, stumps, and branches throughout New England's forests. These mushrooms are characterized by their brownish caps and distinctive ring-like sheaths around their stems, which is why some species are called "sheathed woodtufts." They play an important ecological role as saprophytes, helping to break down dead wood and recycle nutrients back into the forest ecosystem.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their partial veil that forms a ring or sheath on the stem, their preference for hardwood substrates, and their brownish spore prints. Unlike some similar-looking mushrooms, Kuehneromyces species have a membranous ring that often becomes torn or tattered with age.
children.funFact: The genus name Kuehneromyces honors German mycologist Robert Kühner, a pioneering researcher who made significant contributions to understanding the relationships between different mushroom groups in the mid-20th century.

children.name: Phaeocollybia
children.description: Phaeocollybia is a genus of distinctive mushrooms commonly known as rootshanks, named for their characteristic long, tapering root-like stem that extends deep underground. These woodland fungi are mycorrhizal partners with trees, forming beneficial relationships with their host plants' root systems. They typically have brownish caps and produce brown spores.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The defining feature of rootshanks is their remarkably long, slender stem that tapers to a root-like extension buried deep in the soil, often extending 6-12 inches below ground. This underground 'pseudorhiza' makes them unmistakable among forest mushrooms.
children.funFact: Rootshanks can be incredibly difficult to collect intact because their underground stem extensions are so long and fragile that they often break when you try to dig them up completely.

children.name: Deconica
children.description: Deconica is a genus of small mushrooms that includes species adapted to very different environments. These fungi produce modest, often brownish mushrooms with caps that typically measure just a few centimeters across.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Deconica mushrooms are distinguished by their small size, brownish spore prints, and their ability to thrive in specialized habitats that many other mushrooms cannot tolerate.
children.funFact: Despite being in the same genus, these mushrooms have evolved to live in completely opposite environments - one thrives in alpine conditions on mountains while the other specializes in decomposing animal waste.

children.name: Hemistropharia
children.description: Hemistropharia is a small genus of mushrooms that includes just a few species worldwide. These fungi are wood-decomposers that help break down dead plant material in forest ecosystems. They produce medium-sized mushrooms with caps that typically have distinctive whitish edges or margins.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their caps with pale, often whitish margins that contrast with the darker center portions. They also have specific microscopic features that distinguish them from closely related mushroom genera.
children.funFact: The genus name Hemistropharia comes from Greek roots meaning 'half-twisted,' likely referring to some characteristic of their spore-bearing structures.

children.name: Flammula
children.description: Flammula is a small genus of mushrooms known for their scaly caps and preference for growing on or near woody debris. These fungi are saprobic, meaning they feed on dead organic matter and help decompose wood in forest ecosystems. In New England, this genus is represented by just one species that has a special relationship with alder trees.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Flammula are characterized by their distinctive scaly or flaky caps that give them their common name 'scalycaps.' They typically have brown spores and grow in clusters on decaying wood or soil rich in woody debris.
children.funFact: The genus name 'Flammula' comes from Latin meaning 'little flame,' likely referring to the flame-like or flickering appearance of their scaly cap surfaces.

children.name: Hemipholiota
children.description: Hemipholiota is a small genus of wood-decay fungi that grows on hardwood trees, particularly aspens and poplars. These mushrooms are parasitic, meaning they attack and weaken living trees while also decomposing dead wood. They produce medium-sized, brownish mushrooms with distinctive caps and stems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike their close relatives in the genus Pholiota, Hemipholiota species have a unique combination of features including their preference for poplar trees and specific microscopic characteristics of their spores and cap structure.
children.funFact: The Destructive Pholiota lives up to its name by being one of the most aggressive tree pathogens in North America, capable of killing healthy aspen and poplar trees within just a few years of infection.

children.description: The Hymenogastraceae family includes a diverse collection of mushrooms that are often small to medium-sized with brown spores and typically grow on wood, soil, or moss. Many members of this family have caps that range from yellow and orange to brown colors, and they're commonly found in forests, gardens, and even on lawns throughout New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: What sets this family apart is their rusty-brown to dark brown spore prints and their preference for decomposing organic matter. Many species in this group have a ring around the stem and show a distinctive rusty or cinnamon-colored spore deposit.
children.funFact: This family includes both some of the most toxic mushrooms you can find (like the deadly Poisonpies) and some that contain psychoactive compounds, making proper identification absolutely crucial for any mushroom enthusiast.

children.name: Mycenaceae
Mycena
children.description: Bonnets are a diverse group of small, delicate mushrooms that typically have thin, bell-shaped or conical caps and slender stems. Most species in this genus are saprobes, meaning they decompose dead organic matter like fallen logs, leaf litter, and other plant debris in forests. They're often found growing in clusters and play an important role in nutrient cycling in woodland ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Bonnets can be distinguished from other small mushrooms by their typically thin, translucent caps that often have radial grooves, and their white spore prints. Many species also have distinctive characteristics like colored latex that bleeds when cut, strong odors, or specific color changes when bruised.
children.funFact: Several bonnet species earn their dramatic common names from their ability to "bleed" colored liquids when damaged - the Bleeding Fairy Helmet oozes dark red droplets, while the Milking Bonnet produces white latex, creating a striking visual effect in the forest.

children.name: Panellus
children.description: Oysterlings are small, bracket-like fungi that grow in overlapping clusters on dead hardwood trees and logs. These tough, leathery mushrooms have a distinctive oyster or fan shape and typically appear in shades of brown, tan, or violet. They are saprophytic fungi, meaning they help decompose dead wood and return nutrients to the forest ecosystem.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Oysterlings are distinguished from other bracket fungi by their small size, thin flesh, and tendency to grow in densely packed, overlapping groups. Unlike many bracket fungi, they have true gills on the underside rather than pores.
children.funFact: The Luminescent Panellus can actually glow in the dark with a greenish bioluminescent light, though this ghostly glow is often too faint to see with the naked eye and is more pronounced in younger specimens.

children.name: Roridomyces
children.description: Roridomyces is a small genus of delicate mushrooms that includes the aptly named Dripping Bonnet. These tiny fungi are characterized by their distinctive habit of producing water droplets that hang from their gills and cap edges, creating a dewdrop-like appearance. They are saprophytic mushrooms that help decompose organic matter in forest environments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The key feature that sets Roridomyces apart from other small mushrooms is their unique ability to produce and maintain visible water droplets on their fruiting bodies, particularly along the gill edges.
children.funFact: The genus name 'Roridomyces' literally means 'dewy mushroom' in Latin, perfectly describing their characteristic droplet-covered appearance that makes them look like they're perpetually covered in morning dew.

children.name: Hemimycena
children.description: Halfbonnets are a genus of tiny, delicate mushrooms that get their name from their small, bell-shaped or bonnet-like caps. These diminutive fungi are typically found growing on decaying wood, logs, and woody debris in forests. They play an important role as decomposers, helping to break down dead plant material.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Halfbonnets are distinguished from other small mushrooms by their characteristic milky or translucent white appearance and their preference for growing directly on rotting wood rather than soil.
children.funFact: Despite their tiny size - often less than an inch tall - halfbonnets can be surprisingly numerous, sometimes appearing in dense clusters that look like miniature fairy rings on fallen logs.

children.name: Resinomycena
children.description: Resinomycena is a small genus of tiny mushrooms that grow on dead wood and plant debris in forest environments. These delicate fungi are characterized by their small size and their ability to produce a resinous or sticky substance, which gives them their name.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their resinous secretions and their preference for growing on specific plant materials, particularly rhododendron debris. They have very small, delicate fruiting bodies that can be easily overlooked in the forest.
children.funFact: The single New England species, Resinomycena rhododendri, is so specialized that it almost exclusively grows on dead rhododendron leaves and twigs, making it a very picky eater in the fungal world!

children.description: Mycenaceae is a diverse family of small to medium-sized mushrooms that includes many of the delicate, bell-shaped fungi you'll find growing on decaying wood, leaves, and other organic matter in New England forests. Most members of this family are saprophytes, meaning they help break down dead plant material and return nutrients to the forest ecosystem. They typically have thin, fragile caps and slender stems, often appearing in clusters on rotting logs or forest debris.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their typically small size, thin flesh, and white spore prints. Many species have distinctive features like bleeding latex when cut, strong odors, or caps that become translucent when wet.
children.funFact: Many Mycena species are bioluminescent, creating an eerie green glow in dark forests - this phenomenon is called 'foxfire' and occurs when enzymes in the mushroom react with oxygen.

children.name: Tricholomataceae
Tricholoma
children.description: Knights are a diverse group of mushrooms that typically have sturdy, fleshy caps and grow in partnership with tree roots in forests. Most species have white or pale-colored spores and thick, often bulky stems that give them their robust, knight-like appearance. They're commonly found under both hardwood and coniferous trees throughout New England's woodlands.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Knights can be distinguished from other mushrooms by their combination of white spore prints, thick stems, and gills that are typically notched or attached to the stem in a distinctive way. Many species also have a somewhat waxy or greasy feel to their caps.
children.funFact: Some Knights, like the American matsutake, are prized edible mushrooms with a distinctive spicy-sweet aroma, while others like the Yellow Knight were once considered edible but are now avoided due to potential toxicity concerns.

children.name: Pseudotricholoma
children.description: Pseudotricholoma is a small genus of mushrooms that grows on the ground in forests, forming partnerships with tree roots. These fungi help trees absorb nutrients from the soil while receiving sugars in return, making them important partners in forest ecosystems. They produce medium-sized mushrooms with gills underneath their caps.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Despite their name suggesting similarity to Tricholoma mushrooms, Pseudotricholoma species have different microscopic features and genetic makeup that place them in their own distinct group. They can be identified by their specific gill attachment and spore characteristics.
children.funFact: The name Pseudotricholoma literally means 'false Tricholoma' because these mushrooms were originally thought to belong to the Tricholoma genus until DNA studies revealed they deserved their own separate classification.

children.name: Leucopaxillus
children.description: Leucopaxillus is a genus of large, white mushrooms that grow on the ground in forests. These impressive fungi are known for their substantial size and pale coloration, forming thick, meaty caps that can reach impressive dimensions.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their notably large size, white to cream-colored caps, and thick, sturdy stems. Unlike many other white mushrooms, Leucopaxillus species have a particularly robust, substantial appearance.
children.funFact: The name Leucopaxillus literally means 'white little stake,' referring to their pale color and the sturdy, stake-like appearance of their thick stems.

children.description: The Tricholomataceae are a diverse family of mushrooms that includes some of the most common woodland fungi you'll encounter in New England. These mushrooms typically have white spore prints and grow from the ground, often forming partnerships with tree roots or decomposing organic matter in forest soils.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their white spores, gills that are attached to the stem, and terrestrial growth habit. Unlike some other mushroom families, they don't have a ring around the stem and their gills don't easily separate from the cap.
children.funFact: Some Tricholomataceae mushrooms, particularly in the Tricholoma genus, are known for their strong, distinctive odors that can range from pleasant and flour-like to pungent and soap-like, helping mycologists identify different species in the field.

children.name: Psathyrellaceae
Psathyrella
children.description: Brittlestems are small to medium-sized mushrooms that get their name from their characteristically fragile stems that break easily when handled. These fungi are typically saprobic, meaning they decompose dead organic matter like wood, leaf litter, and other plant debris. Most species in this genus have dark spores and relatively thin, delicate caps that often appear in shades of brown, tan, or gray.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Brittlestems are distinguished from other mushrooms by their extremely fragile, brittle stems that snap cleanly with little pressure, and their dark purple-brown to black spore prints. Their gills typically start light-colored and darken as the spores mature.
children.funFact: Some brittlestem species, like the Beach Brittlestem, are specially adapted to grow in sandy coastal environments where few other mushrooms can survive the salt spray and shifting sands.

children.name: Coprinopsis
children.description: Inkcaps are fascinating mushrooms that literally dissolve themselves as they mature, turning their own caps into a black, inky liquid. These delicate fungi typically have thin, fragile caps with gills that start light-colored but quickly darken and liquefy from the bottom up. Most species in this group are short-lived, often appearing overnight and dissolving away within a day or two.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other mushrooms that simply dry out or decay, inkcaps have a unique process called autodigestion where they release enzymes that turn their own tissues into a dark, ink-like fluid. This self-dissolving process helps them disperse their spores more effectively.
children.funFact: The Common Ink Cap was historically used to make actual writing ink, and some species contain a compound that makes people violently ill if they consume alcohol within several days of eating the mushroom.

children.name: Coprinellus
children.description: Coprinellus is a genus of small, delicate mushrooms commonly known as inkcaps or crumble caps. These fungi are characterized by their fragile caps that often dissolve into an inky, black liquid as they mature, and they typically grow in clusters on decaying wood, plant debris, or enriched soil.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike their close relatives in the genus Coprinus, Coprinellus mushrooms have smaller, more delicate fruiting bodies and lack a true ring around the stem. Their caps autodigest (dissolve themselves) more rapidly and completely than other inkcap genera.
children.funFact: The mica cap gets its name from the tiny, glittering particles that cover its cap when young, making it sparkle like mica mineral crystals in the sunlight.

children.name: Parasola
children.description: Parasola is a genus of small, delicate mushrooms commonly known as inkcaps due to their distinctive habit of dissolving into a black, ink-like liquid as they mature. These fungi typically have thin, pleated or ribbed caps that start out bell-shaped or conical and often appear overnight in grass, mulch, or decaying organic matter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other inkcap mushrooms, Parasola species are generally smaller and more fragile, with caps that are deeply pleated or grooved from the margin nearly to the center. They also tend to have very thin stems and dissolve more quickly than their larger inkcap relatives.
children.funFact: The pleated inkcap can complete its entire life cycle from sprouting to dissolving into black liquid in less than 24 hours, earning it the nickname 'fairy inkcap' for its ephemeral nature.

children.name: Homophron
children.description: Homophron is a small genus of mushrooms that includes species commonly known as brittlestems. These fungi are characterized by their fragile stems that break easily when handled and their typically brown to chestnut-colored caps.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their particularly brittle, fragile stems and their brownish cap colors, which help separate them from other small brown mushrooms in the forest.
children.funFact: The name 'brittlestem' perfectly describes these delicate mushrooms - their stems are so fragile that they often break just from the wind or a gentle touch!

children.name: Lacrymaria
children.description: Lacrymaria is a genus of mushrooms known for their distinctive dark spores and gills that appear to 'weep' or drip with moisture. These fungi are decomposers that break down organic matter in forest environments. The name literally means 'tear-drop' in reference to their weeping appearance.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their dark, nearly black spores and gills that become mottled with droplets of moisture, giving them their characteristic weeping appearance. They also typically have fragile stems and caps that are often bell-shaped or conical.
children.funFact: The weeping widow gets its dramatic common name because its gills literally appear to cry tears - droplets of water containing spores that help the mushroom reproduce.

children.name: Candolleomyces
children.description: Candolleomyces is a small genus of mushrooms that includes delicate fungi with brittle, fragile stems that break easily when handled. These mushrooms typically have thin caps and grow on decaying wood or in areas with rich organic matter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their extremely fragile stems that snap cleanly with little pressure, earning them common names like 'brittlestem.' They differ from similar-looking mushrooms by their particularly delicate structure and specific spore characteristics.
children.funFact: The genus name Candolleomyces honors Augustin Pyramus de Candolle, a famous 19th-century Swiss botanist who developed one of the first comprehensive plant classification systems.

children.name: Typhrasa
children.description: Typhrasa is a small genus of mushrooms that includes species with distinctively wrinkled or textured caps. These fungi are saprobic, meaning they obtain nutrients by decomposing organic matter in forest environments. They are closely related to the more common Psathyrella mushrooms and share similar ecological roles.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Typhrasa can be distinguished from their Psathyrella relatives by their characteristically wrinkled, often cotton-like or gossamer cap surfaces. The caps typically have a more pronounced textured appearance compared to the smoother caps of most Psathyrella species.
children.funFact: The species name 'gossypina' comes from the Latin word for cotton, referring to the fluffy, cotton-like appearance of the mushroom's wrinkled cap surface.

children.description: The Brittlestems and Allies family includes a diverse group of mushrooms known for their fragile stems that break easily when handled. Many members of this family have dark spores and gills that often turn black or dissolve into an inky liquid as the mushroom matures.
children.distinguishingFeatures: This family is characterized by their brittle, easily broken stems and typically dark brown to black spore prints. Many species have gills that deliquesce (dissolve) into a dark, inky fluid as they age.
children.funFact: Some inkcap mushrooms in this family were historically used to make ink for writing, as their dissolving gills produce a natural black liquid that can be used with a quill pen.

children.name: Agaricaceae
Agaricus
children.description: Field and button mushrooms are a diverse group of gilled fungi that includes many familiar species, from the common white button mushrooms found in grocery stores to wild meadow mushrooms growing in grassy areas. These mushrooms typically have white to brown caps, dark brown to black spores, and often grow in soil rich with organic matter like compost, manure, or decaying plant material. Many species in this group are edible and prized by foragers, though proper identification is essential since some can cause digestive upset.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Agaricus mushrooms are distinguished by their chocolate-brown to black spore prints and gills that start pink when young and darken to brown or black as spores mature. Most species also have a ring around the stem and tend to bruise yellow when cut or damaged.
children.funFact: The humble white button mushroom, cremini, and portobello mushrooms sold in stores are all the same species (Agaricus bisporus) - just harvested at different stages of maturity!

children.name: Leucocoprinus
children.description: Leucocoprinus is a genus of delicate, small to medium-sized mushrooms that are commonly found in greenhouses, potted plants, and rich organic soils. These fungi are saprobic decomposers, meaning they break down dead organic matter like compost, mulch, and decaying plant material. Most species in this group have distinctive parasol-like caps that are often white, cream, or pale yellow when young.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Leucocoprinus are distinguished by their fragile, thin flesh, white spore prints, and caps that often have a powdery or scaly surface texture. Unlike many other mushrooms, they frequently appear in cultivated environments and greenhouse settings rather than wild forest habitats.
children.funFact: The flowerpot parasol (Leucocoprinus birnbaumii) is so closely associated with greenhouse cultivation that it has spread worldwide through the plant trade and is now one of the most cosmopolitan mushroom species on Earth.

children.name: Chlorophyllum
children.description: Chlorophyllum is a genus of large, impressive mushrooms commonly known as parasol mushrooms due to their distinctive umbrella-like caps that can reach impressive sizes. These fungi are characterized by their tall, sturdy stems and caps that often feature scales or shaggy textures, making them some of the most recognizable mushrooms in New England forests.
children.distinguishingFeatures: What sets Chlorophyllum apart from other parasol-like mushrooms is their unique spore colors, which range from green to olive-brown rather than the white spores of true parasol mushrooms in the genus Macrolepiota.
children.funFact: The Green-spored Parasol produces distinctly green spores that are easily visible when the mushroom drops its spore print, making it one of the few mushrooms you can identify just by the color of its spores!

children.name: Macropsalliota
children.description: Macropsalliota is a genus of large, fleshy mushrooms that are closely related to common button mushrooms but grow much bigger. These impressive fungi typically have thick, sturdy stems and caps that can reach several inches across, making them some of the more substantial mushrooms you might encounter in New England forests.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike their smaller mushroom relatives, Macropsalliota species are notably large and robust, with many developing reddish or pinkish coloration when bruised or cut. They also tend to have a more complex ring structure around their stems compared to common store-bought mushrooms.
children.funFact: The reddening lepiota gets its name from its distinctive habit of turning pink or reddish when you touch or cut it, almost like the mushroom is blushing!

children.name: Macrolepiota
children.description: Macrolepiota is a genus of large, impressive mushrooms commonly known as parasol mushrooms. These fungi are characterized by their tall stature, distinctive umbrella-like caps that can reach impressive sizes, and prominent rings around their stems. They are saprobic fungi, meaning they feed on decaying organic matter in soil and leaf litter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Macrolepiota mushrooms are distinguished from other large mushrooms by their moveable stem rings and scaly cap surfaces that often have a distinct pattern. Their stems are typically hollow or have a loose pith, and the caps often have a prominent central umbo (raised center).
children.funFact: The caps of some Macrolepiota species can grow over a foot in diameter, earning them the nickname 'parasol mushrooms' because they truly look like natural umbrellas sprouting from the forest floor.

children.name: Leucoagaricus
children.description: Leucoagaricus is a genus of small to medium-sized mushrooms that are typically white or pale-colored with free gills that don't attach to the stem. These mushrooms often have a ring around the stem and produce white spore prints, making them part of the larger group of white-spored mushrooms.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Leucoagaricus can be distinguished from similar white mushrooms by their free gills, the presence of a stem ring, and their white spore print, along with specific microscopic features of their spores.
children.funFact: The name Leucoagaricus literally means 'white Agaricus,' reflecting their pale coloration and their close evolutionary relationship to the common button mushrooms found in grocery stores.

children.description: The Agaricaceae family includes some of our most familiar mushrooms, from the button mushrooms you find at the grocery store to the field mushrooms that pop up in lawns and meadows. These fungi are characterized by their classic mushroom shape with a cap, stem, and gills underneath, and they typically have a ring around the stem where a protective veil once covered the young gills.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are set apart by their dark brown to black spore prints and free gills that don't attach to the stem. Most also have a prominent ring on the stem and white to pale-colored caps that may have scales or patches.
children.funFact: The common button mushroom (Agaricus bisporus) that you buy at the store is actually the same species as portobello mushrooms - portobellos are just mature button mushrooms that have been allowed to grow larger and open their caps!

children.name: Inocybaceae
Inocybe
children.description: Fiber Caps are a large genus of small to medium-sized mushrooms that get their name from the distinctive fibrous texture of their caps, which often appear silky, woolly, or scaly. These fungi form partnerships with tree roots and are commonly found in forests throughout New England, typically growing from soil rather than decaying wood. Most species in this group have brown or grayish caps with a characteristic conical or bell shape when young.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Fiber Caps can be distinguished from other mushrooms by their fibrous, often radially streaked cap surface and their tendency to have a distinctive spermatic or unpleasant odor. Unlike many other forest mushrooms, they typically have brown spore prints and angular spores when viewed under a microscope.
children.funFact: Many Fiber Cap species are notoriously difficult to identify even for expert mycologists, as they often look very similar to each other and require microscopic examination of their uniquely shaped spores to tell them apart.

children.name: Inosperma
children.description: Inosperma is a genus of small to medium-sized mushrooms commonly known as fibrecaps, named for their characteristic fibrous-textured caps that often appear silky or streaky. These mushrooms are typically brown or grayish in color and grow from the forest floor, forming partnerships with tree roots. They're part of the larger cortinarius family and play important roles as mycorrhizal partners with New England's trees.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Fibrecaps are distinguished by their distinctly fibrous, silky cap surfaces that give them a streaked appearance, along with their typically brownish colors and tendency to bruise or stain when handled. Unlike many similar mushrooms, they often have a somewhat radish-like or earthy odor.
children.funFact: The name 'fibrecap' perfectly describes these mushrooms' most notable feature - their caps look like they're made of tiny fibers all radiating outward from the center, creating beautiful natural patterns.

children.name: Pseudosperma
children.description: Pseudosperma is a small genus of mushrooms commonly known as fibrecaps, named for their distinctive caps that often split or crack as they mature. These mushrooms are typically small to medium-sized with brownish caps and are found growing on decaying wood in forests. They belong to the larger family of mushrooms that includes many look-alike species.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Fibrecaps can be identified by their tendency to develop radial cracks or splits in their caps as they age, creating a distinctive fibrous appearance. They also typically have brownish spores and grow specifically on rotting wood rather than soil.
children.funFact: The name 'Pseudosperma' literally means 'false seed,' referring to the appearance of their spores under a microscope.

children.name: Mallocybe
children.description: Mallocybe is a small genus of mushrooms that are typically small to medium-sized with brownish caps and gills that attach to the stem. These fungi are decomposers that help break down organic matter in forest environments, playing an important role in nutrient cycling.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Mallocybe are distinguished from related groups by their unique combination of brownish coloration, attached gills, and specific microscopic spore characteristics that require expert identification.
children.funFact: The genus name Mallocybe comes from Greek words meaning 'woolly head,' referring to the slightly fuzzy or fibrillose texture often found on the caps of these mushrooms.

children.description: Fibercaps and their allies are a family of small to medium-sized mushrooms that typically have brown, tan, or grayish caps with a distinctive fibrous or scaly texture. Most species in this family grow on the ground in forests, forming beneficial partnerships with tree roots. They produce brown spore prints and often have a somewhat earthy or musty smell.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These mushrooms are easily recognized by their characteristic fibrous, radially-streaked cap surfaces that often appear torn or scaly. Unlike many other brown-spored mushrooms, they typically have straight-edged gills that don't easily separate from the cap.
children.funFact: Many fibercaps are considered among the most dangerous mushrooms to eat, as some species contain muscarine, a toxin that can cause severe poisoning even in small amounts.

children.name: Strophariaceae
Pholiota
children.description: Scalycaps are wood-decomposing mushrooms known for their distinctive scaly caps that give them their common name. These fungi typically grow in clusters on dead or dying hardwood trees, playing an important role in forest ecosystems by breaking down organic matter and recycling nutrients back into the soil.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other mushroom groups, scalycaps are characterized by their prominently scaly or shaggy cap surfaces, often with yellowish to brown coloration. They also typically have a ring around the stem and rusty-brown spore prints.
children.funFact: The flaming scalycap gets its dramatic name from its bright yellow-orange cap covered in fiery red-orange scales, making it one of the most colorful mushrooms in New England forests.

children.name: Stropharia
children.description: Roundheads are a group of mushrooms that typically grow on decaying wood, mulch, or rich soil in forests and gardens. These fungi are characterized by their smooth, often colorful caps that can range from blue-green to wine-red to brown, and they play an important role in breaking down organic matter in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Roundheads are distinguished by their dark purple-brown to black spore prints and the presence of a ring around the stem in most species. Their caps often have a distinctive smooth, rounded appearance when young, giving the group its common name.
children.funFact: The Wine-cap Stropharia is so good at breaking down organic matter that it's cultivated by gardeners as both a food source and a natural way to compost wood chips and straw.

children.name: Hypholoma
children.description: Hypholoma is a genus of small to medium-sized mushrooms that typically grow in dense clusters on decaying wood, especially stumps and logs. These fungi are saprophytes, meaning they break down dead organic matter and play an important role in forest decomposition. Most species in this group have caps that range from yellow to brick-red colors and produce dark spores.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Hypholoma mushrooms are distinguished by their clustered growth habit on wood, their often yellowish caps with darker centers, and their dark purplish-brown to blackish spore prints. Unlike some similar wood-loving mushrooms, they typically have thin partial veils when young that leave subtle ring zones on the stems.
children.funFact: The Sulphur Tuft (Hypholoma fasciculare) is considered toxic and has a notably bitter taste, which helps distinguish it from the edible Brick Cap - a good reminder that even closely related mushrooms can have very different culinary and safety properties!

children.name: Leratiomyces
children.description: Leratiomyces is a small genus of mushrooms that includes species commonly found growing on wood chips and mulch in urban and suburban areas. These fungi are saprobic decomposers, meaning they break down dead organic matter and play an important role in nutrient cycling.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus typically have reddish-brown to orange caps and grow in clusters on woody debris. They can be distinguished from similar mushrooms by their specific spore characteristics and DNA sequences.
children.funFact: Chip Cherries got their common name because they're frequently found fruiting on wood chips used in landscaping, making them one of the most likely mushrooms you'll encounter in park mulch beds and garden paths.

children.name: Protostropharia
children.description: Protostropharia is a small genus of mushrooms that are specialized decomposers, particularly skilled at breaking down nutrient-rich organic matter like dung and decaying plant material. These brown-capped fungi play an important ecological role by recycling nutrients back into forest and grassland ecosystems. They are commonly found growing on or near manure, compost, and other fertile substrates throughout New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their smooth, brown to yellowish-brown caps and their strong preference for growing on dung or very nutrient-rich soils. Unlike many other small brown mushrooms, Protostropharia species have dark purple-brown to black spore prints and often display a distinctive ring around the stem.
children.funFact: The Dung Roundhead gets its common name from its perfectly round, dome-shaped cap when young, and it's so specialized for growing on manure that finding one is often a reliable indicator that animals have recently grazed in the area.

children.name: Phaeonematoloma
children.description: Phaeonematoloma is a small genus of mushrooms that belongs to the stropharioid group of fungi. These mushrooms are characterized by their brownish caps and dark spores, and they typically grow on decaying wood in forest environments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus can be distinguished from similar brown mushrooms by their specific combination of dark brownish caps, whitish stems that may bruise blue-green, and their preference for growing on rotting hardwood logs.
children.funFact: The genus name Phaeonematoloma literally means 'dark thread fringe,' referring to the distinctive dark-edged appearance of the mushroom's cap margin.

children.name: Bogbodia
children.description: Bogbodia is a small genus of marine bryozoans, which are tiny colonial animals that filter-feed from the water. These creatures form encrusting colonies on hard surfaces like rocks, shells, and other underwater structures in marine environments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Bogbodia is distinguished by its specific colonial growth patterns and the unique structure of its individual zooids (the tiny animals that make up the colony).
children.funFact: Despite being animals, bryozoan colonies like Bogbodia often look more like plants or coral, creating delicate lace-like patterns as they grow across underwater surfaces.

children.description: The Strophariaceae are a diverse family of mushrooms that typically grow on wood, soil, or organic debris. Most members of this family produce dark-colored spores (usually brown to black) and have gills that are attached to the stem, giving them a distinctive appearance when mature.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These mushrooms are characterized by their dark spore prints and the way their gills connect to the stem. Many species also have a partial veil when young that leaves a ring around the stem as the mushroom matures.
children.funFact: Some members of this family, particularly certain Psilocybe species (though not common in New England), contain compounds that have been used in medical research for treating depression and PTSD.

children.name: Omphalotaceae
Gymnopus
children.description: Gymnopus is a genus of small to medium-sized mushrooms that are tough and leathery, often growing on decaying wood, leaves, or other organic matter in forests. These fungi are known for their ability to revive and continue releasing spores even after drying out completely, earning some species the nickname 'parachute mushrooms.' Most have thin, wiry stems and relatively small caps that can range from white to brown or reddish colors.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other mushrooms, Gymnopus species have a remarkable ability to resurrect after drying out - their caps can expand again and resume spore production when moisture returns. They also typically have very tough, fibrous stems that are difficult to break cleanly.
children.funFact: The horsehair fungus (Gymnopus androsaceus) has stems so thin and black they look exactly like horse hair, and these tiny mushrooms can spring back to life even after being completely dried out for months.

children.name: Collybiopsis
children.description: Parachutes are small to medium-sized mushrooms that typically grow on decaying wood, leaves, or other organic matter in forests. These delicate fungi are characterized by their thin, often translucent caps and slender stems, giving them an ethereal, umbrella-like appearance that inspired their common name.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other small woodland mushrooms, Parachutes have distinctively tough, wiry stems that can bend without breaking easily. Their gills are usually widely spaced and often connect to the stem in various ways, creating subtle but important identification features.
children.funFact: The Wood Woolly-foot gets its name from the fuzzy, hair-like coating on its stem base, which helps it grip onto decaying wood surfaces like tiny biological velcro.

children.name: Rhodocollybia
children.description: Rhodocollybia is a genus of woodland mushrooms that grow from decaying organic matter on forest floors. These medium-sized fungi typically have brownish or grayish caps with white to pale gills underneath, and they play an important role in breaking down dead plant material in New England's forests.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other woodland mushrooms, Rhodocollybia species have a distinctive reddish-brown spore print and often develop characteristic spots or color changes as they age.
children.funFact: The Spotted Collybia gets its name from the dark reddish-brown spots that develop on its white cap and stem as it matures, creating a distinctive polka-dot appearance.

children.name: Mycetinis
children.description: Mycetinis is a small genus of mushrooms that are typically found growing on decaying wood or plant material in forests. These fungi are characterized by their small to medium size and their ability to produce distinctive odors, particularly garlic-like scents in some species.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Mycetinis are distinguished from other small woodland mushrooms by their strong, often garlic-like odors and their preference for growing on specific types of decaying organic matter.
children.funFact: The vampire's bane mushroom gets its dramatic name from its intense garlic smell, playing on the folklore that garlic repels vampires!

children.name: Omphalotus
children.description: Jack-o'-lantern mushrooms are bright orange fungi that grow in clusters on decaying wood, particularly around the base of hardwood trees and stumps. They get their spooky name from their vibrant orange color that resembles Halloween pumpkins, and they're known for being toxic to humans if eaten.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These mushrooms can be distinguished from similar orange fungi by their distinctive gills that run down the stem and their habit of growing in dense, overlapping clusters on wood rather than from the ground.
children.funFact: Jack-o'-lantern mushrooms actually glow in the dark with a greenish bioluminescent light that can be seen with the naked eye in complete darkness, though this eerie glow is quite faint and best observed in fresh specimens.

children.name: Connopus
children.description: Connopus is a small genus of mushrooms that includes species with distinctive clustered growth patterns and brownish caps. These fungi are saprophytic, meaning they decompose dead organic matter in forest environments. In New England, this genus is represented by a single species that grows on decaying wood.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Connopus mushrooms are characterized by their tendency to grow in dense clusters or clumps, often with overlapping caps that create layered formations on their substrate.
children.funFact: The name 'Connopus' comes from Greek words meaning 'cone foot,' referring to the distinctive shape of the mushroom's stem base.

children.name: Lentinula
children.description: Lentinula is a small genus of wood-decomposing mushrooms that grow on dead hardwood trees and logs. These fungi are saprophytes, meaning they break down dead organic matter and play an important role in forest ecosystems by recycling nutrients back into the soil. The most famous member of this genus is the shiitake mushroom, which has been cultivated for food and medicine for over 1,000 years.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Lentinula mushrooms have distinctive brown, scaly caps and white to cream-colored gills that don't extend down the stem. They produce white spore prints and have a characteristic pleasant, earthy aroma that distinguishes them from other brown wood-growing mushrooms.
children.funFact: The name 'shiitake' comes from the Japanese words 'shii' (referring to the shii tree where they naturally grow) and 'take' (meaning mushroom), and these mushrooms contain compounds that have been shown to boost immune system function.

children.name: Paragymnopus
children.description: Paragymnopus is a small genus of mushrooms that are part of the marasmius family, known for their thin, tough stems and small caps. These fungi are decomposers that break down organic matter in forest environments, particularly dead wood and plant debris. They're characterized by their ability to dry out completely and then revive when moisture returns.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus have very thin, wiry black or dark brown stems and small, often perforated or translucent caps. Unlike many mushrooms, they can completely dehydrate and then spring back to life when rehydrated.
children.funFact: The stinking parachute gets its name from both its small parachute-like cap and its distinctive garlic-like odor that can be detected from several feet away.

children.description: The Omphalotaceae are a diverse family of mushrooms that includes both common woodland decomposers and some truly remarkable species. These fungi typically have white spore prints and often grow on decaying wood, fallen logs, or leaf litter, playing important roles in forest ecosystems by breaking down organic matter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their white spores and often tough, leathery textures. Many species have distinctive features like deeply attached gills or stems that extend down into the substrate.
children.funFact: This family includes the famous jack-o'-lantern mushrooms that glow green in the dark, as well as shiitake mushrooms, one of the world's most cultivated edible fungi!

children.name: Physalacriaceae
Armillaria
children.description: Honey mushrooms are a group of parasitic fungi that attack and eventually kill trees and woody shrubs throughout New England's forests.
