children.funFact: The genus name Heimiomyces comes from Greek words meaning 'wall fungus,' referring to their habit of growing on the vertical surfaces of decaying logs and stumps.

children.description: Xeromphalinaceae is a small family of mushroom-forming fungi that includes tiny, delicate species often found growing on decaying wood, moss, or other organic matter. These mushrooms are typically small with thin, often translucent caps and slender stems, and they play important roles as decomposers in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their small size, thin-fleshed fruiting bodies, and distinctive spore characteristics. They often have a somewhat waxy or translucent appearance and typically grow in clusters or scattered groups on their substrate.
children.funFact: Some Xeromphalina species can continue producing spores even in very cold temperatures, allowing them to fruit later in the season than many other mushrooms.

children.name: Cyphellaceae
Baeospora
children.description: Baeospora is a small genus of delicate mushrooms that specialize in growing on decaying conifer debris like pine cones, needles, and woody material. These tiny fungi play an important role in forest ecosystems by helping break down fallen conifer material and recycling nutrients back into the soil. Both New England species are small, fragile mushrooms with thin stems and caps that rarely exceed an inch in diameter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other small woodland mushrooms, Baeospora species have a strong preference for coniferous substrates and are rarely found growing on hardwood debris. They can be distinguished by their delicate structure, whitish spore prints, and their specific habitat association with pine, spruce, and fir materials.
children.funFact: The Conifercone Cap gets its name from its habit of growing directly on old pine cones, sometimes sprouting dozens of tiny mushrooms from a single cone like a miniature fairy garden.

children.name: Chondrostereum
children.description: Chondrostereum is a genus of fungi that forms thin, leathery bracket-like growths on dead and dying hardwood trees. These fungi are wood-rotting species that help break down fallen logs and weakened trees in forest ecosystems. They produce distinctive purplish spores and have a smooth, often colorful upper surface.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many bracket fungi, Chondrostereum species form very thin, flexible fruiting bodies that are leathery rather than woody or cork-like. The underside lacks visible pores or gills, instead having a smooth spore-bearing surface.
children.funFact: The Silverleaf Fungus gets its name from causing infected fruit trees to develop silvery, metallic-looking leaves before the tree eventually dies.

children.name: Mycopan
children.description: Mycopan is a small genus of mushrooms that includes just one species found in New England - the Scabby Bonnet. These are small to medium-sized mushrooms that typically grow on decaying wood in forest environments. They belong to the larger group of fungi that help break down dead organic matter in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their distinctive scabby or rough-textured cap surface, which gives the Scabby Bonnet its common name. They have a bonnet-like cap shape when mature.
children.funFact: Despite being called a 'bonnet,' these mushrooms actually start out with a more rounded cap that gradually flattens as they mature, creating their characteristic hat-like appearance.

children.name: Cheimonophyllum
children.description: Cheimonophyllum is a small genus of fungi that contains just one species in New England - the snowy oysterling. These are oyster-like mushrooms that grow on dead wood, particularly hardwood trees and branches.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other oyster mushrooms, members of this genus are distinguished by their white spores and their preference for fruiting during cooler months when most other fungi are dormant.
children.funFact: The genus name Cheimonophyllum literally means 'winter leaf,' reflecting these mushrooms' remarkable ability to fruit during cold weather when snow may still be on the ground.

children.description: The Cyphellaceae are a family of fungi that produce small, cup-shaped or bracket-like fruiting bodies. These fungi are typically decomposers that break down dead wood and organic matter in forest environments. Most members of this family are relatively small and inconspicuous, often growing on decaying logs, branches, or leaf litter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their distinctive cup-shaped, funnel-shaped, or small bracket-like fruiting bodies that lack a traditional mushroom cap and stem structure. Unlike many other fungi, they typically have a smooth or slightly wrinkled fertile surface rather than gills or pores.
children.funFact: Some Cyphellaceae fungi, like those in the genus Chondrostereum, can cause a plant disease called 'silver leaf' that gives infected tree leaves a distinctive silvery appearance.

children.name: Galeropsidaceae
Panaeolus
children.description: Mottlegills are small to medium-sized mushrooms that get their name from their distinctively speckled or mottled gills, which show a characteristic pattern of light and dark areas as the spores mature. These fungi are commonly found growing in grassy areas, pastures, and lawns throughout New England, often appearing after rain. They're part of the larger group of dark-spored mushrooms and play an important role in decomposing organic matter in soil.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The mottled appearance of their gills sets them apart from other dark-spored mushrooms, as the gills develop patches of different colors when spores ripen unevenly. Unlike many other small brown mushrooms, mottlegills typically have thin, fragile stems and caps that often develop a distinctive bell or cone shape.
children.funFact: The Mower's Mushroom earned its common name because it frequently pops up in freshly mowed lawns, sometimes appearing just hours after grass cutting when conditions are right.

children.description: Galeropsidaceae is a small family of mushrooms that includes the mottlegills, characterized by their dark-spored gills and typically slender stems. These mushrooms are commonly found growing on dung, rich soil, or decaying organic matter in fields, lawns, and pastures. They are small to medium-sized fungi that play an important role in breaking down organic waste in the environment.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their mottled or spotted gill appearance (hence 'mottlegills'), dark brown to black spore prints, and their preference for nutrient-rich substrates like manure.
children.funFact: Some mottlegill species contain psychoactive compounds, making proper identification crucial, though many species in this family are completely harmless decomposers.

children.name: Callistosporiaceae
Callistosporium
children.description: Callistosporium is a small genus of woodland mushrooms that are closely related to oyster mushrooms. These fungi typically grow on decaying wood and are known for their distinctive spore-bearing structures and often colorful caps that can range from olive to purple-tinged.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their unique spore characteristics and their tendency to have more vibrant coloration around the cap margins compared to their close relatives.
children.funFact: The name 'Callistosporium' literally means 'beautiful spore,' referring to the attractive microscopic spores that help mycologists identify these mushrooms.

children.name: Pseudolaccaria
children.description: Pseudolaccaria is a small genus of mushrooms that were once thought to be part of the Laccaria genus but have since been recognized as distinct. These fungi form partnerships with tree roots and produce small to medium-sized mushrooms with gills underneath their caps. They typically grow from the soil in forested areas where they help trees absorb nutrients.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true Laccaria mushrooms, Pseudolaccaria species have different spore characteristics and genetic makeup that set them apart. They tend to have thicker, more robust stems and caps compared to their Laccaria relatives.
children.funFact: The name 'Pseudolaccaria' literally means 'false Laccaria' because these mushrooms were originally misidentified as members of the Laccaria genus before DNA analysis revealed they deserved their own separate group.

children.description: The Callistosporiaceae family consists of small, colorful mushrooms that grow on decaying wood in forests. These fungi are decomposers that help break down dead organic matter, playing an important role in forest ecosystems. They typically produce thin, delicate fruiting bodies with caps that range from yellow to orange to reddish-brown colors.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their small size, bright colors, and their preference for growing on rotting wood rather than soil. They have thin, fragile caps and produce white spore prints.
children.funFact: Despite their small and delicate appearance, these mushrooms are incredibly efficient decomposers that can break down tough woody materials like lignin and cellulose.

children.name: Fistulinaceae
Fistulina
children.description: Fistulina is a small genus of unique bracket fungi that produces thick, fleshy fruiting bodies on hardwood trees. These fungi are known for their distinctive appearance and texture, which often resembles raw meat, earning them common names like 'beefsteak fungus.'
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most bracket fungi that have tubes throughout their cap, Fistulina species have individual tube-like pores that can be separated from each other, giving them a distinctive honeycomb-like appearance when viewed from below.
children.funFact: When cut, these fungi often 'bleed' a red juice that looks remarkably like blood from raw meat, making them one of the most dramatic-looking fungi in New England forests.

children.name: Porodisculus
children.description: Porodisculus is a genus of small, inconspicuous lichens that grow as thin crusts on tree bark and wood surfaces. These lichens form grayish or whitish patches that blend in well with their substrate, making them easy to overlook during casual observation.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their crustose growth form and distinctive reproductive structures called perithecia, which appear as tiny black dots embedded in the lichen surface.
children.funFact: Despite being so small and easily overlooked, Porodisculus lichens are actually composite organisms made up of both fungi and algae living together in a mutually beneficial partnership.

children.name: Pseudofistulina
children.description: Pseudofistulina is a small genus of bracket fungi that produces distinctive shelf-like fruiting bodies on hardwood trees. These fungi are wood decomposers that help break down dead and dying trees in forest ecosystems. The genus contains only a few species worldwide, with just one species found in New England forests.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true bracket fungi, Pseudofistulina species have a unique spore-bearing surface with small pores that can appear almost tooth-like under magnification. The fruiting bodies are typically thick, fleshy when fresh, and have a distinctive reddish-brown coloration.
children.funFact: Despite its name meaning 'false little tube,' Pseudofistulina was once thought to be closely related to the beefsteak fungus (Fistulina) but genetic studies revealed it belongs to a completely different fungal family.

children.description: The Fistulinaceae are a small family of bracket fungi that grow as shelf-like structures on trees. These fungi are known for their distinctive pore surfaces that release spores, and they typically have a fleshy to leathery texture when fresh.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family have pores that are easily separated from each other, unlike the tightly connected pore layers found in most other bracket fungi. Their fruiting bodies also tend to be more fleshy and less woody than typical shelf fungi.
children.funFact: The most famous member of this family, Fistulina hepatica (beefsteak fungus), earned its name because its red, marbled flesh looks remarkably similar to raw beef and even "bleeds" a red juice when cut.

children.name: Cyphellopsidaceae
Dendrothele
children.description: Dendrothele is a small genus of corticioid fungi that form thin, crust-like growths on dead wood. These fungi are wood decomposers that help break down fallen branches and logs in forest ecosystems. They typically appear as whitish to cream-colored patches spreading across the surface of decaying wood.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Dendrothele species are distinguished by their smooth to slightly wrinkled surface texture and their tendency to form relatively thick, waxy crusts compared to many other corticioid fungi. They also have distinctive microscopic features including specific spore shapes and hyphal structures.
children.funFact: Despite their plain appearance, Dendrothele fungi play a crucial role as nature's recyclers, slowly but steadily breaking down woody debris and returning nutrients to the forest soil.

children.name: Merismodes
children.description: Merismodes is a small genus of cup fungi that forms tiny, clustered fruiting bodies on decaying wood and plant material. These delicate fungi are characterized by their small, cup-shaped or disc-like structures that often grow in dense groups, making them appear almost like miniature flower clusters.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Merismodes can be distinguished from other small cup fungi by their tendency to form dense, fascicled (bundled) clusters and their preference for growing on woody substrates in forest environments.
children.funFact: Despite their tiny size, Merismodes fungi play an important role in forest ecosystems by helping to decompose fallen branches and woody debris, recycling nutrients back into the soil.

children.description: Cyphellopsidaceae is a small family of fungi that form thin, crusty growths on wood and bark. These fungi are decomposers that help break down dead plant material in forest ecosystems, playing an important role in nutrient cycling.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family produce their spores on smooth or slightly wrinkled surfaces rather than in pores or gills, and they typically form very thin, patch-like fruiting bodies that can be easily overlooked.
children.funFact: Despite being small and inconspicuous, these fungi are actually quite common on dead branches and logs throughout New England forests, quietly doing their work as nature's recyclers.

children.name: Resupinataceae
Resupinatus
children.description: Resupinatus is a genus of tiny mushrooms that grow directly attached to wood without stems, appearing as small bracket-like or oyster-shaped caps. These delicate fungi are saprophytes, meaning they decompose dead wood and plant material, playing an important role in forest ecosystems. They're among the smallest bracket fungi you'll encounter in New England forests.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike larger oyster mushrooms, Resupinatus species are extremely small (often less than an inch across) and grow directly from wood surfaces without visible stems. Their caps are typically fan-shaped or kidney-shaped and have a distinctly tough, leathery texture despite their small size.
children.funFact: The genus name 'Resupinatus' means 'bent backward,' referring to how these tiny mushrooms curve and twist as they grow directly from vertical wood surfaces.

children.description: The Resupinataceae are a small family of delicate mushrooms that typically grow on decaying wood in forests. These tiny fungi are characterized by their bracket-like or fan-shaped caps that grow directly from wood surfaces without visible stems, often appearing almost sessile or with very short stalks.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other small wood-dwelling mushrooms, members of this family have their caps oriented in a distinctive way - often appearing upside-down or rotated compared to typical mushroom growth patterns, which is reflected in their name meaning 'upside-down.'
children.funFact: Despite their small size, these mushrooms play an important role as decomposers, helping to break down fallen branches and dead wood in New England's forests throughout the growing season.

children.name: Omphalinaceae
Infundibulicybe
children.description: Funnels are mushrooms that get their name from their distinctive funnel-shaped caps that curve downward and inward, creating a depression in the center. These fungi are decomposers that help break down organic matter in forest soils, typically growing in groups among leaf litter and decaying wood. They're part of the larger group of gilled mushrooms and play an important ecological role in nutrient cycling.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The key feature that sets Funnels apart is their characteristic funnel or vase-shaped caps with deeply depressed centers, unlike the flat or dome-shaped caps of most other gilled mushrooms. Their gills typically run down the stem (called decurrent gills), following the funnel shape of the cap.
children.funFact: Some Funnel mushrooms can actually help improve soil quality by forming beneficial relationships with tree roots, trading nutrients while simultaneously decomposing fallen leaves and organic matter.

children.description: The Omphalinaceae family consists of small to medium-sized mushrooms that typically have a funnel or cup-like shape when mature. These fungi are decomposers that help break down organic matter in forest environments, often growing on decaying wood, leaf litter, or soil rich in organic material.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their distinctive funnel-shaped caps that often develop a central depression, along with gills that typically run down the stem (called decurrent gills).
children.funFact: Many Omphalinaceae mushrooms start out with a flat or slightly rounded cap that gradually develops into a deep funnel shape as they age, completely transforming their appearance during their lifecycle.

children.name: Sarcomyxaceae
Sarcomyxa
children.description: Sarcomyxa is a small genus of oyster-like mushrooms that fruit late in the season when most other fungi have finished for the year. These hardy mushrooms grow in overlapping clusters on dead hardwood trees, particularly favoring beech, maple, and other deciduous species.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true oyster mushrooms, Sarcomyxa species have a tough, rubbery texture and lack the pleasant aroma of their more common relatives. They also fruit much later in the season, often persisting into winter.
children.funFact: The Late Oyster earned its common name by being one of the last mushrooms to appear each year, sometimes fruiting well into December even after snow has fallen.

children.name: Tectella
children.description: Tectella is a small genus of mushrooms that includes species commonly known as veiled panus mushrooms. These fungi are characterized by their shelf-like or bracket-shaped fruiting bodies that grow on decaying wood, particularly hardwood trees and logs.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Tectella are distinguished by their tough, leathery texture and the presence of a partial veil when young that often leaves remnants on the cap edge as the mushroom matures.
children.funFact: The name 'Tectella' comes from the Latin word meaning 'little roof,' referring to the way these mushrooms form overlapping, roof-like brackets on tree trunks and fallen logs.

children.description: Sarcomyxaceae is a small family of wood-decaying fungi that includes some distinctive mushrooms found growing on dead hardwood trees. These fungi are saprophytes, meaning they help break down dead organic matter and return nutrients to the forest ecosystem. Members of this family typically produce tough, leathery fruiting bodies that can persist for extended periods.
children.distinguishingFeatures: This family is characterized by their white spore prints and distinctive gill structure, along with their preference for growing on hardwood substrates. Unlike many other wood-decaying fungi, Sarcomyxaceae members often have a somewhat rubbery or gelatinous texture.
children.funFact: The genus Sarcomyxa gets its name from Greek words meaning 'flesh slime,' referring to the somewhat gelatinous texture of these otherwise solid-looking mushrooms.

children.name: Volvariellaceae
Volvariella
children.description: Rosegills are distinctive mushrooms that get their name from their characteristic pink or rose-colored spores and gills. These fungi are saprophytes that decompose dead organic matter, often growing on decaying wood or other mushrooms. All rosegills have a distinctive cup-like structure called a volva at the base of their stem, which is a remnant of the universal veil that initially enclosed the young mushroom.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Rosegills can be identified by their combination of pink spores, white gills that turn pinkish with age, and the prominent cup-shaped volva at the stem base. Unlike similar-looking mushrooms, they lack a ring around the stem and have free gills that don't attach to the stem.
children.funFact: The Piggyback Rosegill gets its common name from its unusual habit of growing directly on top of other mushrooms, literally hitchhiking on its fungal neighbors rather than growing from the ground or wood.

children.description: The Volvariellaceae family consists of mushrooms that grow on decaying organic matter like rotting wood, compost, and plant debris. These fungi are characterized by their distinctive volva (cup-like structure) at the base of the stem and their role as important decomposers in forest ecosystems. The family is best known for the Rosegill mushrooms, which get their name from their pinkish spore color.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their prominent volva at the stem base, pink spores, and free gills that don't attach to the stem. Unlike many other mushroom families, they typically lack a ring around the stem.
children.funFact: Some Rosegill mushrooms are among the fastest-growing fungi, capable of completing their entire life cycle from spore to mature mushroom in just a few days under ideal conditions.

children.name: Campanellaceae
Tetrapyrgos
children.description: Tetrapyrgos is a small genus of tiny mushrooms that are part of the larger Marasmius family. These delicate fungi are characterized by their small size and distinctive dark-colored stalks that support small, often whitish caps.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their consistently dark, nearly black stems (called stipes) and their very small stature compared to other Marasmius mushrooms.
children.funFact: The name 'Tetrapyrgos' comes from Greek words meaning 'four towers,' though the connection to the mushroom's appearance remains somewhat mysterious to mycologists.

children.description: Campanellaceae is a small family of delicate, tiny mushrooms that are among the smallest fungi you'll encounter in New England forests. These minuscule mushrooms typically grow on decaying wood, leaves, or other organic matter, where they help break down dead plant material and recycle nutrients back into the ecosystem.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their extremely small size and bell-shaped or parachute-like caps, often measuring just a few millimeters across. They have thin, delicate stems and produce white spore prints.
children.funFact: The Fairy Parachutes get their whimsical name from their tiny, translucent caps that look like miniature umbrellas or parachutes scattered across the forest floor.

children.name: Cystodermella
children.description: Cystodermella is a small genus of mushrooms commonly known as powdercaps, named for their distinctively granular or powdery cap surfaces. These small to medium-sized fungi are saprobic, meaning they feed on decaying organic matter in forest environments, helping to break down dead plant material and recycle nutrients back into the ecosystem.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Cystodermella are recognized by their granular, powdery cap surfaces and typically have a ring around the stem. They differ from similar-looking mushrooms by their specific microscopic features and their preference for growing on decaying wood or rich forest humus.
children.funFact: The cinnabar powdercap gets its name from its beautiful reddish-orange color that resembles cinnabar mineral, making it one of the most visually striking small mushrooms in New England forests.

children.name: Biannulariaceae
Catathelasma
children.description: Catathelasma is a small genus of large, robust mushrooms that grow on the ground in coniferous forests. These impressive fungi are known for their thick, fleshy caps and sturdy stems, making them some of the most substantial mushrooms you might encounter in New England's woods.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their exceptionally large size, thick white flesh, and the presence of a partial veil that leaves a ring on the stem. They also have distinctive spore prints and grow exclusively in association with conifer trees.
children.funFact: The single New England species, Catathelasma ventricosum, can grow caps up to 16 inches across and weigh several pounds, earning it the nickname 'swollen-belly knight' due to its bulbous stem base.

children.name: Bonomyces
children.description: Bonomyces is a small genus of fungi that produces distinctive funnel-shaped mushrooms in early spring. These fungi are saprophytic, meaning they help decompose organic matter in forest ecosystems, playing an important role in nutrient cycling.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their unique funnel-shaped caps and their early spring fruiting period, often appearing when snow is still melting in New England forests.
children.funFact: The spring funnel is one of the earliest mushrooms to emerge each year, sometimes pushing up through patches of remaining snow to begin the new growing season.

children.description: Biannulariaceae is a small family of mushroom-forming fungi that includes some of the most distinctive and robust mushrooms you might encounter. These fungi are characterized by their thick, fleshy caps and stems that often feature double rings (annuli) around the stem, which gives the family its name.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their double-ringed stems and extremely thick, meaty texture that sets them apart from other mushroom families. They typically produce large, substantial fruiting bodies with a particularly dense and firm consistency.
children.funFact: The genus Catathelasma in this family includes some mushrooms that can weigh several pounds when fully mature, making them among the heaviest individual mushrooms you can find in New England forests.

children.name: Pseudoclitocybaceae
Pseudoclitocybe
children.description: Goblets are a small genus of mushrooms known for their distinctive cup or goblet-shaped caps that develop deep, funnel-like depressions as they mature. These fungi are decomposers that help break down organic matter in forest environments, typically growing on decaying wood or rich soil.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other cup-shaped mushrooms, Goblets have true gills on the underside of their caps and grow on stalks, rather than being sessile cups that sit directly on their substrate.
children.funFact: The name 'cyathiformis' literally means 'cup-shaped' in Latin, perfectly describing how these mushrooms transform from flat caps into deep, goblet-like vessels as they age.

children.name: Aspropaxillus
children.description: Aspropaxillus is a genus of large, funnel-shaped mushrooms that are among the most impressive fungi you can find in New England forests. These mushrooms are characterized by their distinctive funnel or trumpet-like shape and substantial size, making them stand out from other forest floor fungi.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their large, deeply funnel-shaped caps and robust stature, which sets them apart from smaller, flatter mushroom species in the region.
children.funFact: The Giant Funnel is one of the largest mushrooms found in New England, with caps that can grow over a foot wide and create impressive natural funnels on the forest floor.

children.description: Pseudoclitocybaceae is a small family of fungi that includes mushrooms with a distinctive cup or funnel-like shape. These fungi are saprophytes, meaning they help decompose organic matter in forest environments, playing an important role in nutrient cycling.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their pale-colored, thin-fleshed fruiting bodies that often have a depressed or sunken center, giving them their characteristic goblet-like appearance.
children.funFact: Despite having only 2 species in New England, this family was only recently recognized by scientists as distinct from other mushroom families, showing how much we're still learning about fungal relationships.

children.name: Melanoleucaceae
Melanoleuca
children.description: Cavaliers are a genus of woodland mushrooms that grow on the ground in forests throughout New England. These fungi have white spores and typically feature brownish caps with white to cream-colored stems, often appearing in late summer and fall.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Cavaliers can be distinguished from similar mushrooms by their white spore prints and their tendency to have caps that are brownish or grayish-brown rather than purely white or brightly colored.
children.funFact: The name 'Cavalier' reflects their somewhat noble appearance, as these mushrooms often stand tall and proud among the leaf litter of deciduous forests.

children.description: The Melanoleucaceae are a family of mushroom-forming fungi that typically produce medium to large-sized mushrooms with gills underneath their caps. These fungi are saprophytic, meaning they decompose organic matter like fallen leaves and wood debris in forest ecosystems. Most species in this family have white spores and sturdy stems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their combination of white spore prints, attached gills that often run slightly down the stem, and typically robust, fibrous stems. Unlike some similar mushroom families, they lack a ring around the stem and have gills that are usually crowded together.
children.funFact: The name 'Melanoleuca' literally means 'black-white' in Greek, referring to the contrasting dark caps and white gills that are characteristic of many species in this family.

children.name: Stephanosporaceae
Lindtneria
children.description: Lindtneria is a small genus of fungi that includes species commonly known as sweetheart fungi due to their distinctive heart-shaped fruiting bodies. These fungi are typically found growing on decaying wood in forest environments, where they play an important role in breaking down organic matter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their unique heart-shaped or fan-shaped fruiting bodies and distinctive spore characteristics, including the rough-textured spores that give the Golden Sweetheart its scientific name 'trachyspora.'
children.funFact: The Golden Sweetheart gets its charming common name from its distinctive golden-yellow, heart-shaped fruiting bodies that seem to glow against the dark bark of decaying logs.

children.name: Myriococcum
children.description: Myriococcum is a genus of tiny fungi that forms small, dark, spherical structures called perithecia on decaying organic matter. These microscopic fungi are part of the larger group of ascomycete fungi and play an important role in breaking down dead plant material in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Myriococcum fungi are characterized by their distinctive tiny black spherical fruiting bodies that contain numerous small spores. They can be distinguished from similar fungi by their specific spore arrangement and the structure of their reproductive organs.
children.funFact: Despite being incredibly small and often overlooked, Myriococcum fungi are essential decomposers that help recycle nutrients back into the soil, making them available for new plant growth.

children.description: Stephanosporaceae is a small family of fungi that includes microscopic species found in soil and decaying organic matter. These fungi are characterized by their unique spore-producing structures and play important roles in breaking down dead plant material in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their distinctive spore arrangements and specialized reproductive structures that set them apart from other soil-dwelling fungi.
children.funFact: Despite being microscopic, these fungi are essential decomposers that help recycle nutrients in New England's forests, working quietly beneath our feet to keep ecosystems healthy.

children.name: Coprinaceae
Coprinus
children.description: Inky caps are fascinating mushrooms that literally dissolve themselves as they mature, turning their caps into a black, ink-like liquid. These mushrooms have a unique way of dispersing their spores - instead of simply dropping them, they digest their own cap tissue from the bottom up, creating a dripping black fluid that carries the spores away.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other mushrooms that simply dry out or decay when old, inky caps actively liquefy themselves through a process called deliquescence, turning their gills and cap edges into black, drippy ink.
children.funFact: The black liquid produced by inky caps was historically used as actual writing ink, and some people still use it today for calligraphy and art projects.

children.description: The Coprinaceae family consists of delicate mushrooms that have a unique way of dispersing their spores - they literally dissolve themselves! These fungi are commonly called inky caps because their gills turn black and liquify into an ink-like substance as the mushroom matures. They're typically small to medium-sized mushrooms with thin, fragile caps and closely packed gills.
children.distinguishingFeatures: What sets inky caps apart from other mushrooms is their autodigestion process - they release enzymes that break down their own gill tissues, turning them into a dark, drippy liquid. This dramatic self-destruction happens within hours or days of the mushroom emerging.
children.funFact: The black ink produced by some inky cap species was historically used as actual writing ink, and some artists still use it today for drawing and calligraphy!

children.name: Schizophyllaceae
Schizophyllum
children.description: Schizophyllum is a genus containing just one widespread species, the splitgill mushroom. These small, fan-shaped fungi are easily recognized by their distinctive gills that appear split or forked lengthwise, creating a unique fuzzy appearance on the underside of the cap.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The split gills that give this genus its name are truly unique among mushrooms - the gill edges can actually curl and uncurl based on moisture levels to protect the spore-producing surfaces.
children.funFact: The splitgill mushroom is one of the most widespread fungi on Earth, found on every continent except Antarctica, and can revive from a completely dried state when moisture returns.

children.description: Schizophyllaceae is a small family of fungi known for their unique fan-shaped mushrooms with distinctive split gills. These fungi are wood decomposers that play an important role in breaking down dead wood in forest ecosystems. The family is represented in New England by just one species, but it's a remarkable one that can be found worldwide.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are easily recognized by their unusual gills that appear to split lengthwise down the middle, creating a forked or divided appearance. This split-gill feature is quite rare among mushrooms and makes them unmistakable in the field.
children.funFact: The single species in this family, Schizophyllum commune, is considered one of the most widely distributed mushrooms on Earth and can actually survive being completely dried out, then revive when moisture returns.

children.name: Radulomycetaceae
Radulomyces
children.description: Radulomyces is a genus of crust fungi that grow as thin, spreading patches on decaying wood. These fungi have a distinctive surface texture that feels rough or sandpaper-like to the touch, which is where their name comes from (radula means 'scraper' in Latin). They play an important role in forest ecosystems by breaking down dead wood and recycling nutrients back into the soil.
children.distinguishingFeatures: What sets Radulomyces apart from other crust fungi is their uniquely rough, granular surface texture that resembles fine sandpaper. Unlike smoother crust fungi, their spore-bearing surface has tiny projections that create this characteristic bumpy feel.
children.funFact: Despite being called the 'Asian Beauty,' Radulomyces copelandii was actually first discovered and described from specimens found in North America, showing how fungal names don't always match their geographic origins!

children.description: Radulomycetaceae is a small family of fungi that forms thin, crust-like fruiting bodies on decaying wood. These fungi are part of the larger group of wood-decay fungi that help break down dead trees and logs in forest ecosystems. They produce their spores on a smooth or slightly wrinkled surface that lies flat against the wood substrate.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their smooth to finely wrinkled spore-bearing surface and their distinctive spore characteristics when viewed under a microscope. Unlike many related wood-decay fungi, they don't form pores, teeth, or gills.
children.funFact: Despite being a entire fungal family, Radulomycetaceae contains only a single genus with just a few species worldwide, making it one of the smallest families in the fungal kingdom.

children.name: Pruinomycena
children.description: Pruinomycena is a small genus of delicate mushrooms that produce tiny, fragile fruiting bodies. These fungi are saprobic, meaning they feed on decaying organic matter in forest environments, helping to break down dead plant material.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their extremely small size, thin stems, and caps that have a distinctive powdery or frosted appearance (pruinose surface). They differ from other small mushroom genera by their unique combination of microscopic features and habitat preferences.
children.funFact: The genus name 'Pruinomycena' literally means 'frosted mushroom,' referring to the powdery white coating that gives these tiny fungi their distinctive appearance.

children.name: Cystostereaceae
Cystostereum
children.description: Cystostereum is a small genus of fungi that form thin, leathery bracket-like growths on dead hardwood trees and branches. These fungi are wood decomposers that help break down fallen logs and dead wood in forest ecosystems. They produce their spores on a smooth, fertile surface on the underside of their brackets.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Cystostereum fungi are recognized by their thin, flexible fruiting bodies that have a smooth spore-bearing surface rather than pores or gills. They also have distinctive microscopic features including special sterile cells called cystidia that give the genus its name.
children.funFact: The name 'Cystostereum' literally means 'bladder stereum,' referring to the balloon-like sterile cells found in these fungi that help scientists identify them under a microscope.

children.description: Cystostereaceae is a small family of wood-decay fungi that forms thin, crust-like growths on dead wood. These fungi are saprobic, meaning they break down dead organic matter and play an important role in forest decomposition. They produce their spores on a smooth or slightly wrinkled surface that spreads across the substrate like a thin skin.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their smooth to slightly bumpy spore-bearing surface and their unique microscopic structures called cystidia, which are specialized sterile cells that project from the fertile surface.
children.funFact: Despite being tiny and easily overlooked, these crust fungi are essential forest recyclers, helping to break down fallen logs and return nutrients to the soil for new plant growth.

children.name: Hertzogia
children.description: Hertzogia is a small genus of mosses found in specialized habitats. These tiny plants form cushions or mats on rocks and soil, and like all mosses, they lack true roots and instead absorb water and nutrients directly through their leaves.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Hertzogia mosses are distinguished by their unique leaf structure and growth pattern, forming dense, compact cushions in harsh environments where few other plants can survive.
children.funFact: Despite being tiny and easily overlooked, Hertzogia mosses are incredibly hardy and can survive in extreme conditions by going dormant during dry periods and quickly reviving when moisture returns.

children.name: Aphroditeola
children.description: Aphroditeola is a genus of small marine polychaete worms that belong to the scale worm family. These segmented worms live on the ocean floor and are covered with overlapping scale-like structures called elytra that protect their bodies. They are part of the diverse group of bristle worms that play important roles in marine ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Aphroditeola worms are distinguished by their relatively small size and specific arrangement of protective scales along their backs. They differ from other scale worms in their particular scale patterns and body proportions.
children.funFact: The genus name Aphroditeola means 'little Aphrodite,' referencing their relationship to the larger and more spectacular sea mouse worms in the genus Aphrodita, which were named after the Greek goddess of beauty due to their iridescent, hair-like bristles.

children.description: The Common Gilled Mushrooms and Allies represent the largest and most diverse group of fungi that most people recognize as 'mushrooms.' This order includes the classic umbrella-shaped mushrooms with gills underneath their caps, as well as some surprising relatives like puffballs, bird's nest fungi, and coral-like species that have evolved different spore-dispersal strategies.
children.distinguishingFeatures: What unites this diverse group is their shared evolutionary history and similar spore-producing structures, even though some members have moved away from the typical gilled mushroom form. Unlike other major mushroom groups, they typically have thin-walled spores and specific microscopic features in their gill structure.
children.funFact: This order includes both the delicious grocery store button mushrooms and shiitake, as well as some of the world's most deadly poisonous species like the destroying angel mushrooms - showing how diverse and evolutionarily successful this group has become!

children.name: Russulales
Russulaceae
Russula
children.description: Brittlegills are a large genus of mushrooms known for their characteristically brittle, chalk-like flesh that snaps cleanly when broken, rather than tearing like most other mushrooms. These colorful fungi form beneficial partnerships with tree roots and can be found in forests throughout New England, displaying caps in nearly every color of the rainbow from bright reds and purples to greens, yellows, and whites. Most have white or pale yellow spores and relatively short, thick stems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other mushrooms, brittlegills have flesh that breaks with a clean, crisp snap like chalk, and their gills are typically quite brittle as well. They also lack the milky latex that their close relatives, the milk caps (Lactarius), produce when cut or damaged.
children.funFact: Some brittlegills have earned rather unflattering common names based on their taste or smell - 'The Sickener' causes severe stomach upset if eaten raw, while the 'Stinking Brittlegill' smells like rotting fish, and the 'Camembert Brittlegill' has the distinctive aroma of aged cheese!

children.name: Lactarius
children.description: Common Milkcaps are a diverse group of mushrooms that all share one remarkable trait: when their flesh is cut or broken, they release a milky latex that oozes from the wound. This "milk" can be white, orange, yellow, blue, or even clear, and often helps identify the specific species. These mushrooms form beneficial partnerships with tree roots and are commonly found in forests throughout New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other mushrooms, Milkcaps release a distinctive latex or "milk" when damaged, which can range from white to brightly colored. This latex production, combined with their typically brittle flesh and often funnel-shaped caps, makes them easy to distinguish from similar-looking mushroom groups.
children.funFact: The Indigo Milk Cap produces bright blue milk that's so vivid it can stain your hands, and this blue latex actually turns green when exposed to air!

children.name: Lactifluus
children.description: Lactifluus is a genus of mushrooms known as milkcaps that release a milky or watery latex when their flesh is cut or broken. These fungi form important partnerships with tree roots, helping forests thrive while producing distinctive mushrooms with caps that often have concentric zones or wrinkled surfaces. They're commonly found throughout New England's woodlands from summer through fall.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike their close relatives in the genus Lactarius, Lactifluus species typically have white spore prints and their milk latex tends to be less acrid or bitter. Many species in this genus also have a more watery consistency to their latex compared to the thicker, more colorful milk of true Lactarius mushrooms.
children.funFact: The Weeping Milk Cap gets its name because it produces so much clear latex that it literally appears to 'weep' when touched, and this abundant liquid has a distinctly fishy smell that intensifies as the mushroom ages.

children.description: The Russulaceae family includes some of the most recognizable mushrooms in New England forests, known for their distinctive brittle flesh that snaps cleanly like chalk when broken. Many members of this family produce a milky latex when cut or damaged, while others have colorful, often brightly pigmented caps that can range from deep reds to brilliant yellows.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most other mushroom families, Russulaceae members have a unique flesh texture that breaks cleanly rather than tearing fibrous strands, and many species exude a white or colored milk when damaged.
children.funFact: Some milkcap mushrooms change the color of their 'milk' when exposed to air - starting white but turning yellow, blue, or even purple within minutes of being cut!

children.name: Stereaceae
Stereum
children.description: Stereum is a genus of bracket fungi that form thin, leathery, shelf-like growths on dead and dying hardwood and coniferous trees. These fungi appear as overlapping, bracket-shaped structures that often have a smooth or slightly fuzzy upper surface and can range in color from white and cream to brown and orange.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other bracket fungi, Stereum species are typically thin and flexible when fresh, with a distinctly smooth underside that lacks the pores or teeth found in related groups.
children.funFact: Several Stereum species are called "bleeding" fungi because they release a red or orange liquid when cut or damaged, making them easy to identify in the field.

children.name: Aleurodiscus
children.description: Aleurodiscus is a genus of crust fungi that form thin, flat growths directly on the bark of trees and shrubs. These fungi are wood decomposers that help break down dead and dying plant material in forest ecosystems. They typically appear as smooth, disc-like or patch-like formations that can range from whitish to orange in color.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other crust fungi, Aleurodiscus species have a distinctive smooth, waxy texture and often produce colorful fruiting bodies that stand out against tree bark. They also have unique microscopic features including specialized cells called cystidia that help identify different species.
children.funFact: The Orange Disco gets its playful common name from its bright orange color and disc-like appearance, making it look like a tiny natural dance floor growing on tree bark!

children.name: Xylobolus
children.description: Xylobolus is a small genus of crust fungi that forms thin, parchment-like layers on decaying wood. These fungi are wood decomposers that help break down dead trees and fallen logs in forest ecosystems. They typically grow as flat, crusty patches that can be peeled away from the wood surface like old paint or paper.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Xylobolus fungi are distinguished by their ceramic or parchment-like texture and their ability to separate cleanly from the wood substrate. Unlike many other crust fungi, they have a distinctive brittle, almost glass-like quality when dry.
children.funFact: The name 'Xylobolus' literally means 'wood-thrower,' referring to how these fungi can be easily peeled or thrown off from the wood surface they grow on.

children.description: The Stereaceae are a family of bracket fungi that create thin, leathery fruiting bodies on dead wood. These fungi are important decomposers in forest ecosystems, breaking down fallen logs and dead branches. Most species in this family form shelf-like or crust-like growths that are typically smooth or have tiny pores on their undersides.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other bracket fungi, members of Stereaceae typically have smooth undersurfaces or very fine pores, rather than the larger, obvious pores seen in polypores. Their fruiting bodies are also generally thinner and more flexible than the thick, woody brackets of related families.
children.funFact: Some Stereum species can actually bleed! When fresh and cut or bruised, they release reddish or orange droplets that look remarkably like blood, earning species like Stereum gausapatum the common name 'bleeding bracket fungus.'

children.name: Auriscalpiaceae
Lentinellus
children.description: Lentinellus is a genus of small to medium-sized mushrooms that grow on decaying wood, particularly hardwood logs and stumps. These fungi are characterized by their distinctive gilled undersides with teeth-like projections along the gill edges, giving them a serrated appearance when viewed closely.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike typical gilled mushrooms, Lentinellus species have tiny tooth-like projections along their gill edges, making them appear serrated under magnification. They also tend to have tough, leathery textures and often grow in overlapping clusters or shelf-like formations.
children.funFact: The aniseed cockleshell (Lentinellus cochleatus) gets its name from its strong licorice-like scent, which can be detected from several feet away when the mushroom is fresh.

children.name: Artomyces
children.description: Artomyces is a genus of coral fungi that create beautiful branching structures resembling underwater coral or tiny trees. These fungi grow from decaying wood and have distinctive crown-like tips at the end of their branches, which is where they produce their spores.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other coral fungi, Artomyces species have flattened, crown-shaped tips that look like tiny crowns or crests at the end of each branch. This unique crown structure sets them apart from the pointed or rounded tips found in other coral fungus genera.
children.funFact: The crown-tipped coral fungus can continue growing and fruiting from the same spot on a log for many years, sometimes producing new flushes of growth season after season.

children.name: Gloiodon
children.description: Gloiodon is a small genus of unusual fungi that produce tooth-like or spine-covered fruiting bodies rather than typical mushroom caps and gills. These fungi are wood decomposers that help break down dead organic matter in forest ecosystems. They belong to a group of fungi known as tooth fungi due to their distinctive spiny undersides.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Gloiodon fungi are distinguished by their gelatinous, rubbery texture combined with tooth-like spines hanging from the underside of their brackets or caps. This unique combination of jelly-like consistency and spiny structure sets them apart from other tooth fungi.
children.funFact: Despite looking like they might be slimy or wet, Gloiodon fungi have a distinctive rubbery bounce when touched, earning them the common name 'jelly tooth fungi.'

children.name: Auriscalpium
children.description: Auriscalpium is a small genus of fungi that contains just one species worldwide - the distinctive Earpick Fungus. These unusual mushrooms grow exclusively on old pine cones, forming small brownish caps with spines underneath instead of typical gills or pores. They play an important role in breaking down tough cone material in coniferous forests.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other tooth fungi that grow on wood, Auriscalpium species are the only spine-bearing mushrooms that specialize in growing on old pine cones. Their long, slender stems and preference for cone substrates make them unmistakable.
children.funFact: The name 'Earpick Fungus' comes from its resemblance to the small spoon-like tools once used to clean ears, and it can take up to two years to fully decompose a single pine cone.

children.description: The Auriscalpiaceae is a family of fungi that includes some of the most uniquely shaped mushrooms you'll encounter in New England's forests. These fungi are characterized by their unusual spore-bearing surfaces, which can range from tooth-like projections to coral-like branches, rather than the typical gills or pores found in most mushrooms. Most species in this family are wood decomposers, playing important roles in breaking down dead trees and branches.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike typical gilled mushrooms, members of this family produce spores on teeth, spines, or coral-like branches. Their fruiting bodies often have distinctive, sculptural forms that make them easily recognizable in the field.
children.funFact: The genus Auriscalpium contains the "ear-pick fungus," named because its spiny cap resembles an ancient Roman ear-cleaning tool called an auriscalpium!

children.name: Albatrellaceae
Neoalbatrellus
children.description: Neoalbatrellus is a small genus of polypore fungi that grow on wood and are notable for their distinctive blue coloration. These mushrooms form bracket-like or shelf-like fruiting bodies on decaying hardwood logs and stumps. Both New England species in this genus share the characteristic blue hues that make them stand out among other wood-decomposing fungi.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The blue coloration of their fruiting bodies is the most distinctive feature that sets Neoalbatrellus apart from other polypore genera. This blue pigmentation is quite rare among wood-decomposing fungi in New England forests.
children.funFact: The blue color in Neoalbatrellus mushrooms can fade over time or when the fungus is dried, making fresh specimens much more vibrant and easier to identify than older ones.

children.name: Albatrellus
children.description: Albatrellus is a genus of terrestrial mushrooms that grow from the ground rather than on wood like many other polypores. These fungi have a distinctive appearance with their bracket-like or shelf-like caps and tiny pores underneath instead of gills, making them part of the polypore family.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most polypores that grow on dead wood, Albatrellus species are terrestrial and emerge directly from soil. They typically have thick, fleshy caps with white to yellowish pore surfaces that may bruise when handled.
children.funFact: The Sheep Polypore gets its name because it was historically used as food for sheep and other livestock during harsh winters when other food sources were scarce.

children.name: Albatrellopsis
children.description: Albatrellopsis is a small genus of polypore fungi that produces tough, bracket-like mushrooms with distinctive pores on the underside instead of gills. These fungi are wood decomposers that help break down dead hardwood trees in forest ecosystems. They form shelf-like fruiting bodies that can persist for months or even years on their host trees.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Albatrellopsis fungi are distinguished from other polypores by their confluent (merging) pore structure and their preference for growing on hardwood trees rather than conifers. Their fruiting bodies have a distinctive tough, leathery texture and often display concentric zones of color.
children.funFact: The single New England species, Albatrellopsis confluens, gets its name from the way its pores flow together and merge, creating an almost maze-like pattern on the underside of the mushroom.

children.name: Laeticutis
children.description: Laeticutis is a genus of bracket fungi that grows on dead hardwood trees, particularly birch and beech. These fungi form shelf-like structures on tree trunks and have a distinctive pore surface underneath instead of gills. They play an important role in forest ecosystems by decomposing dead wood.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Laeticutis fungi are distinguished by their bright white to cream-colored pore surface and relatively soft, spongy texture when fresh. Unlike many other bracket fungi, they have a somewhat gelatinous consistency and lack the hard, woody texture of shelf fungi like turkey tail.
children.funFact: The name Laeticutis means 'joyful skin' in Latin, referring to the bright, cheerful appearance of these fungi's pore surface.

children.description: The Albatrellaceae are a family of fungi that produce distinctive bracket-like or shelf-like fruiting bodies, often growing from the ground or on decaying wood. These mushrooms typically have a firm, fleshy texture when fresh and feature small pores on their undersides instead of gills, releasing spores through these tiny openings.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other bracket fungi, members of this family often have a more centralized stem and a fleshier consistency. Their pore surfaces are typically white to yellowish and bruise or stain when touched.
children.funFact: Some Albatrellaceae species are edible when young and are considered delicacies in certain regions, though they can become quite tough and woody as they mature.

children.name: Hericiaceae
Hericium
children.description: Hericium is a genus of distinctive white fungi that look nothing like typical mushrooms with caps and stems. Instead, these fascinating decomposers produce cascading masses of tooth-like spines or coral-like branches that hang from tree trunks and logs. All four New England species are wood-rotting fungi that help break down dead hardwood trees in our forests.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other tooth fungi, Hericium species grow in large, shaggy masses with long, hanging spines rather than having teeth on the underside of a cap. Their pure white color and dramatic, icicle-like appearance makes them unmistakable in the forest.
children.funFact: Lion's mane mushroom (Hericium erinaceus) is being studied for its potential to support brain health and memory, as it contains compounds that may stimulate nerve growth factor production.

children.name: Laxitextum
children.description: Laxitextum is a small genus of crust fungi that forms thin, spreading patches on dead wood. These fungi are wood decomposers that help break down fallen logs and branches in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus have a loose, web-like texture with distinctively colored surfaces that often show contrasting light and dark zones.
children.funFact: The name 'Laxitextum' literally means 'loose weave,' referring to the open, net-like structure of these fungi's fruiting bodies.

children.description: Tooth fungi are a fascinating family of fungi that produce spores on tooth-like or spine-like projections instead of gills or pores. These white, cascading structures hang downward from the fungus, creating some of the most distinctive and easily recognizable mushrooms in New England forests. They're primarily decomposers that break down dead wood, playing an important role in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most mushrooms that have gills underneath their caps or pores on their undersides, tooth fungi produce their spores on hanging, tooth-like spines that point downward. This unique spore-bearing surface makes them unmistakable in the forest.
children.funFact: Lion's Mane mushroom (Hericium erinaceus), a member of this family, is not only edible and delicious with a texture similar to crab or lobster, but it's also being studied for potential benefits to brain health and nerve regeneration.

children.name: Peniophoraceae
Peniophora
children.description: Peniophora is a genus of crust fungi that form thin, smooth patches on the bark of dead or dying trees and branches. These fungi are wood decomposers that help break down fallen logs and dead wood in forest ecosystems. They typically create colorful, flat crusts that can range from white and pink to brown and gray.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Peniophora fungi are distinguished by their smooth, waxy texture and their tendency to form thin, tightly attached crusts that follow the contours of the bark. Unlike many other crust fungi, they often have distinctive colors and may develop a slightly peeling edge as they mature.
children.funFact: Despite their common name 'crust fungi,' some Peniophora species like the Red Tree Brain Fungus can develop wrinkled, brain-like textures that make them look more dramatic than typical flat crusts.

children.name: Scytinostroma
children.description: Scytinostroma is a genus of crust fungi that form thin, flat patches on decaying wood. These fungi grow as resupinate (lying flat against their substrate) fruiting bodies that spread across the surface of dead branches and logs like a thin skin or crust.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their smooth to slightly wrinkled surface texture and their ability to form continuous, film-like crusts that can peel away from the wood substrate when mature.
children.funFact: The name Scytinostroma comes from Greek words meaning 'leather mat,' referring to the tough, flexible texture of these fungi when they dry out.

children.description: The Peniophoraceae are a family of wood-decaying fungi that form thin, crust-like fruiting bodies on dead wood. These fungi are important decomposers in forest ecosystems, breaking down fallen logs and branches by secreting enzymes that digest cellulose and lignin. They typically grow as flat, leathery patches that are tightly attached to their woody substrate.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other crust fungi, members of Peniophoraceae often have distinctively colored spores and specialized microscopic structures called cystidia that project from their surface. Their fruiting bodies tend to be smoother and more uniform than related families.
children.funFact: Some Peniophora species can actually change color dramatically as they age, starting out bright orange or pink and fading to gray or brown over time.

children.name: Bondarzewiaceae
Bondarzewia
children.description: Bondarzewia is a genus of large, bracket-like fungi that form impressive shelf-like structures on trees. These mushrooms are wood decomposers that help break down dead and dying hardwood trees, particularly oaks. They're known for their substantial size and distinctive layered appearance.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Bondarzewia fungi are distinguished by their large, overlapping bracket formations and their preference for growing at the base of oak trees. Unlike many other bracket fungi, they have a more fleshy texture when fresh and often display concentric zones on their upper surface.
children.funFact: Berkeley's Polypore can grow to enormous sizes, with some specimens reaching over 3 feet across and weighing up to 50 pounds, making it one of the largest mushrooms in North America!

children.name: Wrightoporia
children.description: Wrightoporia is a genus of fungi that forms bracket-like structures on dead or dying hardwood trees. These fungi are wood decomposers that help break down fallen logs and branches in forest ecosystems. They produce spores through tiny pores on the underside of their fruiting bodies.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Wrightoporia fungi are characterized by their thin, flexible bracket-like fruiting bodies and their distinctive microscopic features, including unique spore shapes and specialized cells called cystidia.
children.funFact: This genus was named after mycologist Jim Wright, who made significant contributions to the study of bracket fungi in North America.

children.name: Heterobasidion
children.description: Heterobasidion is a genus of wood-rotting fungi that are serious pathogens of coniferous trees, particularly pines, spruces, and firs. These fungi cause root and butt rot, attacking the base and roots of trees and often spreading through root contact between neighboring trees. They produce bracket-like fruiting bodies that are typically brown and woody in texture.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Heterobasidion fungi are distinguished by their ability to cause extensive root rot in conifers and their characteristic brown, perennial bracket fruiting bodies with white pore surfaces underneath.
children.funFact: Heterobasidion root rot can spread underground through forest stands for decades, creating expanding circles of dead and dying trees that foresters call 'infection centers' - some of which can be detected from aerial photographs.

children.description: The Bondarzewiaceae are a family of wood-decay fungi that specialize in breaking down the structural components of trees and woody plants. These fungi typically form tough, bracket-like or crust-like fruiting bodies and play important ecological roles as decomposers in forest ecosystems. Most members of this family are found growing on dead or dying hardwood and coniferous trees.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their white rot decay pattern, which breaks down both cellulose and lignin in wood, leaving behind a pale, fibrous residue. They typically have a dimitic hyphal system (containing two types of hyphae) and produce white spore prints.
children.funFact: Some Bondarzewia species, like Berkeley's polypore, can produce massive fruiting bodies weighing over 50 pounds that emerge from the base of oak trees like giant woody flowers.

children.name: Lachnocladiaceae
Dichostereum
children.description: Dichostereum is a small genus of crust fungi that forms thin, papery layers on decaying wood. These fungi create flat, spreading patches that look almost like paint or skin peeling off tree bark, with colors ranging from whitish to brownish-gray.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other crust fungi, Dichostereum has a unique spore-bearing surface with tiny pores that are often arranged in maze-like patterns, and its fruiting body tends to peel away from the wood substrate more easily than related species.
children.funFact: Despite their simple appearance, Dichostereum fungi play an important role as decomposers, helping to break down tough wood fibers and return nutrients to forest soils.

children.name: Vararia
children.description: Vararia is a genus of crust fungi that form thin, flat patches on the undersides of decaying logs and branches. These fungi spread like a coating or skin over the wood surface, playing an important role in breaking down dead wood in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Vararia fungi are distinguished by their smooth to slightly wrinkled, crust-like appearance that adheres tightly to wood surfaces. Unlike many other crust fungi, they have a distinctive microscopic structure with unique spore-bearing cells.
children.funFact: Despite their inconspicuous appearance, Vararia fungi are essential forest recyclers, helping to decompose fallen trees and return nutrients to the soil for new plant growth.

children.description: Lachnocladiaceae is a small family of fungi that includes species with very different appearances and lifestyles. These fungi can form either thin, crust-like patches on wood surfaces or create distinctive coral-like branching structures that resemble tiny underwater gardens growing from decaying logs and branches.
children.distinguishingFeatures: What unites this diverse family is their shared evolutionary history and similar microscopic reproductive structures, despite their dramatically different outward appearances ranging from flat crusts to intricate branched forms.
children.funFact: Some members of this family can completely change their growth form depending on environmental conditions, switching from flat crusts to elaborate branching structures as they mature.

children.name: Echinodontiaceae
Echinodontium
children.description: Echinodontium is a genus of bracket fungi that creates distinctive woody, hoof-shaped growths on tree trunks. These fungi are parasites that cause heart rot in living trees, particularly conifers, and continue to decompose the wood after the tree dies.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are recognized by their extremely hard, woody fruiting bodies that have a characteristic spiny or tooth-like underside instead of pores or gills.
children.funFact: The name Echinodontium literally means "spiny tooth," referring to the sharp, tooth-like projections on the underside of their fruiting bodies that release spores.

children.description: Echinodontiaceae is a small family of wood-decay fungi that produce distinctive tooth-like or spine-covered fruiting bodies. These fungi are parasites and decomposers of woody plants, particularly conifers, where they cause heart rot by breaking down the wood's cellulose and lignin. They play an important ecological role in forest ecosystems by recycling nutrients from dead and dying trees.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their unique fruiting bodies that have a spiny or tooth-like fertile surface, rather than the gills or pores found in many other fungi. The spines hang downward and release spores from their surfaces.
children.funFact: The genus name 'Echinodontium' literally means 'spiny tooth,' referring to the characteristic needle-like projections that make these fungi look somewhat like natural pincushions growing on tree trunks.

children.description: Russulales is a diverse order of fungi that includes some of New England's most recognizable mushrooms, from the colorful brittlegills to the peculiar tooth fungi that look like white icicles hanging from trees. These fungi play crucial roles as decomposers and mycorrhizal partners, helping trees absorb nutrients while breaking down organic matter in forests. Despite their varied appearances, they share similar reproductive structures and genetic relationships.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other mushroom orders, Russulales species often have distinctive spore-bearing surfaces - some have traditional gills, others have tooth-like projections, and some form crusts on wood. Many members also have brittle flesh that crumbles easily when handled, and several families produce a milky latex when cut.
children.funFact: The tooth fungi in this order, like the Lion's Mane mushroom, are not only edible delicacies but are also being studied for their potential to support brain health and nerve regeneration.

children.name: Boletales
Boletaceae
Boletus
children.description: The Boletus genus includes some of New England's most prized edible mushrooms, commonly known as porcini and boletes. These chunky, often barrel-shaped mushrooms have thick stems and caps with pores underneath instead of gills, giving their undersides a sponge-like appearance. They form beneficial partnerships with tree roots and are typically found in forests during summer and fall.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other mushrooms, boletes have tiny pores under their caps rather than gills or teeth. Many species in this genus bruise blue when cut or damaged, and they generally have thick, robust stems that are often bulbous at the base.
children.funFact: The famous King Bolete (Boletus edulis) is so highly valued by chefs that it's sometimes called the "king of mushrooms" and can sell for over $20 per pound when fresh!

children.name: Leccinum
children.description: Leccinum is a genus of chunky, robust mushrooms commonly known as scaber stalks or rough-stemmed boletes. These mushrooms are easily recognized by their thick stems covered in dark, rough scales or dots, and their spongy pore surface underneath the cap instead of gills. They form beneficial partnerships with trees, particularly birches, aspens, and other hardwoods.
children.distinguishingFeatures: What sets Leccinum apart from other boletes is their distinctively scaly or dotted stems that feel rough to the touch, along with their strong association with specific tree partners. Many species also have the unique characteristic of turning black or blue when the flesh is cut or bruised.
children.funFact: Many Leccinum mushrooms are so closely tied to their tree partners that you can often identify the species just by knowing which tree they're growing near - like the Brown Birch-bolete which grows exclusively with birch trees!

children.name: Tylopilus
children.description: Tylopilus is a genus of mushrooms commonly known as bitter boletes, named for their characteristically bitter taste that makes most species inedible. These are medium to large mushrooms with spongy pore surfaces instead of gills, and they typically have brown, reddish, or grayish caps with sturdy stems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other bolete mushrooms, Tylopilus species are distinguished by their bitter taste and often produce pink or reddish spore prints rather than the brown or olive prints of most boletes.
children.funFact: The bitter taste that gives these mushrooms their common name is so intense that even a tiny nibble can leave your mouth puckering for quite a while - nature's way of saying 'don't eat me!'

children.name: Aureoboletus
children.description: Aureoboletus is a genus of bolete mushrooms that typically have golden-yellow or bright yellow pore surfaces underneath their caps instead of gills. These fungi form beneficial partnerships with tree roots and are commonly found growing in forests throughout New England. Like other boletes, they have a thick, fleshy stem and cap structure that makes them easily recognizable.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Aureoboletus are distinguished from other boletes by their characteristic bright golden-yellow pore surfaces and often have stems that are similarly colored or marked with yellow tones.
children.funFact: The name 'Aureoboletus' literally means 'golden bolete,' perfectly describing the striking golden-yellow pores that give these mushrooms their distinctive appearance.

children.name: Neoboletus
children.description: Neoboletus is a genus of mushrooms that produce their spores in tubes rather than on gills, creating a sponge-like appearance underneath the cap. These boletes are characterized by their tendency to bruise blue when cut or damaged, and they typically have robust, often colorful stems and caps.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Neoboletus are distinguished from other bolete genera by their strong blue bruising reaction and often bright yellow, red, or orange coloration on both caps and stems.
children.funFact: The dramatic blue bruising that occurs when these mushrooms are touched or cut happens within seconds and is caused by chemical reactions involving compounds that help protect the fungus from being eaten.

children.name: Xerocomellus
children.description: Xerocomellus is a genus of medium-sized mushrooms known as boletes, which have spongy pores under their caps instead of gills. These fungi form beneficial partnerships with tree roots and are characterized by their tendency to develop cracks in their caps as they mature, often revealing colorful flesh underneath.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus typically show distinctive cracking patterns on their caps and may bruise blue when cut or damaged, setting them apart from other bolete genera.
children.funFact: The Red-cracking Bolete gets its name from the beautiful red cracks that develop across its brown cap, creating a mosaic-like pattern that makes it one of the most visually striking boletes in New England forests.

children.name: Leccinellum
children.description: Leccinellum is a genus of medium-sized mushrooms that form beneficial partnerships with trees, especially oaks and other hardwoods. These fungi have the characteristic bolete structure with pores instead of gills underneath their caps, and they typically develop distinctive color changes when their flesh is cut or bruised.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Leccinellum are distinguished from other boletes by their specific host tree relationships and their tendency to develop yellow, blue, or reddish staining when damaged. They also typically have scaly or rough stems that help separate them from smooth-stemmed bolete genera.
children.funFact: The Saffron Bolete gets its name from the bright golden-yellow color that appears when you cut into its flesh, creating a dramatic transformation that can happen within seconds of exposure to air.

children.name: Hortiboletus
children.description: Hortiboletus is a genus of small to medium-sized mushrooms that belong to the bolete family, meaning they have pores instead of gills under their caps. These mushrooms typically have reddish or pinkish coloring on their caps or stems and are commonly found in woods and fields throughout New England. They form beneficial partnerships with tree roots, helping forests stay healthy.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other boletes, Hortiboletus species are generally smaller and often display distinctive reddish, pink, or rosy hues on their caps, stems, or pores.
