Their pores may bruise blue when damaged, and they typically have a more delicate appearance than the robust boletes in related genera.
children.funFact: The Ruby Bolete gets its name from its beautiful ruby-red cap that can look like a precious gem glinting on the forest floor.

children.name: Xerocomus
children.description: Xerocomus is a genus of medium-sized mushrooms that belong to the bolete family, characterized by their spongy pore surface underneath the cap instead of gills. These fungi form beneficial partnerships with tree roots and are typically found growing on the ground in forests throughout New England. All members of this genus are terrestrial mushrooms that play important ecological roles as decomposers and mycorrhizal partners.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other boletes, Xerocomus species often have caps with a velvety or suede-like texture and tend to be smaller and more delicate in appearance. Many species in this genus also show distinctive color changes when the flesh is cut or bruised.
children.funFact: The name 'Xerocomus' literally means 'dry hair' in Greek, referring to the characteristic dry, velvety texture of their mushroom caps that feels almost like suede fabric.

children.name: Retiboletus
children.description: Retiboletus is a genus of boletes (mushrooms with pores instead of gills) that are known for their distinctive network-like patterns on their stems and their tendency to bruise blue when cut or damaged. These mushrooms typically have thick, sturdy stems and grow in association with tree roots in forest environments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other boletes, Retiboletus species have prominent raised, net-like ridges (reticulation) covering their stems, which gives the genus its name. They also characteristically turn bright blue when bruised or cut, a reaction caused by chemical compounds in the mushroom.
children.funFact: The name 'Retiboletus' literally means 'net bolete,' referring to the intricate mesh-like pattern that decorates their stems like natural lacework.

children.name: Hemileccinum
children.description: Hemileccinum is a genus of bolete mushrooms that produce their spores in tubes rather than on gills. These fungi form beneficial partnerships with tree roots, helping forests thrive while creating the distinctive mushrooms we see above ground. All members of this genus have caps and stems, with pore surfaces underneath their caps instead of the blade-like gills found on many other mushrooms.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Hemileccinum boletes are distinguished from other bolete genera by their specific microscopic spore characteristics and DNA sequences. They typically have較 firm flesh and pore surfaces that may change color when bruised or cut.
children.funFact: The Ashtray Bolete gets its unusual name from its cap's resemblance to an old ceramic ashtray, complete with a rim-like edge and grayish coloration.

children.name: Chalciporus
children.description: Chalciporus is a small genus of boletes (mushrooms with pores instead of gills) that are typically small to medium-sized with reddish to brownish caps. These mushrooms form beneficial partnerships with tree roots and are commonly found in mixed and coniferous forests throughout New England. All members of this genus have tubes and pores on the underside of their caps rather than the blade-like gills found on many other mushrooms.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Chalciporus boletes are distinguished by their typically reddish coloration and their notably peppery or bitter taste when raw. Unlike many other bolete genera, they tend to be smaller in size and often have pores that may bruise or change color when damaged.
children.funFact: The Peppery Bolete gets its name from its intensely hot, peppery taste that can make your mouth burn if you bite into it raw, though this spiciness disappears completely when the mushroom is cooked.

children.name: Lanmaoa
children.description: Lanmaoa is a genus of bolete mushrooms that are relatively new to science, having been separated from other bolete groups based on DNA studies. These mushrooms typically have fleshy caps and produce spores in tubes rather than gills, and they form beneficial partnerships with tree roots in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Lanmaoa can be distinguished from other boletes by their specific microscopic features and genetic characteristics that were only recently discovered through molecular analysis.
children.funFact: This genus was only established in 2014, making it one of the most recently recognized groups of mushrooms, showing that scientists are still discovering new ways to organize the fungal tree of life.

children.name: Strobilomyces
children.description: Strobilomyces is a genus of distinctive bolete mushrooms that are easily recognized by their unique appearance. These fungi have caps covered in dark, shaggy scales that give them a pinecone-like or woolly appearance, and their white flesh dramatically turns black when cut or bruised.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other boletes, Strobilomyces mushrooms have conspicuously scaly, almost furry-looking caps and flesh that turns black when damaged rather than blue or remaining unchanged.
children.funFact: The name Strobilomyces literally means 'pinecone fungus' because of the overlapping dark scales on the cap that resemble the scales of a pinecone.

children.name: Xanthoconium
children.description: Xanthoconium is a small genus of bolete mushrooms that form beneficial partnerships with tree roots in forest ecosystems. These fungi have the characteristic bolete structure with pores instead of gills under their caps, and they help trees absorb nutrients from the soil in exchange for sugars.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their yellowish pore surfaces that may bruise blue when damaged, and their often colorful caps that can range from reddish-brown to purplish hues.
children.funFact: The name Xanthoconium comes from Greek words meaning 'yellow dust,' referring to the yellowish spore powder these mushrooms release.

children.name: Imleria
children.description: Imleria is a genus of medium-sized mushrooms that belong to the bolete family, characterized by their spongy pore surface underneath the cap instead of gills. These mushrooms typically have brown to reddish-brown caps and often bruise blue when cut or damaged. They form beneficial partnerships with tree roots and are commonly found in forests throughout New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Imleria boletes are distinguished from other bolete genera by their specific combination of brown coloration, blue bruising reaction, and particular spore characteristics visible under a microscope. They also tend to have a more velvety or slightly sticky cap surface compared to some other bolete groups.
children.funFact: The Bay Bolete was once classified in the genus Boletus, but genetic studies revealed it deserved its own genus - Imleria was named in honor of Hungarian mycologist Lajos Imler who contributed significantly to bolete research.

children.name: Neoporphyrellus
children.description: Neoporphyrellus is a genus of boletes, which are mushrooms that have pores instead of gills underneath their caps. These fungi form beneficial partnerships with tree roots and are characterized by their dark-colored caps and stems that often bruise or stain when cut or handled.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other bolete genera, Neoporphyrellus species typically have very dark, almost black caps and stems, giving them a distinctive velvety appearance that sets them apart from their more colorful bolete relatives.
children.funFact: The Black Velvet Bolete gets its common name from its remarkably dark, velvety cap surface that can appear almost jet black, making it one of the darkest-colored boletes you'll find in New England forests.

children.name: Butyriboletus
children.description: Butter Boletes are a small group of mushrooms known for their rich, buttery yellow flesh that often bruises blue when cut or damaged. These are bolete mushrooms, meaning they have pores instead of gills under their caps, and they form beneficial partnerships with tree roots in the forest. They're prized by mushroom hunters for their excellent edible qualities and distinctive appearance.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other boletes, Butter Boletes have particularly rich yellow flesh throughout the mushroom that typically turns blue when exposed to air. Their caps often display warm brown to reddish-brown colors that help distinguish them from other bolete genera.
children.funFact: The name 'Butyriboletus' literally means 'butter bolete' in Latin, referring to the rich, creamy yellow color of their flesh that resembles fresh butter.

children.name: Phylloporus
children.description: Gilled Boletes are fascinating fungi that blur the line between two major mushroom groups. Unlike typical boletes that have spongy pores under their caps, these mushrooms have gills like traditional mushrooms, yet they're genetically related to the bolete family.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These mushrooms are unique because they have gills instead of the tubes and pores found in other boletes, making them look more like typical gilled mushrooms at first glance.
children.funFact: Gilled Boletes represent an evolutionary bridge between gilled mushrooms and typical boletes, showing how fungi can evolve different spore-releasing structures while maintaining their genetic relationships.

children.name: Cyanoboletus
children.description: Cyanoboletus is a genus of boletes (mushrooms with pores instead of gills) that are famous for their dramatic color-changing abilities. When these mushrooms are cut or bruised, they quickly turn bright blue due to chemical reactions in their tissues. They're medium to large-sized mushrooms that grow on the ground in forests, typically under hardwood or mixed trees.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These boletes are distinguished from other bolete genera by their intense and rapid blue staining reaction when damaged. The blue coloration is much more pronounced and immediate compared to the slower, less dramatic color changes seen in most other boletes.
children.funFact: The ink stain bolete gets its common name because the blue bruising eventually turns black, creating dark stains that look like spilled ink on the mushroom's surface.

children.name: Caloboletus
children.description: Bitter Boletes are a small group of mushrooms that look tempting but taste terrible. These fungi have the classic bolete structure with spongy pores under their caps instead of gills, but they're united by their intensely bitter flavor that makes them inedible.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other boletes that may be mild or pleasant-tasting, all Bitter Boletes have an unmistakably harsh, bitter taste that persists even after cooking.
children.funFact: The genus name 'Caloboletus' comes from Greek words meaning 'beautiful bolete' - a bit ironic since their beautiful appearance is completely undermined by their awful taste!

children.name: Porphyrellus
children.description: Porphyrellus is a small genus of bolete mushrooms that produce spores and have caps that typically display dark, dusky colors. These fungi form beneficial partnerships with tree roots and can be found growing in forests throughout New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their distinctively dark-colored spores and caps that tend toward dusky browns and purples, setting them apart from the lighter-spored boletes in related genera.
children.funFact: The genus name 'Porphyrellus' comes from the Greek word for purple, referring to the purplish-brown tones often seen in these mushrooms' caps and spores.

children.name: Harrya
children.description: Harrya is a small genus of bolete mushrooms that grows in association with hardwood trees, particularly oaks. These mushrooms have the classic bolete structure with a cap and stem, and tiny pores on the underside instead of gills. They form beneficial partnerships with tree roots, helping forests thrive through nutrient exchange.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Harrya boletes are distinguished by their bright yellow pore surface that bruises blue when touched, and their distinctive coloration and staining reactions that separate them from other bolete genera.
children.funFact: The genus Harrya was only recently established in 2012, named after mycologist Harry Thiers, separating these mushrooms from the larger Boletus genus based on DNA analysis.

children.name: Exsudoporus
children.description: Exsudoporus is a genus of boletes, which are mushrooms with pores instead of gills under their caps. These fungi form beneficial partnerships with tree roots and are known for their distinctive appearance and the way their flesh changes color when cut or bruised.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their ability to exude droplets of liquid from their pore surfaces when young and fresh, which gives the genus its name meaning 'sweating pores.'
children.funFact: The name Exsudoporus literally means 'sweating pores' in Latin, referring to the distinctive droplets of moisture these mushrooms release from their undersides when they're young and actively growing.

children.name: Sutorius
children.description: Sutorius is a genus of bolete mushrooms that produce their spores in tubes rather than on gills like many other mushrooms. These fungi form beneficial partnerships with tree roots, helping forests thrive by exchanging nutrients with their plant partners. Members of this genus are characterized by their sturdy stems and caps with pore surfaces underneath.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Sutorius boletes are distinguished from other bolete genera by their specific microscopic spore characteristics and unique DNA sequences. They typically have thick, robust stems and caps that don't dramatically change color when bruised or cut.
children.funFact: The genus name Sutorius comes from the Latin word for 'cobbler' or 'shoemaker,' possibly referring to the tough, leather-like texture of some species' caps.

children.name: Baorangia
children.description: Baorangia is a genus of mushrooms that belongs to the bolete family, characterized by having pores instead of gills underneath their caps. These mushrooms form beneficial partnerships with tree roots, helping forests exchange nutrients through underground networks. They're medium to large-sized mushrooms that are prized by foragers for their meaty texture.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Baorangia mushrooms are distinguished from other boletes by their distinctive color-changing properties when cut or bruised, often shifting from yellow to blue. They also have a unique spore print color and specific microscopic features that separate them from closely related bolete genera.
children.funFact: The genus Baorangia was only recently established in 2014 when DNA studies revealed that these mushrooms were distinct enough from other boletes to deserve their own separate group!

children.name: Pulveroboletus
children.description: Pulveroboletus is a small genus of bolete mushrooms known for their distinctive powdery spore surfaces. These fungi have the typical bolete structure with pores instead of gills underneath their caps, and they form beneficial partnerships with tree roots in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their bright yellow pore surfaces that become covered in a characteristic powdery coating of spores as they mature, giving them their 'powdery' name.
children.funFact: The powdery sulfur bolete gets its name from the bright sulfur-yellow powder that coats its pores and can literally dust off onto your fingers when you touch it!

children.name: Pseudoboletus
children.description: Pseudoboletus is a small genus of bolete mushrooms that includes some of the most unusual fungi in the bolete family. These mushrooms are parasites that grow directly on other mushrooms, specifically on earthball fungi, rather than forming their own independent relationship with tree roots like most boletes.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike typical boletes that grow from the ground in partnership with trees, Pseudoboletus species are parasitic and grow directly on top of other fungi, particularly earthballs (Scleroderma species).
children.funFact: The Parasitic Bolete is one of the few mushrooms that is a parasite of another mushroom, making it a rare example of a fungus that 'eats' another fungus rather than decomposing plant matter or partnering with tree roots.

children.name: Austroboletus
children.description: Austroboletus is a small genus of bolete mushrooms that produce their spores in tubes rather than on gills. These fungi form beneficial partnerships with tree roots, helping forests absorb nutrients while receiving sugars in return. They're characterized by their soft, fleshy caps and the distinctive way their flesh changes color when cut or bruised.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other boletes, Austroboletus mushrooms typically have very delicate, graceful stems and caps that bruise dramatically when handled. They also tend to be smaller and more fragile than their sturdier bolete relatives.
children.funFact: Despite their name suggesting they're from Australia, Austroboletus mushrooms are found in North America too - the 'Austro' actually refers to their southern distribution patterns rather than the Australian continent.

children.name: Bothia
children.description: Bothia is a small genus of marine gastropod mollusks, commonly known as sea snails. These small marine creatures live in ocean waters and are characterized by their spiral shells and soft bodies that can retract into their protective shells when threatened.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of genus Bothia are distinguished by their distinctive shell shape and specific anatomical features that separate them from other sea snail genera in their family.
children.funFact: Like many sea snails, Bothia species use a rasping tongue-like structure called a radula to scrape food particles from surfaces as they feed.

children.name: Boletellus
children.description: Boletellus is a genus of mushrooms that are closely related to the more familiar boletes, but with some unique characteristics. These fungi form partnerships with tree roots and produce mushrooms with pores instead of gills on the underside of their caps. Like other boletes, they play important roles as decomposers and nutrient recyclers in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Boletellus mushrooms are distinguished from typical boletes by their tendency to have more fibrous, tough stems and caps that often crack or develop a scaly appearance as they mature. They also typically have smaller pores and different spore characteristics compared to their Boletus relatives.
children.funFact: The single New England species, Boletellus chrysenteroides, gets its scientific name from its golden-yellow pores, with 'chrysenteroides' meaning 'golden-boweled' in reference to this distinctive coloration.

children.name: Buchwaldoboletus
children.description: Buchwaldoboletus is a small genus of bolete mushrooms that have adapted to grow on decaying wood rather than forming partnerships with tree roots like most other boletes. These mushrooms have the characteristic pore surface underneath their caps instead of gills, but they're unusual among boletes for being decomposers of dead wood.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most boletes that form mycorrhizal relationships with living trees, Buchwaldoboletus species are saprobic, meaning they feed on dead and decaying wood. This wood-dwelling habit makes them quite rare and distinctive among the bolete family.
children.funFact: The Wood Bolete was only recently discovered to be distinct enough to warrant its own genus, having been moved from other bolete genera as DNA analysis revealed its unique evolutionary position.

children.name: Pulchroboletus
children.description: Pulchroboletus is a small genus of bolete mushrooms that are closely related to the king boletes but have their own distinct characteristics. These mushrooms have the typical bolete features of caps with pore surfaces instead of gills underneath, and they form beneficial partnerships with tree roots.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished from other boletes by their specific microscopic spore characteristics and DNA sequences that separate them from the closely related Boletus genus.
children.funFact: The genus name Pulchroboletus means 'beautiful bolete,' reflecting the attractive appearance of these mushrooms with their often colorful caps and stems.

children.name: Alessioporus
children.description: Alessioporus is a small genus of bolete mushrooms that form mycorrhizal relationships with trees. These fungi have the characteristic spongy pore surface on the underside of their caps instead of gills, and they help forest trees absorb nutrients from the soil.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their unique combination of reddish and yellowish colors, along with specific microscopic features of their spores and cap structure that separate them from other bolete genera.
children.funFact: This genus was only recently described by scientists in 2014, showing that there are still new groups of fungi being discovered and classified even in well-studied regions like New England.

children.description: Boletes are a diverse family of mushrooms best known for having tiny pores on their undersides instead of the familiar gills found on most mushrooms. These pores look like tiny holes and release spores, giving the underside a sponge-like appearance that's easy to spot. Most boletes form beneficial partnerships with tree roots, helping forests thrive while producing some of our most prized edible mushrooms.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most mushrooms with gills or other spore-bearing structures, boletes have a distinctive pore surface that looks like a natural sponge. Many species also have thick, sturdy stems and caps that separate cleanly from the stem when picked.
children.funFact: The famous porcini mushroom, prized by chefs worldwide, belongs to this family and can grow to enormous sizes - some specimens have been found weighing over 10 pounds!

children.name: Suillaceae
Suillus
children.description: Slippery Jacks are a diverse group of mushrooms known for their slimy or greasy cap surfaces when wet, which gives them their common name. These fungi form beneficial partnerships with coniferous trees, helping the trees absorb nutrients from the soil while receiving sugars in return. They typically have spongy pores under their caps instead of gills, and many species have distinctive rings around their stems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other bolete mushrooms, Slippery Jacks have characteristically sticky or slimy cap surfaces and often display partial veils that leave rings on their stems. They are also specifically associated with coniferous trees rather than hardwoods.
children.funFact: The slippery, mucilaginous coating on their caps acts as a protective barrier against insects and helps the mushroom retain moisture during dry periods.

children.description: The Suillaceae family consists of mushrooms that form mutually beneficial partnerships with tree roots, particularly conifers like pines and firs. These fungi are characterized by their soft, spongy undersides with tiny pores instead of gills, and many species have a distinctive slimy or sticky cap surface that gives them their common name 'slippery jacks.'
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other bolete families, Suillaceae mushrooms typically have a ring around the stem and often display a characteristic slimy cap surface. Their pore surfaces are usually yellow and may stain blue when bruised.
children.funFact: Many slippery jacks are so closely tied to specific tree species that finding certain mushrooms can help you identify what trees are growing nearby - some species only grow with particular types of pines or other conifers!

children.name: Sclerodermataceae
Scleroderma
children.description: Earthballs are round, potato-like fungi that grow on the ground in forests and woodlands. These tough-skinned mushrooms start out solid inside but develop dark, powdery spores as they mature, eventually cracking open to release their spores into the air.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true puffballs, earthballs have thick, leathery outer skins that crack in irregular patterns rather than having a neat opening at the top. Their spore mass is typically darker and more marbled than the white interior of young puffballs.
children.funFact: Many earthballs form partnerships with tree roots, trading nutrients in underground fungal networks that can extend for miles through the forest floor.

children.name: Calostoma
children.description: Calostoma is a unique genus of fungi that produces distinctive stalked fruiting bodies that look like colorful jellied treats on stems. These unusual fungi are commonly called stalked puffball-in-aspic because their spore-containing heads are surrounded by a gelatinous layer that resembles aspic jelly.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike typical puffballs that sit directly on the ground, Calostoma species are elevated on distinct stalks and have their spore mass encased in a jelly-like outer layer that eventually dissolves away.
children.funFact: The single New England species, stalked puffball-in-aspic, gets its bright red color from cinnabar-red pigments and was once thought to be so rare that finding one was considered a mycological treasure hunt prize.

children.description: The Sclerodermataceae are a family of fungi that produce tough, ball-shaped fruiting bodies that develop underground or at ground level. These fungi form partnerships with tree roots and play important roles in forest ecosystems. The family includes earthballs and the unusual stalked puffball genus Calostoma.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true puffballs, members of this family have very thick, leathery outer walls and their spores develop in a dark, firm mass inside rather than as fluffy powder.
children.funFact: Some Calostoma species are called 'prettymouth' fungi because they have bright red or orange openings at the top that look like colorful lips when the spores are ready to be released.

children.name: Gyroporaceae
Gyroporus
children.description: Gyroporus is a genus of boletes - mushrooms with pores instead of gills under their caps. These fungi form beneficial partnerships with tree roots and are known for their distinctive hollow stems that develop as they mature. Most species in this group are edible and can be found growing in forests throughout New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most other boletes, Gyroporus mushrooms develop characteristic hollow or chambered stems as they age. Many species also bruise blue when cut or damaged, which is a helpful identification feature.
children.funFact: The Cornflower Bolete gets its name from the brilliant blue color it turns when bruised or cut, creating a striking contrast with its typically brown cap and pale stem.

children.description: The Gyroporaceae are a family of mushrooms that produce spores in tubes rather than on gills, similar to boletes. These fungi form partnerships with tree roots, helping forests thrive while creating the familiar umbrella-shaped mushrooms we see above ground. Most members of this family are found in woodlands where they play important roles as decomposers and mycorrhizal partners.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true boletes, Gyroporaceae mushrooms have a unique spore-bearing surface that can be easily separated from the cap, and their flesh often turns blue when cut or bruised.
children.funFact: Some Gyroporus mushrooms have hollow stems that make them surprisingly light for their size, earning them the nickname 'hollow-stem boletes.'

children.name: Rhizopogonaceae
Rhizopogon
children.description: Bearded truffles are underground fungi that form round to oval fruiting bodies beneath the soil surface, typically found near coniferous trees. Unlike true truffles, these fungi have a distinctive fibrous or 'bearded' appearance on their outer surface and form important partnerships with tree roots.
children.distinguishingFeatures: They can be distinguished from true truffles by their fibrous, often hairy outer coating and their spore-bearing tissue that remains soft and gel-like rather than becoming powdery when mature.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'false truffles,' bearded truffles are actually more closely related to common mushrooms than they are to the expensive culinary truffles found in European cuisine.

children.description: The Rhizopogonaceae family consists of underground fungi that form truffle-like fruiting bodies instead of typical mushrooms with caps and stems. These fungi live in close partnership with tree roots, especially conifers like pines and firs, helping trees absorb nutrients while receiving sugars in return. They're commonly called false truffles because they grow beneath the soil surface like true truffles but belong to a different fungal group.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true mushrooms that release spores into the air, these fungi keep their spores enclosed within their underground fruiting bodies. They depend on small mammals like squirrels and chipmunks to dig them up and spread their spores through their droppings.
children.funFact: Some species in this family can actually help forest trees survive in poor soils by dramatically increasing the tree's ability to absorb water and nutrients - a single teaspoon of forest soil can contain miles of these fungal threads!

children.name: Tapinellaceae
Tapinella
children.description: Tapinella is a small genus of bracket-like fungi that grow on decaying wood, particularly conifers. These mushrooms have a distinctive rolled or inrolled margin when young, giving them their common name 'rollrim' fungi. They typically have a velvety or fuzzy texture and brown coloration.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other bracket fungi, Tapinella species have gills or gill-like structures on the underside rather than pores. Their margins characteristically roll inward when young, and they often have a notably soft, velvety texture on their caps and stems.
children.funFact: The Velvet-footed Tap gets its name from its distinctively dark, velvety stem base that feels like soft fabric to the touch.

children.name: Pseudomerulius
children.description: Pseudomerulius is a small genus of wood-decay fungi that forms thin, spreading fruiting bodies on dead hardwood logs and branches. These fungi have a distinctive appearance with their wrinkled, brain-like or coral-like surface texture that can range from golden yellow to orange-brown colors. They play an important ecological role as decomposers, breaking down dead wood in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true coral fungi or bracket fungi, Pseudomerulius species form thin, crust-like fruiting bodies that are tightly attached to the wood surface with characteristic wrinkled or ridged patterns. Their soft, gelatinous texture when fresh also sets them apart from similar-looking wood-decay fungi.
children.funFact: Despite their small size and inconspicuous nature, Pseudomerulius fungi are incredibly efficient decomposers that can completely break down fallen branches within a few years, recycling nutrients back into the forest soil.

children.description: Tapinellaceae is a small family of fungi that includes some distinctive mushrooms with unique cap and stem structures. These fungi are saprophytic, meaning they get their nutrients by decomposing dead organic matter like fallen logs and leaf litter in forest environments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their often funnel-shaped or irregularly shaped caps that may have a wrinkled or folded appearance, and they typically have decurrent gills that run down the stem.
children.funFact: The most well-known member of this family, Tapinella atrotomentosa (velvet-footed pax), was once classified with the boletes before DNA analysis revealed its true evolutionary relationships.

children.name: Gomphidiaceae
Gomphidius
children.description: Spikes are a small group of distinctive mushrooms with tall, cone-shaped caps and thick, waxy gills that run partway down the stem. These fungi form partnerships with conifer trees, particularly spruces and larches, helping the trees absorb nutrients from the soil. All three New England species have characteristically slimy or sticky caps when wet.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most mushrooms, Spikes have thick, waxy gills that are widely spaced and often appear to melt or run down the stem. Their caps are distinctly cone or spike-shaped, giving them their common name.
children.funFact: Spike mushrooms turn black when bruised or dried, and their spores are so dark that they can leave black prints on the gills of nearby white mushrooms growing in the same area.

children.name: Chroogomphus
children.description: Chroogomphus is a small genus of mushrooms known for their distinctive cone or spike-like appearance when young. These fungi form beneficial partnerships with pine trees, growing from the forest floor near their roots and helping the trees absorb nutrients from the soil.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other mushrooms, Chroogomphus species have a characteristic pointed, cone-shaped cap when young that gives them their common name of 'pine spikes.' They also have a unique olive-brown to blackish spore print that helps distinguish them from similar-looking fungi.
children.funFact: The name Chroogomphus comes from Greek words meaning 'colored peg,' referring to their distinctive pointed shape and often colorful appearance ranging from orange to reddish-brown.

children.description: The Gomphidiaceae is a small family of mushrooms that includes two main groups found in New England: the spikes (Gomphidius) and Chroogomphus species. These mushrooms are characterized by their thick, waxy gills that often appear to run down the stem, and they typically have dark, smoky spores. They form special partnerships with tree roots, helping forests stay healthy while getting nutrients in return.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most other mushroom families, Gomphidiaceae members have distinctively thick, waxy gills and produce very dark, almost black spores. Their gills also tend to be more widely spaced than typical mushrooms and often extend down the stem.
children.funFact: These mushrooms are often found growing near or even parasitizing boletes (mushrooms with pores instead of gills), creating an unusual three-way relationship between the Gomphidiaceae mushroom, the bolete, and tree roots.

children.name: Hygrophoropsidaceae
Hygrophoropsis
children.description: Hygrophoropsis is a small genus of mushrooms that are famous mimics in the fungal world. These fungi produce orange to yellowish-brown caps with gill-like structures underneath, giving them the appearance of the prized edible chanterelles that many foragers seek.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true chanterelles which have forked ridges, Hygrophoropsis species have true gills that are thin, closely spaced, and often fork near the stem. Their gills are also typically more orange in color and their flesh is softer than true chanterelles.
children.funFact: The False Chanterelle was once thought to be mildly toxic, but recent research suggests it's actually edible, though much less flavorful than its prized look-alike.

children.name: Leucogyrophana
children.description: Leucogyrophana is a small genus of wood-decay fungi that specialize in breaking down dead wood in forest environments. These fungi produce thin, crust-like fruiting bodies that grow directly on the surface of rotting logs and branches. They play an important role in forest ecosystems by recycling nutrients from fallen trees back into the soil.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their pale-colored, smooth to slightly wrinkled fruiting bodies that form thin crusts on wood surfaces. They can be distinguished from similar wood-decay fungi by their specific microscopic features and their preference for certain types of decaying hardwoods.
children.funFact: Despite being nearly invisible to casual observers, Leucogyrophana fungi are incredibly efficient decomposers that can break down some of the toughest components of wood, including lignin, which gives trees their structural strength.

children.description: The Hygrophoropsidaceae are a small family of fungi that includes both mushroom-forming species and wood-decay fungi with different growth forms. Despite their varied appearances, they share similar cellular structures and genetic characteristics that group them together. This family represents an interesting example of how closely related fungi can evolve very different lifestyles and forms.
children.distinguishingFeatures: This family is unique in containing both gilled mushrooms (like the false chanterelle) and crust-like fungi that grow flat against wood surfaces. The diverse growth forms within a single family make it unusual among fungal groups.
children.funFact: The most famous member of this family is the false chanterelle (Hygrophoropsis aurantiaca), which gets its name because it mimics the appearance of true chanterelles but has true gills instead of the fork-like ridges found on real chanterelles.

children.name: Diplocystidaceae
Astraeus
children.description: Barometer Earthstars are fascinating fungi that look like wooden flowers or stars when they open up. These mushrooms have a unique two-layer structure with an outer layer that splits into pointed rays, revealing a round spore sac in the center that releases dusty spores when disturbed.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other earthstars, Barometer Earthstars are highly sensitive to moisture and will dramatically open and close their rays based on humidity levels, acting like natural weather predictors.
children.funFact: These fungi earned their "barometer" name because their rays curl inward when dry weather approaches and spread wide open when rain is coming, making them living weather stations you can find in the forest!

children.description: Diplocystidaceae is a family of unique fungi that includes the fascinating barometer earthstars. These mushrooms have a distinctive star-like appearance when mature, with outer layers that split open to reveal a central spore-containing structure. They're called 'barometer' earthstars because their outer rays open and close in response to humidity changes in the air.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other earthstar fungi, members of this family have a double-layered outer wall (peridium) that creates their characteristic star-shaped opening pattern. The outer layer splits into pointed rays that curl back dramatically when conditions are right.
children.funFact: Barometer earthstars act like natural weather instruments - their rays close up tight during dry conditions and spread wide open when humidity is high, helping to protect their spores until conditions are perfect for dispersal.

children.name: Paxillaceae
Paxillus
children.description: Rollrims are distinctive mushrooms named for their characteristic rolled-under cap edges that create a distinctive rim around the mushroom. These brown to copper-colored fungi are typically found growing on the ground in deciduous and mixed forests, often forming partnerships with tree roots.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The strongly inrolled cap margins that persist even in mature specimens make rollrims easy to identify, along with their brown spore print and gills that run down the stem slightly.
children.funFact: The Brown Roll-Rim was once considered edible and commonly eaten in Europe, but is now known to contain toxins that can cause serious immune reactions, especially with repeated consumption.

children.name: Hydnomerulius
children.description: Hydnomerulius is a small genus of wood-decay fungi that creates distinctive crusty growths on dead coniferous wood. These fungi are characterized by their unique surface texture that combines smooth areas with tiny tooth-like projections, earning them the common name 'toothcrust.'
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike typical bracket fungi, Hydnomerulius species form thin, crusty patches that lie flat against the wood surface rather than projecting outward. Their spore-bearing surface has a distinctive combination of smooth areas and small teeth or spines.
children.funFact: The genus name Hydnomerulius combines 'Hydnum' (referring to tooth fungi) and 'Merulius' (a crust fungus genus), perfectly describing these fungi that bridge the gap between toothed and crusty fungal forms.

children.description: The Paxillaceae family includes mushrooms with distinctive gills that can be easily separated from the cap, often appearing to roll or peel away from the edges. These fungi are typically found growing on wood or in soil, and they play important roles as decomposers in forest ecosystems. Most members of this family have brownish or yellowish caps and produce brown spore prints.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most gilled mushrooms, Paxillaceae members have gills that separate easily from the cap and often fork or branch. The gills typically extend down the stem and have a distinctive rolled or inrolled cap margin that gives rollrims their common name.
children.funFact: Some rollrim mushrooms were once considered edible, but scientists discovered they contain toxins that can cause serious health problems, leading to their reclassification as poisonous fungi.

children.name: Coniophoraceae
Coniophora
children.description: Coniophora is a genus of wood-decay fungi that specialize in breaking down the cellulose in wood while leaving behind the lignin, creating what's known as brown rot. These fungi are commonly found growing on dead or dying wood in forests, and some species can also cause damage to wooden structures in buildings. They typically form thin, web-like fungal mats or small, inconspicuous fruiting bodies.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Coniophora fungi are distinguished by their ability to cause brown rot rather than white rot, leaving wood with a characteristic brown, crumbly texture. Their spores are typically smooth and brown, and they often produce olive-brown to dark brown fruiting surfaces.
children.funFact: The wet rot fungus (Coniophora puteana) gets its name because it requires much higher moisture levels than dry rot fungi, and can actually help indicate water damage problems in buildings before they become visible to the naked eye.

children.name: Penttilamyces
children.description: Penttilamyces is a genus of microscopic fungi that live as parasites or decomposers in forest environments. These tiny organisms are part of the complex web of microorganisms that help break down organic matter in woodland soils.
children.distinguishingFeatures: This genus is distinguished by its specific cellular structures and genetic characteristics that set it apart from other microscopic fungi, though detailed identification typically requires laboratory analysis.
children.funFact: Despite being invisible to the naked eye, these microscopic fungi play a crucial role in nutrient cycling, helping to return essential elements from dead organic matter back to the forest ecosystem.

children.description: The Coniophoraceae are a family of wood-decay fungi that specialize in breaking down dead wood in forest environments. These fungi produce brownish, crust-like fruiting bodies that grow directly on rotting logs, stumps, and other woody debris. They play a crucial role in forest ecosystems by decomposing cellulose and helping recycle nutrients back into the soil.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their brown rot decay pattern, which breaks down cellulose while leaving behind brown, crumbly wood residue. Their fruiting bodies are typically thin, crusty, and brownish in color, often with a smooth or slightly wrinkled surface.
children.funFact: Some Coniophora species are known as 'wet rot' fungi and can cause significant damage to wooden structures in buildings, particularly in areas with high moisture levels.

children.name: Pisolithaceae
Pisolithus
children.description: Pisolithus is a genus of distinctive earthball fungi that form large, round to irregularly shaped fruiting bodies that emerge from the soil. These fungi are important mycorrhizal partners with trees, forming beneficial relationships with roots to help both the fungus and tree exchange nutrients. They're commonly found in sandy soils and disturbed areas throughout New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other earthball fungi, Pisolithus species have a unique internal structure with numerous small chambers (peridioles) packed with spores, giving the inside a compartmentalized appearance when cut open. Their fruiting bodies also tend to be larger and more irregularly shaped than typical puffballs.
children.funFact: These fungi earned the common name 'dyeball' because their dark spore mass was historically used to create natural dyes for coloring fabrics and other materials.

children.description: Pisolithaceae is a family of earthball fungi that produce distinctive round, ball-like fruiting bodies instead of typical mushrooms with caps and stems. These fungi form important partnerships with tree roots, helping trees absorb nutrients from the soil in exchange for sugars. They're commonly found in forests and are especially associated with pine and oak trees.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other puffball-like fungi, members of Pisolithaceae have a thick, leathery outer skin and their interior breaks down into a powdery mass of spores that is often dark colored. Their fruiting bodies tend to be larger and more robust than typical puffballs.
children.funFact: Some Pisolithus species are known as 'dead man's foot' because of their dark, irregular appearance when mature, and they're so hardy they can even grow in disturbed soils like roadsides and mining sites.

children.name: Boletinellaceae
Boletinellus
children.description: Boletinellus is a small genus of mushrooms that forms special partnerships with tree roots, helping forests thrive through nutrient exchange. These fungi are easily recognized by their unique cap structure that looks wrinkled and brain-like, quite different from typical mushroom caps. In New England, this genus is represented by just one species that specifically grows near ash trees.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike typical mushrooms with smooth caps, Boletinellus species have distinctively wrinkled, convoluted caps that resemble coral or brain tissue. They also have a decurrent growth pattern where the pore surface extends down the stem.
children.funFact: The ash-tree bolete has such a strong relationship with ash trees that finding this mushroom can actually help you identify ash trees in the forest, as it rarely grows more than a few feet away from ash roots.

children.description: Boletinellaceae is a small family of fungi that includes mushrooms with a unique combination of features from different fungal groups. These fungi have caps and stems like typical mushrooms, but their spore-bearing surface has shallow pores rather than gills, and they form important partnerships with tree roots.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their porous undersides that are much shallower than typical bolete mushrooms, often appearing almost gill-like, and their tendency to have somewhat decurrent pores that run down the stem.
children.funFact: The single New England species in this family, Boletinellus merulioides, is commonly called the 'ash-tree bolete' because it forms a special relationship exclusively with ash trees and is often found growing right from the tree's roots.

children.name: Serpulaceae
Serpula
children.description: Serpula is a genus of marine tube-building worms that create hard, white calcareous tubes attached to rocks, shells, and other underwater surfaces. These segmented worms live permanently inside their self-built tubes, extending feathery feeding tentacles called radioles to filter plankton and organic particles from the water. They are commonly found in shallow coastal waters throughout the North Atlantic.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Serpula worms can be distinguished from other tube worms by their distinctive funnel-shaped operculum (a lid-like structure) that they use to seal their tube opening when threatened. Their tubes are typically smooth, white, and irregularly coiled or twisted.
children.funFact: When disturbed, Serpula worms can snap their colorful feeding tentacles back into their tubes and slam their operculum shut faster than the blink of an eye, creating a perfect seal against predators and harsh conditions.

children.description: Serpulaceae is a family of marine worms that build hard, white, tube-like shells made of calcium carbonate on rocks, shells, and other underwater surfaces. These worms live permanently inside their self-constructed tubes, extending colorful, feathery feeding structures called radioles to filter tiny food particles from the water.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other tube-building marine worms, serpulids create tubes made of calcium carbonate (limestone) rather than softer materials, and they have a specialized plug called an operculum that can seal their tube opening for protection.
children.funFact: When disturbed, these worms can snap back into their tubes faster than the blink of an eye, creating a distinctive popping sound underwater.

children.description: The Boletales are a diverse order of fungi that includes the classic mushrooms with pores instead of gills under their caps, like the familiar boletes, as well as some unusual forms like puffballs and bracket fungi. Most members of this group form beneficial partnerships with tree roots, helping forests thrive by exchanging nutrients with their plant partners. This order represents one of the most ecologically important groups of fungi in New England's woodlands.
children.distinguishingFeatures: While many Boletales have the characteristic pore surface instead of gills, the group is actually defined by genetic relationships rather than appearance alone. This means some members look quite different from the typical bolete mushroom, including species that form crusts on wood or grow as puffballs.
children.funFact: Some boletes can instantly turn bright blue when cut or bruised due to chemical reactions with oxygen, creating a dramatic color change that can startle first-time mushroom hunters but is completely harmless.

children.name: Polyporales
Polyporaceae
Trametes
children.description: Trametes is a genus of bracket fungi that forms tough, leathery shelf-like structures on dead and dying trees throughout New England's forests. These fungi are decomposers that play a crucial role in breaking down wood, with most species displaying distinctive pore surfaces underneath their colorful caps rather than gills.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other bracket fungi, Trametes species typically have thin, flexible fruiting bodies with small, round pores on the underside that may become maze-like or gill-like in some species. They're also distinguished by their often vibrant colors and banded patterns on the upper surface.
children.funFact: The famous turkey-tail fungus (Trametes versicolor) gets its name from its concentric bands of brown, tan, and gray that resemble the fanned tail feathers of a wild turkey, and it's one of the most common fungi you'll encounter on dead hardwood logs in New England.

children.name: Ganoderma
children.description: Ganoderma fungi are distinctive bracket or shelf fungi that grow on trees and fallen logs throughout New England's forests. These woody, polypore mushrooms are known for their shiny, lacquered appearance and their role as decomposers that break down dead and dying wood. Many species in this group have been prized for centuries in traditional medicine, particularly the reishi mushrooms.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Ganoderma species are easily recognized by their glossy, varnish-like surface that often appears reddish-brown to mahogany colored. Unlike other bracket fungi, they have a distinctive shiny coating that makes them look almost artificial or painted.
children.funFact: The artist's bracket earned its name because its white underside can be drawn on with a fingernail or stick, creating permanent brown lines that make it a natural canvas for woodland artwork.

children.name: Polyporus
children.description: Polyporus is a genus of bracket fungi that grow on dead or dying hardwood trees throughout New England's forests. These mushrooms have a distinctive shelf-like or bracket appearance with tiny pores on their undersides instead of gills, and they play an important role as decomposers in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other bracket fungi, Polyporus species typically have a central or off-center stem connecting the cap to the wood, rather than growing directly from the tree trunk. Their pore surface is usually white to cream-colored and the pores are relatively large and easily visible.
children.funFact: The umbrella polypore can form massive clusters weighing over 40 pounds, earning it the nickname 'hen of the woods' in some regions, though it's not the same species commonly sold in grocery stores under that name.

children.name: Cerioporus
children.description: Cerioporus is a genus of bracket fungi that form shelf-like structures on dead or dying hardwood trees. These polypore fungi have distinctive pore surfaces underneath instead of gills, and they play important roles as decomposers in forest ecosystems. Members of this genus are typically found growing on deciduous trees like elm, maple, and beech.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Cerioporus species are characterized by their large, overlapping bracket-like fruiting bodies and relatively large, angular pores on the underside. Unlike some other polypores, they tend to have softer, more flexible flesh when fresh and often display distinctive patterns or coloration on their upper surfaces.
children.funFact: The Dryad's Saddle gets its common name from folklore - it was said to be large and sturdy enough for woodland fairies (dryads) to use as a seat!

children.name: Fomes
children.description: Fomes is a genus of bracket fungi that form hard, woody shelf-like structures on trees. These fungi are saprophytes that decompose dead wood, playing an important role in forest ecosystems by recycling nutrients back into the soil. All species in this genus produce tough, perennial fruiting bodies that can persist for many years.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Fomes fungi are distinguished by their extremely hard, hoof-shaped brackets with thick walls and small pores on the underside. Unlike many other bracket fungi, Fomes species have fruiting bodies that are notably dense and woody, often requiring significant force to break.
children.funFact: The Hoof Fungus (Fomes fomentarius) has been used by humans for thousands of years as tinder for starting fires, and was even found in the equipment of Ötzi the Iceman, a 5,300-year-old mummy discovered in the Alps.

children.name: Neofavolus
children.description: Neofavolus is a genus of bracket fungi that grow on dead hardwood trees, forming shelf-like structures on trunks and branches. These polypore fungi are characterized by their distinctive pore surfaces underneath their caps, which release spores for reproduction. All three New England species play important roles as decomposers, breaking down dead wood in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their relatively large, angular to hexagonal pores on the underside of their fruiting bodies, which are typically larger and more geometric than the round pores found in many other polypore fungi.
children.funFact: The hexagonal-pored polypore gets its name from its remarkably geometric pore structure that can resemble a natural honeycomb pattern when viewed up close.

children.name: Lentinus
children.description: Woodcaps and Sawgills are tough, leathery mushrooms that specialize in breaking down dead hardwood trees and branches. These fungi are easily recognized by their distinctive gills that often have serrated or toothed edges, giving them their 'sawgill' nickname. They're important decomposers in forest ecosystems, helping recycle nutrients from fallen wood.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most gilled mushrooms, Lentinus species have tough, leathery textures and can survive freezing temperatures. Their gills typically have jagged, serrated edges rather than smooth surfaces, and they often grow directly from dead wood without visible stems.
children.funFact: The Winter Polypore can actually continue growing during mild winter days, making it one of the few mushrooms you might find fruiting in New England's snowy forests.

children.name: Picipes
children.description: Picipes is a genus of bracket fungi that form shelf-like structures on dead and decaying wood. These polypore fungi are important decomposers in forest ecosystems, breaking down lignin and cellulose in fallen logs and dead trees. They typically have tough, leathery fruiting bodies with small pores on the underside instead of gills.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Picipes are distinguished from other polypores by their specific pore structure and the microscopic characteristics of their spores. They tend to have relatively large, angular pores and often display brownish coloration.
children.funFact: The Bay Polypore gets its name from its rich reddish-brown color that resembles a bay horse, and it can persist on dead wood for several years while continuing to release spores.

children.name: Daedaleopsis
children.description: Daedaleopsis is a genus of bracket fungi that grows on dead hardwood trees, particularly willows and birches. These fungi are distinctive for their maze-like pore structure on the underside, which gives them their common name reference to mazes. They play an important role in forest ecosystems by decomposing dead wood.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The key feature that sets Daedaleopsis apart is their unique pore structure that forms intricate, maze-like patterns rather than simple round holes like most other bracket fungi. Their pores are also quite large and elongated, creating distinctive labyrinthine channels.
children.funFact: The genus name Daedaleopsis literally means 'resembling Daedalus' - a reference to the craftsman from Greek mythology who built the famous labyrinth, perfectly describing these fungi's maze-like undersides.

children.name: Coriolopsis
children.description: Coriolopsis is a small genus of bracket fungi that form tough, leathery shelf-like structures on dead hardwood trees. These fungi are wood decomposers that help break down fallen logs and dead branches in the forest, playing an important role in nutrient cycling.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus have relatively thin, flexible brackets with a smooth to slightly bumpy cap surface and tiny pores underneath. They can be distinguished from similar bracket fungi by their brownish flesh that often shows distinct color zones when cut.
children.funFact: Despite their tough, leathery appearance, Coriolopsis brackets can persist on dead wood for several years, slowly working to decompose their host tree from the outside in.

children.name: Cryptoporus
children.description: Cryptoporus is a small genus of polypore fungi that creates distinctive bracket-like fruiting bodies on coniferous trees. These fungi are wood decomposers that help break down dead and dying wood in forest ecosystems. They are characterized by their unique veil-like covering that partially encloses their pore surface.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most other polypore fungi, Cryptoporus species have a partial veil that covers the pore-bearing surface, creating a distinctive enclosed chamber. This veil gives them their common name 'veiled polypores' and makes them easily recognizable among bracket fungi.
children.funFact: The veiled chamber created by Cryptoporus serves as protection for beetles and other small insects that help disperse the fungus's spores, creating a mutually beneficial relationship.

children.name: Datroniella
children.description: Datroniella is a small genus of bracket fungi that forms tough, shelf-like structures on dead hardwood trees. These fungi are wood decomposers that help break down fallen logs and dead branches in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Datroniella fungi are distinguished by their thick, corky texture and distinctive pore structure on the underside, which is different from the more common polypore fungi.
children.funFact: The single New England species, Datroniella scutellata, was only recently recognized as distinct from other bracket fungi and represents one of the lesser-known members of our forest fungal community.

children.name: Hexagonia
children.description: Hexagonia is a genus of bracket fungi that forms distinctive shelf-like structures on dead and dying hardwood trees. These polypore fungi are wood decomposers that help break down fallen logs and standing dead trees in forest ecosystems. They are characterized by their tough, leathery texture and pore surface underneath instead of gills.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Hexagonia fungi are easily recognized by their large, angular pores on the underside that give them their name, as these pores are noticeably larger and more geometric than those of most other bracket fungi.
children.funFact: The name 'Hexagonia' refers to the six-sided, honeycomb-like appearance of the large pores on the underside of these fungi, though the pores aren't always perfectly hexagonal in shape.

children.name: Datronia
children.description: Datronia is a small genus of bracket fungi that grow on dead hardwood trees, forming shelf-like structures on bark. These fungi are wood decomposers that help break down fallen logs and dead branches in forest ecosystems. They produce distinctive pore surfaces underneath their bracket-shaped fruiting bodies.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Datronia fungi are recognized by their unique maze-like pore pattern on the underside of their brackets, which gives them their common name 'mazegills.' Unlike many other bracket fungi with simple round pores, Datronia species have elongated, winding pores that create an intricate labyrinth pattern.
children.funFact: The maze-like pore structure of Datronia fungi can contain over 1,000 individual chambers per square inch, creating an incredibly efficient system for releasing millions of microscopic spores into the forest air.

children.name: Perenniporia
children.description: Perenniporia is a genus of wood-decay fungi that produce tough, bracket-like fruiting bodies on dead or dying hardwood trees. These fungi are important decomposers in forest ecosystems, breaking down woody material and recycling nutrients back into the soil. They form perennial structures that can persist for several years, growing larger each season.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Perenniporia fungi are distinguished by their thick, woody bracket fruiting bodies with multiple layers of pore tubes that build up year after year. Unlike annual polypore fungi, their fruiting bodies are long-lasting and add new pore layers each growing season.
children.funFact: The name Perenniporia literally means 'perennial pores,' referring to how these fungi add new layers of pore-bearing tissue each year, creating a multi-story structure that can be read like tree rings to determine the fungus's age.

children.description: Bracket fungi are tough, shelf-like mushrooms that grow horizontally from tree trunks, stumps, and logs like natural shelves or brackets. These persistent fungi are nature's recyclers, slowly breaking down dead and dying wood with their powerful enzymes. Most have tiny pores on their undersides instead of gills, releasing millions of spores into the air.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike soft, fleshy mushrooms that appear and disappear quickly, bracket fungi are typically hard, woody, and can persist for months or even years. Their distinctive shelf-like growth pattern and pore-covered undersides make them easy to recognize.
children.funFact: Turkey tail fungi, one of the most common bracket fungi, got their name because their colorful, banded caps look remarkably like the fanned tail feathers of wild turkeys.

children.name: Fomitopsidaceae
Fomitopsis
children.description: Fomitopsis is a genus of woody bracket fungi that grow as shelf-like structures on trees and dead wood throughout New England's forests. These tough, perennial fungi are important decomposers that break down cellulose and lignin in wood, playing a crucial role in forest ecosystems. Most species in this group form hard, woody conks that can persist for many years on their host trees.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Fomitopsis fungi are distinguished by their typically whitish to cream-colored pore surfaces and their ability to cause a brown rot in wood, breaking down cellulose while leaving behind the brown lignin. Many species also develop distinctive color bands or zones on their upper surfaces as they age.
children.funFact: The birch polypore (Fomitopsis betulina) was found in the gear of Ötzi the Iceman, a 5,300-year-old mummy, suggesting ancient peoples used this fungus for medicinal purposes or as tinder for starting fires.

children.name: Antrodia
children.description: Antrodia is a genus of wood-decay fungi that forms bracket-like fruiting bodies on dead hardwood trees. These fungi are important decomposers in forest ecosystems, breaking down cellulose and lignin in fallen logs and dead standing trees. They typically produce white, shelf-like structures that grow horizontally from tree trunks.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Antrodia fungi create distinctive white rot in wood and have pore surfaces (rather than gills) on the underside of their bracket fruiting bodies. Their fruiting bodies are typically annual, meaning they form fresh each year rather than persisting for multiple seasons.
children.funFact: Antrodia fungi are so efficient at decomposing wood that they can completely break down a fallen log over several years, returning all its nutrients back to the forest soil.

children.description: Bracket polypores are wood-decomposing fungi that form shelf-like or bracket-shaped fruiting bodies on dead or dying trees. These fungi are essential decomposers in forest ecosystems, breaking down the cellulose and lignin in wood through a process called brown rot, which leaves the wood crumbly and brown.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other bracket fungi that cause white rot, members of this family typically cause brown rot, leaving behind cube-shaped pieces of degraded wood. Their fruiting bodies are usually tough and woody, with pore surfaces rather than gills.
children.funFact: Some species in this family, like the red-belted polypore, can live for decades and add new growth layers each year, making them like the tree rings of the fungal world.

children.name: Meruliaceae
Phlebia
children.description: Phlebia is a genus of crust fungi that form thin, spreading patches on decaying wood. These fungi have distinctive wrinkled, folded, or bumpy surfaces rather than the smooth appearance of many other crust fungi. They play an important role in forest ecosystems by decomposing dead wood and recycling nutrients.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Phlebia fungi are recognized by their characteristically wrinkled, bumpy, or coral-like surface texture, which sets them apart from the smooth crusts of many related wood-decay fungi. Many species also display vibrant colors ranging from white and pink to bright orange-red.
children.funFact: Despite their crusty appearance, some Phlebia species like the Coral-pink Merulius develop such elaborate folds and wrinkles that they almost look like tiny coral reefs growing on rotting logs.

children.name: Merulius
children.description: Merulius is a genus of wood-decay fungi that forms thin, sheet-like fruiting bodies with distinctively wrinkled or folded surfaces. These fungi typically grow on dead hardwood, spreading across bark and wood surfaces in irregular patches. They play an important role in forest ecosystems by breaking down fallen logs and branches.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Merulius fungi are recognized by their wrinkled, brain-like surface texture that distinguishes them from smooth crust fungi, and their thin, flexible fruiting bodies that can be peeled away from the wood substrate.
children.funFact: The Trembling Crust gets its name because its jelly-like texture causes it to quiver or tremble when touched, even though it's actually quite firmly attached to the wood it grows on.

children.name: Sarcodontia
children.description: Sarcodontia is a small genus of tooth fungi that forms crusty, bracket-like growths on dead hardwood trees. These fungi are characterized by their white to yellowish fruiting bodies that develop distinctive tooth-like or spine-like projections on their underside instead of gills or pores.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other tooth fungi, Sarcodontia species form flat, crusty brackets that are often irregular in shape and grow directly from the wood surface. Their teeth are typically short and densely packed, giving the underside a fuzzy appearance.
children.funFact: The Yellow Toothcrust gets its common name from its tendency to develop yellow staining as it ages, particularly around the margins of the fruiting body.

children.name: Mycoacia
children.description: Mycoacia is a small genus of crust fungi that form thin, flat growths on decaying wood. These fungi are characterized by their unique spore-bearing surface covered in tiny tooth-like projections called aculei, giving them a somewhat spiny texture when viewed up close.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike smooth crust fungi, Mycoacia species have distinctive small, sharp projections on their fertile surface that point downward, creating a texture similar to fine sandpaper.
children.funFact: The genus name 'Mycoacia' literally means 'fungal needle,' referring to the tiny spike-like structures that cover their spore-producing surface.

children.name: Climacodon
children.description: Climacodon is a genus of tooth fungi that produces distinctive shelf-like or bracket-shaped fruiting bodies on hardwood trees. These fungi are wood decomposers that help break down dead and dying trees in forest ecosystems. Instead of gills or pores, they have tooth-like projections on their undersides that release spores.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Climacodon fungi are distinguished by their large, overlapping bracket formations and prominent white tooth-like spines hanging from the underside. They typically grow in impressive tiered clusters that can span several feet across on tree trunks.
children.funFact: The Northern Tooth fungus can produce fruiting bodies that persist for multiple years, growing larger each season and sometimes reaching over 3 feet across on a single tree.

children.name: Hydnophlebia
children.description: Hydnophlebia is a genus of tooth fungi that produce their spores on tiny tooth-like projections rather than gills or pores. These fungi form thin, spreading crusts on decaying wood, creating patches that look almost like they're painted onto the surface.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other tooth fungi that form mushroom-like structures, Hydnophlebia species grow as flat, crust-like patches with very small teeth that are barely visible to the naked eye.
children.funFact: The spreading yellow tooth gets its golden color from bright yellow pigments that can actually stain your fingers if you handle fresh specimens!

children.name: Aurantiporus
children.description: Aurantiporus is a small genus of bracket fungi that grow as shelf-like structures on dead hardwood trees. These polypore fungi are wood decomposers that help break down fallen logs and dead branches in the forest, playing an important role in nutrient cycling.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their bright orange to yellow-orange coloration and soft, spongy texture when fresh. They have small, round pores on the underside rather than gills, and typically grow in overlapping clusters.
children.funFact: The name 'Aurantiporus' literally means 'orange pore,' perfectly describing the distinctive bright orange color that makes these fungi stand out against the brown bark of dead trees.

children.description: The Meruliaceae are a diverse family of wood-decay fungi that break down dead wood in forests throughout New England. These fungi produce spores on surfaces that can be smooth, wrinkled, toothed, or porous, and they play a crucial role in recycling nutrients back into forest ecosystems. Most species in this family form thin, crust-like fruiting bodies that spread across the surface of rotting logs and branches.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their variable spore-bearing surfaces and their ability to cause white rot in wood, breaking down both cellulose and lignin. Unlike many other wood-decay fungi, they often produce fruiting bodies that are resupinate (lying flat against the wood surface) rather than forming typical mushroom caps.
children.funFact: Some Meruliaceae fungi can actually change the structure of their spore-bearing surface as they mature, starting smooth and developing wrinkles, pores, or even tooth-like projections over time.

children.name: Irpicaceae
Ceriporia
children.description: Waxpores are small bracket fungi that grow on decaying hardwood trees, creating thin, shelf-like structures that feel waxy to the touch. These fungi are important decomposers in forest ecosystems, breaking down dead wood and returning nutrients to the soil. They typically have small, round pores on their undersides instead of gills, and often display beautiful colors ranging from white to purple.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Waxpores are distinguished from other bracket fungi by their distinctly waxy texture and relatively small size. Their pores are typically very small and round, and many species in this genus display purple or violet coloration.
children.funFact: The mauve waxpore gets its name from its striking purple coloration, which can fade to brown with age, making younger specimens much more vibrant and eye-catching.

children.name: Irpex
children.description: Irpex is a genus of wood-decomposing fungi that form bracket-like or crust-like fruiting bodies on dead hardwood trees and logs. These fungi are characterized by their unique spore-bearing surface that combines both pores and tooth-like projections, creating a distinctive textured appearance. They play an important role in forest ecosystems by breaking down dead wood and recycling nutrients back into the soil.
children.distinguishingFeatures: What sets Irpex apart from other bracket fungi is their hybrid spore-bearing surface that features both small pores and irregularly shaped teeth or ridges. This combination of pore and tooth structures is relatively uncommon among wood-decomposing fungi.
children.funFact: The name 'Irpex' comes from the Latin word for 'harrow,' referring to the tooth-like projections on their undersurface that resemble the spikes on an old-fashioned farming tool used to break up soil.

children.name: Gloeoporus
children.description: Gloeoporus is a small genus of bracket fungi that form shelf-like structures on dead or dying hardwood trees. These fungi are wood decomposers that help break down fallen logs and branches in New England's forests. They typically produce relatively thin, often overlapping brackets with distinctive pore surfaces underneath.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Gloeoporus fungi are characterized by their gelatinous or waxy texture when fresh and their distinctive pore surface that can change color with age or handling. Unlike many other bracket fungi, they tend to have a softer, more flexible consistency.
children.funFact: The name 'Gloeoporus' literally means 'glue pore,' referring to the sticky or gelatinous texture of these fungi when they're fresh and actively growing.

children.name: Trametopsis
children.description: Trametopsis is a small genus of bracket fungi that grows on dead hardwood trees, forming shelf-like structures on tree trunks and logs. These fungi are wood decomposers that help break down dead wood in forest ecosystems. They produce tough, leathery fruiting bodies that can persist for months or even years.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Trametopsis fungi are distinguished from similar bracket fungi by their distinctive pore surface that starts white but ages to brown or grayish colors, and their preference for hardwood substrates rather than conifers.
children.funFact: The single New England species, Deer-colored Trametes, gets its name from its brownish coloration that resembles the coat of a deer.

children.name: Meruliopsis
children.description: Meruliopsis is a small genus of crust fungi that forms thin, flat growths on dead wood. These fungi have a wrinkled or bumpy surface texture and play an important role in decomposing fallen logs and branches in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their distinctive wrinkled to tuberculate (bumpy) fertile surface and their ability to form resupinate (flat, crust-like) fruiting bodies on decaying wood.
children.funFact: The only New England species, Yew Crust, gets its name from its frequent association with decaying yew wood, though it can also grow on other coniferous substrates.

children.name: Byssomerulius
children.description: Byssomerulius is a small genus of fungi that forms thin, crust-like growths on decaying wood. These fungi are wood decomposers that help break down dead trees and fallen logs in forest ecosystems. They produce distinctive net-like or honeycomb patterns on their surface as they spread across their woody substrate.
children.distinguishingFeatures: What sets Byssomerulius apart from other crust fungi is its characteristic net-like or reticulated surface pattern, which looks like a natural honeycomb spread across the wood. This netted appearance is created by raised ridges that form irregular polygonal shapes across the fungal surface.
children.funFact: The name 'Byssomerulius' combines 'bysso' meaning fine threads (referring to its fibrous texture) and 'merulius' meaning blackbird, a reference shared with other wood-decay fungi in this family.
