children.description: The Irpicaceae family consists of wood-decomposing fungi that create bracket-like or crust-like fruiting bodies on dead trees and fallen logs. These fungi are important decomposers in forest ecosystems, breaking down cellulose and lignin in wood. Most species in this family have distinctive pore surfaces or tooth-like projections underneath their fruiting bodies instead of traditional gills.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their varied pore structures, which can range from round holes to angular or maze-like patterns, and some species have distinctive tooth-like or spine-like projections. Unlike many other bracket fungi families, Irpicaceae species often have softer, more flexible textures when fresh.
children.funFact: Some species in this family, like those in the genus Ceriporia, produce waxy or resinous substances that give them their common name 'waxpores' and help protect the fungus from drying out.

children.name: Phanerochaetaceae
Bjerkandera
children.description: Bjerkandera is a small genus of bracket fungi that grow as shelf-like structures on dead hardwood trees. These polypore fungi are decomposers that help break down fallen logs and dying trees, playing an important role in forest recycling. They typically have a smoky or grayish appearance and relatively thin, flexible brackets.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Bjerkandera species are recognized by their thin, flexible brackets with a distinctive smoky gray to brownish coloration and small, round pores on the underside. Unlike many other bracket fungi, they tend to have a softer, less woody texture when fresh.
children.funFact: The genus name Bjerkandera honors the Norwegian botanist Clovis Bjerkandera, and these fungi are sometimes called 'smoky brackets' because their grayish coloration resembles wisps of smoke against tree bark.

children.name: Phlebiopsis
children.description: Phlebiopsis is a genus of crust fungi that form thin, flat patches on dead wood, resembling paint or frosting spread across the surface. These fungi are important decomposers in forest ecosystems, breaking down cellulose and lignin in fallen logs and branches. They typically appear as white, cream, or pale yellow crusty growths that can cover large areas of decaying wood.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Phlebiopsis can be distinguished from other crust fungi by their smooth to slightly bumpy surface texture and their tendency to form extensive, continuous patches rather than individual fruiting bodies. They also have distinctive microscopic features including their spore shape and the structure of their hyphal system.
children.funFact: Phlebiopsis gigantea is used commercially as a biological control agent to prevent root rot in conifer plantations, applied to freshly cut stumps to outcompete harmful fungi that cause disease.

children.name: Phanerochaete
children.description: Phanerochaete is a genus of wood-decay fungi that specialize in breaking down the tough lignin in dead wood, playing a crucial role in forest recycling. These fungi typically form thin, crust-like growths that spread across the surface of decaying logs and branches. They're part of the white-rot fungi group, which can completely decompose wood into simple nutrients.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Phanerochaete fungi are distinguished by their smooth to slightly wrinkled, crust-like appearance that hugs tightly to wood surfaces. Unlike many other wood-decay fungi, they don't form shelf-like brackets or mushroom caps, instead creating thin, paint-like coatings.
children.funFact: These tiny decomposers are nature's master chemists - they produce powerful enzymes that can break down lignin, one of the toughest natural polymers on Earth, making them valuable for biotechnology research into breaking down plant materials.

children.name: Hapalopilus
children.description: Hapalopilus is a small genus of polypore fungi that grow as bracket-like shelves on dead hardwood trees. These fungi are wood decomposers that help break down fallen logs and dead branches in forest ecosystems. They produce soft, spongy fruiting bodies with tiny pores on the underside instead of gills.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Hapalopilus fungi are characterized by their distinctively soft, lightweight texture and orange to reddish-brown coloration. Unlike many other polypores that become hard and woody, these mushrooms remain tender and can be easily compressed by hand.
children.funFact: The tender nesting polypore gets its name because its soft, cushiony texture makes it so comfortable that small animals and insects often use it as a cozy resting spot or nesting material.

children.name: Donkia
children.description: Donkia is a small genus of freshwater diatoms, which are microscopic algae with beautiful glass-like cell walls made of silica. These single-celled organisms are found in clean, flowing waters like streams and springs. Like other diatoms, they play an important role in aquatic ecosystems as primary producers, converting sunlight into energy through photosynthesis.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Donkia species are distinguished by their distinctive valve structure and symmetrical patterns etched into their silica cell walls. They typically prefer oligotrophic (nutrient-poor) freshwater environments and are considered indicators of high water quality.
children.funFact: The intricate geometric patterns on Donkia's glass-like cell walls are so precise and beautiful that Victorian microscopists used diatoms like these to create decorative slides that were considered works of art.

children.name: Terana
children.description: Terana is a small genus of crust fungi that forms thin, flat patches on dead wood. These fungi create smooth, waxy-looking crusts that spread across the surface of decaying logs and branches in forest environments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Terana fungi are easily recognized by their distinctive bright blue coloration, which is quite rare among crust fungi that are typically white, brown, or orange.
children.funFact: The stunning cobalt blue color of Terana coerulea is so vivid and unusual in the fungal world that it's sometimes called the 'Cobalt Crust' and can appear almost artificially colored when found in the wild.

children.name: Porostereum
children.description: Porostereum is a small genus of bracket fungi that forms thin, leathery shelf-like structures on dead hardwood trees. These fungi are wood decomposers that help break down fallen logs and dead branches in forest ecosystems. They have a distinctive appearance with their flat, overlapping brackets that grow directly from the wood surface.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Porostereum brackets are characterized by their thin, flexible texture and smooth to slightly wrinkled surface that lacks the thick, woody consistency of many other bracket fungi. The underside has tiny pores rather than gills, and the brackets often have a brownish to grayish coloration.
children.funFact: Porostereum spadiceum is sometimes called the 'thin-maze flat polypore' because its pore surface can develop a maze-like pattern as it ages, creating an intricate geometric design on the underside of the bracket.

children.description: The Phanerochaetaceae family consists of wood-decomposing fungi that play a crucial role in breaking down dead trees and woody debris in New England's forests. These fungi typically form flat, crust-like or shelf-like fruiting bodies that grow directly on the surface of decaying wood. They are highly efficient decomposers, using powerful enzymes to break down tough wood fibers like lignin and cellulose.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their ability to cause white rot in wood, leaving behind pale, stringy, bleached-looking decay. Unlike brown rot fungi that leave wood crumbly and brown, Phanerochaetaceae species break down both the lignin and cellulose, creating a whitish, fibrous decay pattern.
children.funFact: Some species in this family, particularly in the genus Phanerochaete, are being studied by scientists for their potential to break down environmental pollutants and even help clean up oil spills due to their powerful lignin-degrading enzymes.

children.name: Postiaceae
Cyanosporus
children.description: Cyanosporus is a genus of bracket fungi that forms shelf-like fruiting bodies on dead or dying hardwood trees. These polypore fungi are wood decomposers that help break down fallen logs and weakened trees in forest ecosystems. All members of this genus have pores on their undersides instead of gills, and they play an important role as nature's recyclers.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Cyanosporus are characterized by their bluish to grayish coloration and relatively soft, fleshy texture when fresh. They can be distinguished from other polypores by their specific color patterns and their preference for hardwood hosts.
children.funFact: The Blue Cheese Polypore gets its name from its distinctive blue-gray coloration that can resemble the veining in blue cheese, though it's completely unrelated to the dairy product!

children.name: Ptychogaster
children.description: Ptychogaster is a genus of bracket fungi that represents the early, sterile stage of certain polypore mushrooms. These fungi appear as white, cotton-like growths on dead hardwood trees, earning them the common name 'powderpuff brackets' due to their fluffy, cloud-like appearance.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike mature bracket fungi with their woody, shelf-like fruiting bodies, Ptychogaster forms soft, white, powdery masses that lack the typical pore surface used for spore production.
children.funFact: Ptychogaster albus is actually the juvenile form of the artist's bracket fungus (Ganoderma applanatum) - it's the same organism at different life stages, like a caterpillar and butterfly!

children.name: Fuscopostia
children.description: Fuscopostia is a small genus of wood-decay fungi that forms bracket-like fruiting bodies on dead hardwood trees. These polypore fungi are saprophytes, meaning they play an important ecological role by breaking down dead wood and recycling nutrients back into the forest ecosystem. They get their common name from their tendency to cause brown staining in the wood they decompose.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Fuscopostia fungi are distinguished by their soft, fragile texture and their characteristic ability to cause brown rot in the wood they inhabit. Unlike many other polypores, their fruiting bodies are quite delicate and can easily crumble when handled.
children.funFact: The genus name Fuscopostia literally means 'dark brown post' in Latin, referring to both the brown staining these fungi cause in wood and their tendency to grow on dead tree trunks that resemble fence posts.

children.name: Osteina
children.description: Osteina is a small genus of fungi that includes just one species found in New England. These fungi are part of the larger group of cup fungi, which produce their spores in small, cup-shaped or disc-like structures. They typically grow on decaying organic matter in forest environments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Osteina fungi are distinguished by their pale, whitish to cream-colored fruiting bodies that have a distinctive texture and appearance when mature.
children.funFact: The name 'Osteina' comes from a Latin word meaning 'bony,' likely referring to the pale, bone-like color of these small fungi.

children.name: Spongiporus
children.description: Spongiporus is a genus of bracket fungi that creates shelf-like fruiting bodies on dead or dying trees. These fungi are wood decomposers that help break down dead wood in forest ecosystems. They have a spongy, porous underside where spores are released.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Spongiporus fungi are distinguished by their particularly soft, spongy texture and large, angular pores on the underside of their brackets. Unlike many other bracket fungi, they tend to have a more cushion-like appearance rather than hard, woody shelves.
children.funFact: The name 'Spongiporus' literally means 'spongy pores,' perfectly describing the soft, compressible texture of these fungi's spore-bearing surface.

children.name: Amaropostia
children.description: Amaropostia is a genus of bracket fungi that grow as shelf-like structures on dead and dying hardwood trees. These fungi are wood decomposers that help break down fallen logs and standing dead trees in forest ecosystems. They produce tough, leathery fruiting bodies that can persist for months or even years.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their bitter taste and white to cream-colored pore surface that bruises yellow when touched or damaged. The pores are typically small and round, and the bracket itself has a whitish to pale brown upper surface.
children.funFact: The name 'Amaropostia' literally means 'bitter post,' referring to both the characteristically bitter taste of these fungi and their preference for growing on wooden posts and dead tree trunks.

children.name: Postia
children.description: Postia is a genus of bracket fungi that forms shelf-like or bracket-shaped fruiting bodies on dead and decaying wood. These fungi are important decomposers in forest ecosystems, breaking down cellulose and lignin in fallen logs and dead trees. They typically produce white or pale-colored spores and create a brown rot in the wood they colonize.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Postia fungi are distinguished from other bracket fungi by their white to cream-colored pore surfaces and their ability to cause brown rot rather than white rot in wood. Their fruiting bodies are often thin and can be either perennial or annual depending on the species.
children.funFact: Despite being microscopic organisms for most of their lives, Postia fungi can dramatically weaken massive trees and logs, with some species capable of reducing wood strength by up to 80% before any visible decay becomes apparent to the human eye.

children.description: The Postiaceae are a family of wood-decaying fungi that specialize in breaking down the cellulose in dead wood, causing what's known as brown rot. These fungi typically produce bracket-like or shelf-like fruiting bodies that grow directly from the surfaces of logs, stumps, and dead trees. They play a crucial role in forest ecosystems by recycling nutrients from fallen timber back into the soil.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike white rot fungi that break down both cellulose and lignin, Postiaceae fungi leave behind the brown lignin while consuming the white cellulose, giving decayed wood a characteristic brown, crumbly texture. Their fruiting bodies are usually tough and woody, often with small pores on the underside instead of gills.
children.funFact: Some Postiaceae fungi can continue digesting wood for years after the visible fruiting body has disappeared, with the fungal network inside the wood slowly turning entire logs into rich, chocolate-brown humus.

children.name: Incrustoporiaceae
Skeletocutis
children.description: Skeletocutis is a genus of small, wood-decay fungi that form thin, bracket-like or crust-like growths on dead hardwood and coniferous trees. These fungi are decomposers that help break down fallen logs and dead wood in New England's forests. They typically have white to grayish colors and create tiny pores on their undersides to release spores.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Skeletocutis are distinguished by their extremely thin, often resupinate (lying flat against the wood) fruiting bodies and their very small, round pores that are barely visible to the naked eye. Unlike many bracket fungi, they rarely form thick, shelf-like projections.
children.funFact: Despite their small and inconspicuous appearance, Skeletocutis fungi are essential forest recyclers that can continue breaking down wood for years, slowly turning fallen trees back into soil nutrients.

children.name: Tyromyces
children.description: Tyromyces is a genus of white-rot fungi that produce bracket-like fruiting bodies on dead and dying hardwood trees. These fungi are important decomposers in forest ecosystems, breaking down lignin and cellulose in wood with their powerful enzymes. They typically form annual, shelf-like structures that are soft when fresh but become harder with age.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Tyromyces fungi are distinguished by their white to cream-colored pore surfaces and relatively soft, fleshy texture when young. Unlike many other bracket fungi, they tend to be annual rather than perennial, and their pores are typically small and round.
children.funFact: The name Tyromyces literally means 'cheese fungus' in Greek, referring to the soft, cheese-like texture of fresh specimens before they dry out and harden.

children.description: The Incrustoporiaceae family consists of wood-dwelling fungi that create thin, crust-like fruiting bodies on dead trees and fallen logs. These fungi are important decomposers in forest ecosystems, breaking down woody material and recycling nutrients back into the soil. They produce their spores in tiny pores on the underside of their bracket-like or crusty growths.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their white-rot decay pattern and their thin, often resupinate (lying flat against the substrate) fruiting bodies with small, round pores. Unlike many other bracket fungi, they typically don't form large, shelf-like structures but instead create relatively inconspicuous, flat growths.
children.funFact: Some species in this family can actually help trees by forming beneficial relationships with their roots, trading nutrients for sugars while simultaneously decomposing dead wood nearby.

children.name: Steccherinaceae
Steccherinum
children.description: Steccherinum is a genus of tooth fungi that create distinctive spreading, crust-like fruiting bodies on decaying wood. These fungi are characterized by their tooth-like or spine-like projections on the underside, which give them a fuzzy or bristly appearance when viewed up close.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other tooth fungi that form bracket-like structures, Steccherinum species grow as thin, spreading crusts that conform closely to the wood surface. Their teeth are typically shorter and more densely packed than those of related genera.
children.funFact: Despite their small size and inconspicuous appearance, Steccherinum fungi play a crucial role in forest ecosystems by breaking down the cellulose in dead wood, helping to recycle nutrients back into the soil.

children.name: Etheirodon
children.description: Etheirodon is a genus of moss that belongs to the family Hypnaceae, known for their delicate, feathery appearance. These mosses typically form loose, irregularly branched mats on various surfaces in moist environments. They are small but important components of forest ecosystems, helping to retain moisture and provide habitat for tiny organisms.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Etheirodon mosses are distinguished by their irregularly pinnate (feather-like) branching pattern and their distinctive leaf arrangement that gives them a somewhat disheveled or loose appearance compared to more regularly branched moss relatives.
children.funFact: The name 'Etheirodon' comes from Greek words meaning 'sieve tooth,' referring to the distinctive structure of their spore-bearing capsules that has tooth-like projections resembling a fine mesh.

children.name: Antrodiella
children.description: Antrodiella is a genus of bracket fungi that form shelf-like growths on decaying wood. These fungi are wood decomposers that help break down dead trees and logs in forest ecosystems. They produce spores through tiny pores on their undersurface rather than gills.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Antrodiella fungi are distinguished by their annual bracket growth habit and their particular pore structure and spore characteristics that separate them from other bracket fungi genera.
children.funFact: Despite being called bracket fungi, Antrodiella species sometimes grow in a partially upright or semi-resupinate position, meaning they can appear to be growing both horizontally from the wood surface and vertically up the trunk.

children.name: Loweomyces
children.description: Loweomyces is a small genus of wood-decaying fungi that forms thin, crust-like fruiting bodies on dead hardwood trees and branches. These fungi are saprobic decomposers, meaning they break down dead organic matter and play an important role in forest nutrient cycling. They produce small, white to cream-colored spores and have a distinctive microscopic structure.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Loweomyces fungi are distinguished by their smooth to slightly wrinkled surface texture and their specific spore characteristics when viewed under a microscope. Unlike many other crust fungi, they have a unique combination of thin-walled spores and specialized microscopic structures called cystidia.
children.funFact: The genus Loweomyces was named in honor of American mycologist Josiah Lincoln Lowe, who made significant contributions to our understanding of wood-decaying fungi in the early 20th century.

children.name: Mycorrhaphium
children.description: Mycorrhaphium is a genus of fungi that forms beneficial partnerships with plant roots, helping them absorb nutrients from the soil. These microscopic fungi create extensive networks of thread-like structures that extend far beyond what plant roots can reach on their own. In return for helping plants gather water and minerals, they receive sugars and other nutrients from their plant partners.
children.distinguishingFeatures: This genus is characterized by its specific branching patterns and spore structures that can only be seen under a microscope. It forms a particular type of mycorrhizal association that is distinct from other root-partnering fungi in how it connects to and penetrates plant root cells.
children.funFact: Like an underground internet, Mycorrhaphium fungi can connect multiple plants together, allowing them to share resources and even chemical warning signals about insect attacks or diseases.

children.description: The Steccherinaceae family consists of wood-decomposing fungi that play crucial roles as nature's recyclers in New England forests. These fungi typically grow on dead or dying hardwood and coniferous trees, breaking down tough woody material and returning nutrients to the forest ecosystem. Most members of this family produce distinctive fruiting bodies with various pore and tooth-like structures on their undersides.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other wood-decay fungi, Steccherinaceae members often have unique spore-bearing surfaces that can range from smooth to toothed to maze-like patterns. They're distinguished from similar families by their specific microscopic features and their preference for creating intricate, often overlapping bracket-like formations on tree surfaces.
children.funFact: Some Steccherinaceae fungi can continue decomposing wood for decades, with their mycelia (fungal threads) spreading through entire fallen logs and creating interconnected networks that can span multiple trees in the forest.

children.name: Laetiporaceae
Laetiporus
children.description: Laetiporus is a genus of bracket fungi commonly known as chicken of the woods, named for their meat-like texture and taste when cooked. These bright yellow and orange shelf fungi grow as overlapping brackets on tree trunks and fallen logs, feeding on the wood as saprotrophs or parasites. All species in this genus are edible when young and are prized by foragers as a vegetarian substitute for chicken.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Laetiporus are distinguished by their vibrant yellow to orange coloration, soft and succulent texture when fresh, and their growth pattern of overlapping shelf-like brackets. Unlike many other bracket fungi, they lack a tough, woody texture and have small, round pores on their undersides.
children.funFact: Chicken of the woods is one of the few wild mushrooms that can be safely identified by beginners because there are no poisonous look-alikes with the same bright yellow-orange coloration and bracket growth pattern.

children.description: Laetiporaceae is a family of bracket fungi that includes the well-known chicken-of-the-woods mushrooms. These fungi are wood decomposers that typically form shelf-like or bracket-shaped fruiting bodies on trees and logs. They play an important ecological role by breaking down dead and dying wood in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their bright yellow to orange colors and their ability to form large, overlapping bracket-like structures on wood. Unlike many other bracket fungi, they have a softer, more tender texture when fresh.
children.funFact: Chicken-of-the-woods mushrooms get their common name because their texture and flavor are remarkably similar to chicken meat, making them a popular wild edible for foragers and vegetarians alike.

children.name: Meripilaceae
Meripilus
children.description: Meripilus is a genus of large, bracket-like fungi that grow on hardwood trees and stumps, particularly favoring oak trees. These polypore fungi form overlapping, fan-shaped caps that can grow quite large and are known for their distinctive staining reactions when bruised or cut.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their tendency to stain dark colors (black, red, or yellow) when damaged, which helps distinguish them from other polypore fungi that don't show such dramatic color changes.
children.funFact: The Black-staining Polypore can form massive fruiting bodies weighing over 100 pounds, making it one of the largest fungi you might encounter in New England forests.

children.description: Meripilaceae is a family of bracket fungi that form large, overlapping shelf-like structures on trees and stumps. These polypore fungi are wood decomposers that play important roles in forest ecosystems by breaking down dead and dying wood. They typically grow in clusters or rosettes at the base of trees or on large roots.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their large, fan-shaped caps that grow in overlapping clusters, and their whitish pore surface underneath that bruises black when touched or damaged.
children.funFact: Some Meripilus species can form massive fruiting bodies weighing over 50 pounds, making them among the largest mushrooms you might encounter in New England forests!

children.name: Cerrenaceae
Cerrena
children.description: Cerrena is a genus of bracket fungi that forms tough, leathery shelf-like structures on dead and dying hardwood trees. These fungi are important decomposers in forest ecosystems, breaking down wood and returning nutrients to the soil. They produce spores through a maze-like pore surface on the underside of their fruiting bodies.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Cerrena fungi are distinguished by their unique pore surface that appears as an intricate maze or labyrinth pattern, rather than the round holes typical of most bracket fungi. This maze-like structure gives them their common name and makes them easily recognizable.
children.funFact: The Mossy Maze Polypore can continue growing and producing spores for several years on the same piece of wood, with individual fruiting bodies potentially living for up to a decade.

children.name: Irpiciporus
children.description: Irpiciporus is a small genus of polypore fungi that creates shelf-like brackets on dead hardwood trees. These fungi are wood decomposers that help break down fallen logs and dead branches in forest ecosystems. They have distinctive pore surfaces underneath their fruiting bodies that release spores.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their soft, fleshy texture when fresh and their tendency to develop tooth-like projections that hang down from the pore surface. The pores are typically large and angular, giving the underside a distinctive honeycomb-like appearance.
children.funFact: The only New England species, Irpiciporus mollis, is sometimes called the 'soft polypore' because its fruiting body feels spongy and flexible when fresh, unlike many other bracket fungi that are woody and hard.

children.name: Somion
children.description: Somion is a genus of very small, primitive flies that belong to the family Scatopsidae, commonly known as dung flies or minute black scavenger flies. These tiny insects are typically dark-colored and are often found in decaying organic matter where they help break down decomposing materials. They play an important ecological role as decomposers in forest and garden ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Somion flies can be distinguished from other scatopsid flies by their distinctive wing venation patterns and their extremely small size, often measuring less than 2 millimeters in length.
children.funFact: Despite their common name association with dung, Somion flies are actually more commonly found in leaf litter and compost piles than in animal waste, making them valuable allies for gardeners and forest health.

children.description: The Cerrenaceae family consists of bracket fungi that grow as shelf-like structures on dead or dying hardwood trees. These fungi are important decomposers in forest ecosystems, breaking down wood and recycling nutrients back into the soil. They typically have a leathery or woody texture and can persist on trees for many months or even years.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their pore surface (rather than gills) and their bracket-like growth form that extends horizontally from tree trunks. They tend to have a more leathery texture compared to the softer polypore fungi in related families.
children.funFact: Some Cerrenaceae fungi can actually continue growing and producing spores even after the host tree has completely died and fallen to the ground.

children.name: Phaeolaceae
Phaeolus
children.description: Phaeolus is a small genus of bracket fungi that grows on conifers, particularly pine trees. These fungi are wood-rotting species that cause brown rot, breaking down the cellulose in wood and leaving behind a crumbly, brown residue. They're most commonly found growing at the base of living or dead coniferous trees.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Phaeolus are distinguished by their large, shelf-like fruiting bodies that often have a velvety or fuzzy upper surface when young, and their preference for coniferous hosts. Unlike many other bracket fungi, they typically produce yellowish to orange-brown spore prints.
children.funFact: Both species in this genus have historically been used to create natural dyes, producing beautiful yellow, orange, and brown colors for wool and other textiles.

children.description: Phaeolaceae is a small family of wood-decay fungi that specialize in breaking down dead hardwood trees. These fungi produce distinctive bracket-like fruiting bodies that emerge from tree trunks and fallen logs. They play an important ecological role as decomposers in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their tough, shelf-like fruiting bodies with distinctive pore surfaces underneath instead of gills. They cause a brown rot in wood, leaving behind a crumbly, cube-like decay pattern.
children.funFact: The most well-known member of this family, Phaeolus schweinitzii, is sometimes called the 'dyer's polypore' because it produces beautiful yellow, orange, and brown dyes that were historically used to color wool and fabric.

children.name: Ischnodermataceae
Ischnoderma
children.description: Ischnoderma is a small genus of bracket fungi that grow as shelf-like structures on dead and dying hardwood trees. These polypore fungi are wood decomposers that help break down fallen logs and weakened trees in forest ecosystems. Both New England species are relatively large, thick brackets with distinctive aromatic properties.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their thick, fleshy brackets and strong, pleasant fragrances - one smells resinous while the other has a sweet benzoin-like scent. Unlike many other bracket fungi, Ischnoderma species tend to be quite substantial and meaty in texture.
children.funFact: The Benzoin Bracket gets its name from its sweet, vanilla-like fragrance that resembles benzoin resin, making it one of the most pleasantly scented fungi you'll encounter in New England forests.

children.description: The Ischnodermataceae is a small family of wood-decaying fungi that includes shelf or bracket fungi found growing on dead and dying trees. These fungi are important decomposers in forest ecosystems, breaking down tough woody materials and recycling nutrients back into the soil. They typically form tough, leathery fruiting bodies that can persist for months or even years.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their white rot decay pattern, which breaks down both cellulose and lignin in wood, leaving behind whitish, stringy wood fibers. They have distinctive microscopic features including thick-walled spores and specialized hyphal structures.
children.funFact: Some Ischnoderma species can continue growing and producing spores for several years from the same fruiting body, making them among the longest-lived fungal structures in New England forests.

children.name: Sparassidaceae
Sparassis
children.description: Cauliflower mushrooms are distinctive fungi that grow as large, ruffled masses resembling heads of cauliflower or sea coral. These parasitic mushrooms typically grow at the base of conifers like pine and spruce, where they cause heart rot in their host trees. They can reach impressive sizes, sometimes weighing several pounds when fully developed.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike typical cap-and-stem mushrooms, cauliflower mushrooms have a highly branched, coral-like structure with thin, wavy, ribbon-like lobes. Their unique ruffled appearance makes them virtually impossible to confuse with any other mushroom group.
children.funFact: A single cauliflower mushroom can weigh up to 50 pounds and provide enough food for multiple meals, making them a prized find for foragers despite their rarity.

children.description: The Sparassidaceae family consists of fungi that produce distinctive coral-like or cauliflower-shaped fruiting bodies with many branched, ruffled layers. These mushrooms grow as large, pale masses that can weigh several pounds and are found at the base of trees, particularly conifers. They are wood-decay fungi that help break down dead organic matter in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike typical cap-and-stem mushrooms, members of this family form highly branched, coral-like structures with thin, wavy edges that resemble sea coral or heads of cauliflower. Their unique architecture maximizes surface area for spore production.
children.funFact: A single cauliflower mushroom can contain thousands of individual branches and may live for several weeks, continuing to grow and produce spores throughout its extended fruiting period.

children.name: Panaceae
Panus
children.description: Panus is a small genus of tough, bracket-like mushrooms that grow on dead hardwood trees and logs. These fungi are characterized by their leathery texture and fan-shaped caps that often have fuzzy or hairy surfaces. They play an important role as decomposers in forest ecosystems, breaking down dead wood.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike typical soft oyster mushrooms, Panus species have a distinctly tough, almost leathery texture that makes them quite durable. Their caps often display fuzzy or velvety surfaces, and they typically have decurrent gills that run down the stem.
children.funFact: Despite their tough texture when fresh, some Panus species become more tender when cooked and have been used as food in various cultures, though they require longer cooking times than softer mushrooms.

children.description: The Panaceae family consists of bracket fungi that grow on dead or dying hardwood trees, particularly oak and beech. These mushrooms have a distinctive fan or bracket-like shape and tough, leathery texture that helps them persist through changing weather conditions.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their bracket-like growth form, tough texture, and small, round pores on the underside instead of gills. They typically have a velvety or fuzzy upper surface when young.
children.funFact: These fungi can persist for months or even years on dead trees, slowly decomposing the wood and playing a crucial role in forest recycling.

children.name: Grifolaceae
Grifola
children.description: Grifola is a genus of mushrooms that form distinctive clusters of overlapping, fan-shaped caps that branch from a central base. These fungi grow at the base of trees, particularly oaks, and are prized both for their culinary value and their impressive size. They are polypore fungi, meaning they have tiny pores instead of gills on their undersides.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other polypore mushrooms that form shelf-like brackets on tree trunks, Grifola species create massive, multi-layered rosettes that can weigh dozens of pounds. Their overlapping, ruffled caps give them a distinctive lettuce-like or hen-like appearance.
children.funFact: A single hen of the woods mushroom can weigh up to 100 pounds and contain enough food to feed a family for weeks!

children.description: The Grifolaceae is a small family of polypore fungi that includes some of our most prized edible mushrooms. These fungi are characterized by their bracket-like or rosette-forming growth pattern and their ability to decompose wood, playing an important role in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family typically form large, overlapping bracket-like caps that grow in rosette or fan-like clusters from tree bases or stumps. Unlike many other polypores, they often have a more fleshy, tender texture when young.
children.funFact: The single New England representative of this family, commonly known as hen-of-the-woods or maitake, can form massive fruiting bodies weighing over 50 pounds at the base of oak trees!

children.name: Climacocystaceae
Climacocystis
children.description: Climacocystis is a small genus of bracket fungi that grows on dead and dying coniferous trees, particularly spruces and firs. These fungi are wood decomposers that help break down fallen logs and weakened trees in northern forests. They form shelf-like or bracket-shaped fruiting bodies that emerge from the bark of their host trees.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Climacocystis fungi are distinguished by their white to cream-colored pore surface and their preference for coniferous hosts in cooler climates. Unlike many other bracket fungi, they have a distinctive layered appearance and relatively large pores that are easily visible to the naked eye.
children.funFact: The name Climacocystis means 'ladder cyst,' referring to the ladder-like arrangement of cells visible under a microscope in the fungus's internal structure.

children.description: Climacocystaceae is a small family of fungi that includes wood-decay species that break down dead trees and woody debris in forest ecosystems. These fungi are polypores, meaning they produce their spores in tiny pores on the underside of their fruiting bodies rather than on gills like mushrooms.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their bracket-like or shelf-like fruiting bodies that grow directly from dead wood, with a distinctive pore structure underneath for spore release.
children.funFact: This family contains only one genus with very few species worldwide, making it one of the smaller and more specialized groups of wood-decay fungi.

children.name: Podoscyphaceae
Abortiporus
children.description: Abortiporus is a small genus of polypore fungi that forms distinctive rosette-shaped fruiting bodies on decaying wood. These fungi are saprophytes, meaning they help decompose dead organic matter and recycle nutrients back into the forest ecosystem. They are characterized by their unique growth pattern that creates overlapping, bracket-like structures.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most polypore fungi that form simple shelf-like brackets, Abortiporus creates complex rosette formations with multiple overlapping lobes. The fruiting bodies also have the unusual ability to change color when bruised or handled, hence the common name "blushing" for some species.
children.funFact: The name Abortiporus literally means "aborted pores" because young specimens often have irregular or incompletely formed pore surfaces that don't develop the typical tube structure seen in other polypore fungi.

children.description: Podoscyphaceae is a small family of polypore fungi that create bracket-like fruiting bodies on decaying wood. These fungi are decomposers that help break down dead trees and fallen logs in forest ecosystems. They have a unique growth pattern where their fruiting bodies often appear cup-shaped or bracket-like with distinctive pore surfaces underneath.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their distinctive pore structure and the way their fruiting bodies attach to wood substrates. Unlike many other polypores, they often have a more irregular, sometimes aborted or malformed appearance to their brackets.
children.funFact: The name 'Podoscyphaceae' comes from Greek words meaning 'foot cup,' referring to the distinctive cup-like or stemmed appearance of some species in this family.

children.name: Aegeritaceae
Aegerita
children.description: Aegerita is a small genus of crust fungi that forms thin, white to cream-colored patches on decaying wood. These fungi are saprophytes, meaning they break down dead organic matter and play an important role in forest decomposition. They produce their spores on a smooth or slightly wrinkled surface that spreads across the substrate like a crusty coating.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Aegerita fungi are distinguished by their pure white to pale cream coloration and smooth to finely wrinkled spore-bearing surface. Unlike many other crust fungi, they tend to form relatively thick, chalky-white patches that can be quite conspicuous on dark wood.
children.funFact: Despite its common name 'couscous crust,' this fungus gets its nickname from its granular, bead-like appearance that resembles the tiny pasta grains of couscous when viewed up close.

children.description: Aegeritaceae is a small family of fungi that includes species commonly known as poplar mushrooms or velvet foot mushrooms. These fungi are typically found growing on dead or dying hardwood trees, where they play an important role as decomposers breaking down wood.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their small to medium-sized fruiting bodies with dark, velvety stems and pale caps. They often grow in clusters and have white spore prints.
children.funFact: Some species in this family can continue growing even in freezing temperatures, making them one of the few mushrooms you might find fruiting during winter months in New England.

children.name: Pycnoporellaceae
Pycnoporellus
children.description: Pycnoporellus is a small genus of bracket fungi that grow as shelf-like structures on dead coniferous trees. These fungi are wood decomposers that help break down fallen logs and dead branches in forest ecosystems. They produce distinctive bracket-shaped fruiting bodies with pores on the underside instead of gills.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their bright orange to reddish-brown coloration and relatively soft, fleshy texture when fresh. They typically have large, angular pores on the underside and grow exclusively on coniferous wood.
children.funFact: The name Pycnoporellus means 'little dense pore,' referring to the closely packed pore structure on the underside of these colorful bracket fungi.

children.description: Pycnoporellaceae is a small family of bracket fungi that forms shelf-like fruiting bodies on dead and dying wood. These fungi are important decomposers in forest ecosystems, breaking down cellulose and lignin in wood to recycle nutrients back into the soil.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family produce distinctive bracket-shaped mushrooms with a tough, leathery texture and small, round pores on the underside instead of gills. The pore surface is typically white to cream colored when fresh.
children.funFact: Despite being a globally distributed family, Pycnoporellaceae contains only a handful of species worldwide, making it one of the smaller families in the bracket fungi group.

children.name: Fibroporiaceae
Fibroporia
children.description: Fibroporia is a genus of wood-decay fungi that specialize in breaking down the cellulose in dead wood, causing what's known as brown rot. These fungi play an important role in forest ecosystems by decomposing fallen logs and dead trees, recycling nutrients back into the soil. They typically form thin, white to cream-colored fungal mats or crusts on the surface of decaying wood.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Fibroporia fungi are distinguished by their fibrous, cotton-like texture and their ability to cause brown rot, which leaves behind a characteristic brown, crumbly wood residue. Unlike white rot fungi that break down both cellulose and lignin, these fungi primarily target cellulose.
children.funFact: The brown, cube-like chunks of wood left behind by Fibroporia and other brown rot fungi were historically called 'touchwood' and were used as tinder for starting fires because the decayed wood catches flame easily.

children.description: Fibroporiaceae is a small family of wood-decay fungi that specialize in breaking down dead wood in forest ecosystems. These fungi produce bracket-like or crust-like fruiting bodies that grow directly on rotting logs and stumps. They play an important role as decomposers, helping recycle nutrients back into the forest soil.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their fibrous, tough texture and distinctive pore structure on the underside of their fruiting bodies. They create a white rot in wood, breaking down both cellulose and lignin components.
children.funFact: Despite being a small family with only one species in New England, Fibroporiaceae fungi are incredibly efficient decomposers that can completely break down fallen trees over several years, earning them the nickname 'nature's recyclers.'

children.name: Adustoporiaceae
Amyloporia
children.description: Amyloporia is a genus of wood-decay fungi that forms thin, crust-like growths on dead wood. These fungi are characterized by their porous undersurface with tiny holes (pores) instead of gills, and they play an important role in breaking down fallen logs and branches in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus have a distinctive pale yellowish color and form very thin, closely attached crusts on wood surfaces. Unlike many other pore fungi, they create relatively small, round pores that give the surface a finely perforated appearance.
children.funFact: The name 'Amyloporia' comes from Greek words meaning 'starch pores,' referring to the starchy reaction these fungi can show when tested with iodine solutions.

children.description: Adustoporiaceae is a small family of wood-decomposing fungi that form bracket-like or crust-like fruiting bodies on dead hardwood trees. These fungi are important decomposers in forest ecosystems, breaking down cellulose and lignin in fallen logs and dead branches. They typically produce white or cream-colored spores and have a distinctive pore structure on their undersides.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their unique combination of microscopic features, including specific spore shapes and the arrangement of their pore-bearing surface. They differ from related bracket fungi families in their particular wood-rotting chemistry and cellular structure.
children.funFact: Despite being a small family with only one species found in New England, Adustoporiaceae fungi can live for many years on the same piece of wood, slowly but steadily recycling nutrients back into the forest ecosystem.

children.name: Hyphodermataceae
Hyphoderma
children.description: Hyphoderma is a genus of crust fungi that forms thin, smooth patches on decaying wood. These fungi grow flat against the surface of dead branches and logs, creating what looks like a thin coating or skin over the wood.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other crust fungi, Hyphoderma species have a very smooth, waxy appearance and lack the pores or wrinkles found in related groups. Their fruiting bodies are typically white to cream-colored and feel somewhat waxy to the touch.
children.funFact: Despite their simple appearance, Hyphoderma fungi play a crucial role in forest ecosystems by breaking down the tough lignin in wood, helping return nutrients to the soil.

children.description: Hyphodermataceae is a family of fungi that form thin, crust-like growths on dead wood and other organic matter. These fungi are decomposers that help break down fallen logs and branches in forest ecosystems. They typically produce their spores on smooth, waxy surfaces that spread across their substrate like a thin skin.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their smooth, waxy spore-bearing surfaces that lack the pores, gills, or other complex structures found in many other fungi. They form thin, closely attached crusts that can be difficult to peel away from the wood they're growing on.
children.funFact: Despite their simple appearance, these crust fungi are incredibly important forest recyclers, capable of breaking down tough wood fibers that many other organisms cannot digest.

children.description: Shelf fungi are a diverse group of wood-decomposing fungi that typically form bracket-like or shelf-like fruiting bodies on trees and logs. Most species in this order produce their spores in tiny tubes or pores on the underside of their fruiting bodies, rather than on gills like many mushrooms. These fungi play a crucial role as nature's recyclers, breaking down dead wood and returning nutrients to the forest ecosystem.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike gilled mushrooms, most shelf fungi have a pore surface (like a natural sponge) where spores are produced. Their fruiting bodies are often tough, woody, and can persist for months or even years, unlike the soft, short-lived mushrooms of other groups.
children.funFact: Some shelf fungi, like the Artist's Conk, can live for decades and add a new layer of growth each year, creating rings that can be counted like tree rings to determine the fungus's age.

children.name: Hymenochaetales
Hymenochaetaceae
Phellinus
children.description: Phellinus is a genus of bracket fungi that are serious tree pathogens, causing heart rot in living hardwood trees throughout New England's forests. These tough, woody fungi form shelf-like or hoof-shaped fruiting bodies that persist for years on tree trunks, slowly decomposing the wood from the inside out. Each species in this genus typically specializes in attacking specific types of trees, such as aspens, willows, or birches.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Phellinus brackets are characterized by their extremely hard, woody texture and dark, often blackish upper surfaces that develop deep cracks with age. Unlike many other bracket fungi, they have rusty-brown spore-bearing surfaces underneath and their fruiting bodies can live for decades.
children.funFact: Some Phellinus fruiting bodies can live for over 30 years, making them among the longest-lived fungal structures in New England forests!

children.name: Trichaptum
children.description: Trichaptum is a genus of bracket fungi that grow as shelf-like structures on dead and dying trees throughout New England's forests. These fungi are important decomposers that help break down wood, playing a crucial role in forest ecosystems by recycling nutrients back into the soil.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are recognized by their distinctive pore surface that often has a purple or violet tint, especially when young, and may have tooth-like projections around the pore openings.
children.funFact: The violet-toothed polypore gets its name from the beautiful purple coloration on its underside when fresh, though this striking color fades to brown as the fungus ages.

children.name: Onnia
children.description: Onnia is a genus of bracket fungi that form thick, woody shelf-like structures on coniferous trees, particularly spruces and firs. These polypore fungi are parasites and decomposers that cause brown rot in their host trees, breaking down the cellulose and leaving behind the brownish lignin. They're commonly found in northern forests and are important players in forest ecosystem cycling.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Onnia species are distinguished by their thick, often velvety or fuzzy upper surfaces and their preference for coniferous hosts. Unlike many other bracket fungi, they typically have a distinctive triangular shape when viewed from the side and often develop concentrically zoned surfaces.
children.funFact: The Woolly Velvet Polypore gets its name from its incredibly soft, fuzzy upper surface that feels remarkably similar to velvet fabric when fresh.

children.name: Inonotus
children.description: Inonotus is a genus of bracket fungi that are parasites and decomposers of hardwood trees, particularly favoring birch, oak, and other deciduous species. These fungi form woody, shelf-like growths on tree trunks and branches, often appearing as hard, crusty brackets with distinctive coloring. They play an important ecological role by breaking down dead and dying wood in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Inonotus fungi are characterized by their hard, woody texture and typically rusty-brown to black coloration, often with a crusty or warty surface. Unlike many other bracket fungi, they tend to have small pores on their underside and often cause a white rot in their host trees.
children.funFact: The most famous member of this genus is chaga (Inonotus obliquus), which forms black, charcoal-like masses on birch trees and has been used for centuries in traditional medicine and as a coffee substitute.

children.name: Hydnoporia
children.description: Hydnoporia is a genus of crust fungi that grow as flat, spreading patches on decaying wood. These fungi have a distinctive surface covered in tiny teeth or spines that point downward, giving them a fuzzy or bristly appearance when viewed up close.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike smooth crust fungi, Hydnoporia species have small tooth-like projections on their underside where spores are produced. This gives them a rougher texture compared to their flat, smooth relatives.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'glue crust' fungi, these species actually help break down wood by secreting enzymes, playing an important role as nature's recyclers in forest ecosystems.

children.name: Fuscoporia
children.description: Fuscoporia is a genus of polypore fungi that form tough, woody bracket fungi on dead and dying hardwood trees. These fungi are wood decomposers that play an important role in forest ecosystems by breaking down dead wood and recycling nutrients back into the soil. They typically produce perennial fruiting bodies that can persist for several years.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Fuscoporia species are characterized by their rusty brown to yellowish colors and their tendency to form crusty, shelf-like growths that are firmly attached to their host trees. They have small, round pores on their undersides and produce spores that are also brownish in color.
children.funFact: The Mustard Yellow Polypore can live for decades on the same tree, slowly growing outward each year and adding new layers to its fruiting body like tree rings.

children.name: Porodaedalea
children.description: Porodaedalea is a genus of bracket fungi that grows as shelf-like structures on coniferous trees, particularly pines and spruces. These woody fungi are parasites and decomposers that cause heart rot in their host trees, playing an important role in forest ecosystems by breaking down dead wood. They form tough, perennial fruiting bodies that can persist for many years on tree trunks.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Porodaedalea are distinguished by their preference for coniferous hosts and their distinctive pore structure on the underside of the bracket. Unlike some similar bracket fungi, they typically have small, round pores and produce brown, woody fruiting bodies with a corky texture.
children.funFact: The Pine Bracket can live for decades on a single tree, with some specimens estimated to be over 30 years old, making them among the longest-lived fungi in New England forests.

children.name: Hymenochaete
children.description: Hymenochaete is a genus of crust fungi that form thin, leathery patches on the bark of hardwood trees, particularly oaks. These fungi appear as flat, brownish crusts that spread across tree surfaces and play an important role in decomposing dead wood in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their rusty-brown coloration and the presence of specialized sterile structures called setae that appear as dark, bristle-like projections under magnification.
children.funFact: Despite their name suggesting they damage trees, Hymenochaete fungi are actually beneficial decomposers that only grow on dead wood and help recycle nutrients back into the forest ecosystem.

children.name: Fomitiporia
children.description: Fomitiporia is a genus of wood-decay fungi that forms hard, crusty patches on tree bark and dead wood. These fungi are specialized decomposers that break down the tough lignin in wood, playing an important role in forest ecosystems by recycling nutrients from fallen trees and branches.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus form particularly hard, perennial fruiting bodies that persist for multiple years and have tiny, round pores on their surface. They are distinguished from other crust fungi by their extremely dense, woody texture and their ability to cause white rot in hardwood trees.
children.funFact: Some Fomitiporia species can live for decades on the same tree, gradually expanding their crusty patches year after year while continuously breaking down the wood beneath.

children.name: Pseudoinonotus
children.description: Pseudoinonotus is a small genus of bracket fungi that grows on hardwood trees, particularly oaks. These fungi are wood-decaying organisms that form large, shelf-like fruiting bodies on tree trunks and help break down dead wood in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their thick, fleshy bracket-shaped fruiting bodies with a velvety or fuzzy surface texture. They typically have a brownish coloration and produce spores from tiny pores on the underside rather than gills.
children.funFact: The oak bracket can produce fruiting bodies that weigh over 50 pounds and live for several years, growing larger each season like tree rings.

children.name: Mensularia
children.description: Mensularia is a small genus of bracket fungi that grows on hardwood trees, particularly alders. These fungi form shelf-like or bracket-shaped fruiting bodies that extend horizontally from tree trunks and help decompose dead wood in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Mensularia brackets have a distinctive radial pattern of ridges and furrows on their upper surface, giving them a fan-like appearance that helps distinguish them from other bracket fungi.
children.funFact: The Alder Bracket is so specialized that it almost exclusively grows on alder trees, making it a reliable indicator species for identifying alder wood even after the tree has died.

children.name: Fulvifomes
children.description: Fulvifomes is a genus of bracket fungi that forms hard, woody shelf-like structures on tree trunks. These fungi are wood-decomposers that feed on dead or dying hardwood trees, particularly black locust trees. They have a distinctive cracked, crusty cap surface and play an important role in forest ecosystems by breaking down dead wood.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their deeply cracked, often blackened cap surface that develops distinctive fissures as they age. Unlike many other bracket fungi, Fulvifomes species have extremely hard, woody fruiting bodies that persist for many years.
children.funFact: The Cracked Cap Polypore can live for decades on a single tree, with some specimens estimated to be over 20 years old based on their layered growth rings.

children.name: Fomitiporella
children.description: Fomitiporella is a genus of wood-decay fungi that forms hard, bracket-like fruiting bodies on dead and dying trees. These fungi are important decomposers in forest ecosystems, breaking down woody material and recycling nutrients back into the soil. They produce their spores in tiny pores on the underside of their shelf-like structures.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Fomitiporella fungi are characterized by their extremely hard, woody fruiting bodies that persist for many years on trees. Unlike many other bracket fungi, they have very small, round pores and a distinctively tough, almost stone-like texture.
children.funFact: The fruiting bodies of Fomitiporella fungi are so hard and durable that they can persist on dead trees for decades, earning them a reputation as some of the most long-lasting fungi in the forest.

children.name: Inocutis
children.description: Inocutis is a genus of bracket fungi that grow as tough, woody shelf-like structures on trees. These fungi are decomposers that break down dead wood, playing an important role in forest ecosystems by recycling nutrients back into the soil.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Inocutis fungi are characterized by their extremely hard, woody texture and perennial growth habit, meaning they persist for multiple years rather than appearing seasonally like many other fungi.
children.funFact: The name Inocutis literally means "fibrous skin," referring to the tough, leathery surface texture of these remarkably durable fungi.

children.name: Asterodon
children.description: Asterodon is a genus of tooth fungi, a group of mushrooms that produce spores on tiny tooth-like or spine-like projections instead of gills or pores. These fungi are wood decomposers that help break down dead organic matter in forest ecosystems. They typically grow on decaying hardwood logs and stumps.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Asterodon species are distinguished by their unique spore-bearing teeth that hang downward from the cap surface, and their characteristic rusty-brown to orange coloration.
children.funFact: The name 'Asterodon' literally means 'star tooth,' referring to the distinctive star-shaped or pointed teeth that cover the underside of these fascinating fungi.

children.name: Phellinopsis
children.description: Phellinopsis is a small genus of wood-decay fungi that forms tough, bracket-like fruiting bodies on dead hardwood trees. These fungi are saprophytes, meaning they play an important ecological role by breaking down dead wood and recycling nutrients back into the forest ecosystem.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Phellinopsis fungi are characterized by their thick, woody brackets with a distinctive layered structure and rust-brown to dark brown colors. Unlike many other bracket fungi, they have a unique spore structure and grow exclusively on hardwood trees.
children.funFact: The single New England species, Phellinopsis conchata, can live for many years on the same dead tree, slowly growing larger and adding new layers to its bracket each growing season.

children.description: The Hymenochaetaceae are a family of fungi that specialize in breaking down wood, playing a crucial role as nature's recyclers in New England's forests. Most members of this family are bracket fungi or polypores that form tough, shelf-like fruiting bodies on tree trunks and fallen logs. They're particularly skilled at decomposing the lignin in wood, which makes them essential for nutrient cycling in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family typically have rusty-brown spore prints and often produce distinctive brown or rust-colored pigments. Many species in this group cause a characteristic brown rot in wood, and their fruiting bodies tend to be perennial and woody rather than soft and fleshy.
children.funFact: Some Hymenochaetaceae fungi, like certain Inonotus species, have been used in traditional medicine for centuries and are still being studied today for their potential anti-inflammatory and immune-boosting compounds.

children.name: Rickenellaceae
Rickenella
children.description: Mosscap mushrooms are tiny, delicate fungi that form small orange or yellowish caps on thin stems. They typically grow among mosses and other small plants in moist, shaded areas like forest floors and wetlands. These miniature mushrooms are part of the larger group of gilled fungi but are much smaller than most mushrooms people commonly notice.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Mosscap mushrooms are distinguished by their extremely small size (caps usually less than half an inch across) and their bright orange to yellow-orange coloration. Unlike many other small mushrooms, they have widely spaced gills and very thin, wiry stems.
children.funFact: Despite being so tiny that they're easily overlooked, mosscap mushrooms play an important ecological role by helping decompose organic matter in moss communities and providing food for small insects and other tiny forest creatures.

children.name: Alloclavaria
children.description: Alloclavaria is a small genus of club fungi that produces distinctive spindle-shaped fruiting bodies. These fungi are saprophytes, meaning they break down dead organic matter in forest environments, playing an important role in nutrient cycling.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other club fungi, Alloclavaria species have a characteristic spindle or club shape that is often twisted or curved, and they typically display purple to violet coloration.
children.funFact: The Purple Spindles were once thought to be related to coral fungi, but DNA studies revealed they belong to their own unique evolutionary lineage.

children.name: Cotylidia
children.description: Cotylidia is a small genus of bracket fungi that forms distinctive rosette-shaped fruiting bodies on decaying wood. These fungi are saprobic decomposers, breaking down dead organic matter and playing an important role in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their unique rosette or flower-like growth pattern, with overlapping bracket-like caps arranged in circular formations that resemble wooden roses.
children.funFact: The name Cotylidia comes from the Greek word 'kotyle' meaning cup or bowl, referring to the distinctive cup-like shape of the individual brackets that make up the rosette formation.

children.name: Resinicium
children.description: Resinicium is a genus of crust fungi that forms thin, flat patches on decaying wood. These fungi are wood decomposers that help break down dead trees and logs in forest ecosystems. They produce their spores from a smooth or slightly wrinkled surface that spreads like a thin crust over the wood.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Resinicium fungi are distinguished by their smooth to slightly bumpy spore-bearing surface and their ability to produce a resinous or waxy texture. Unlike many other crust fungi, they often have distinctive color patterns and a somewhat glossy appearance.
children.funFact: The name 'Resinicium' comes from the Latin word for resin, referring to the waxy or resinous texture that these fungi often develop on their surface.

children.name: Muscinupta
children.description: Muscinupta is a genus of tiny moths in the family Nepticulidae, known for their incredibly small size and specialized feeding habits. These minute moths are among the smallest lepidopterans in North America, with wingspans often measuring less than a quarter inch. The larvae are leaf miners, creating distinctive tunnels and patterns inside plant leaves as they feed.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their extremely small size even among other nepticulid moths, and their larvae specifically mine the leaves of mosses and small herbaceous plants rather than trees or shrubs.
children.funFact: Despite being called the 'Minute Mossmaid,' the larvae don't actually feed on moss - the name likely refers to the moth's tiny, delicate appearance and preference for low-growing plants in moist, moss-rich habitats.

children.description: The Rickenellaceae are a diverse family of small fungi that includes both tiny mushrooms and crust-like species that grow flat against surfaces. Many members of this family have a special relationship with mosses, either growing directly on them or in moss-rich environments. Despite their different appearances, they share similar microscopic features and genetic relationships.
children.distinguishingFeatures: This family is distinguished by its mix of mushroom-forming species and crust fungi, along with their frequent association with bryophytes (mosses and liverworts). Many have distinctive spore shapes and specialized structures for attaching to or growing among moss plants.
children.funFact: Some Rickenellaceae fungi are so tiny that their mushroom caps are smaller than a pinky nail, and they often go completely unnoticed unless you're specifically looking for them among moss cushions.

children.name: Coltriciaceae
Coltricia
children.description: Coltricia is a genus of bracket fungi that form distinctive funnel-shaped or circular caps with tiny pores on the underside instead of gills. These mushrooms have a leathery, tough texture and typically display warm brown to cinnamon colors. They're commonly found growing on decaying wood or emerging from the ground near rotting roots.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other polypore fungi, Coltricia species have a central stem and funnel-shaped caps rather than growing as shelf-like brackets directly from wood. Their consistently brown to cinnamon coloration and tough, leathery texture also help separate them from similar fungi.
children.funFact: The Brown Funnel Polypore can live for several years, with its caps becoming darker and more weathered each season while continuing to produce spores.

children.description: Coltriciaceae is a family of fungi that produces distinctive bracket-like or funnel-shaped mushrooms, often called velvet-foot polypores. These fungi are wood decomposers that play an important role in forest ecosystems by breaking down dead wood and recycling nutrients back into the soil. They typically have tough, leathery fruiting bodies with small pores on the underside instead of gills.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their funnel or bracket-shaped caps with a velvety or fuzzy texture, and they have a distinctive radial pattern of ridges or zones on their upper surface. Unlike many other polypore fungi, they often have a central or off-center stem.
children.funFact: Some Coltricia species are known as 'tiger's eye' fungi because their caps display beautiful concentric zones of brown, orange, and yellow colors that create striking patterns reminiscent of the gemstone.

children.name: Rigidoporaceae
Rigidoporus
children.description: Rigidoporus is a genus of bracket fungi that grow as shelf-like structures on trees and fallen logs. These fungi are wood decomposers that break down dead and dying hardwood trees, playing an important role in forest recycling. They form tough, perennial fruiting bodies that can persist for several years.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Rigidoporus fungi are characterized by their hard, woody texture and small, round pores on the underside instead of gills. Unlike many other bracket fungi, they have a particularly rigid structure that feels almost rock-hard when mature.
children.funFact: The Poplar Bracket can live for decades on a single tree, slowly expanding its shelf-like body year after year while continuously decomposing the wood beneath it.

children.description: Rigidoporaceae is a family of wood-decay fungi that produces bracket-like or shelf-like fruiting bodies on dead and dying trees. These fungi are important decomposers in forest ecosystems, breaking down tough woody material with their powerful enzymes. They typically form hard, woody structures that can persist for years on tree trunks and logs.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their rigid, woody texture and small, round pores on the underside of their fruiting bodies instead of gills. The pore surface is typically white to cream-colored and doesn't bruise when touched.
children.funFact: Despite their tough, almost wood-like appearance, these fungi can live for many years and continue growing, with some specimens adding new layers of pore-bearing tissue each growing season.

children.name: Schizoporaceae
Xylodon
children.description: Xylodon is a genus of fungi that form thin, crust-like growths on dead wood, resembling a layer of paint or coating spread across the surface. These wood-decomposing fungi have a unique surface texture that combines smooth areas with tiny pores, giving them their distinctive appearance. They play an important role in breaking down fallen logs and branches in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike typical crust fungi that have either completely smooth surfaces or distinct pores, Xylodon species have a mixed surface texture with both smooth patches and small, irregular pores scattered throughout.
children.funFact: The name 'Xylodon' literally means 'wood tooth' in Greek, referring to the tiny tooth-like projections that can be seen under magnification on their fruiting surfaces.

children.description: Schizoporaceae is a family of fungi that includes wood-decomposing species with distinctive pore structures. These fungi typically form crusty or bracket-like growths on dead wood, playing an important role in forest ecosystems by breaking down fallen logs and branches.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their unique pore arrangement and spore-bearing structures that help distinguish them from other wood-decay fungi families.
children.funFact: Despite being relatively uncommon, these fungi are essential forest recyclers, helping to return nutrients from dead wood back to the soil for new plant growth.

children.name: Basidioradulum
children.description: Basidioradulum is a small genus of crust fungi that grow as thin, flat patches on decaying wood. These fungi produce tiny tooth-like projections on their surface, giving them a rough, bumpy texture that helps distinguish them from smooth crust fungi.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other crust fungi that have smooth or pored surfaces, Basidioradulum species have distinctive small teeth or spines that stick out from their fruiting body surface.
children.funFact: The genus name Basidioradulum literally means 'little scraper with a club base,' referring to both the tooth-like surface texture and the club-shaped spore-producing cells typical of this fungal group.

children.name: Peniophorellaceae
Peniophorella
children.description: Peniophorella is a small genus of wood-decay fungi that forms thin, crust-like fruiting bodies on dead hardwood trees and branches. These fungi are saprotrophic decomposers, meaning they break down dead organic matter and play an important role in forest nutrient cycling. They belong to the corticioid fungi, a group known for their flat, skin-like appearance when growing on wood surfaces.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Peniophorella species are distinguished from other crust fungi by their smooth to slightly wrinkled surface texture and their microscopic features, including distinctive spores and specialized structures called cystidia that project from the fungal surface.
children.funFact: Despite being microscopic in thickness, these crust fungi can spread across surprisingly large areas of a single log or branch, sometimes covering several square feet of wood surface.

children.description: Peniophorellaceae is a small family of crust fungi that form thin, flat patches on decaying wood. These fungi are decomposers that help break down dead trees and branches in forest ecosystems. They produce their spores on smooth, waxy surfaces that spread across the wood like a coating.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their smooth, waxy fruiting bodies and their unique spore-bearing structures called basidia that have distinctive shapes under microscopic examination.
children.funFact: Despite being a recognized fungal family, Peniophorellaceae contains only a single known genus with very few species worldwide, making it one of the smallest families in the fungal kingdom.

children.name: Chaetoporellaceae
Kneiffiella
children.description: Kneiffiella is a small genus of bacteria that belongs to the Rhodobacteraceae family, commonly found in marine and freshwater environments. These microscopic organisms are part of the diverse world of proteobacteria, playing important roles in aquatic ecosystems through their metabolic activities.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their specific genetic characteristics and cellular structure that separate them from other closely related bacterial genera in the Rhodobacteraceae family.
children.funFact: Despite being invisible to the naked eye, Kneiffiella bacteria contribute to the complex web of microbial life that helps maintain the health of aquatic ecosystems in New England.

children.description: Chaetoporellaceae is a small family of marine bryozoans, which are tiny colonial animals that build intricate calcium carbonate structures on underwater surfaces. These filter-feeding creatures form delicate, often lace-like colonies that can be found encrusting rocks, shells, and other hard surfaces in coastal waters.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their distinctive zooid (individual animal) structure and the specific arrangement of their feeding apparatus. They typically form thin, encrusting colonies with a characteristic pattern of pores and chambers.
children.funFact: Despite being animals, bryozoan colonies like those in Chaetoporellaceae are often mistaken for seaweeds or corals due to their plant-like or coral-like appearance when observed underwater.
