children.description: Hymenochaetales is an order of fungi that includes many important wood-decomposing species, from tiny crust-like fungi that grow flat against tree bark to distinctive bracket fungi with pore-covered undersides. Most members of this group are serious wood decomposers that break down the tough lignin in trees, playing a crucial role in forest ecosystems by recycling dead wood back into soil nutrients.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other bracket fungi, members of Hymenochaetales typically have brown, rust-colored, or dark spore prints and often produce distinctive brown pigments in their tissues. Many species also have a tough, leathery texture and can persist on dead wood for years.
children.funFact: Some species in this order, like the artist's conk (Ganoderma applanatum), have such a hard, stable surface that people can actually draw or carve on them to create lasting artwork!

children.name: Cantharellales
Hydnaceae
Cantharellus
children.description: Chanterelles are beloved edible mushrooms known for their distinctive funnel or vase-like shape and forked, ridge-like gills that run down the stem. These woodland fungi form partnerships with tree roots, helping forests thrive while creating some of nature's most prized culinary treasures. They come in beautiful colors ranging from golden yellow to bright red to ghostly white.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true mushrooms with blade-like gills, chanterelles have thick, forked ridges or wrinkles on their undersides that look more like veins. Their caps are typically funnel-shaped with wavy, irregular edges, and they're generally much meatier and more substantial than look-alike species.
children.funFact: Chanterelles are nearly impossible to cultivate commercially because they require complex partnerships with living tree roots, making wild foraging the primary way these gourmet mushrooms reach our tables.

children.name: Hydnum
children.description: Hedgehog mushrooms are a fascinating group of fungi that get their name from the distinctive spines or teeth hanging beneath their caps, rather than the typical gills or pores found on most mushrooms. These woodland fungi are typically found growing on the forest floor, often in association with trees, and range in color from pure white to peachy orange to reddish-brown. All members of this genus share the characteristic tooth-like structures that release spores, creating their unique hedgehog-like appearance.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other mushrooms with flat gills or tiny pores, hedgehog mushrooms have numerous small, downward-pointing spines or teeth on the underside of their caps. This spiny undersurface immediately sets them apart from any other mushroom group you might encounter in New England forests.
children.funFact: Many hedgehog mushrooms are considered excellent edibles with a mild, pleasant flavor, and they're nearly impossible to confuse with any poisonous species thanks to their unique spiny undersides.

children.name: Craterellus
children.description: Trumpets are a genus of funnel or trumpet-shaped mushrooms that are highly prized by foragers for their excellent culinary qualities. These fungi have distinctive hollow, vase-like caps that often appear wrinkled or wavy, and they typically grow from the forest floor in clusters during late summer and fall.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other mushrooms, trumpets have smooth undersurfaces without visible gills, pores, or spines, and their caps are characteristically funnel-shaped and hollow all the way down to the base.
children.funFact: Black trumpets are sometimes called 'black chanterelles' or 'trumpets of death' despite being perfectly edible and delicious - the ominous name comes from their dark, almost charcoal-colored appearance that can make them nearly invisible on the forest floor.

children.name: Clavulina
children.description: Clavulina is a genus of coral fungi that create beautiful branching, antler-like structures rising from the forest floor. These fascinating fungi lack the typical mushroom cap and instead form intricate networks of white, gray, or tan branches that resemble underwater coral formations. They play important ecological roles as decomposers, breaking down organic matter in woodland environments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other coral fungi, Clavulina species have branches that fork repeatedly in a distinctive pattern and lack the bright colors often seen in related groups. Their branches are typically smooth to slightly wrinkled and tend to be more delicate and finely divided than other coral fungi.
children.funFact: Despite their name 'coral fungi,' these organisms are more closely related to mushrooms than to ocean corals, and some species can actually form partnerships with plant roots, acting as beneficial mycorrhizal partners.

children.name: Multiclavula
children.description: Multiclavula is a small genus of unique fungi that forms partnerships with algae, creating tiny club-shaped or coral-like structures. These fascinating organisms blur the line between fungi and lichens, growing as small white or pale fruiting bodies that often emerge from moss or decaying wood.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike typical mushrooms, Multiclavula species contain green algae within their tissues and produce simple, unbranched club-shaped fruiting bodies. They're distinguished from true lichens by their mushroom-like spore-producing structures.
children.funFact: These remarkable fungi are sometimes called 'lichen mushrooms' because they represent an evolutionary bridge between traditional fungi and lichens, combining characteristics of both groups.

children.name: Sistotrema
children.description: Sistotrema is a genus of crust fungi that form thin, spreading patches on decaying wood. These fungi have a distinctive surface texture covered in tiny tooth-like projections that help distinguish them from other wood-decomposing fungi. They play an important role in forest ecosystems by breaking down dead wood and returning nutrients to the soil.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike smooth crust fungi, Sistotrema species have surfaces covered in small, tooth-like or peg-like projections called teeth or pegs. This gives them a rougher, more textured appearance compared to their smooth-surfaced relatives.
children.funFact: The aromatic earthfan gets its name from its pleasant, sweet fragrance that can often be detected before the fungus is even spotted on a log or stump.

children.description: The Hydnaceae family includes some of New England's most distinctive and sought-after edible mushrooms, including the beloved golden chanterelles and spiny hedgehog mushrooms. These fungi are characterized by their unique spore-bearing surfaces, which can be smooth, wrinkled, spiny, or ridged rather than having traditional gills or pores. Most members of this family form beneficial partnerships with tree roots, helping forests thrive while producing their colorful fruiting bodies.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike typical mushrooms with gills or bracket fungi with pores, Hydnaceae members have diverse spore-bearing surfaces including tooth-like spines, wrinkled undersides, or smooth surfaces. Many have distinctive funnel or trumpet shapes that make them easily recognizable in the forest.
children.funFact: Chanterelles are one of the few wild mushrooms that are nearly impossible to cultivate commercially, making forest foraging the primary way people have enjoyed these golden treasures for thousands of years.

children.name: Botryobasidiaceae
Botryobasidium
children.description: Botryobasidium is a genus of small, inconspicuous fungi that form thin, crust-like patches on decaying wood and bark. These fungi are decomposers that help break down dead organic matter in forest ecosystems. They produce their spores on tiny, club-shaped structures called basidia.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are recognized by their extremely thin, almost film-like fruiting bodies that spread across surfaces like paint. They can only be reliably identified through microscopic examination of their distinctive spore-producing structures.
children.funFact: Despite being nearly invisible to the naked eye, Botryobasidium fungi play a crucial role as nature's recyclers, quietly working behind the scenes to decompose fallen branches and dead bark throughout New England's forests.

children.description: Botryobasidiaceae is a family of fungi that produces their spores on thin, web-like structures that spread across rotting wood and plant debris. These fungi are decomposers that help break down dead organic matter in forest ecosystems, playing an important role in nutrient cycling. Most members of this family form very thin, almost invisible fruiting bodies that look like delicate white or pale films on decaying surfaces.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other fungi that form mushrooms or brackets, members of Botryobasidiaceae create extremely thin, film-like fruiting bodies that are often barely visible to the naked eye. Their spores are produced on smooth surfaces rather than on gills or pores.
children.funFact: These fungi are so thin and translucent that they're often called 'cobweb fungi' - you might walk right past them without noticing their delicate, gossamer-like presence on rotting logs!

children.name: Tulasnellaceae
Tulasnella
children.description: Tulasnella is a genus of microscopic fungi that forms essential partnerships with orchids and other plants. These tiny fungi live in soil and plant roots, helping their plant partners absorb nutrients and water from the environment. Without these fungal allies, many orchids simply cannot survive in the wild.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Tulasnella fungi produce distinctive spores that form in clusters and have a unique jelly-like texture when wet. They lack the complex fruiting bodies found in mushrooms and other more familiar fungi.
children.funFact: These seemingly simple fungi are actually orchid matchmakers - they're so essential to orchid reproduction that orchid seeds won't even germinate without them!

children.description: Tulasnellaceae is a family of tiny fungi that form crucial partnerships with orchids and other plants. These microscopic fungi live in soil and plant roots, helping their plant partners absorb nutrients and water from the environment.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other fungi, members of this family have very simple, thread-like structures and lack the complex reproductive bodies that most fungi produce. They reproduce primarily through simple spores and vegetative growth.
children.funFact: Many orchid seeds cannot germinate without forming a partnership with Tulasnellaceae fungi, making these tiny organisms essential for orchid survival and reproduction.

children.name: Ceratobasidiaceae
Rhizoctonia
children.description: Rhizoctonia is a genus of soil-dwelling fungi that are primarily known as plant pathogens, causing various diseases in crops, turf grasses, and other plants. These fungi live in the soil and attack plant roots and stems, often thriving in warm, humid conditions. They are particularly notorious for causing damaging diseases in agricultural and landscaping settings.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other plant pathogenic fungi, Rhizoctonia species don't produce spores in the traditional sense, instead spreading primarily through direct contact of their thread-like fungal structures (hyphae) with plant tissue.
children.funFact: Rhizoctonia solani can attack over 200 different plant species, making it one of the most versatile plant pathogens in the world - from your backyard lawn to major food crops like potatoes and rice.

children.description: The Ceratobasidiaceae are a family of fungi that primarily live as parasites or symbionts with plants. Most members of this family don't produce visible mushrooms, instead forming microscopic structures and thread-like networks in soil or plant tissues. They play important ecological roles by interacting closely with plant roots and other fungi.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other fungi, members of this family typically lack clamp connections (small bridge-like structures) between their cells. They also produce their spores on simple, often fork-shaped structures rather than in complex fruiting bodies.
children.funFact: Some species in this family can act as both helpful partners and harmful pathogens to the same plant, depending on environmental conditions - switching from friend to foe when the plant becomes stressed.

children.description: The Cantharellales is an order of fungi that includes some of New England's most beloved mushrooms, particularly the golden chanterelles, as well as various tooth fungi and many microscopic species. These fungi are unified by their shared evolutionary history and similar reproductive structures, though they display a remarkable variety of forms from conspicuous forest mushrooms to tiny fungi that live symbiotically with plant roots.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other fungal orders, the Cantharellales includes species with diverse spore-bearing surfaces - some have gills, others have teeth or spines, and some are completely smooth. Many members form important partnerships with trees, helping forest ecosystems thrive through mycorrhizal relationships.
children.funFact: This order includes both the prized golden chanterelles that mushroom hunters seek and tiny orchid mycorrhizal fungi that are essential partners for wild orchids - without these microscopic fungi, many of New England's beautiful native orchids simply cannot survive.

children.name: Thelephorales
Boletopsidaceae
Hydnellum
children.description: Hydnellum is a genus of distinctive mushrooms known as tooth fungi, characterized by their spiny undersides instead of gills or pores. These fungi form symbiotic relationships with tree roots and are typically found growing from the forest floor, often appearing crusty or velvety on top with hanging spines beneath that release spores.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other tooth fungi, Hydnellum species have a tough, leathery texture and often display vibrant colors ranging from bright orange and blue to deep reds and browns. Many species also produce colorful juices when cut or bruised.
children.funFact: The Red-juice Tooth (Hydnellum peckii) is nicknamed the 'bleeding tooth fungus' because it oozes bright red droplets that look remarkably like blood, especially when the mushroom is young and actively growing.

children.name: Boletopsis
children.description: Boletopsis is a small genus of unusual mushrooms that look like boletes but are actually more closely related to tooth fungi. These distinctive fungi have pores on their undersides like true boletes, but their spores and internal structure reveal their different evolutionary history. They're relatively uncommon finds that typically grow on the ground in coniferous and mixed forests.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true boletes, Boletopsis mushrooms have white spore prints and their pore surface doesn't typically bruise when damaged. They also tend to have a more fibrous, less fleshy texture than most boletes.
children.funFact: Despite looking like boletes, DNA studies revealed that Boletopsis mushrooms are actually "evolutionary mimics" - they independently evolved the same pore structure as true boletes but belong to a completely different fungal lineage!

children.name: Sarcodon
children.description: Sarcodon is a genus of tooth fungi that produce spores on tiny tooth-like or spine-like projections hanging down from the underside of their caps, rather than on gills or in pores. These mushrooms are typically found growing on the ground in forests, often forming partnerships with tree roots. They have a distinctive appearance with their spiny undersides and often scaly or rough cap surfaces.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most mushrooms that have gills or pores, Sarcodon fungi have hundreds of small, pointed teeth or spines hanging from their caps where spores are produced. Their caps are often covered in overlapping scales that give them a shingled appearance.
children.funFact: The name 'Sarcodon' comes from Greek words meaning 'flesh tooth,' referring to the fleshy, tooth-like spines that make these fungi look like they have tiny fangs!

children.description: The Boletopsidaceae family consists of fungi that produce their spores on tooth-like structures or in tubes rather than on typical mushroom gills. These mushrooms are typically found growing on the ground in forests, often forming beneficial partnerships with tree roots. Most members of this family have tough, leathery textures and earthy colors ranging from brown to gray.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike typical mushrooms with gills, these fungi have either spiny teeth hanging down from the cap (like Hydnellum and Sarcodon) or tiny pores on the underside (like Boletopsis). Their flesh is often quite firm and doesn't bruise easily when handled.
children.funFact: Some Hydnellum species are called 'bleeding tooth fungi' because they can exude bright red or orange droplets that look remarkably like blood when the mushroom is young and actively growing.

children.name: Bankeraceae
Phellodon
children.description: Phellodon is a genus of unique fungi known as tooth fungi, which produce spores on tiny tooth-like or spine-like projections hanging down from the underside of their caps instead of gills or pores. These mushrooms typically have a tough, leathery texture and grow on the ground in forests, often forming partnerships with tree roots.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other mushrooms that have gills or pores, Phellodon species have distinctive hanging spines or teeth on their undersides that give them their common name of 'tooth fungi.'
children.funFact: Many Phellodon species have a distinctive spicy or bitter taste, and some were historically used as natural food seasonings before commercial spices became widely available.

children.description: Bankeraceae is a family of fungi that includes tooth fungi, which produce spores on spine-like projections rather than gills or pores. These mushrooms typically have a cap and stem structure, with the distinctive teeth or spines hanging down from the underside of the cap. They are important decomposers in forest ecosystems, breaking down organic matter in the soil.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are easily recognized by their tooth-like or spine-like structures (called teeth) on the underside of the cap, which replace the more familiar gills found in many other mushrooms. The spores are produced on these hanging teeth rather than on flat surfaces.
children.funFact: Some species in this family, particularly in the genus Phellodon, have a distinctive bitter or peppery taste that helps deter animals from eating them.

children.name: Thelephoraceae
Thelephora
children.description: Thelephora is a genus of fungi that produces distinctive, often fan-shaped or vase-like mushrooms with a leathery texture. These fungi are commonly found growing on soil or decaying wood in forests, where they help decompose organic matter and form beneficial partnerships with tree roots.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other mushrooms, Thelephora species have a smooth spore-bearing surface on the underside rather than gills or pores, and their fruiting bodies often have a distinctive fibrous, leather-like texture that can persist for months.
children.funFact: The Common Fiber Vase gets its name from its cup or vase-like shape and fibrous texture, and it's often one of the first fungi that beginning mushroom hunters learn to identify because of its distinctive appearance and abundance in New England forests.

children.description: The Thelephoraceae are a family of fungi that form partnerships with tree roots, helping forests thrive through these mutually beneficial relationships. These mushrooms typically have tough, leathery textures and often grow in overlapping clusters or bracket-like formations on the ground or on wood. They're important decomposers that help recycle nutrients in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other mushroom families, Thelephoraceae fungi have smooth spore-bearing surfaces without gills, pores, or teeth. Their fruiting bodies are often thin and flexible with a distinctive leathery or papery texture.
children.funFact: Some Thelephoraceae species can actually change color dramatically when bruised or cut, shifting from brown to bright purple or other vivid hues due to chemical reactions in their tissues.

children.name: Polyozellaceae
Polyozellus
children.description: Blue chanterelles are distinctive fungi that form clusters of blue to purple-black, vase-shaped caps that often grow together in overlapping masses. Unlike true chanterelles, these mushrooms have a darker coloration and tend to form dense, interconnected clusters rather than growing as individual specimens. They are found in coniferous forests, particularly under spruce and fir trees.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Blue chanterelles are easily distinguished from other chanterelle-like fungi by their striking blue to purple-black coloration and their tendency to grow in fused, overlapping clusters rather than as separate individual mushrooms.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'blue chanterelles,' these mushrooms are not actually closely related to true chanterelles and belong to a completely different fungal family.

children.description: The Polyozellaceae family contains distinctive blue to purple-black mushrooms that grow in dense, clustered formations. These fungi are closely related to chanterelles but have their own unique characteristics that set them apart from their golden cousins.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true chanterelles, members of this family display striking blue to purple-black coloration and form large, overlapping clusters that can weigh several pounds.
children.funFact: Blue chanterelles are so rare and distinctive that finding a cluster is considered a prized discovery among mushroom hunters, as they're one of the few naturally blue-colored edible mushrooms in North America.

children.description: Thelephorales is an order of fungi that includes some of the most distinctive mushrooms you'll encounter in New England forests. These fungi are primarily ectomycorrhizal, meaning they form beneficial partnerships with tree roots, helping forests thrive by exchanging nutrients with their plant partners.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this order are known for their tough, leathery textures and often unusual forms, ranging from coral-like branching structures to funnel-shaped caps with spines instead of gills underneath.
children.funFact: Some Thelephorales fungi, like the hedgehog mushrooms, have tiny spines hanging from their caps instead of the typical gills or pores, giving them a distinctive fuzzy appearance that makes them easy to identify.

children.name: Auriculariales
Auriculariaceae
Exidia
children.description: Exidia is a genus of jelly fungi that form soft, gelatinous fruiting bodies on dead wood throughout New England's forests. These fascinating fungi get their jelly-like texture from their ability to absorb and hold large amounts of water, allowing them to swell when wet and shrink when dry. They play an important role as decomposers, breaking down dead branches and logs.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Exidia species are distinguished from other jelly fungi by their typically brain-like or folded surface texture and their tendency to form flattened, spreading masses rather than upright structures. Unlike some jelly fungi, they often have a somewhat firmer consistency and more defined shape.
children.funFact: These remarkable fungi can lose up to 90% of their water content during dry periods and appear completely dried up, but they'll spring back to their full gelatinous form within hours of the next rainfall.

children.name: Auricularia
children.description: Wood ear fungi are distinctive jelly-like mushrooms that grow as ear-shaped brackets on dead and living hardwood trees. These rubbery, translucent fungi have a smooth, gelatinous texture and can bounce back to their original shape when pressed. They're saprophytes that help decompose dead wood while sometimes acting as weak parasites on living trees.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other bracket fungi, wood ears have a distinctly gelatinous, ear-like appearance with a smooth, rubbery texture that feels almost cartilaginous. Their translucent, jelly-like consistency and ability to shrivel when dry but rehydrate when wet sets them apart from harder, woodier bracket fungi.
children.funFact: Wood ear fungi can completely dry out and appear dead during drought conditions, but they'll magically spring back to life and resume their normal gelatinous texture within hours of rain or high humidity.

children.name: Exidiopsis
children.description: Exidiopsis is a genus of jelly fungi that creates some of nature's most delicate and ephemeral formations. These fungi produce thin, gelatinous fruiting bodies that often appear as translucent, hair-like structures growing on decaying wood.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other jelly fungi that form blob-like or ear-shaped masses, Exidiopsis species create extremely fine, thread-like formations that can resemble frost or delicate hair growing from wood surfaces.
children.funFact: The single New England species, Hair Ice, creates magical winter displays by extruding water through its fungal threads to form incredibly delicate ice sculptures that look like silky white hair sprouting from fallen branches.

children.description: The Auriculariaceae are a family of jelly fungi known for their gelatinous, rubbery texture and ear-like or brain-like appearance. These fascinating fungi grow on dead and decaying wood, where they play an important role in breaking down organic matter in forest ecosystems. Unlike many mushrooms, they can absorb water and swell up when wet, then shrink and become leathery when dry.
children.distinguishingFeatures: What sets this family apart is their unique gelatinous consistency and their ability to dramatically change texture based on moisture levels. Their fruiting bodies are typically ear-shaped, cup-shaped, or have folded, brain-like surfaces rather than the typical cap-and-stem structure of most mushrooms.
children.funFact: Wood ear fungi have been cultivated and eaten in Asian cuisine for over 1,000 years, and they're so resilient that dried specimens can be rehydrated and return to their original jelly-like texture even after months of storage.

children.name: Pseudohydnum
children.description: Pseudohydnum is a unique genus of fungi that combines characteristics of both jelly fungi and tooth fungi. These fascinating organisms have a gelatinous, translucent texture like jelly fungi, but produce their spores on tooth-like projections underneath their caps rather than on smooth surfaces.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other jelly fungi that have smooth undersides, Pseudohydnum species have distinctive spiny or tooth-like structures hanging from their caps. This combination of gelatinous texture with toothed spore-bearing surface makes them unmistakable among fungi.
children.funFact: The Toothed Jelly Fungus can actually be eaten raw and has a mild, pleasant flavor, making it one of the few gelatinous fungi that's considered a delicacy in some cuisines.

children.name: Hyaloriaceae
Myxarium
children.description: Myxarium is a genus of unique jelly fungi that create translucent, brain-like fruiting bodies on decaying wood. These fascinating fungi have a gelatinous texture and appear almost crystal-clear, earning them names that reflect their glass-like appearance.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other jelly fungi, Myxarium species have an exceptionally clear, almost transparent appearance that looks like crystal or glass rather than the typical opaque or colored jellies of related groups.
children.funFact: The Crystal Brain Fungus can actually freeze solid in winter and then thaw out in spring to continue growing, making it one of nature's most resilient gelatinous organisms.

children.description: Hyaloriaceae is a small family of jelly fungi that produce translucent, gelatinous fruiting bodies. These fungi are saprophytes, meaning they feed on dead organic matter, particularly decaying wood where they help break down cellulose and other plant materials.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their clear to translucent, jelly-like appearance and their unique spore-bearing structures called basidia that are arranged in a distinctive pattern.
children.funFact: The name 'Hyaloriaceae' comes from the Greek word 'hyalos' meaning glass, referring to the crystal-clear, glass-like appearance of these delicate fungi.

children.name: Guepinia
children.description: Guepinia is a small genus of jelly fungi that produce distinctive, gelatinous fruiting bodies with a unique brain-like or convoluted appearance. These fungi are saprobic, meaning they decompose dead organic matter, particularly decaying hardwood logs and branches. They have a characteristic rubbery, translucent texture that becomes more pronounced when wet.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Guepinia fungi are distinguished from other jelly fungi by their brain-like, folded surface structure and their typically orange to pinkish coloration. Unlike smoother jelly fungi, they have deeply wrinkled, convoluted surfaces that create their distinctive appearance.
children.funFact: Despite their name 'jelly fungi,' Guepinia species can actually survive periods of drought by drying out completely, then rehydrating and resuming growth when moisture returns.

children.name: Protohydnum
children.description: Protohydnum is a small genus of jelly fungi that combines features of both jelly fungi and tooth fungi in a unique way. These unusual fungi produce soft, gelatinous fruiting bodies that have tiny tooth-like projections on their undersides instead of the typical smooth surface found in most jelly fungi.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other jelly fungi that have smooth spore-bearing surfaces, Protohydnum species have small tooth-like spines that hang down from their gelatinous caps, making them look like tiny jellyfish with tentacles.
children.funFact: Protohydnum represents an evolutionary bridge between jelly fungi and tooth fungi, showing how different fungal groups can share unexpected characteristics.

children.name: Basidiodendron
children.description: Basidiodendron is a genus of tiny, often overlooked fungi that form delicate, branching structures resembling miniature coral or antlers. These microscopic fungi are typically found growing on decaying wood, bark, or other organic matter in forest environments. They belong to a group of fungi that produce their spores on club-shaped structures called basidia.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other small wood-dwelling fungi, Basidiodendron species create distinctively branched, coral-like fruiting bodies that are often translucent or whitish in appearance. Their spores are typically round or nearly round, which helps distinguish them from similar branching fungi.
children.funFact: These fungi are so small that their intricate branching structures are often best appreciated under a magnifying glass or microscope, revealing a hidden miniature forest of coral-like growths.

children.description: The Auriculariales are an order of jelly fungi known for their distinctive gelatinous, rubbery texture that can bounce back when touched. These fascinating fungi are often found growing on dead or dying wood, where they form ear-like, bracket-like, or coral-shaped fruiting bodies. Many species in this group are edible and have been harvested for food and traditional medicine for centuries.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other fungi, members of Auriculariales have a unique jelly-like consistency that remains flexible even when dry, and they can rehydrate after periods of drought. Their spore-producing structures are also distinctive, often appearing smooth or slightly wrinkled rather than having gills, pores, or teeth like other mushroom groups.
children.funFact: The famous "wood ear" mushroom (Auricularia auricula-judae) in this order can shrivel up completely during dry periods and then plump back up to full size after just a few minutes of rain!

children.name: Phallales
Phallaceae
Phallus
children.description: Phallus is a genus of distinctive mushrooms commonly known as stinkhorns that emerge from underground egg-like structures. These fungi are easily recognized by their tall, phallic-shaped fruiting bodies topped with a dark, slimy cap that produces a strong, foul odor resembling rotting meat.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of the Phallus genus are distinguished from other stinkhorns by their simple, unbranched structure and their emergence from a white, egg-like sac called a volva that remains at the base.
children.funFact: Despite their unpleasant smell to humans, stinkhorns produce their foul odor specifically to attract flies and other insects, which help spread their spores after being lured in by the scent they mistake for carrion.

children.name: Mutinus
children.description: Mutinus is a genus of distinctive fungi commonly known as stinkhorns that emerge from underground egg-like structures to produce tall, slender fruiting bodies. These mushrooms are characterized by their phallic appearance and strong, unpleasant odor that attracts flies and other insects. The spores are carried on a slimy, dark coating that covers the tip of the mushroom.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other stinkhorn genera, Mutinus species have relatively simple, unbranched fruiting bodies that lack the cage-like or latticed structures seen in related groups. They also tend to be more slender and elongated compared to the broader, more complex forms of other stinkhorns.
children.funFact: Despite their foul smell that's often compared to rotting meat, Mutinus mushrooms are actually edible when harvested in their early egg stage before the odor develops, and they're considered a delicacy in some cultures.

children.name: Satyrus
children.description: Satyrus is a genus of stinkhorn fungi known for their distinctive wrinkled, brain-like appearance and strong, unpleasant odor. These unusual mushrooms emerge from underground egg-like structures and develop into grotesque, fleshy fruiting bodies that attract flies with their smell. They're part of nature's cleanup crew, decomposing organic matter in forest soils.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Satyrus are distinguished from other stinkhorns by their deeply wrinkled, convoluted surfaces that give them a brain-like or coral-like appearance, rather than the smooth caps or net-like structures found in other stinkhorn genera.
children.funFact: Despite their revolting smell to humans, stinkhorns like those in Satyrus are considered delicacies in some cultures and can be eaten when still in their egg stage before the odor develops.

children.description: Stinkhorns are a fascinating family of fungi that start their lives as egg-like structures buried in soil or leaf litter, then dramatically emerge as tall, often phallic-shaped fruiting bodies. These fungi are famous for their strong, unpleasant odor that smells like rotting meat or garbage. They produce their spores in a slimy, dark coating that attracts flies and other insects.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other mushrooms that release spores into the air, stinkhorns rely on their foul smell and slimy spore mass to attract insects that carry their spores away on their bodies. Their rapid growth from egg to full fruiting body in just hours or days is also distinctive.
children.funFact: Some stinkhorns can grow up to 8 inches tall in just a few hours, making them among the fastest-growing organisms on Earth!

children.name: Clathraceae
Clathrus
children.description: Cage stinkhorns are bizarre-looking fungi that emerge from underground egg-like structures to form intricate, cage-like or finger-like fruiting bodies. These fungi produce a foul-smelling, slimy spore mass that attracts flies and other insects, which help spread their spores to new locations. They belong to a group of fungi known for their unusual shapes and offensive odors.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other stinkhorn fungi that form simple stalks or phallus-like structures, cage stinkhorns create complex three-dimensional frameworks with multiple arms, columns, or latticed cages. Their spore-bearing surface is typically found on the inner surfaces of these elaborate structures rather than at a single tip.
children.funFact: The devil's-fingers stinkhorn was originally native to Australia and New Zealand but has spread to other continents, likely through human commerce, and can now be found growing in New England gardens and woodlands.

children.name: Pseudocolus
children.description: Pseudocolus is a small genus of stinkhorn fungi known for their unusual and striking appearance. These fungi produce fruiting bodies that emerge from underground egg-like structures and develop into distinctive orange or reddish structures with multiple arms or columns. Like other stinkhorns, they produce foul-smelling spores to attract flies and other insects for dispersal.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike typical stinkhorns that form single hollow stems, Pseudocolus species create multiple branched or latticed arms that spread outward from a central base. The arms are often brightly colored in orange or red hues and have a spongy, honeycomb-like texture.
children.funFact: The stinky squid gets its name from its tentacle-like arms and powerful rotting smell, but despite its oceanic nickname, it's actually a land-dwelling fungus that can appear almost overnight after heavy rains.

children.description: The Clathraceae are a family of distinctive fungi known for their bizarre, cage-like or latticed fruiting bodies that emerge from underground egg-like structures. These unusual mushrooms produce a foul-smelling slime that attracts flies and other insects, which help disperse their spores. They're part of the stinkhorn group and are among the most architecturally complex fungi you'll encounter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike typical mushrooms with caps and stems, Clathraceae fungi form intricate hollow cages, lattices, or arm-like structures that are often brightly colored in reds, oranges, or pinks. They all produce the characteristic rotting meat odor that gives stinkhorns their name.
children.funFact: These fungi can grow incredibly fast, with some species capable of pushing up through soil and reaching full size in just a few hours, earning them the nickname 'explosive fungi.'

children.name: Lysuraceae
Lysurus
children.description: Lysurus is a genus of distinctive fungi known as stinkhorns that produce tall, colorful fruiting bodies with a foul-smelling surface. These unusual mushrooms start as egg-like structures underground before rapidly expanding into their characteristic forms with finger-like or cage-like projections. The smelly, slimy coating on their surfaces attracts flies and other insects that help spread their spores.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other stinkhorn genera, Lysurus species typically have multiple arms or columns that branch out from a central stem, often forming star-like or cage-like patterns. Their fruiting bodies are usually brightly colored in reds, oranges, or pinks, making them quite eye-catching despite their unpleasant odor.
children.funFact: The lantern stinkhorn can grow from a small egg to its full height of up to 6 inches in just a few hours, making it one of the fastest-growing fungi in New England forests.

children.description: Lysuraceae is a family of fungi known for producing some of the most bizarre and striking mushrooms you'll encounter in New England's forests. These fungi are characterized by their unusual fruiting bodies that often have cage-like, latticed, or tentacle-like structures emerging from egg-shaped bases. They belong to the stinkhorn group and typically produce foul-smelling spores to attract flies and other insects for dispersal.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike typical mushrooms with caps and stems, Lysuraceae fungi have highly modified fruiting bodies with intricate geometric patterns, lattice-work structures, or finger-like projections. They emerge from distinctive white, egg-like structures and often emit strong, unpleasant odors.
children.funFact: The red cage fungus (Clathrus ruber) in this family looks like a bright red basketball made of latticed bars and smells like rotting meat to attract flies that help spread its spores.

children.description: Stinkhorns and allies are a fascinating group of fungi that produce some of nature's most unusual and eye-catching mushrooms. These fungi are famous for their strong, often unpleasant odors that smell like rotting meat or sewage, which they use to attract flies and other insects. Instead of releasing spores into the wind like most mushrooms, they rely on these insects to carry their spores to new locations.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike typical mushrooms, members of this group often have bizarre, sculptural shapes including cage-like structures, finger-like projections, or phallic forms. They produce a slimy, dark spore mass called gleba that creates their characteristic foul smell.
children.funFact: Some stinkhorn species can grow from egg to full size in just a few hours, with growth rates so rapid you can literally watch them emerge from the ground!

children.name: Gomphales
Gomphaceae
Ramaria
children.description: Coral fungi in the genus Ramaria are fascinating mushrooms that look remarkably like underwater coral reefs, with branching, finger-like structures rising from the forest floor. These colorful fungi break down organic matter in the soil and form beneficial partnerships with tree roots. They typically grow in clusters and can range from white and yellow to pink, red, and purple hues.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike typical mushrooms with caps and stems, Ramaria species have a distinctive coral-like branching pattern with multiple upright branches that fork repeatedly. Their spores are produced on the surface of these branches rather than on gills or in pores.
children.funFact: Some coral fungi can change color dramatically when bruised or cut, with certain species turning bright blue, green, or black when their tissue is damaged.

children.name: Turbinellus
children.description: Turbinellus is a small genus of distinctive funnel-shaped mushrooms that were once classified as chanterelles but are now recognized as their own group. These fungi are characterized by their trumpet-like caps that become deeply depressed or funnel-shaped with age, and their thick, fleshy stems that taper downward.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true chanterelles, Turbinellus mushrooms have true gills rather than shallow ridges, and they typically have much thicker, more robust stems. Their caps are also more deeply funnel-shaped and often covered in distinctive scales.
children.funFact: The Scaly Chanterelle can grow to impressive sizes, with some specimens reaching over a foot across, making it one of the largest mushrooms you might encounter in New England forests.

children.name: Gomphus
children.description: Gomphus is a genus of distinctive mushrooms known for their unusual funnel or trumpet-like shape. These fungi are characterized by their thick, fleshy fruiting bodies that often have a wrinkled or folded appearance, resembling clustered ears or trumpets emerging from the ground.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other mushrooms, Gomphus species have a smooth or only slightly wrinkled spore-bearing surface rather than gills or pores. Their thick, rubbery texture and distinctive funnel shape make them easy to distinguish from other forest fungi.
children.funFact: The common name 'pig's ears' comes from the mushroom's resemblance to the floppy, wrinkled ears of a pig, and despite their unusual appearance, they are considered choice edible mushrooms by foragers.

children.description: The Gomphaceae family includes distinctive fungi with club-shaped, vase-shaped, or coral-like fruiting bodies that often have a rubbery or firm texture. These fungi are typically found growing on the ground in forests, where they form partnerships with tree roots to help both the fungus and tree obtain nutrients.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many mushrooms with caps and stems, Gomphaceae fungi have unique shapes - some look like colorful coral branches, others like trumpets or vases. Their spores are produced on the outer surface of these structures rather than on gills or in pores.
children.funFact: Some coral fungi in this family can have dozens of branching tips, earning them nicknames like 'yellow coral' or 'pink-tipped coral fungus' based on their vibrant colors.

children.name: Clavariadelphaceae
Clavariadelphus
children.description: Clavariadelphus is a genus of distinctive club-shaped fungi that look more like small wooden clubs or pestle-shaped tools than typical mushrooms. These fungi lack the familiar cap-and-stem structure, instead growing as thick, fleshy, club-like structures that can range from a few inches to nearly a foot tall. They're saprophytic fungi, meaning they help decompose organic matter in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike the branched coral fungi they're often confused with, Clavariadelphus species are unbranched and club-shaped, typically with a thick, rounded or flattened top and a narrower base. They're also generally much larger and more robust than most other club fungi.
children.funFact: The truncated club fungus gets its name from its distinctive flat-topped appearance, as if someone took a knife and sliced off the top of the club!

children.description: Clavariadelphaceae is a small family of club-shaped fungi that look like simple coral or antlers growing from the ground. These fungi are saprobes, meaning they help decompose dead organic matter in forest soils, playing an important role in nutrient cycling. They produce their spores on the outer surface of their club-like fruiting bodies.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike branched coral fungi, members of this family typically have simple, unbranched club shapes that taper from a narrow base to a broader top. They can be distinguished from similar club fungi by their microscopic features and genetic characteristics.
children.funFact: Some species in this family were historically eaten as food and are sometimes called 'sweet tooth' fungi, though they're not commonly harvested today.

children.name: Lentariaceae
Lentaria
children.description: Lentaria is a small genus of coral fungi that produce distinctive branched, coral-like fruiting bodies. These fungi are saprobes, meaning they decompose dead organic matter in forest environments, playing an important role in nutrient cycling.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other coral fungi, Lentaria species have relatively simple, less densely branched structures with smooth spore-bearing surfaces rather than the more complex branching patterns seen in related genera.
children.funFact: The name 'Lentaria' comes from the Latin word meaning 'flexible' or 'pliant,' referring to the somewhat bendable nature of their coral-like branches.

children.description: Lentariaceae is a small family of coral fungi that produce branched, finger-like fruiting bodies resembling tiny antlers or coral formations. These fungi are wood decomposers that help break down dead organic matter in forest ecosystems. They typically grow on decaying logs, stumps, and woody debris in wooded areas.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their coral-like branching structure and their specific microscopic spore characteristics. Unlike some other coral fungi, Lentariaceae species have smooth, cylindrical branches that divide repeatedly in a distinctive pattern.
children.funFact: Despite their coral-like appearance, these fungi are more closely related to typical mushrooms than to ocean corals, and their branching structure maximizes surface area for spore release.

children.description: Gomphales is an order of fungi that includes some of the most distinctive and oddly-shaped mushrooms you'll encounter in New England forests. These fungi are known for their unusual forms, ranging from club-like structures to funnel-shaped caps, and they often have a tough, leathery texture rather than the soft, fleshy feel of typical mushrooms.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Gomphales are distinguished by their often irregular, non-standard mushroom shapes and their typically tough, rubbery texture. Unlike many other fungi, they frequently lack the classic cap-and-stem structure and instead grow as clubs, funnels, or coral-like branches.
children.funFact: The pig's ear mushroom (Gomphus clavatus) in this order gets its common name from its funnel-shaped cap that resembles the ear of a pig, and it's considered a delicacy in some parts of Europe.

children.name: Corticiales
Corticiaceae
Corticium
children.description: Corticium is a genus of crust fungi that form thin, smooth patches on dead wood, resembling paint or varnish spread across the surface. These fungi play an important role as decomposers in forest ecosystems, breaking down fallen logs and branches. All three New England species in this genus create distinctive flat, crusty growths that hug tightly to their wooden substrates.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other crust fungi, Corticium species typically have very smooth, waxy surfaces without visible pores, teeth, or other projecting structures. Their fruiting bodies are characteristically thin and closely adhere to the wood surface.
children.funFact: Despite their simple appearance, Corticium fungi are incredibly efficient recyclers - they can break down complex wood compounds like lignin and cellulose, gradually turning fallen trees back into soil nutrients.

children.name: Punctularia
children.description: Punctularia is a genus of bracket fungi that form thin, crust-like growths on dead hardwood trees and logs. These fungi are decomposers that help break down wood by secreting enzymes, playing an important role in forest nutrient cycling. Members of this genus are characterized by their relatively flat, spreading growth form that adheres closely to the wood surface.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Punctularia fungi can be distinguished from other crust fungi by their distinctive surface textures and coloration patterns. They often develop zones of different colors and have a somewhat fuzzy or velvety appearance when actively growing.
children.funFact: Despite having common names like 'Tree Bacon' and 'Purple Fuzz,' these fungi are not edible and get their colorful nicknames from their distinctive striped patterns and fuzzy textures that make them easy to spot on fallen logs.

children.name: Marchandiomyces
children.description: Marchandiomyces is a genus of fungi that forms distinctive coral-like or branched fruiting bodies. These small fungi are parasitic, growing on and deriving nutrients from liverworts, particularly those in the Marchantia genus.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most fungi that grow on decaying matter, Marchandiomyces species are specialized parasites that specifically target living liverworts. Their coral-like branching structure is also quite unique among fungi.
children.funFact: This genus was named after the liverwort genus Marchantia because of its highly specialized relationship with these ancient non-flowering plants.

children.name: Erythricium
children.description: Erythricium is a small genus of crust fungi that forms thin, smooth patches on decaying wood. These fungi are saprophytes, meaning they play an important role in forest ecosystems by breaking down dead organic matter and recycling nutrients back into the soil.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Erythricium fungi are distinguished by their smooth, waxy texture and bright orange to reddish coloration when fresh. Unlike many other crust fungi, they have a relatively simple structure without pores or teeth on their surface.
children.funFact: The name 'Erythricium' comes from the Greek word 'erythros' meaning red, referring to the distinctive reddish-orange color that makes these small fungi stand out against the brown bark they grow on.

children.name: Cytidia
children.description: Cytidia is a small genus of cup fungi that creates distinctive bright red, cup-shaped fruiting bodies on decaying wood. These tiny fungi are saprobic decomposers, helping break down dead organic matter in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Cytidia fungi are easily recognized by their brilliant scarlet-red coloration and small, shallow cup shape that typically measures less than an inch across.
children.funFact: Despite their tiny size, Cytidia fungi produce some of the most vibrant red colors found in the fungal kingdom, making them stand out dramatically against the brown bark they typically grow on.

children.name: Galzinia
children.description: Galzinia is a small genus of marine bryozoans, tiny colonial animals that form encrusting growths on hard surfaces underwater. These filter-feeding creatures create calcium carbonate skeletons and live in organized colonies where each individual animal (called a zooid) has a specialized role in the colony's survival.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Galzinia colonies form thin, sheet-like encrustations that spread across rocks, shells, and other hard substrates in marine environments. The colonies have a distinctive branching pattern and specialized defensive structures that help protect the feeding individuals.
children.funFact: Despite being animals, Galzinia colonies can look remarkably plant-like or coral-like as they spread across underwater surfaces, often being mistaken for algae or small corals by casual observers.

children.description: The Corticiaceae family consists of fungi that form thin, crust-like growths on dead wood, bark, and other surfaces. These fungi are decomposers that help break down organic matter in forest ecosystems, playing a crucial role in nutrient cycling. Most species in this family produce their spores on smooth or slightly textured surfaces that lie flat against their substrate.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike mushrooms with caps and stems, Corticiaceae fungi grow as flat, often colorful crusts that spread across surfaces like paint. They typically have smooth spore-bearing surfaces rather than pores, gills, or spines.
children.funFact: Some Corticiaceae species can change color dramatically as they age, starting as bright white or yellow crusts and eventually turning deep orange, red, or brown over time.

children.description: Corticiales are an order of fungi that primarily form thin, crust-like growths on wood and other surfaces. These fungi are typically found growing flat against tree bark, fallen logs, and dead wood, where they play important roles as decomposers in forest ecosystems. Most members of this group produce their spores on smooth or slightly wrinkled surfaces rather than in more complex structures like gills or pores.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike mushrooms with caps and stems, Corticiales fungi grow as flat, often papery crusts that spread across surfaces like paint or patches. Their spore-bearing surfaces are typically smooth to slightly wrinkled, lacking the distinct gills, pores, or other elaborate structures found in many other fungal groups.
children.funFact: Some Corticiales fungi can actually help protect trees from disease by competing with harmful pathogens for space and resources on bark surfaces, acting as natural biological shields.

children.name: Sebacinales
Sebacinaceae
Sebacina
children.description: Sebacina is a genus of jelly fungi that includes both coral-like and crust-forming species. These fungi are characterized by their gelatinous texture and ability to form symbiotic relationships with plant roots, helping trees and other plants absorb nutrients from the soil.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other jelly fungi, many Sebacina species can form both above-ground fruiting bodies and below-ground mycorrhizal networks. They're unique in combining a jelly-like consistency with diverse growth forms ranging from coral-like branches to flat crusts.
children.funFact: Some Sebacina species are master multitaskers - they can simultaneously help orchid seeds germinate, assist tree roots in nutrient uptake, and produce their own distinctive jelly-textured mushrooms above ground.

children.name: Helvellosebacina
children.description: Helvellosebacina is a small genus of fungi that forms partnerships with plant roots, helping them absorb nutrients from the soil. These microscopic fungi are part of the vast underground network that connects forest plants and trees, playing a crucial role in healthy ecosystem functioning.
children.distinguishingFeatures: This genus is characterized by its unique spore-bearing structures and specific molecular signatures that distinguish it from other root-associated fungi. Members of this group have distinctive cellular features that can only be properly identified through microscopic examination and DNA analysis.
children.funFact: Despite being invisible to the naked eye, Helvellosebacina fungi may be quietly supporting the growth of familiar New England forest plants right beneath our feet as we walk through the woods.

children.description: The Sebacinaceae family consists of small, inconspicuous fungi that form important partnerships with plant roots. These fungi help plants absorb nutrients from the soil while receiving sugars in return, creating mutually beneficial relationships called mycorrhizas. Most members of this family are rarely seen above ground, spending their lives as microscopic threads in the soil.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other fungi, Sebacinaceae members rarely produce visible mushrooms or fruiting bodies. Instead, they are primarily recognized by their unique spore structures and their specialized ability to form partnerships with a wide variety of plant species.
children.funFact: Some Sebacinaceae fungi can simultaneously partner with multiple different plant species at once, essentially creating underground communication networks that allow plants to share resources with each other.

children.description: Sebacinales are a group of fungi that form some of the most important partnerships with plants in nature. These fungi create mycorrhizal relationships, where they connect with plant roots and help them absorb water and nutrients from the soil in exchange for sugars. Most members of this order are microscopic and live entirely underground or within plant tissues.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other mycorrhizal fungi, Sebacinales can form partnerships with an incredibly wide range of plants, from orchids to trees to ferns. They also have unique cellular structures and don't produce the large, visible mushrooms that many other fungal groups create.
children.funFact: Many orchids absolutely depend on Sebacinales fungi to germinate from their tiny seeds - without these fungal partners, the orchid seeds cannot develop into mature plants.

children.name: Atheliales
Byssocorticiaceae
Byssocorticium
children.description: Byssocorticium is a small genus of crust fungi that form thin, flat patches on the surface of decaying wood. These fungi appear as whitish to grayish crusty growths that spread across bark and wood surfaces like a thin coating. They play an important role in forest ecosystems by helping to decompose dead wood and return nutrients to the soil.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their smooth, thin crusty texture and their tendency to form extensive flat patches rather than brackets or other fungal shapes. They have a distinctive microscopic structure with specialized cells that help identify them from other crust fungi.
children.funFact: Despite their plain appearance, Byssocorticium fungi are incredibly efficient decomposers that can break down some of the toughest components of wood, including lignin, which gives trees their strength and rigidity.

children.description: Byssocorticiaceae is a small family of fungi that form thin, cotton-like or web-like growths on decaying wood. These fungi are decomposers that help break down dead plant material in forest ecosystems. They typically appear as delicate, whitish films or patches spreading across the surface of rotting logs and branches.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their extremely thin, almost transparent fruiting bodies that look like fine cotton or silk threads stretched over wood surfaces. Unlike many other wood-decay fungi, they form very flat, film-like structures rather than brackets, shelves, or other three-dimensional forms.
children.funFact: Despite their delicate, almost ghostly appearance, these tiny fungi are incredibly efficient decomposers that can break down some of the toughest components of wood that other organisms can't digest.

children.name: Atheliaceae
Athelia
children.description: Athelia is a genus of tiny crust fungi that form thin, web-like patches on decaying wood and plant debris. These microscopic decomposers play an important role in breaking down organic matter in forest ecosystems, though they're often overlooked due to their extremely small size and inconspicuous appearance.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Athelia produce incredibly thin, almost transparent fruiting bodies that look like delicate cobwebs stretched across their substrate. Unlike many other crust fungi, they lack visible pores or gills and instead release spores from a smooth surface.
children.funFact: The cobweb duster gets its name from its striking resemblance to abandoned spider webs, and it's so thin that it can be nearly invisible unless you know exactly what to look for.

children.description: Atheliaceae is a family of crust fungi that form thin, flat patches on dead wood, bark, and other organic matter. These inconspicuous fungi appear as whitish, grayish, or brownish films that spread across surfaces like a thin coating. They play important roles as decomposers in forest ecosystems, breaking down dead plant material.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their extremely thin, crust-like growth form and smooth spore-bearing surfaces that lack pores, gills, or other obvious structures. They can only be reliably identified by examining their microscopic features.
children.funFact: Despite being nearly invisible to casual observers, Atheliaceae fungi are among the most common decomposers in forests, quietly working behind the scenes to recycle nutrients from fallen branches and bark.

children.name: Pilodermataceae
Piloderma
children.description: Piloderma is a genus of mycorrhizal fungi that form beneficial partnerships with tree roots, helping them absorb water and nutrients from the soil. These fungi are essential components of forest ecosystems, creating underground networks that connect different plants and facilitate nutrient exchange. They typically produce small, inconspicuous fruiting bodies that are rarely noticed by casual observers.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Piloderma species are characterized by their smooth, waxy-looking fruiting bodies and their specialized relationship with coniferous trees. They can be distinguished from other mycorrhizal fungi by their unique spore characteristics and the specific way they form connections with host plant roots.
children.funFact: These fungi act like a 'wood wide web,' creating underground networks that can span entire forests and allow trees to share resources and even send chemical warning signals to each other about pest attacks.

children.description: Pilodermataceae is a small family of fungi that forms important partnerships with tree roots, helping forests thrive through mycorrhizal relationships. These fungi live underground, creating extensive networks of thread-like structures that connect with plant roots to exchange nutrients. They play a crucial but often invisible role in forest ecosystems throughout New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their smooth, relatively simple fruiting bodies and their specific microscopic features, including distinctive spores and cellular structures that separate them from other mycorrhizal fungi families.
children.funFact: Despite being essential partners for many forest trees, Pilodermataceae fungi are rarely seen above ground since they do most of their important work in the hidden world beneath the forest floor.

children.description: Atheliales is an order of crust-like fungi that form thin, often nearly invisible layers on decaying wood, bark, and other organic matter. These fungi are important decomposers in forest ecosystems, breaking down dead plant material and recycling nutrients back into the soil. Most members of this group produce their spores on smooth or slightly textured surfaces that lie flat against their substrate.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other fungi, Atheliales typically form very thin, film-like fruiting bodies that can be difficult to spot with the naked eye. Their spore-bearing surfaces are usually smooth or have only minimal texture, lacking the pores, gills, or other prominent structures found in more conspicuous fungi.
children.funFact: Many Atheliales fungi are so thin and translucent that they're often called 'cobweb fungi' - you might walk past hundreds of them in the forest without ever noticing they're there!

children.name: Geastrales
Geastraceae
Geastrum
children.description: Earthstars are fascinating fungi that start as small, round puffballs buried in soil or leaf litter. As they mature, their outer layer splits and peels back like a star, revealing a central spore sac that releases powdery spores when disturbed. These woodland decomposers help break down organic matter while creating some of nature's most distinctive fungal displays.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike regular puffballs that remain round, earthstars have an outer layer that dramatically splits into pointed rays, creating their characteristic star shape. The number of rays and the presence of collars or other features help distinguish different earthstar species.
children.funFact: Earthstars are hygroscopic, meaning their rays curl inward during dry conditions to protect the spores, then unfurl again when moisture returns - acting like natural weather indicators!

children.name: Sphaerobolus
children.description: Cannonball fungi are tiny, remarkable fungi that have developed one of nature's most dramatic spore dispersal mechanisms. These small, cup-shaped fungi literally shoot their spores out like cannonballs, using built-up pressure to launch them distances of up to 15 feet. They're wood-decomposers that help break down dead organic matter in forests.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other fungi that release spores passively through wind or water, cannonball fungi actively catapult their spores using a specialized launching mechanism. The fruiting body turns itself inside-out with explosive force to fire a sticky mass of spores toward bright surfaces.
children.funFact: The cannonball fungus can launch its spores at speeds of up to 35 miles per hour, making it one of the fastest projectiles in the natural world relative to its size!

children.description: The Geastraceae family includes some of nature's most dramatic fungi, featuring species that undergo spectacular transformations when releasing their spores. These fungi start as round, enclosed structures but dramatically split open into star-like shapes or explosive mechanisms to disperse their reproductive material. Members of this family are found in forests and woodlands throughout New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other puffball-related fungi, Geastraceae members have outer walls that split and peel back in distinctive patterns - either forming pointed star rays (earthstars) or creating spring-loaded catapult mechanisms (cannonball fungi).
children.funFact: Cannonball fungi can actually shoot their spore-filled capsules up to 20 feet away with an audible 'pop' sound, making them some of the most explosive organisms in the forest!

children.description: Geastrales is an order of fascinating fungi commonly known as earthstars. These mushrooms start as round, enclosed structures that dramatically split open into star-like shapes, revealing a central spore sac in the middle. They're related to puffballs but have evolved this unique star-opening mechanism to help disperse their spores.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike regular puffballs that simply crack open, earthstars have an outer layer that splits into pointed rays that bend backward, creating their characteristic star appearance. This stellar opening mechanism sets them apart from all other fungi.
children.funFact: Some earthstars are hygroscopic, meaning their star-shaped rays will close up in dry weather and reopen when it's humid, acting like natural weather indicators!

children.name: Amylocorticiales
Amylocorticiaceae
Plicatura
children.description: Plicatura is a small genus of fungi that forms thin, crust-like growths on decaying wood. These fungi are characterized by their wrinkled or folded surface texture, which gives them their name from the Latin word meaning 'folded' or 'pleated.'
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other crust fungi, Plicatura species have distinctly wrinkled or crimped surfaces rather than smooth ones. They typically form thin, resupinate (lying flat against the substrate) fruiting bodies that can be white to cream-colored.
children.funFact: The crimped gill fungus gets its name from its distinctive wrinkled appearance that resembles crimped fabric or accordion folds, making it one of the more easily recognizable crust fungi in the forest.

children.name: Anomoloma
children.description: Anomoloma is a small genus of fungi that forms distinctive fruiting bodies with unique structural characteristics. These fungi are saprophytic, meaning they help decompose organic matter in forest ecosystems. The genus contains only a few known species worldwide, making it a relatively rare find for nature enthusiasts.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Anomoloma fungi are distinguished by their unusual spore-bearing structures and distinctive microscopic features that set them apart from other similar decomposer fungi. Their fruiting bodies have a characteristic appearance that helps mycologists identify them in the field.
children.funFact: The name 'Anomoloma' literally means 'irregular border,' referring to the unusual edge characteristics of these fungi's fruiting structures.

children.description: Amylocorticiaceae is a family of fungi that produce thin, crust-like fruiting bodies that spread across the surface of decaying wood. These fungi are decomposers that help break down dead trees and branches in forest ecosystems. Most species in this family form smooth or slightly wrinkled patches on bark and wood surfaces.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their corticioid (crust-like) growth form and specific microscopic features including particular spore shapes and hyphal structures. They can be distinguished from similar crust fungi by their unique combination of cellular characteristics visible under a microscope.
children.funFact: Despite their inconspicuous appearance as thin crusts on wood, these fungi play a crucial role as nature's recyclers, breaking down tough wood fibers and returning nutrients to the forest soil.

children.description: Amylocorticiales is a small order of fungi that forms thin, crust-like patches on decaying wood. These fungi are important decomposers in forest ecosystems, breaking down dead wood and returning nutrients to the soil. They typically grow as flat, spreading layers that closely adhere to the surface of logs and branches.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this order are characterized by their corticioid (crust-like) growth form and specific microscopic features including particular spore shapes and cellular structures. They can be distinguished from other crust fungi by their unique combination of chemical reactions and DNA sequences.
children.funFact: Despite being relatively recently described as a distinct order, these inconspicuous fungi have likely been quietly decomposing New England's forests for millions of years, often going unnoticed by casual observers due to their subtle, bark-like appearance.

children.name: Gloeophyllales
Gloeophyllaceae
Gloeophyllum
children.description: Gloeophyllum is a genus of wood-decomposing fungi that specialize in breaking down dead coniferous wood. These bracket fungi form shelf-like or bracket-shaped fruiting bodies that grow directly from the surface of rotting logs and stumps. They play an important ecological role by recycling nutrients from dead conifer trees back into forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other bracket fungi, Gloeophyllum species have a distinctive undersurface with gill-like or maze-like pores rather than simple round pores. They also specifically target coniferous wood and can cause brown rot, which breaks down cellulose while leaving behind brown lignin.
children.funFact: Gloeophyllum fungi are so efficient at decomposing conifer wood that they can actually digest the toxic compounds that conifers produce to defend themselves, making them specialized recyclers in coniferous forests.

children.name: Neolentinus
children.description: Neolentinus is a small genus of wood-decomposing fungi that grow on coniferous trees, particularly pines and other softwoods. These mushrooms are characterized by their tough, leathery texture and their ability to break down lignin in dead wood, playing an important role in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Neolentinus have distinctive gills that run partway down the stem and tough, fibrous caps that can persist for months. They differ from similar wood-dwelling fungi by their combination of decurrent gills and exceptionally durable fruiting bodies.
children.funFact: The common name 'Trainwrecker' for Neolentinus lepideus comes from its ability to cause serious structural damage to railroad ties and wooden bridges by breaking down the wood's lignin.

children.name: Boreostereum
children.description: Boreostereum is a small genus of wood-decay fungi that forms flat, crust-like growths on dead hardwood trees. These fungi are decomposers that help break down fallen logs and branches in forest ecosystems. They produce their spores from a smooth, waxy surface that spreads across the wood substrate.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Boreostereum can be distinguished from other crust fungi by its distinctive radial, fan-like growth pattern and its smooth, waxy spore-bearing surface that lacks the pores or teeth found in many related wood-decay fungi.
children.funFact: Despite being a relatively obscure fungus, Boreostereum radiatum has been found to have potential antimicrobial properties and has been studied for possible medical applications.

children.description: The Gloeophyllaceae are a family of wood-decay fungi that specialize in breaking down dead wood, particularly conifers. These tough, bracket-like fungi are excellent decomposers that play a crucial role in forest ecosystems by recycling nutrients from fallen trees and branches. Most members of this family produce distinctive shelf-like or bracket fruiting bodies that persist for long periods.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other bracket fungi, Gloeophyllaceae members typically have a lamellate (gilled) or maze-like pore surface rather than simple round pores. They also tend to cause brown rot in wood, breaking down cellulose while leaving behind the brown lignin framework.
children.funFact: Some Gloeophyllum species are so effective at breaking down wood that they're considered serious timber pests, capable of destroying wooden structures like railroad ties and building lumber even in relatively dry conditions.

children.description: Gloeophyllales is a small order of wood-decay fungi that are specialized decomposers of dead wood. These fungi are characterized by their ability to cause brown rot, breaking down the cellulose in wood while leaving behind the brown lignin. They play an important ecological role in forest ecosystems by recycling nutrients from fallen trees and branches.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this order are distinguished by their brown rot decay pattern and their typically bracket-like or shelf-like fruiting bodies that grow directly from dead wood. Unlike white rot fungi, they selectively decompose cellulose while leaving the woody lignin largely intact.
children.funFact: Some species in this order can cause significant structural damage to wooden buildings and are considered important wood-destroying fungi in construction, making them both ecologically beneficial and economically problematic.

children.name: Stereopsidales
Stereopsidaceae
Stereopsis
children.description: Stereopsis is a small genus of crust fungi that forms thin, flat growths on decaying wood. These fungi play an important role in forest ecosystems by helping to decompose fallen logs and branches, returning nutrients to the soil.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus produce distinctive spore-bearing structures that appear as smooth, waxy crusts on wood surfaces, often with characteristic coloration that can help distinguish between species.
children.funFact: The genus name Stereopsis comes from Greek words meaning 'solid appearance,' referring to the firm, crust-like texture of these fungi when they're actively growing.

children.description: Stereopsidaceae is a small family of crust fungi that grow as thin, spreading patches on decaying wood. These fungi form bracket-like or resupinate (lying flat) fruiting bodies that help decompose fallen logs and branches in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their smooth to slightly wrinkled spore-bearing surface and their tendency to form overlapping, shelf-like structures on wood substrates.
children.funFact: Despite being relatively inconspicuous, these fungi play a crucial role as nature's recyclers, breaking down tough wood fibers and returning nutrients to the forest soil.

children.description: Stereopsidales is a small order of mosses that includes just one family found in New England. These are tiny, often overlooked mosses that typically grow in cushions or mats on soil, rocks, or decaying wood in forest environments.
