children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this order are characterized by their small size, simple leaf structure, and distinctive spore capsules that often have a unique opening mechanism for releasing spores.
children.funFact: Despite being incredibly small and easily missed by casual observers, these mosses play an important role in forest ecosystems by helping to retain moisture and providing microhabitats for even tinier organisms.

children.name: Xenasmatellales
Xenasmatellaceae
Xenasmatella
children.description: Xenasmatella is a small genus of fungi that produces thin, web-like fruiting bodies on decaying wood. These delicate fungi create gossamer-thin layers that spread across rotting logs and branches, appearing almost like cobwebs made of fungal tissue.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other wood-decomposing fungi, Xenasmatella species form extremely thin, translucent fruiting bodies that lack the typical mushroom shape or bracket form of most wood fungi.
children.funFact: The yellow cobweb fungus gets its common name from its remarkably thin, web-like appearance that can be so delicate it's easily mistaken for actual spider webs at first glance.

children.description: Xenasmatellaceae is a small family of wood-decomposing fungi that live as parasites or decomposers on other fungi, particularly wood-decay species. These tiny organisms form thin, crust-like growths on dead wood where other fungi are already present. They play a specialized role in forest ecosystems by recycling nutrients from both wood and other fungal matter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most wood-decay fungi that directly break down wood cellulose, members of this family are mycoparasites that primarily feed on other fungi. They produce distinctive microscopic structures and have a unique lifestyle that sets them apart from typical wood-decomposing species.
children.funFact: This entire family contains only one genus with very few species worldwide, making it one of the rarest groups of fungi you might encounter in New England forests.

children.description: Xenasmatellales is a small order of fungi that includes species forming thin, web-like or crust-like growths on decaying wood. These fungi are part of the basidiomycetes group and play an important role in breaking down dead organic matter in forest ecosystems. They are typically found growing on the undersides of fallen logs and branches.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this order are characterized by their extremely thin, almost transparent fruiting bodies that form delicate, web-like sheets. Unlike many other wood-decomposing fungi, they produce very inconspicuous structures that can be easily overlooked.
children.funFact: This order is so rare and little-studied that it contains only one family worldwide, making it one of the most exclusive groups in the fungal kingdom.

children.name: Tremellodendropsidales
Tremellodendropsidaceae
Tremellodendropsis
children.description: Tremellodendropsis is a genus of jelly fungi that form distinctive coral-like branches extending upward from the ground. These fungi have a unique gelatinous texture that becomes firm when dry, and they grow on decaying wood in forest environments. Unlike true corals, these are terrestrial fungi that play an important role in decomposing organic matter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: This genus is distinguished from other jelly fungi by its upright, branched coral-like growth form rather than the typical ear-shaped or bracket-like structures of most jelly fungi. The branching pattern and terrestrial habitat make it easily recognizable among gelatinous fungi.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'coral fungi,' Tremellodendropsis species are actually more closely related to ear fungi and other jelly fungi than to the true coral fungi, showing how similar forms can evolve independently in different fungal lineages.

children.description: Tremellodendropsidaceae is a small family of jelly fungi that forms unique coral-like or branched fruiting bodies. These fungi have a distinctive gelatinous texture when fresh and are saprobic, meaning they decompose dead organic matter in forest environments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other jelly fungi that form ear-shaped or brain-like masses, members of this family create distinctive branched, coral-like structures that somewhat resemble tiny antlers or sea coral.
children.funFact: This family is so rare and distinctive that it contains only one genus worldwide, making every specimen a special find for mycologists and nature enthusiasts.

children.description: Tremellodendropsidales is a small order of jelly fungi that forms coral-like or branched fruiting bodies. These fungi have a gelatinous texture and are saprophytic, meaning they decompose dead organic matter in forest environments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other jelly fungi, members of this order have distinctly branched, coral-like structures rather than brain-like or ear-shaped forms. They also have unique microscopic features in their spore-bearing structures that set them apart from related groups.
children.funFact: This order is so rare and poorly studied that it contains only a single family worldwide, making it one of the most exclusive groups in the fungal kingdom.

children.name: Hysterangiales
Phallogastraceae
Phallogaster
children.description: Phallogaster is a genus of small, pouch-like fungi that forms underground fruiting bodies. These unusual fungi develop as hollow, sac-shaped structures that remain beneath the soil surface for most of their lifecycle, only occasionally pushing through to the surface when mature.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most mushrooms that form caps and stems above ground, Phallogaster species develop as enclosed, balloon-like pouches that typically stay hidden underground until they're ready to release their spores.
children.funFact: The name 'Phallogaster' literally means 'phallus stomach,' referring to its unusual pouch-like shape that's quite different from typical mushroom forms.

children.description: Phallogastraceae is a small family of unusual fungi that produce their spores inside enclosed, egg-like structures. These fungi are related to stinkhorns but remain mostly underground or hidden in soil and leaf litter. They represent an evolutionary link between more familiar mushroom forms and the bizarre stinkhorn fungi.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike their stinkhorn relatives that emerge above ground with foul-smelling spore masses, members of this family keep their spores contained within closed, often irregularly-shaped fruiting bodies that remain largely concealed.
children.funFact: These mysterious fungi are so rare and secretive that many species were only recently discovered, and scientists are still learning about their life cycles and ecological roles.

children.description: Hysterangiales is an order of fungi that includes species with unusual fruiting bodies that develop underground or partially buried in soil. These fungi produce their spores in enclosed chambers rather than releasing them directly into the air like many other mushrooms.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike typical mushrooms that release spores from gills or pores, members of this order keep their spores enclosed within the fruiting body until maturity. They often rely on animals to disperse their spores rather than wind dispersal.
children.funFact: Some fungi in this order produce fruiting bodies that smell like rotting meat or other strong odors to attract insects and animals that help spread their spores.

children.name: Trechisporales
Hydnodontaceae
Trechispora
children.description: Trechispora is a genus of small, crust-like fungi that form thin, whitish patches on decaying wood. These fungi are part of the natural decomposition process in forests, breaking down dead organic matter and recycling nutrients back into the ecosystem. They produce tiny spores from microscopic structures on their surface.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Trechispora fungi are recognized by their distinctive spores which have unique ornamental patterns and projections when viewed under a microscope. Unlike many other crust fungi, they have a particular spore shape that helps mycologists identify them.
children.funFact: Despite being nearly invisible to casual observers, Trechispora fungi play a crucial role as nature's recyclers, quietly working to break down fallen branches and logs in New England's forests.

children.description: Hydnodontaceae is a small family of wood-decomposing fungi that break down dead organic matter in forest ecosystems. These fungi typically form thin, crust-like growths on decaying wood and have microscopic spores with distinctive spiny or warty surfaces. They play an important role as decomposers, helping to recycle nutrients back into the forest soil.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their unique spore ornamentation, featuring spines, warts, or other surface projections that are visible under a microscope. They also have a specific type of hyphal structure and typically grow as resupinate (crust-like) fungi on wood substrates.
children.funFact: Despite being tiny and often overlooked, these fungi are nature's recyclers, capable of breaking down tough wood fibers that many other organisms cannot digest, making them essential partners in maintaining healthy forest ecosystems.

children.description: Trechisporales is a small order of fungi that includes species with unique spore-bearing structures. These fungi typically produce their spores on specialized surfaces that can appear smooth, wrinkled, or with small tooth-like projections. Most members of this group are decomposers that help break down dead wood and organic matter in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Trechisporales are distinguished by their distinctive spore-producing surfaces and specific microscopic characteristics of their spores. They differ from other fungal orders in their particular combination of structural features and genetic relationships.
children.funFact: Despite being a diverse group worldwide, Trechisporales is represented by only a single species in New England, making it one of the rarest fungal orders in the region.

children.name: Sistotremastrales
Sistotremastraceae
Sertulicium
children.description: Sertulicium is a genus of marine hydrozoans, which are small colonial animals related to jellyfish and corals. These creatures form branching, plant-like colonies that attach to rocks, shells, or other hard surfaces on the ocean floor. Each colony is made up of many tiny individual polyps that work together to capture food and reproduce.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Sertulicium colonies have a distinctive feathery or fern-like branching pattern with small cup-shaped structures (called hydrotheca) arranged along the branches where individual polyps live.
children.funFact: Despite looking like delicate underwater plants, Sertulicium colonies are actually made up of hundreds of tiny animals that can retract into their protective cups when threatened.

children.description: Sistotremastraceae is a small family of crust fungi that form thin, flat patches on decaying wood. These fungi are part of the corticioid group, meaning they grow as smooth or wrinkled crusts rather than forming mushrooms with caps and stems. They play an important role in breaking down dead wood in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their smooth to slightly wrinkled crust-like growth form and their microscopic spore-bearing structures. Unlike many other crust fungi, they tend to have a more delicate, film-like appearance when growing on wood surfaces.
children.funFact: Despite being tiny and easily overlooked, these crust fungi are essential decomposers that help recycle nutrients from fallen logs back into the forest soil.

children.description: Sistotremastrales is a small order of fungi that includes species with distinctive crust-like or bracket-shaped fruiting bodies. These fungi are decomposers that help break down dead wood in forest ecosystems, playing an important role in nutrient cycling.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this order are characterized by their unique spore-bearing surface structure and specific microscopic features that distinguish them from other wood-decomposing fungi.
children.funFact: This order is so specialized and uncommon that only one species from this entire group has been found in all of New England!

children.name: Tremellales
Tremellaceae
Tremella
children.description: Tremella fungi are distinctive jelly-like mushrooms that have a gelatinous, translucent appearance when fresh and moist. These fascinating organisms are parasitic fungi that live on other fungi, particularly lichens and wood-decay fungi, creating colorful, wobbly masses that can look like brain coral or folded gelatin.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other jelly fungi, Tremella species have a uniquely folded, brain-like or leafy structure rather than simple blobs, and they specifically parasitize other fungi rather than decomposing wood directly.
children.funFact: The famous 'witch's butter' gets its spooky name from European folklore, where people believed witches would throw this bright yellow, gelatinous fungus at houses to cast spells.

children.description: Tremellaceae is a family of jelly fungi that produce distinctive gelatinous, translucent fruiting bodies that feel soft and rubbery to the touch. These fungi are saprobic decomposers that break down dead wood and organic matter in forest environments. Most species in this family have a characteristic jelly-like or brain-like appearance when fresh and moist.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other fungi, Tremellaceae species have a unique gelatinous texture due to their specialized cell walls that can absorb large amounts of water. They also have a distinctive spore-producing structure called a septate basidium that divides the spores into separate compartments.
children.funFact: Many Tremellaceae fungi can completely dehydrate into hard, shriveled masses during dry periods, then quickly rehydrate and return to their full jelly-like form when moisture returns.

children.name: Phaeotremellaceae
Phaeotremella
children.description: Phaeotremella is a genus of jelly fungi that form distinctive brown to yellowish-brown, gelatinous fruiting bodies on decaying wood. These fungi have a characteristically folded, brain-like or leafy appearance and feel rubbery or jelly-like to the touch. They are saprophytes, meaning they help decompose dead wood and return nutrients to the forest ecosystem.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other jelly fungi, Phaeotremella species are consistently brown to amber in color and have a more distinctly folded, leafy structure rather than being smooth or simply lobed. They also tend to be larger and more persistent than many other gelatinous fungi.
children.funFact: These fungi can actually shrink down to almost nothing during dry periods and then rehydrate and expand back to their full size when moisture returns, allowing them to survive harsh weather conditions.

children.description: Phaeotremellaceae is a family of jelly fungi that produce soft, gelatinous fruiting bodies with a distinctive brain-like or folded appearance. These fungi are saprobic decomposers that break down dead wood, particularly hardwood trees, playing an important role in forest nutrient cycling. They typically appear as brownish, yellowish, or orange-colored masses that feel rubbery or jelly-like to the touch.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other jelly fungi families, Phaeotremellaceae members have a characteristic folded or brain-like surface texture and tend to be brownish or yellowish in color rather than clear or brightly colored. Their spores are produced on club-shaped cells called basidia that have distinctive cross-walls.
children.funFact: These fungi can dry up completely during drought conditions and then rehydrate and resume growth when moisture returns, earning them the nickname 'resurrection fungi.'

children.name: Naemateliaceae
Naematelia
children.description: Naematelia is a genus of jelly fungi that form brain-like or ear-shaped fruiting bodies with a distinctive gelatinous, rubbery texture. These fungi are parasites that grow on other fungi, particularly bracket fungi and wood-decay fungi, rather than directly on wood or other substrates. They can be found year-round, even surviving freezing temperatures by becoming dormant and rehydrating when conditions improve.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other jelly fungi, Naematelia species are parasitic on other fungi rather than being wood decomposers themselves. Their fruiting bodies have a more brain-like, convoluted appearance compared to the smoother surfaces of many other gelatinous fungi.
children.funFact: These remarkable fungi can completely dehydrate during dry periods, shrinking to a fraction of their size, then quickly rehydrate and resume growth when moisture returns!

children.description: Naemateliaceae is a family of jelly fungi that produce distinctive gelatinous fruiting bodies with a brain-like or coral-like appearance. These fungi are saprophytes, meaning they feed on dead organic matter, particularly decaying wood where they help break down cellulose and other plant materials. They're commonly found growing on fallen logs, dead branches, and other woody debris in forests.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their uniquely gelatinous, translucent fruiting bodies that have a distinctly brain-like or coral-like folded surface texture. Unlike other jelly fungi, they tend to have more complex, convoluted shapes rather than simple blob-like forms.
children.funFact: These fungi can actually survive being completely dried out and will spring back to life when rehydrated by rain, making them remarkably resilient to drought conditions.

children.name: Biatoropsis
children.description: Biatoropsis is a small genus of parasitic lichens that specifically target and grow on other lichens, particularly beard lichens (Usnea species). These tiny organisms are parasites rather than the typical lichen partnership, meaning they derive nutrients from their host lichens instead of photosynthesizing on their own.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most lichens that form partnerships between fungi and algae, Biatoropsis species are parasitic fungi that attack and feed on existing lichen partnerships. They form small, disk-shaped fruiting bodies on the surface of their host lichens.
children.funFact: The single New England species, Biatoropsis usnearum, is so specialized that it almost exclusively parasitizes beard lichens, making it a "parasite of a partnership" since lichens themselves are already collaborative organisms.

children.description: Tremellales is an order of jelly fungi that produce soft, gelatinous, often translucent fruiting bodies. These fungi are typically found growing on decaying wood, where they appear as wobbly, brain-like or ear-shaped masses that feel rubbery to the touch. Many species in this group are parasites of other fungi, living off their hosts while producing their own distinctive fruiting structures.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other fungi, Tremellales have a unique jelly-like texture due to their gelatinous cell walls and high water content. Their fruiting bodies can often bounce back to their original shape after being compressed, and many species become nearly invisible when dried but quickly rehydrate after rain.
children.funFact: Some Tremellales fungi, like the popular "wood ear" mushrooms, are considered delicacies in Asian cuisine and are prized for their unique chewy texture and ability to absorb flavors from surrounding ingredients.

children.name: Filobasidiales
Filobasidiaceae
Syzygospora
children.description: Syzygospora is a genus of tiny parasitic fungi that live on other mushrooms and fungi. These microscopic organisms don't form the typical mushroom structures we're familiar with, but instead create small, often unnoticeable growths on their fungal hosts.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike typical mushrooms, Syzygospora species are parasitic fungi that specifically target other fungi as their hosts. They produce their spores directly from simple structures rather than from gills, pores, or other complex fruiting body parts.
children.funFact: The name 'Syzygospora' comes from Greek words meaning 'yoked spores,' referring to how their spores are often joined together in pairs.

children.description: Filobasidiaceae is a family of microscopic fungi that includes yeasts and small, simple fungi that often live as parasites or decomposers. These fungi are characterized by their unique spore-producing structures and their ability to reproduce both sexually and asexually. They play important ecological roles in breaking down organic matter and cycling nutrients through ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family produce distinctive spores called basidiospores on specialized structures, and many species have a yeast-like growth form rather than forming typical mushroom structures. They are distinguished from other fungal families by their specific genetic characteristics and spore development patterns.
children.funFact: Despite being microscopic and often overlooked, some Filobasidiaceae fungi can cause plant diseases, while others are beneficial decomposers that help recycle nutrients in forest soils.

children.description: Filobasidiales is a small order of microscopic fungi that includes yeasts and yeast-like organisms. These fungi are characterized by their simple cellular structure and their ability to reproduce through budding or forming small spores called basidiospores.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other basidiomycete fungi that form mushrooms or other visible fruiting bodies, members of Filobasidiales typically exist as single-celled yeasts or form simple, thread-like structures.
children.funFact: Despite being microscopic, these fungi play important ecological roles as decomposers and can sometimes be found living on plant surfaces or in soil.

children.name: Cystofilobasidiales
Cystofilobasidiaceae
Cystofilobasidium
children.description: Cystofilobasidium is a genus of yeasts that live as parasites or symbionts on plants, particularly feeding on sap and other plant fluids. These microscopic fungi are part of the larger group of basidiomycete yeasts, which reproduce through specialized spores called basidiospores.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other yeasts, Cystofilobasidium species form distinctive thick-walled resting cells called chlamydospores and produce their spores on club-shaped structures called basidia.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'sap yeast,' Cystofilobasidium macerans doesn't just passively feed on plant sap - it can actually help break down plant cell walls, making it both a decomposer and a plant associate.

children.description: Cystofilobasidiaceae is a small family of yeasts that are part of the larger group of fungi. These microscopic organisms are typically found living in soil, on plant surfaces, or in aquatic environments where they play important roles in nutrient cycling. Unlike many familiar fungi that form mushrooms or molds, members of this family exist primarily as single-celled yeasts.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their unique cell wall composition and specific reproductive structures called basidia. They can be distinguished from other yeast families by their particular genetic markers and the way they reproduce sexually.
children.funFact: Despite being microscopic and often overlooked, yeasts in this family can survive in extreme cold conditions and have been found thriving in Arctic soils and glacial environments.

children.description: Cystofilobasidiales is an order of yeasts that includes species capable of surviving in extremely cold environments, including Antarctic soils and glacial ice. These are single-celled fungi that reproduce by budding and can form distinctive balloon-like structures called cystofilobasidia. They play important roles in cold-climate ecosystems where few other microorganisms can survive.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other yeasts, members of this order are particularly well-adapted to freezing temperatures and can remain active at temperatures that would kill most fungi. They also have a unique cell structure with thick walls that help them survive harsh environmental conditions.
children.funFact: Some species in this order have been found living in 15,000-year-old glacial ice, essentially frozen in time yet still viable when thawed!

children.name: Dacrymycetales
Dacrymycetaceae
Dacrymyces
children.description: Dacrymyces is a genus of small, gelatinous fungi that form bright orange to yellow, jelly-like growths on decaying wood. These fungi are commonly called jelly fungi because of their distinctive rubbery, translucent texture that becomes more obvious when wet. All species in this genus are saprobic, meaning they feed on dead organic matter and help decompose fallen logs and branches.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Dacrymyces can be distinguished from other jelly fungi by their bright orange to yellow colors and their preference for growing on coniferous wood. Unlike some other gelatinous fungi, Dacrymyces species typically have a more firm, less watery consistency.
children.funFact: These jelly fungi can completely dry out and become hard and shriveled during dry periods, then quickly rehydrate and return to their plump, gelatinous form when moisture returns.

children.name: Calocera
children.description: Calocera is a genus of distinctive jelly fungi that produce bright yellow or orange, gelatinous fruiting bodies with branched, antler-like or club-shaped forms. These fascinating fungi grow on decaying wood and have a rubbery, jelly-like texture that can bounce back when pressed. Despite their unusual appearance, they play an important role in forest ecosystems by decomposing dead wood.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other jelly fungi, Calocera species have a distinctly branched, coral-like or antler-like growth pattern and are typically bright yellow to orange in color. Their fruiting bodies are more upright and structured compared to the blob-like forms of many other gelatinous fungi.
children.funFact: When fresh, Calocera fungi are so gelatinous and elastic that you can bend and twist them without breaking, but they become hard and brittle when they dry out.

children.name: Guepiniopsis
children.description: Jelly Cones are small, distinctive fungi that produce gelatinous, cone or cup-shaped fruiting bodies. These fungi typically grow on decaying wood and have a translucent, rubbery texture that gives them their common name.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other jelly fungi that form irregular blobs or brackets, Jelly Cones create distinct cone or trumpet-shaped structures. Their firm yet flexible texture and defined shape make them easily recognizable among the gelatinous fungi.
children.funFact: The Trumpet Jelly Cup can actually change its shape throughout the day as it absorbs and releases moisture from the air, expanding when humid and shrinking when dry.

children.name: Femsjonia
children.description: Femsjonia is a small genus of jelly fungi that produce gelatinous, often cup-shaped or cushion-like fruiting bodies. These fungi are saprophytes that help decompose dead wood, playing an important role in forest ecosystems by breaking down organic matter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Femsjonia are distinguished from other jelly fungi by their distinctive cup or disc-shaped fruiting bodies and their specific microscopic spore characteristics.
children.funFact: The genus Femsjonia was named after Norwegian mycologist Egil Femsjon, and these fascinating fungi can actually absorb water and swell up when it rains, then shrink back down during dry periods.

children.name: Dacryopinax
children.description: Dacryopinax is a genus of small, distinctive jelly fungi that produce bright orange to coral-colored fruiting bodies. These fungi are saprobic, meaning they decompose dead organic matter, particularly rotting wood in forest environments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their unique spiny or coral-like appearance, with multiple branched projections that give them a distinctly different look from other jelly fungi that are typically smooth or brain-like.
children.funFact: Despite their delicate, jelly-like appearance, Dacryopinax fungi can survive freezing temperatures and will resume growing when conditions warm up again.

children.description: The Dacrymycetaceae are a family of jelly fungi that produce soft, gelatinous fruiting bodies with a distinctive rubbery or jelly-like texture. These fungi are saprobic, meaning they feed on dead organic matter, particularly decaying wood where they play an important role in forest decomposition. Most species in this family appear as small, colorful blobs or irregular masses on rotting logs and branches.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other jelly fungi, members of Dacrymycetaceae have a unique spore-producing structure called a tuning-fork basidium, which splits into two prongs each bearing a single spore. Their fruiting bodies are typically more persistent and less watery than other gelatinous fungi.
children.funFact: Some species in this family, like certain Calocera fungi, are bright orange or yellow and can be mistaken for small coral fungi, but their jelly-like texture gives them away when touched.

children.description: Dacrymycetales are small, colorful fungi that produce distinctive jelly-like or gelatinous fruiting bodies, often appearing bright orange or yellow. These fungi are wood decomposers, playing an important role in breaking down dead branches and logs in forest ecosystems. They're commonly called 'jelly fungi' because of their soft, bouncy texture when fresh.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other jelly fungi, members of Dacrymycetales have unique forked spores (called tuning-fork spores) that split into two parts. Their spores are also produced on club-shaped structures rather than in enclosed chambers.
children.funFact: The bright orange 'witch's butter' (Dacrymyces chrysospermus) can appear to magically materialize on dead wood after rain, swelling from nearly invisible dried remnants to plump, jelly-like blobs overnight.

children.name: Bartheletiales
Bartheletiaceae
Bartheletia
children.description: Bartheletia is a genus of microscopic fungi that parasitizes ginkgo trees, creating distinctive circular spots on the leaves. These tiny organisms are part of a specialized group of plant pathogens that have evolved specifically to live on ginkgo foliage. Despite their small size, they play an important role in the ecosystem of these ancient trees.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Bartheletia is distinguished by its highly specialized relationship with ginkgo trees and the characteristic circular leaf spots it produces. Unlike many other leaf-spotting fungi, this genus appears to be uniquely adapted to ginkgo hosts.
children.funFact: This genus represents one of the few known fungal parasites of the ancient ginkgo tree, which has survived virtually unchanged for over 200 million years.

children.description: Bartheletiaceae is a small family of fungi that includes just one genus, Bartheletia. These are microscopic fungi that live as parasites or symbionts with other organisms, typically found in soil or decaying organic matter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their unique spore-forming structures and specific cellular arrangements that distinguish them from other fungal families. They have distinctive microscopic features that can only be properly identified through detailed laboratory examination.
children.funFact: This entire fungal family is so rare and understudied that it contains only a single genus with very few known species worldwide, making any discovery of Bartheletiaceae fungi quite special for mycologists.

children.description: Bartheletiales is a small order of fungi that includes some of the most unusual and primitive members of the fungal kingdom. These fungi are characterized by their simple structure and ancient evolutionary lineage, representing an early branch in fungal evolution.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this order have distinctive spore-producing structures and lack many of the complex features found in more advanced fungi. They are distinguished by their unique cellular organization and reproductive methods.
children.funFact: This order is so rare and poorly understood that it contains only one family and very few known species worldwide, making any discovery of these fungi particularly exciting for mycologists.

children.name: Pucciniales
Pucciniaceae
Puccinia
children.description: Orange-Yellow Rusts are a large group of plant parasitic fungi that create distinctive orange, yellow, or reddish pustules on the leaves and stems of their host plants. These fungi are highly specialized, with each species typically infecting only specific types of plants, from grasses and wildflowers to trees and garden plants. They spread through microscopic spores that can travel on wind currents to find new host plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other fungi, Puccinia species often require two completely different host plants to complete their complex life cycle, alternating between them in different seasons. Their characteristic bright orange to yellow spore-filled pustules that erupt through plant surfaces make them easily recognizable in the field.
children.funFact: Some rust fungi in this genus have incredibly complex life cycles with up to five different spore stages, and many species can overwinter as spores in leaf litter, then infect new plants when conditions are right in spring.

children.name: Uromyces
children.description: Uromyces is a genus of rust fungi that are specialized plant parasites, creating distinctive orange, yellow, or brown pustules on their host plants. These fungi have complex life cycles and are highly host-specific, meaning each species typically infects only one type of plant or closely related plant species. You might spot them as colorful spots or patches on leaves, stems, or other plant parts throughout New England's forests and fields.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other rust fungi that require two different host plants to complete their life cycle, most Uromyces species can complete their entire life cycle on a single host plant. They produce characteristic single-celled spores (called teliospores) that distinguish them from other rust genera that produce multi-celled spores.
children.funFact: The Jack-in-the-Pulpit Rust creates such distinctive orange spots on its host that experienced naturalists can often identify the presence of jack-in-the-pulpit plants from a distance just by spotting the bright rust pustules on the leaves!

children.description: The Pucciniaceae family consists of rust fungi that are specialized plant parasites, creating those distinctive orange, yellow, or reddish pustules you might notice on leaves, stems, and other plant parts. These fungi have complex life cycles that often require multiple host plants to complete their development, making them fascinating examples of biological interdependence.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other fungi, rust fungi in this family are obligate parasites that cannot survive without living plant hosts, and they produce colorful spore-filled pustules that burst through the surface of infected plants.
children.funFact: Some rust fungi in this family have incredibly complex life cycles involving up to five different spore types and requiring two completely different host plants - for example, some wheat rusts must alternate between wheat and barberry plants to complete their full reproductive cycle.

children.name: Gymnosporangiaceae
Gymnosporangium
children.description: Cedar rusts are a fascinating group of fungi that live complex double lives, requiring two different types of host plants to complete their life cycle. These rusts typically alternate between juniper trees (where they form distinctive orange, gelatinous structures) and members of the rose family like apples, pears, and hawthorns (where they create colorful spots and growths on leaves and fruits).
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other rust fungi that can complete their life cycle on a single host, cedar rusts are obligate heteroecious, meaning they absolutely must alternate between juniper species and rose family plants to reproduce successfully.
children.funFact: The famous cedar-apple rust creates alien-looking orange, jelly-like 'horns' that emerge from round galls on juniper branches during wet spring weather, shooting spores toward nearby apple trees like nature's own science fiction scene.

children.description: The Gymnosporangiaceae are a family of rust fungi that cause distinctive plant diseases known as cedar rusts. These fungi are obligate parasites that require two different host plants to complete their complex life cycle, typically alternating between cedar trees (junipers) and members of the rose family like apples, hawthorns, and serviceberries.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other rust fungi, cedar rusts produce highly conspicuous, often bright orange or yellow spore-bearing structures that can be quite large and gelatinous when wet. They are also notable for their strict requirement of specific alternate hosts from two completely different plant families.
children.funFact: Cedar-apple rust creates bizarre orange, jelly-like growths called galls on cedar trees that can expand dramatically in wet weather, looking almost alien as they release their spores.

children.name: Coleosporiaceae
Chrysomyxa
children.description: Chrysomyxa is a genus of rust fungi that are specialized plant parasites, causing disease in both coniferous trees and various shrubs. These fungi have complex life cycles that require two different host plants to complete their development - typically alternating between spruce trees and other plants like blueberries or Labrador tea. They produce colorful spore masses on infected plant tissues, often appearing as orange, yellow, or reddish pustules.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other rust fungi, Chrysomyxa species specifically target spruce trees as their primary host and have evolved very specific relationships with particular alternate host plants. Each species in this genus typically has a narrow range of acceptable host plants for completing its life cycle.
children.funFact: The spruce witch's broom rust can cause dramatic deformities in spruce trees, creating dense clusters of abnormal branches called 'witch's brooms' that can persist for years and become quite large, sometimes resembling giant bird nests in the forest canopy.

children.name: Cronartium
children.description: Cronartium is a genus of rust fungi that cause distinctive gall-like growths and infections on trees, particularly pines and their alternate hosts. These fungi have complex life cycles that require two different host plants to complete their reproduction, often jumping between pine trees and other plants like currants or oaks.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Cronartium species create characteristic orange, blister-like spore masses on their hosts and require alternating between coniferous and deciduous host plants to complete their life cycle, unlike many other fungi that can complete their reproduction on a single host.
children.funFact: White pine blister rust was accidentally introduced to North America from Europe in the early 1900s and has since become one of the most economically damaging diseases of white pine forests, leading to extensive forest management programs.

children.name: Coleosporium
children.description: Coleosporium is a genus of rust fungi that are plant parasites, causing orange or yellow pustules to appear on the leaves and stems of their host plants. These fungi have complex life cycles that typically require two different host plants to complete their reproduction, alternating between coniferous trees (like pines) and various flowering plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other rust fungi, Coleosporium species produce distinctive orange to yellow spore masses that often appear powdery or waxy on infected plant surfaces. They are characterized by their specific host relationships and the particular shape and color of their spore-bearing structures.
children.funFact: These fungi are master manipulators that can actually change the appearance and behavior of infected plants, sometimes making leaves more colorful to attract insects that help spread their spores to new hosts.

children.name: Rossmanomyces
children.description: Rossmanomyces is a small genus of rust fungi that are highly specialized parasites of plants in the wintergreen family. These microscopic fungi live entirely within their host plants, causing distinctive rust-colored spots and lesions on leaves and stems. They have evolved a very intimate relationship with their hosts, being unable to survive without them.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other rust fungi that can infect multiple plant families, Rossmanomyces species are extremely host-specific, targeting only plants in the wintergreen family (Ericaceae). They produce their characteristic rust-colored spores directly on the leaf surface rather than in specialized fruiting bodies.
children.funFact: The wintergreen rust is so perfectly adapted to its host that it can only complete its life cycle on specific wintergreen species, making it one of nature's most specialized parasites.

children.description: Coleosporiaceae is a family of rust fungi that are obligate parasites, meaning they must live on living plant hosts to survive. These fungi have complex life cycles that often require two different host plants to complete their development, typically alternating between conifers like pines and firs, and flowering plants like asters and goldenrods.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their heteroecious life cycles (requiring two host species) and their production of distinctive spore stages including colorful orange or yellow pustules on host plants. They typically have conifers as their primary hosts and herbaceous plants as alternate hosts.
children.funFact: Some Coleosporiaceae species can cause their host plants to produce witches' brooms - dense clusters of abnormally growing branches that look like giant bird nests in the tree canopy.

children.name: Phragmidiaceae
Phragmidium
children.description: Phragmidium is a genus of rust fungi that specifically targets plants in the rose family, including roses, cinquefoils, and strawberries. These parasitic fungi create distinctive orange, yellow, or reddish spots and pustules on leaves and stems of their host plants. They have complex life cycles that typically involve multiple spore stages throughout the growing season.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Phragmidium rusts are distinguished by their multi-celled spores that have distinctive spiny projections, and their exclusive specialization on rose family plants. Unlike many other rust fungi, they complete their entire life cycle on the same host plant family.
children.funFact: Some Phragmidium species, like the multiflora rose rust, are actually used as biological control agents to help manage invasive rose species in natural areas.

children.name: Gymnoconia
children.description: Gymnoconia is a small genus of rust fungi that are plant parasites, causing distinctive rust-colored spots and growths on their host plants. These microscopic organisms are part of the complex world of fungi that play important roles in forest ecosystems, though they can sometimes cause plant diseases.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Gymnoconia are distinguished from other rust fungi by their specific spore structures and the particular way they form their rust-colored fruiting bodies on infected plants.
children.funFact: Like many rust fungi, Gymnoconia species may require multiple different host plants to complete their complex life cycles, essentially 'traveling' from one plant species to another as they reproduce.

children.description: Phragmidiaceae is a family of rust fungi that are specialized plant parasites, creating those distinctive orange, yellow, or reddish pustules you might notice on the leaves and stems of roses and other plants. These fungi have complex life cycles that often involve multiple host plants, and they're obligate parasites, meaning they can only survive by living on their host plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their multi-celled spores that are typically arranged in chains or columns, and they produce distinctive spore-bearing structures called telia that often appear as dark, crusty patches on infected plants.
children.funFact: Some Phragmidiaceae rusts are so host-specific that they can only infect particular species of roses, making them useful to botanists as indicators of plant relationships and evolutionary history.

children.name: Pucciniastraceae
Calyptospora
children.description: Calyptospora is a genus of rust fungi that are highly specialized plant parasites, creating distinctive orange or reddish growths on their host plants. These fungi have complex life cycles that often require multiple different host plants to complete their reproduction. In New England, this genus is represented by a single species that specifically targets huckleberry plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Calyptospora fungi are distinguished by their characteristic columnar or tower-like spore-producing structures that emerge from infected plant tissues. Unlike many other rust fungi, they form very specific, elongated fruiting bodies that give them their distinctive appearance.
children.funFact: The Huckleberry Broom Rust creates dramatic 'witches' brooms' - dense clusters of abnormal branch growth on huckleberry bushes that can persist for years and completely change the shape of the infected plant.

children.name: Melampsorella
children.description: Melampsorella is a small genus of rust fungi that are specialized plant parasites, causing distinctive diseases on coniferous trees. These fungi have complex life cycles that require two different host plants to complete their reproduction, typically alternating between fir trees and other plant species.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished from other rust fungi by their specific host relationships with fir trees and their ability to cause dramatic broom-like growths of abnormal branches on infected trees.
children.funFact: The fir broom rust creates "witches' brooms" - dense clusters of stunted branches that look like giant bird nests in fir trees and can persist for decades, sometimes becoming so large they're mistaken for animal dens.

children.name: Pucciniastrum
children.description: Pucciniastrum is a genus of rust fungi that are specialized plant parasites, causing distinctive rust-colored spots and growths on their host plants. These fungi have complex life cycles that often require two different host plants to complete their reproduction, making them highly specialized pathogens.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their specific host preferences and the characteristic orange to reddish-brown rust pustules they produce on infected plant tissues. Unlike some rust fungi, Pucciniastrum species typically have relatively simple spore structures.
children.funFact: The Wintergreen Rust in this genus creates bright orange spots on wintergreen leaves that look like tiny rust stains, which is exactly how rust fungi got their common name!

children.description: Pucciniastraceae is a family of rust fungi that are specialized plant parasites, causing distinctive rust-colored spots and growths on their host plants. These fungi have complex life cycles that often require two different host plants to complete their development, making them fascinating examples of biological interdependence.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their heteroecious lifestyle, meaning they must alternate between different host plant species to complete their life cycle, and they typically produce distinctive spore structures on both hosts.
children.funFact: Some Pucciniastrum species alternate between spruce trees and wild plants like fireweed, spending part of their lives as yellow blisters on spruce needles and another part as orange pustules on wildflower leaves.

children.name: Milesinaceae
Uredinopsis
children.description: Uredinopsis is a genus of rust fungi that creates distinctive orange or reddish spore masses on the undersides of fern fronds. These specialized parasites have complex life cycles that alternate between fern hosts and coniferous trees, forming different types of spores at different stages. They are part of the larger group of rust fungi, which are among the most host-specific parasites in nature.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other rust fungi that infect flowering plants, Uredinopsis species specifically target ferns as their primary hosts. They produce their telial stage (overwintering spores) on fern fronds, which distinguishes them from related rust genera that complete this stage on different plant types.
children.funFact: Some Uredinopsis species can dramatically alter the appearance of fern fronds, causing them to develop bright orange or yellow patches that look almost like autumn leaves in the middle of summer.

children.name: Naohidemyces
children.description: Naohidemyces is a small genus of rust fungi that specialize in infecting plants in the blueberry family. These microscopic fungi are plant pathogens that cause distinctive rust-colored spots and lesions on their host plants' leaves.
children.distinguishingFeatures: This genus is distinguished from other rust fungi by its specific association with blueberry and related plants, and its unique spore structures and life cycle stages that are adapted to this particular host family.
children.funFact: The genus Naohidemyces was only recently established in 2015, named after Japanese mycologist Naohide Hiratsuka who made significant contributions to rust fungi research.

children.description: Milesinaceae is a small family of rust fungi that are plant pathogens, causing disease on ferns and other plants. These microscopic fungi have complex life cycles that often require multiple different host plants to complete their development. They produce distinctive spore structures that help them spread and infect new plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their specific host preferences, particularly their association with ferns as primary hosts. They also have unique spore morphology and life cycle patterns that differ from other rust fungus families.
children.funFact: Some Milesinaceae rust fungi alternate between fern hosts and completely unrelated flowering plants during their life cycle, making them botanical shape-shifters that can dramatically change their appearance and behavior depending on which plant they're living on.

children.name: Tranzscheliaceae
Tranzschelia
children.description: Tranzschelia is a genus of rust fungi that are specialized plant pathogens, creating distinctive orange, yellow, or reddish pustules on their host plants. These microscopic fungi have complex life cycles that often require two different plant species to complete their reproduction, moving between hosts throughout the seasons.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Tranzschelia are distinguished by their specific host preferences and the characteristic spore structures they produce. They typically alternate between different plant families during their life cycle, with many species requiring both herbaceous plants and woody shrubs or trees.
children.funFact: Some Tranzschelia species are so host-specific that they can only complete their life cycle by alternating between plants as different as meadow rue wildflowers and cherry trees!

children.description: Tranzscheliaceae is a small family of rust fungi that are specialized plant parasites. These microscopic fungi create distinctive rust-colored spots and pustules on the leaves and stems of their host plants, particularly stone fruits like plums and cherries.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other rust fungi, members of Tranzscheliaceae typically require two different host plants to complete their complex life cycle, alternating between woody plants and herbaceous hosts.
children.funFact: These fungi are named after Russian mycologist Vladimir Tranzschel, who made significant contributions to understanding rust fungi in the early 1900s.

children.name: Allodus
children.description: Allodus is a small genus of rust fungi that are highly specialized plant parasites. These microscopic fungi create distinctive orange or reddish spots and pustules on their host plants, living entirely dependent on their plant hosts for survival.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Allodus are distinguished by their very narrow host specificity, with each species typically infecting only one or a few closely related plant species. They produce characteristic rust-colored spore masses that give these fungi their common name.
children.funFact: The single New England species, Mayapple Rust, is so specialized that it can only complete its life cycle on mayapple plants, making it one of nature's most exclusive plant-fungus relationships.

children.name: Pileolariaceae
Pileolaria
children.description: Pileolaria is a genus of rust fungi that are highly specialized plant parasites. These microscopic fungi form distinctive spore-producing structures on their host plants and have complex life cycles that may involve multiple host species.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their specific parasitic relationship with certain plant families and their unique spore structures that differ from other rust fungal genera.
children.funFact: The single New England species, poison ivy rust, actually helps control poison ivy populations by weakening the plants it infects, making this tiny fungus an unlikely ally for hikers and gardeners.

children.description: Pileolariaceae is a small family of marine polychaete worms that build distinctive tube-like homes on hard surfaces underwater. These segmented worms are filter feeders that extend feathery tentacles from their tubes to capture tiny particles of food from the water column.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their unique tube construction and specialized feeding apparatus that distinguishes them from other tube-dwelling marine worms.
children.funFact: Despite being represented by only one species in New England waters, these tiny architects create some of the most intricate microscopic tube structures found in marine environments.

children.name: Melampsoraceae
Melampsora
children.description: Melampsora is a genus of rust fungi that are obligate parasites, meaning they can only survive by living on other plants. These fungi are known for causing rust diseases on various trees and shrubs, particularly poplars and willows. They have complex life cycles that often involve multiple host plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Melampsora species are distinguished from other rust fungi by their specific host preferences and the characteristic orange to reddish spore masses they produce on infected leaves and stems.
children.funFact: Some Melampsora species require two different types of host plants to complete their life cycle - they might spend part of their life on a poplar tree and another part on an entirely different plant species like a fern or wildflower.

children.description: Melampsoraceae is a family of rust fungi that are obligate parasites, meaning they can only survive by living on host plants. These fungi have complex life cycles that often require two different host plants to complete their development, and they cause rust diseases that appear as orange, yellow, or brown pustules on leaves and stems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their heteroecious life cycles (requiring two host plants) and their production of distinctive spore stages including urediniospores and teliospores that create the characteristic rust-colored patches on infected plants.
children.funFact: Some Melampsora species alternate between poplar trees and flax plants during their life cycle, which historically caused significant problems for flax cultivation used in linen production.

children.name: Hyalopsoraceae
Hyalopsora
children.description: Hyalopsora is a small genus of rust fungi that specialize in infecting ferns. These microscopic parasites create distinctive rust-colored spots and growths on fern fronds, completing complex life cycles that may involve multiple host plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many rust fungi that infect flowering plants, Hyalopsora species specifically target ferns as their primary hosts. They produce characteristic orange to rust-colored spore masses on the undersides of infected fern leaves.
children.funFact: Oak fern rust has one of the most complex life cycles in the fungal world, requiring both fern and spruce tree hosts to complete its full reproductive cycle.

children.description: Hyalopsoraceae is a small family of rust fungi that are plant parasites, causing diseases on various host plants. These microscopic fungi have complex life cycles that often involve multiple host plants, and they produce distinctive spores that help them spread and infect new plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their transparent or translucent spores (the name 'Hyalopsora' means 'clear spore') and their specific parasitic relationships with certain plant families.
children.funFact: Despite being plant parasites, rust fungi like those in Hyalopsoraceae play important ecological roles and some species have co-evolved so closely with their hosts that they can only survive on one specific plant species.

children.description: Rust fungi are specialized plant parasites that create distinctive rust-colored or orange pustules on their host plants. These fungi have incredibly complex life cycles that often require two different host plants to complete, making them some of the most intricate parasites in nature. They are obligate parasites, meaning they can only survive by living on other plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other plant parasitic fungi, rust fungi produce characteristic spore-filled pustules that burst through plant surfaces, creating rusty or orange spots. Most species require alternating between two completely different host plant species during their multi-stage life cycle.
children.funFact: Some rust fungi can produce up to five different types of spores during their complex life cycle, with each spore type having a specific role and often infecting different host plants - it's like having multiple personalities!

children.name: Platygloeales
Platygloeaceae
Insolibasidium
children.description: Insolibasidium is a small genus of parasitic fungi that specialize in infecting plants, causing distinctive leaf deformities and blights. These fungi are highly specialized pathogens that have evolved to target specific host plants, forming intimate relationships with their victims.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus create characteristic blight symptoms and leaf deformations on their host plants, distinguishing them from other plant pathogenic fungi that may cause different types of damage.
children.funFact: The single New England species in this genus is so specialized that it targets honeysuckle plants specifically, earning its common name 'Honeysuckle Leaf Blight' for the distinctive twisted and yellowed leaves it creates.

children.description: Platygloeaceae is a small family of jelly fungi that form gelatinous, often translucent fruiting bodies on decaying wood. These fungi are saprophytes, meaning they break down dead organic matter and play an important role in forest decomposition. They have a unique microscopic structure with special spore-bearing cells called basidia that help scientists identify them.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their distinctive basidial structure and gelatinous texture. Unlike many other jelly fungi, they form relatively thin, flattened fruiting bodies rather than thick, brain-like masses.
children.funFact: With only one species found in New England, this family represents one of the rarest groups of fungi in the region, making any discovery of these translucent woodland jewels a special find for nature explorers.

children.name: Eocronartiaceae
Eocronartium
children.description: Eocronartium is a small genus of rust fungi that specialize in parasitizing mosses. These microscopic fungi live inside moss tissues, stealing nutrients and causing disease in their hosts. Unlike many other rust fungi that infect flowering plants, members of this genus have evolved specifically to target bryophytes.
children.distinguishingFeatures: What sets Eocronartium apart from other rust fungi is its exclusive relationship with mosses as hosts, rather than the trees and shrubs that most rusts prefer. The spores and infection structures are also uniquely adapted for the tiny scale of moss plants.
children.funFact: Eocronartium represents one of the most ancient lineages of rust fungi, suggesting that these parasites were already infecting mosses hundreds of millions of years ago when bryophytes dominated early terrestrial ecosystems.

children.description: Eocronartiaceae is a small family of rust fungi that are parasitic on plants, causing distinctive rust-colored spots and growths on their hosts. These fungi have complex life cycles that often involve multiple host plants, and they reproduce by releasing spores that spread to infect new plants. Like other rust fungi, they form special structures that penetrate plant tissues to obtain nutrients.
children.distinguishingFeatures: This family is distinguished from other rust fungi by their specific spore structures and the particular way they form their reproductive organs on host plants. They represent an early evolutionary branch of the rust fungi group.
children.funFact: Despite being such a small family with only one species found in New England, Eocronartiaceae represents an important piece of the evolutionary puzzle, helping scientists understand how rust fungi diversified millions of years ago.

children.description: Platygloeales is a small order of jelly fungi that produce soft, gelatinous fruiting bodies. These fungi are parasites or parasitoids of other fungi, particularly rusts, and play an important role in fungal ecology by helping to control plant diseases.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other jelly fungi, members of Platygloeales specifically target rust fungi as their hosts. They produce distinctive gelatinous structures that emerge from infected rust fungi rather than growing directly on wood or plant material.
children.funFact: These fungi are essentially 'fungal vampires' that attack and consume rust fungi, making them natural biological control agents that help protect plants from rust diseases.

children.name: Atractiellales
Phleogenaceae
Helicogloea
children.description: Helicogloea is a genus of jelly fungi that form distinctive gelatinous, translucent fruiting bodies on decaying wood. These small fungi have a unique twisted or coiled appearance and belong to a group that helps decompose dead plant material in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their helical or spirally twisted, jelly-like fruiting bodies that are typically small and translucent to whitish in color.
children.funFact: The name Helicogloea literally means 'spiral jelly,' perfectly describing these fungi's characteristic twisted, corkscrew-like shape.

children.name: Phleogena
children.description: Phleogena is a genus of small, stalked fungi that grow on decaying wood, particularly hardwood trees like beech and oak. These fungi produce tiny, ball-shaped fruiting bodies that sit atop slender stalks, giving them their common name of 'stalkballs.' They play an important role in forest ecosystems by helping to decompose fallen logs and branches.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Phleogena are distinguished by their characteristic stalked, spherical fruiting bodies and their preference for growing directly from the bark and wood of dead hardwood trees. Unlike many other small wood-decay fungi, they have a distinctly club-like or ball-on-a-stick appearance.
children.funFact: The name Phleogena comes from Greek words meaning 'bark-born,' reflecting these fungi's habit of emerging directly from tree bark as they consume the dead wood beneath.

children.description: Phleogenaceae is a small family of unusual fungi that produce jelly-like or gelatinous fruiting bodies. These fungi are saprophytic, meaning they decompose dead organic matter, particularly wood and plant debris. They belong to a group of fungi known for their distinctive slimy or rubbery textures when fresh.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their gelatinous, often translucent fruiting bodies that can appear brain-like or coral-like in shape. Unlike many other jelly fungi, they have a unique microscopic structure with specialized cells that help distinguish them from similar-looking species.
children.funFact: Despite their slimy appearance, these fungi play an important ecological role as decomposers and some species can actually survive being completely dried out, then rehydrate and continue growing when moisture returns.

children.description: Atractiellales is a small order of fungi that includes some of the most unusual and poorly understood species in the fungal kingdom. These fungi are often found growing on decaying wood, where they form small, inconspicuous fruiting bodies that are easily overlooked by casual observers. They represent an ancient lineage that helps scientists understand the early evolution of fungi.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this order have distinctive spore-bearing structures and produce spores in a unique way that sets them apart from other fungal groups. Their fruiting bodies are typically small and have unusual cellular arrangements that require microscopic examination to properly identify.
children.funFact: Despite being found worldwide, Atractiellales fungi are so rarely encountered and studied that many species may still be unknown to science, making every discovery potentially significant for understanding fungal diversity.

children.name: Erythrobasidiales
Cyphobasidium
children.description: Cyphobasidium is a small genus of microscopic fungi that live as parasites on lichens. These tiny organisms are so small they're invisible to the naked eye, but they play an important role in lichen ecosystems by feeding on their host lichens.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These fungi are distinguished by their unique parasitic lifestyle specifically targeting lichens, and their extremely small size that requires microscopic examination to observe.
children.funFact: The single New England species, Cyphobasidium hypogymniicola, is so specialized that it only parasitizes lichens in the genus Hypogymnia, making it one of nature's most particular eaters!

children.description: Erythrobasidiales is a small order of microscopic yeasts that live as parasites on plants. These tiny fungi are part of the larger group called basidiomycetes, which includes mushrooms and other familiar fungi, but they exist as single-celled organisms rather than forming visible fruiting bodies.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most other basidiomycete fungi that form mushrooms or other large structures, members of this order remain microscopic throughout their life cycle and reproduce by budding like typical yeasts.
children.funFact: This entire order contains only one known genus with just a few species worldwide, making it one of the rarest groups in the fungal kingdom.

children.name: Mixiales
Mixiaceae
Mixia
children.description: Mixia is a unique genus of microscopic fungi that forms specialized partnerships with fern roots. These tiny organisms live in the soil and create beneficial relationships with their fern hosts, helping them absorb nutrients and water more effectively.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike typical mycorrhizal fungi, Mixia forms distinctive coiled structures within fern root cells and belongs to an ancient lineage that represents one of the earliest branches of the fungal tree of life.
children.funFact: Mixia represents such an ancient fungal lineage that studying it helps scientists understand what the very first fungi on Earth might have looked like over 400 million years ago.

children.description: Mixiaceae is a small family of fungi that represents one of the most ancient lineages in the fungal tree of life. These microscopic fungi are parasites that live inside amoebas and other single-celled organisms, forming a unique relationship with their hosts.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most fungi, members of Mixiaceae lack the typical fungal cell wall component chitin and have very simple cellular structures that bridge the gap between fungi and their ancient ancestors.
children.funFact: This family contains some of the most primitive fungi known to science, giving us clues about what the earliest fungi might have looked like over a billion years ago.

children.description: Mixiales is a small order of parasitic plants that have lost the ability to photosynthesize and instead live by drawing nutrients from other plants through their roots. These unusual plants lack chlorophyll and appear as small, pale, scale-like structures emerging from the ground. They represent one of nature's most specialized examples of plant parasitism.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most other parasitic plants that attach to stems or leaves, members of Mixiales are root parasites that form underground connections with their host plants. They also completely lack chlorophyll and leaves, appearing as simple, colorless shoots.
children.funFact: The single New England species in this order is so rare and inconspicuous that it was only discovered in North America in the 1960s, despite being smaller than your thumb and hiding among forest leaf litter.

children.name: Exobasidiales
Exobasidiaceae
Exobasidium
children.description: Exobasidium is a genus of plant parasitic fungi that specialize in infecting members of the heath family, including blueberries, cranberries, and rhododendrons. These fungi cause distinctive galls, leaf curls, and abnormal growths on their host plants, often creating swollen, distorted tissues that can appear pink, red, or whitish.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other plant pathogenic fungi, Exobasidium species produce their spores directly on the surface of infected plant tissue without forming typical mushroom-like fruiting bodies. They create highly specialized relationships with specific host plants in the heath family.
children.funFact: The 'rose bloom' caused by Exobasidium on cranberries gets its name because the infected berries turn bright pink or red and become enlarged, resembling tiny roses among the normal fruit.

children.description: The Exobasidiaceae are a family of plant parasitic fungi that specialize in causing galls, blisters, and deformities on their host plants. These fungi are particularly known for attacking members of the heath family (Ericaceae), including blueberries, cranberries, and rhododendrons. They create distinctive swollen or distorted growth on leaves, stems, or flowers of their hosts.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other plant pathogenic fungi, members of Exobasidiaceae produce their spores directly on the surface of infected plant tissue without forming typical mushroom structures. They create characteristic galls and leaf blisters that are often brightly colored, ranging from pink to white.
children.funFact: Some Exobasidium species actually make their host plant tissues edible and even considered delicacies - the pink or white galls they create on blueberry and huckleberry leaves are sometimes called 'pinkster apples' and can be eaten raw!

children.description: Exobasidiales are a small order of fungi that specialize in causing plant diseases, particularly creating unusual growths and deformities on their host plants. These fungi are biotrophic parasites, meaning they keep their host plants alive while feeding on them, often causing distinctive swellings, leaf curls, or witches' brooms on trees and shrubs.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other fungi, members of Exobasidiales produce their spores directly on the surface of infected plant tissue without forming typical mushroom-like fruiting bodies. They create characteristic plant deformities and galls that are often more noticeable than the fungi themselves.
children.funFact: Some Exobasidiales infections create edible plant growths - azalea galls caused by these fungi are considered a delicacy in parts of Asia and are sometimes called 'mountain vegetables.'

children.name: Microstromatales
Pseudomicrostroma
children.description: Pseudomicrostroma is a small genus of plant pathogenic fungi that causes leaf spot diseases. These microscopic fungi form tiny, dark fruiting bodies on infected leaves and are specialized parasites of specific host plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many leaf spot fungi, Pseudomicrostroma produces distinctive small, shield-like fruiting structures that are embedded in the leaf tissue. The spores are released through small openings in these dark, flattened structures.
children.funFact: The single New England species, Pseudomicrostroma juglandis, is highly specialized and only infects walnut family trees, demonstrating how some fungi have evolved to target very specific plant hosts.

children.description: Microstromatales is a small order of fungi that includes species which form tiny, cushion-like structures on decaying wood and plant material. These fungi are decomposers that help break down organic matter in forest ecosystems. They are characterized by their microscopic fruiting bodies and simple reproductive structures.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this order are distinguished by their extremely small, often overlooked fruiting bodies that appear as minute dots or bumps on their substrate. Unlike many other fungi, they lack complex spore-bearing structures and have relatively simple morphology.
children.funFact: Despite being so small that they're easily overlooked by casual observers, Microstromatales fungi play an important role as nature's recyclers, quietly breaking down dead wood in New England's forests.

children.name: Ustilaginales
Ustilaginaceae
Mycosarcoma
children.description: Mycosarcoma is a genus of plant pathogenic fungi that causes smut diseases in grasses and cereal crops. These fungi produce distinctive black, sooty spores that replace normal plant tissues, creating swollen, tumor-like growths on infected plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other smut fungi, Mycosarcoma species form large, fleshy galls filled with dark spores that completely transform the infected plant parts into abnormal growths.
children.funFact: Corn smut (caused by Mycosarcoma maydis) is considered a delicacy called 'huitlacoche' in Mexican cuisine, where the infected corn kernels are harvested and eaten as a flavorful ingredient in dishes.

children.name: Ustilago
children.description: Ustilago is a genus of smut fungi that are plant parasites, causing diseases primarily in grasses and grains. These fungi produce dark, powdery spores that replace the seeds or other plant parts of their hosts, often creating black, dusty masses where healthy plant tissue should be.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other fungi, Ustilago species specifically target the reproductive parts of plants, transforming seeds and flowers into masses of dark spores. They have a complex life cycle that requires living plant hosts to complete their development.
children.funFact: The name 'Ustilago' comes from the Latin word 'ustus' meaning 'burnt,' referring to the charcoal-black appearance of infected plant parts covered in the fungus's sooty spores.

children.name: Melanopsichium
children.description: Melanopsichium is a genus of parasitic fungi that infects grasses and sedges, causing distinctive dark, powdery spore masses to form on the host plants. These fungi are smut fungi, which means they replace normal plant tissues with masses of dark spores. They have a specialized lifestyle, living entirely within their grass hosts and only becoming visible when they produce their characteristic black spore clusters.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Melanopsichium fungi are distinguished from other smut fungi by their specific association with sedge family plants and their production of particularly dark, almost black spore masses. Unlike many other smut fungi that affect cereal crops, Melanopsichium species are primarily found on wild sedges and rushes.
children.funFact: The name Melanopsichium literally means 'black crumb' in reference to the dark, granular appearance of the spore masses these fungi produce on infected plants.

children.name: Sporisorium
children.description: Sporisorium is a genus of smut fungi that are plant parasites, causing distinctive dark, sooty masses of spores to form on their grass hosts. These fungi live inside grass plants and dramatically alter the appearance of seed heads by replacing normal seeds with black, powdery spore masses. They have a complex life cycle that requires specific grass species to complete their development.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other smut fungi, Sporisorium species typically form their spore masses in the seed heads of grasses rather than on leaves or stems. The spores are usually surrounded by a distinctive membrane that eventually breaks open to release the dark, dusty spores.
children.funFact: Sporisorium fungi are so specialized that each species typically infects only one or a few closely related grass species, making them highly host-specific parasites.

children.description: The Ustilaginaceae are a family of fungi commonly known as smut fungi that specialize in infecting grasses and other plants. These microscopic parasites live inside their host plants and produce dark, powdery spores that often replace the plant's seeds or other structures.
