children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other lichen groups, Lecideales typically have apothecia with prominent dark rims (called lecideine apothecia) and lack the bright, powdery soredia that many other crusty lichens use for reproduction.
children.funFact: Some Lecideales lichens can survive in extremely harsh conditions, including on bare rock faces exposed to intense sunlight and temperature fluctuations, making them among the first colonizers of newly exposed rocky surfaces.

children.name: Rhizocarpales
Rhizocarpaceae
Rhizocarpon
children.description: Map lichens are crusty, slow-growing lichens that form distinctive patches on rocks, creating colorful patterns that resemble maps or aerial photographs. These hardy organisms are actually partnerships between fungi and algae, working together to colonize bare rock surfaces in harsh environments. They're commonly found on granite outcrops, boulders, and stone walls throughout New England's mountains and rocky areas.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Map lichens are characterized by their crustose (crusty) growth form that appears to be painted directly onto rock surfaces, often displaying bright yellow, green, or gray colors arranged in geometric patterns with distinct borders between different colored zones.
children.funFact: Map lichens grow so slowly that scientists use them as natural clocks to date rock surfaces and archaeological sites - some patches may be hundreds or even thousands of years old!

children.name: Rehmia
children.description: Rehmia is a small genus of crustose lichens that form thin, crusty patches on rock surfaces. These lichens are characterized by their map-like appearance, with distinct boundaries and colorful patterns that can range from grayish to reddish tones.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Rehmia are distinguished by their distinctive apothecia (fruiting bodies) that have prominent, often brightly colored margins and their tendency to form irregular, map-like patches on rock substrates.
children.funFact: The Drenched Map Lichen gets its common name from its preference for growing on rocks that are frequently wet from streams, waterfalls, or heavy moisture, creating colorful natural maps on New England's rocky landscapes.

children.name: Poeltinula
children.description: Poeltinula is a small genus of crustose lichens that form thin, crusty patches on rock surfaces. These lichens are part of the diverse world of symbiotic organisms, where fungi and algae work together to create a single living entity that can survive in harsh environments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their dark, blackish crusts with distinctive reproductive structures called perithecia that are embedded in the lichen surface.
children.funFact: This genus was named after the Austrian lichenologist Josef Poelt, who made significant contributions to our understanding of lichen taxonomy in the 20th century.

children.description: Rhizocarpaceae is a family of crusty lichens that form thin, flat patches on rocks and other hard surfaces. These lichens are masters of living in harsh environments, often found growing on exposed stone where few other organisms can survive. They create some of the most long-lasting living things on Earth, with some colonies potentially thousands of years old.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their crustose (crust-like) growth form that adheres tightly to rock surfaces, and their distinctive spore-producing structures called apothecia that often appear as small black or dark brown discs.
children.funFact: Some species in this family, particularly the Map Lichens, are among the slowest-growing organisms on the planet, expanding less than a millimeter per year, which scientists use to date ancient rock surfaces and archaeological sites.

children.description: Rhizocarpales is an order of small aquatic ferns that includes water ferns and mosquito ferns. These tiny floating or semi-aquatic plants produce specialized spore-bearing structures called sporocarps, which look like small pods or capsules. They're among the smallest ferns in the world and play important ecological roles in freshwater habitats.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike typical ferns, members of Rhizocarpales are heterosporous, meaning they produce two different types of spores (large female megaspores and tiny male microspores) rather than one uniform spore type. Their sporocarps are also unique structures that protect the spores until conditions are right for germination.
children.funFact: Some mosquito ferns in this group can double their population size in just 2-3 days under ideal conditions, making them among the fastest-growing plants on Earth!

children.name: Trapeliales
Trapeliaceae
Trapelia
children.description: Trapelia is a small genus of crustose lichens that form thin, crusty patches on rocks and other hard surfaces. These lichens are typically grayish or brownish in color and produce small, round fruiting bodies called apothecia that contain their spores.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Trapelia lichens are distinguished by their simple crustose thalli and distinctive apothecia that often have darker margins. They lack the complex chemical compounds found in many other lichen genera, making them relatively simple but reliable to identify.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'pebble lichens,' these organisms are actually composite life forms made up of fungal partners living symbiotically with algae, working together to break down rock surfaces over decades.

children.name: Trapeliopsis
children.description: Trapeliopsis is a small genus of crustose lichens that form thin, crusty patches on wood and bark. These lichens are characterized by their granular surface texture and small, disk-like fruiting bodies called apothecia. They are typically found growing on decaying wood, old fence posts, and tree bark in forest environments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Trapeliopsis can be distinguished from other crustose lichens by their distinctive granular, warty surface texture and their preference for growing on wood substrates rather than rock or soil.
children.funFact: The Board Lichen gets its common name from its frequent occurrence on old wooden boards, fence posts, and weathered lumber, making it one of the most likely lichens you'll encounter on human-made wooden structures.

children.name: Placynthiella
children.description: Placynthiella is a small genus of crustose lichens that form thin, dark patches on various surfaces. These lichens have a simple structure with tiny fruiting bodies called apothecia that appear as small dark spots scattered across their surface.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their dark, tar-like appearance and extremely thin, crusty growth form that adheres tightly to substrates like bark, wood, and sometimes rock.
children.funFact: The name Placynthiella literally means 'little flat flower,' referring to the small, flat fruiting bodies that dot the lichen's surface like tiny dark blossoms.

children.name: Rimularia
children.description: Rimularia is a genus of crustose lichens that form thin, crusty patches on rock surfaces. These lichens create a symbiotic partnership between fungi and algae, growing slowly but persistently on stone substrates where they can survive harsh weather conditions.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Rimularia are characterized by their distinctive fruiting bodies (apothecia) that have prominent, often raised rims and their preference for growing directly on bare rock surfaces rather than bark or soil.
children.funFact: These hardy lichens can live for decades or even centuries on the same rock surface, slowly weathering the stone beneath them and contributing to soil formation over geological time.

children.description: Trapeliaceae is a family of small, crusty lichens that form thin, often barely visible patches on rocks, tree bark, and soil. These lichens are typically gray, brown, or greenish in color and have tiny, round fruiting bodies that look like small dots or discs scattered across their surface. They're commonly found in New England's forests and rocky areas, though they're often overlooked due to their small size.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their crustose (crusty) growth form and their simple, lecideine apothecia - small, dark, disc-like fruiting structures with thin margins. Unlike some other lichen families, they typically have relatively simple internal chemistry and lack the colorful pigments found in many other crustose lichens.
children.funFact: Despite being tiny and inconspicuous, Trapeliaceae lichens are important pioneers that help break down rock surfaces and create soil, making them some of nature's smallest but most persistent geological engineers.

children.name: Xylographaceae
Xylographa
children.description: Xylographa is a small genus of crustose lichens that form thin, crusty patches on tree bark and wood. These lichens create distinctive elongated, slot-like fruiting bodies called lirellae that look like tiny black lines or dashes scattered across their surface. They are typically found growing on the bark of deciduous trees in forest environments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Xylographa lichens are recognized by their characteristic linear fruiting bodies (lirellae) that appear as narrow, dark slits or dashes on a pale crusty surface. This gives them a distinctive "writing on bark" appearance that sets them apart from other crustose lichens with round or irregular fruiting bodies.
children.funFact: The name Xylographa literally means "wood writing" in Greek, referring to how these lichens' linear fruiting bodies resemble ancient script or mysterious messages written directly onto tree bark.

children.description: Xylographaceae is a small family of crustose lichens that form thin, crusty patches on rock surfaces. These lichens are characterized by their simple structure and ability to grow directly on stone substrates, creating colorful crusts that can be easily overlooked.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their crustose growth form that adheres tightly to rock surfaces and their simple reproductive structures called apothecia that appear as small, disc-like features on the lichen surface.
children.funFact: Despite being easily mistaken for paint or stains on rocks, these tiny lichens are actually complex partnerships between fungi and algae that can slowly dissolve minerals from stone surfaces over decades.

children.description: Trapeliales is an order of crustose lichens that form thin, crusty patches on rocks, bark, and soil. These lichens are typically small and inconspicuous, often appearing as grayish or whitish crusts that blend seamlessly with their substrate. They are found in a variety of habitats from coastal areas to mountain peaks.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this order are characterized by their simple, crustose growth form and distinctive reproductive structures called apothecia that often appear as small, dark discs embedded in or sitting on the crusty surface.
children.funFact: Some Trapeliales lichens are among the most pollution-tolerant species, making them excellent indicators of air quality in urban environments.

children.name: Acarosporales
children.commonName: cobblestone lichens, eiglera lichens, and allies

children.name: Acarosporaceae
Acarospora
children.description: Cobblestone lichens are crustose lichens that form distinctive patterns resembling tiny cobblestones or mosaic tiles on rock surfaces. These hardy lichens create thin, crusty patches made up of small, angular sections that fit together like pieces of a natural puzzle. They're commonly found growing on exposed rocks, walls, and concrete surfaces throughout New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other crustose lichens that form smooth or randomly cracked surfaces, cobblestone lichens create highly organized, geometric patterns with clearly defined boundaries between each small section. Their areolate (divided into small areas) structure gives them their characteristic cobblestone appearance.
children.funFact: Despite their small size and humble appearance, cobblestone lichens are incredibly long-lived and can slowly expand their territory for decades, with some colonies potentially persisting for over a century on the same rock surface.

children.name: Sarcogyne
children.description: Grain-spored lichens are small, crusty lichens that get their name from their distinctive spores, which look like tiny grains when viewed under a microscope. These lichens typically form thin, scaly patches on rocks and other hard surfaces, often appearing grayish or whitish in color.
children.distinguishingFeatures: What sets grain-spored lichens apart from other crusty lichens is their unique spore structure - their spores are round to oval-shaped and have a distinctly grainy or warty surface texture that's visible under magnification.
children.funFact: Despite being tiny and easily overlooked, grain-spored lichens are incredibly hardy survivors that can thrive on bare rock faces where few other organisms can establish themselves.

children.description: The cobblestone lichen family includes lichens that form distinctive crusty patches on rocks, often resembling tiny cobblestones or cracked pavement. These hardy lichens are masters of rock colonization, creating colorful crusts that can range from gray to yellow to orange. They're commonly found growing directly on bare rock surfaces, especially in sunny, exposed locations.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their areolate (cracked into small sections) thallus that looks like miniature cobblestones, and their distinctive spores that are produced in specialized fruiting bodies called apothecia.
children.funFact: These lichens are incredibly slow-growing but extremely long-lived, with some colonies potentially persisting for hundreds of years while gradually expanding across rock surfaces at rates of just millimeters per decade.

children.description: Cobblestone lichens and their allies are a group of crustose lichens that form thin, crusty patches on rocks and other hard surfaces. They get their common name from their distinctive appearance, which often resembles tiny cobblestones or mosaic tiles pressed into the surface they're growing on. These lichens are particularly well-adapted to harsh, exposed environments where other organisms struggle to survive.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other crustose lichens, members of this order typically have their reproductive structures (apothecia) sunken into the lichen body rather than raised above it. Their spores are also characteristically simple and colorless, helping distinguish them from related lichen groups.
children.funFact: Some cobblestone lichens can survive in extremely harsh conditions, including the intense UV radiation and temperature fluctuations of high-altitude mountain peaks and desert rocks.

children.name: Sarrameanales
Sarrameanaceae
Loxospora
children.description: Loxospora is a small genus of crusty lichens that form thin, flat patches on tree bark and rocks. These lichens are characterized by their distinctive ragged or torn-looking edges around their fruiting bodies, which gives them their common name of 'ragged-rim lichens.' They typically appear as grayish or yellowish crusts with small, cup-like structures containing spores.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The key feature that sets Loxospora apart from other crustose lichens is the characteristically irregular, torn or ragged margins around their apothecia (spore-producing structures). This ragged rim appearance is so distinctive that it's reflected in their common names.
children.funFact: Despite their small size and inconspicuous appearance, Loxospora lichens are excellent indicators of air quality and can live for decades on the same tree, slowly growing outward in all directions at a rate of just millimeters per year.

children.description: Sarrameanaceae is a small family of crustose lichens that form thin, crusty growths on tree bark and rock surfaces. These lichens are composed of fungi living in partnership with algae, creating colorful patches that can range from gray to yellow-green on their substrates.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their distinctive spore-producing structures and unique chemical compounds that can be detected through specialized tests, helping to separate them from other crustose lichen families.
children.funFact: Despite being tiny and easily overlooked, these lichens are incredibly long-lived organisms that can persist on the same tree trunk or rock surface for decades, slowly growing outward at just millimeters per year.

children.description: Sarrameanales is a small order of carnivorous plants that includes the famous pitcher plants found in New England's bogs and wetlands. These fascinating plants have evolved specialized leaves that form deep, slippery pitchers to trap and digest insects and other small prey. They've adapted this carnivorous lifestyle to survive in nutrient-poor, acidic soils where most other plants struggle.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this order are distinguished by their highly modified leaves that form pitcher-shaped traps with slippery walls and digestive enzymes at the bottom. Unlike other carnivorous plants that use sticky surfaces or snap traps, these plants rely on pitfall traps to capture their prey.
children.funFact: The purple pitcher plant (Sarracenia purpurea) is so well-adapted to cold climates that it's the only pitcher plant that can survive New England winters, and it's actually the state flower of Newfoundland!

children.name: Hymeneliales
Hymeneliaceae
Tremolecia
children.description: Tremolecia is a small genus of crustose lichens that form thin, crusty patches on rock surfaces. These lichens are specialized for growing on hard substrates like granite and other acidic rocks, where they create distinctive dark-colored crusts with small, embedded reproductive structures.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Tremolecia lichens are distinguished by their dark, often blackish crusts that grow directly on rock surfaces and their small, sunken disc-like fruiting bodies (apothecia) that are typically darker than the surrounding crust.
children.funFact: Despite their modest appearance, Tremolecia lichens are incredibly hardy and can survive in some of the harshest rock environments, slowly breaking down stone surfaces over decades through chemical weathering.

children.name: Ionaspis
children.description: Ionaspis is a small genus of crustose lichens that form thin, crusty patches on rocks and other hard surfaces. These lichens are typically found in aquatic or semi-aquatic environments, often growing on rocks near or in streams, lakes, and other water bodies. They are characterized by their ability to tolerate periodic submersion and wet conditions that would be challenging for many other lichen species.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Ionaspis lichens are distinguished by their preference for wet, aquatic habitats and their ability to survive periodic flooding or submersion. Unlike many other crustose lichens, they have specialized adaptations that allow them to thrive in consistently moist environments.
children.funFact: The name Ionaspis comes from Greek words meaning 'violet shield,' referring to the purple or violet-colored fruiting bodies (apothecia) that these lichens produce.

children.description: Hymeneliaceae is a small family of crustose lichens that form thin, crusty patches on rock surfaces. These hardy lichens are typically found growing on exposed stone in harsh environments like mountaintops and coastal areas. They create some of the most enduring biological partnerships between fungi and algae in nature's most challenging habitats.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their extremely thin, often nearly invisible crusts that seem to be painted directly onto rock surfaces. They produce distinctive disc-shaped fruiting bodies (apothecia) that are often the only visible sign of the lichen's presence.
children.funFact: These lichens are so tightly bonded to their rock substrates that they can literally help break down mountains over thousands of years, playing a crucial role in soil formation by slowly dissolving minerals from solid rock.

children.description: Hymeneliales is a small order of crustose lichens that form thin, crusty patches on rocks and soil. These lichens have a distinctive fruiting structure called an apothecium that sits flush with or slightly raised above the lichen surface, giving them their characteristic appearance.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this order are distinguished by their simple apothecia that lack true margins and have a smooth, often blackish disc. Unlike many other lichen groups, their fruiting bodies appear almost embedded in the lichen crust itself.
children.funFact: Despite being one of the smaller lichen orders, Hymeneliales lichens are remarkably hardy and can survive in some of the harshest environments on Earth, including arctic tundra and high-altitude rocky surfaces.

children.name: Leprocaulales
Leprocaulaceae
Halecania
children.description: Halecania is a small genus of crustose lichens that form thin, often grayish crusts on rock surfaces. These lichens are composite organisms made up of fungi and algae living together in partnership, with the fungal partner providing structure while the algae produce food through photosynthesis.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Halecania lichens are distinguished by their specific spore characteristics and chemical reactions, particularly the presence of certain acids that can be detected through spot tests with chemical reagents.
children.funFact: Like all lichens, Halecania species are incredibly slow-growing pioneers that can colonize bare rock surfaces where few other organisms can survive, sometimes taking decades to reach full maturity.

children.name: Leprocaulon
children.description: Mealy lichens are small, crusty lichens that form thin, powdery patches on tree bark and wood surfaces. They get their name from their distinctive mealy or granular appearance, looking somewhat like flour or fine powder sprinkled on the substrate. These lichens are composite organisms made up of fungi and algae living together in partnership.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other crusty lichens, mealy lichens have a distinctly granular, powdery texture that easily rubs off when touched. They lack the smooth, continuous crust or leaf-like structures found in other lichen groups.
children.funFact: The powdery granules that give mealy lichens their name are actually tiny reproductive structures called soredia, which contain both fungal threads and algal cells ready to start new lichen colonies wherever they land.

children.description: Leprocaulaceae is a small family of lichens that includes some of the most distinctive crusty and shrubby species found in New England. These lichens are characterized by their unique growth forms and specialized reproductive structures that help them thrive in various habitats from tree bark to soil.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their powdery or granular surfaces and distinctive reproductive structures called soralia, which produce small powdery clusters for asexual reproduction.
children.funFact: The Mealy Lichens in this family get their common name from their flour-like, powdery appearance that makes them look like they've been dusted with meal or fine powder.

children.description: Leprocaulales is a small order of crustose lichens that form thin, often powdery or granular crusts on rocks, bark, and other surfaces. These lichens are typically pale colored and create patches that can look almost chalky or dusty. They are found in various habitats from forests to coastal areas throughout New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this order are distinguished by their leprose (powdery) growth form and lack of a well-developed thallus structure. Unlike many other crustose lichens, they rarely produce fruiting bodies and instead reproduce mainly through dispersal of their powdery fragments.
children.funFact: Despite their humble, dust-like appearance, these lichens are actually complex partnerships between fungi and algae that can slowly break down rock surfaces over decades, contributing to soil formation.

children.name: Baeomycetales
Baeomycetaceae
Baeomyces
children.description: Beret lichens are small, distinctive lichens that form tiny mushroom-like structures with brown, rounded caps sitting on short stalks. They grow directly from crusty, granular patches on soil, creating what looks like miniature toadstools scattered across the ground.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most lichens that grow flat against surfaces, beret lichens produce upright, stalked fruiting bodies that resemble tiny mushrooms or berets, making them unmistakable among New England's lichen species.
children.funFact: These lichens are often called 'golf tee lichens' because their distinctive shape looks remarkably like tiny golf tees sprouting from the earth.

children.description: The Baeomycetaceae family consists of small, distinctive lichens that form unique mushroom-like or pin-cushion structures. These lichens have a crusty base (called a thallus) from which tiny stalked reproductive structures emerge, making them look quite different from the flat, leafy, or branching forms of most other lichens.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most lichens that keep their reproductive parts flush with their surface, Baeomycetaceae lichens produce distinctive raised, stalked structures that can look like tiny pins or miniature mushrooms sprouting from their crusty base.
children.funFact: Despite their mushroom-like appearance, these are true lichens - a partnership between fungi and algae - and the stalked structures are actually specialized spore-producing organs unique to this family.

children.description: Baeomycetales is a small order of lichens that form distinctive mushroom-like or club-shaped fruiting structures called mazaedia. These lichens have a unique way of reproducing, producing powdery spores in specialized structures that look quite different from the flat, crusty appearance of most other lichens.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most lichens that form flat, disk-shaped reproductive structures, members of Baeomycetales produce tall, stalked fruiting bodies topped with powdery spore masses that resemble tiny mushrooms.
children.funFact: The powdery spore masses of these lichens can be blown away by wind like dust, earning some species the nickname "powder-headed lichens."

children.name: Dictyocatenulata
children.description: Dictyocatenulata is a genus of microscopic marine diatoms, which are single-celled algae with beautiful glass-like cell walls made of silica. These tiny organisms live in ocean waters and are part of the phytoplankton community that forms the base of marine food webs.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their distinctive chain-like colonial arrangement and intricate net-like patterns on their silica cell walls. The genus name literally means 'net-like chain,' referring to this unique structural feature.
children.funFact: Despite being invisible to the naked eye, diatoms like Dictyocatenulata produce about 20% of the world's oxygen through photosynthesis - more than all the rainforests combined!

children.name: Helotiales
Erysiphaceae
Erysiphe
children.description: Erysiphe is a large genus of fungi that causes powdery mildew diseases on plants. These microscopic fungi create the characteristic white, powdery coating you often see on leaves, stems, and flowers of infected plants throughout New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other fungi that cause plant diseases, Erysiphe species grow primarily on the surface of plant tissues rather than inside them, creating visible white patches that can be easily wiped off.
children.funFact: Each Erysiphe species is typically very host-specific, meaning the powdery mildew on your grape vines is a completely different species than the one on your clover or lilacs, even though they look nearly identical!

children.name: Golovinomyces
children.description: Golovinomyces is a genus of powdery mildew fungi that creates those distinctive white, powdery patches you might notice on plant leaves during humid summer days. These microscopic fungi are plant parasites that feed on a wide variety of wildflowers, herbs, and other plants throughout New England. Unlike many fungi that decompose dead material, these species are specialized to extract nutrients from living plant tissues.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Golovinomyces can be distinguished from other powdery mildews by their specific spore structures and the particular plant families they target. Each species tends to be highly specialized, often infecting only one type or family of host plants.
children.funFact: Despite being plant parasites, Golovinomyces species rarely kill their hosts - instead, they form a long-term relationship that allows the plant to survive while the fungus gets a steady food source, making them more like freeloaders than destroyers.

children.name: Podosphaera
children.description: Podosphaera is a genus of microscopic fungi that cause powdery mildew diseases on a wide variety of plants throughout New England. These fungi create the characteristic white, powdery coating you might notice on leaves, stems, and flowers of infected plants like roses, apples, and many native shrubs. Each species in this genus typically specializes in infecting specific types of plants, forming intimate relationships with their hosts.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other fungal pathogens, Podosphaera species grow primarily on the surface of plant tissues rather than inside them, creating visible white or grayish powdery patches. They produce distinctive spherical fruiting bodies with appendages that help distinguish them from other powdery mildew genera.
children.funFact: Despite being plant pathogens, Podosphaera fungi are so specialized that most species can only infect one or a few closely related plant species - the Apple Powdery Mildew, for instance, primarily targets apples and won't typically infect your roses!

children.name: Phyllactinia
children.description: Phyllactinia is a genus of powdery mildew fungi that create white, powdery coatings on the leaves of trees and shrubs. These plant parasites are highly host-specific, with each species typically infecting only one type of plant, from birches and maples to dogwoods and black locusts. They reproduce by forming tiny black fruiting bodies that look like pepper specks scattered across the white fungal growth.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Phyllactinia species are distinguished from other powdery mildews by their unique appendages that look like tiny needles or pins projecting from their fruiting bodies. These needle-like structures help identify the genus even when the fungal growth appears similar to other powdery mildews.
children.funFact: Despite being parasites, Phyllactinia fungi rarely kill their host plants - instead, they've evolved to keep their hosts alive as long-term food sources, creating a sustainable relationship that can persist for years.

children.name: Neoerysiphe
children.description: Neoerysiphe is a genus of powdery mildew fungi that creates white, powdery patches on the leaves and stems of various plants. These microscopic fungi are plant parasites that draw nutrients from their host plants while living on the surface of leaves and other plant parts. All three New England species in this genus specialize in infecting plants in the mint and snapdragon families.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other powdery mildew genera, Neoerysiphe species have distinctive spore-bearing structures and typically produce their sexual reproductive structures (chasmothecia) with unique appendage patterns that help mycologists identify them under a microscope.
children.funFact: Despite being plant parasites, Neoerysiphe fungi rarely kill their host plants - instead, they've evolved to keep their hosts alive while creating those telltale white powdery coatings that gardeners often notice on their plants during humid summer months.

children.name: Sawadaea
children.description: Sawadaea is a genus of powdery mildew fungi that creates white, powdery coatings on the leaves of various trees and shrubs. These microscopic fungi are plant parasites that feed on their hosts by drawing nutrients from leaf surfaces, often causing the distinctive white dusty appearance that gardeners and hikers commonly notice on affected plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other powdery mildews, Sawadaea species have distinctive spore-bearing structures and typically specialize in infecting woody plants like maples, rather than herbaceous plants.
children.funFact: Despite being parasites, Sawادaea fungi rarely kill their host plants - instead, they've evolved to keep their hosts alive while slowly sapping nutrients, creating a long-term relationship that can persist for years.

children.name: Arthrocladiella
children.description: Arthrocladiella is a genus of small freshwater green algae that forms branching, thread-like structures. These microscopic organisms live in aquatic environments and are part of the diverse world of algae that help form the base of freshwater food webs.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their characteristic branching pattern and jointed appearance, with segments that connect in a chain-like fashion.
children.funFact: Despite being microscopic, these algae play an important role in producing oxygen and providing food for tiny aquatic animals in New England's ponds and streams.

children.name: Blumeria
children.description: Blumeria is a genus of parasitic fungi that causes powdery mildew diseases on grasses and cereal crops. These microscopic fungi live on the surface of their host plants, forming white, powdery patches that give the disease its characteristic appearance.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other fungi, Blumeria species are obligate parasites that can only survive on living host plants and cannot be grown in laboratory cultures without their hosts.
children.funFact: Blumeria graminicola is one of the most economically important plant pathogens worldwide, causing billions of dollars in crop losses annually by infecting wheat, barley, and other cereal grains.

children.description: Powdery mildews are plant-parasitic fungi that create distinctive white, powdery patches on the leaves, stems, and flowers of their host plants. These fungi are obligate parasites, meaning they can only survive by feeding on living plant tissue, and they're among the most common and recognizable plant diseases you'll encounter in New England gardens and forests.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other plant fungi that cause dark spots or rotting, powdery mildews produce characteristic white or grayish powdery growth on plant surfaces that can be easily wiped off with your finger.
children.funFact: Each species of powdery mildew is typically very host-specific, so the powdery mildew on your lilacs is likely a completely different species than the one affecting your phlox, even though they look nearly identical to the naked eye.

children.name: Lachnaceae
Lachnum
children.description: Lachnum is a genus of tiny cup fungi that create delicate, hair-fringed structures on decaying wood and plant material. These miniature mushrooms form small, shallow cups that are often covered with fine hairs, giving them a fuzzy appearance when viewed up close.
children.distinguishingFeatures: What sets Lachnum apart from other cup fungi is their characteristically hairy or bristly exterior surfaces and their preference for growing on woody debris. The fine hairs around the cup margins are visible even without magnification in many species.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'fairy cups,' these fungi are so small that most species measure less than a few millimeters across - you'd need a magnifying glass to truly appreciate their intricate hairy details!

children.name: Lachnellula
children.description: Lachnellula is a small genus of cup fungi that specialize in growing on coniferous trees, particularly spruces and firs. These tiny fungi form small, disk-shaped fruiting bodies that emerge from the bark or wood of their host trees. They play an important role as decomposers in coniferous forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other cup fungi, Lachnellula species are specifically adapted to coniferous hosts and often have a distinctive hairy or fuzzy margin around their cup-shaped fruiting bodies.
children.funFact: Lachnellula resinaria gets its name from its association with resin-rich areas of conifer bark, where it helps break down these sticky, aromatic compounds that would otherwise persist in the forest.

children.name: Capitotricha
children.description: Capitotricha is a genus of tiny marine worms that belong to the polychaete group. These microscopic creatures live in sandy and muddy ocean sediments, where they burrow and feed on organic particles. They are part of the diverse world of marine segmented worms that play important roles in ocean ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Capitotricha are characterized by their distinctive head region with specialized sensory structures called palps, which help them detect food and navigate their sandy environment.
children.funFact: Despite being smaller than a grain of rice, these tiny worms are expert engineers that help aerate ocean sediments as they burrow, creating pathways for oxygen and nutrients to reach deeper layers of the seafloor.

children.name: Proliferodiscus
children.description: Proliferodiscus is a small genus of tiny fungi that forms delicate, disc-shaped fruiting bodies on decaying wood. These microscopic decomposers help break down dead plant material in forest ecosystems, playing an important role in nutrient cycling.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their small, saucer-like appearance and their ability to reproduce both sexually through spores and asexually through specialized structures that bud off from the main body.
children.funFact: The name 'Proliferodiscus' literally means 'proliferating disc,' referring to their unique ability to create new fruiting bodies by budding, like tiny fungal clones sprouting from the parent.

children.name: Neodasyscypha
children.description: Neodasyscypha is a small genus of cup fungi that forms tiny, hair-covered fruiting bodies on decaying wood. These delicate fungi are part of the larger group of disc fungi that help break down dead organic matter in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their small, cup-shaped fruiting bodies that are densely covered with fine hairs, giving them a fuzzy appearance under magnification.
children.funFact: The name Neodasyscypha literally means 'new hairy cup,' referring to the distinctive fuzzy texture that covers these miniature fungal cups.

children.description: Lachnaceae is a family of tiny cup fungi that produce small, disc-shaped fruiting bodies covered in fine hairs or bristles. These microscopic fungi are decomposers that break down dead plant material, particularly wood and other organic matter in forest environments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their distinctively hairy or bristly cup-shaped fruiting bodies, which distinguish them from the smooth-surfaced cups of related fungal families.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'cup fungi,' many Lachnaceae species are so small that you'd need a magnifying glass to see their fuzzy, hair-like structures that give the family its name.

children.name: Arachnopezizaceae
Arachnopeziza
children.description: Arachnopeziza is a small genus of cup fungi that creates tiny, delicate fruiting bodies on decaying wood and plant material. These diminutive fungi are part of nature's decomposition crew, breaking down organic matter in forest ecosystems. They produce small, cup-shaped or disc-like structures that release spores to reproduce.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their very small size and their preference for growing on specific types of decaying plant material. They have distinctive spore characteristics and microscopic features that separate them from other small cup fungi.
children.funFact: Despite their tiny size, Arachnopeziza fungi play an important role in recycling nutrients back into the forest soil, making them essential partners in maintaining healthy woodland ecosystems.

children.name: Durella
children.description: Durella is a small genus of bryozoans, which are tiny colonial animals that live in marine environments. These filter-feeding creatures form encrusting colonies on hard surfaces like rocks, shells, and other underwater structures. Each individual in the colony lives in its own small chamber and extends tentacles to capture plankton and organic particles from the water.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Durella bryozoans are characterized by their calcified, box-like chambers (called zoecia) that have distinctive apertures with teeth or spines around the opening. The colonies form thin, crusty patches that can be distinguished from other bryozoans by the specific shape and ornamentation of their individual chambers.
children.funFact: Despite being animals, bryozoan colonies like Durella are sometimes mistaken for seaweed or coral because they form plant-like or rock-like growths on underwater surfaces.

children.name: Parachnopeziza
children.description: Parachnopeziza is a small genus of cup fungi that produces tiny, disc-shaped fruiting bodies on decaying plant material. These microscopic fungi are saprophytes, meaning they help break down dead organic matter and recycle nutrients back into forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their extremely small size and specific microscopic features of their spores and cellular structure that separate them from other cup fungi.
children.funFact: Despite being so tiny that they're easily overlooked, Parachnopeziza fungi play an important role as nature's recyclers, helping to decompose fallen leaves and twigs in New England's forests.

children.description: Arachnopezizaceae is a family of small cup fungi that typically grow on decaying wood and plant debris in forest environments. These tiny fungi produce small, disc-shaped or cup-shaped fruiting bodies that are often less than a centimeter across and can be easily overlooked among the leaf litter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their minute size and the presence of distinctive hair-like structures on their fruiting bodies, which is reflected in the name 'Arachnopeziza' meaning 'spider cup.'
children.funFact: Despite their tiny size, these fungi play an important ecological role as decomposers, helping to break down organic matter and recycle nutrients in forest ecosystems.

children.name: Mollisiaceae
Mollisia
children.description: Mollisia is a genus of small, cup-shaped fungi that grow as tiny discs on dead wood and plant material. These diminutive decomposers are often overlooked due to their small size, typically measuring just a few millimeters across. They play an important role in breaking down organic matter in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Mollisia fungi are characterized by their small, disc-like fruiting bodies that sit directly on the substrate without stalks. Unlike many other cup fungi, they remain quite flat and don't develop the deep cup shape of larger species.
children.funFact: Despite their tiny size, Mollisia fungi are incredibly abundant - you might find dozens of these miniature discs clustered together on a single piece of rotting wood, creating what looks like a galaxy of tiny grey planets.

children.name: Phialocephala
children.description: Phialocephala is a genus of dark, microscopic fungi that form important partnerships with tree roots in New England's forests. These fungi are endophytes, meaning they live inside plant tissues without causing disease, and they're particularly common in coniferous trees like pines and spruces.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus produce distinctive dark, flask-shaped spore-producing structures called phialides. They can be identified by their dark-colored mycelia and their specific way of forming spores in chains from these specialized structures.
children.funFact: Despite being invisible to the naked eye, Phialocephala fungi can make up a significant portion of the fungal community in forest soils and may help trees survive environmental stress by enhancing their ability to absorb nutrients and water.

children.description: The Mollisiaceae are a family of small, cup-shaped fungi that typically grow on dead wood, bark, and plant debris. These tiny decomposers help break down organic matter in forest ecosystems, playing an important role in nutrient cycling. Most members produce small, disk-like fruiting bodies that are often difficult to spot without close examination.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their small, shallow cup or disk-shaped fruiting bodies (apothecia) that lack a stem. They differ from similar cup fungi by their typically smooth, waxy appearance and their preference for growing directly on decaying plant material.
children.funFact: Some species in the genus Phialocephala form beneficial partnerships with tree roots, helping plants absorb nutrients while receiving sugars in return - a relationship that can help trees survive in nutrient-poor soils.

children.name: Helotiaceae
Hymenoscyphus
children.description: Hymenoscyphus is a genus of small, cup-shaped fungi that produce tiny disc-like fruiting bodies, typically measuring just a few millimeters across. These delicate fungi are saprophytes, meaning they feed on dead organic matter like fallen leaves, twigs, and nuts. They play an important role in forest ecosystems by helping to decompose plant material and return nutrients to the soil.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Hymenoscyphus are distinguished by their small, shallow cup or disc-shaped fruiting bodies with smooth, often translucent surfaces. Unlike many other cup fungi, they typically have very short stalks or are nearly sessile (stalkless).
children.funFact: The 'nut disco' (Hymenoscyphus fructigenus) gets its common name from its habit of growing on old acorns and other nuts, where its small white discs look like tiny dance floors for forest creatures!

children.name: Tatraea
children.description: Tatraea is a small genus of fungi that contains just one species found in New England. These are microscopic fungi that live as parasites or symbionts, often found in association with other organisms in forest environments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: This genus is characterized by its large spores (as suggested by the species name 'macrospora') and its specific microscopic structures that distinguish it from other small fungal genera.
children.funFact: Tatraea macrospora is so rare and specialized that it represents the only known species in its entire genus in New England, making it a unique find for mycologists exploring the region's fungal diversity.

children.description: Helotiaceae is a family of small cup fungi that typically produce tiny, disc-shaped fruiting bodies on decaying plant material. These delicate fungi are commonly found growing on dead twigs, leaves, and other organic debris in forest environments. They play an important role as decomposers, helping to break down dead plant matter and recycle nutrients back into the ecosystem.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their small, cup-shaped or disc-shaped fruiting bodies that are usually less than a few millimeters across. Unlike many other cup fungi, Helotiaceae species often have smooth, waxy surfaces and tend to grow directly from decaying plant tissues.
children.funFact: Some species in the Hymenoscyphus genus within this family are responsible for serious tree diseases, including the ash dieback disease that has devastated European ash trees, showing how these tiny fungi can have enormous ecological impacts.

children.name: Sclerotiniaceae
Sclerencoelia
children.description: Sclerencoelia is a small genus of cup fungi that specialize in growing on dead wood, particularly hardwood trees and shrubs. These fungi form small, dark-colored cup-shaped fruiting bodies that help decompose woody plant material in forest ecosystems. They play an important role as decomposers, breaking down dead branches and bark.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their small, blackish cup-shaped fruiting bodies and their preference for growing on dead hardwood substrates. They can be distinguished from similar cup fungi by their consistently dark coloration and woody habitat preferences.
children.funFact: The Spring Aspencup gets its name because it typically appears in early spring on dead aspen and poplar wood, often emerging while snow is still on the ground.

children.name: Botrytis
children.description: Botrytis is a genus of fungi that includes plant pathogens known for causing gray mold diseases on fruits, vegetables, and flowers. These fungi produce fuzzy, grayish spores that spread easily through air and water, making them common problems in gardens, greenhouses, and stored produce.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Botrytis fungi are characterized by their distinctive gray, velvety spore masses that develop on infected plant tissue. They typically attack soft, dying, or stressed plant parts and can spread rapidly in cool, humid conditions.
children.funFact: Despite being a destructive plant pathogen, Botrytis cinerea is actually welcomed by some winemakers who call it 'noble rot' because it can concentrate sugars in grapes to create prized dessert wines.

children.name: Monilinia
children.description: Monilinia is a genus of plant pathogenic fungi that specialize in causing brown rot diseases in fruit-bearing plants. These fungi are particularly notorious for attacking stone fruits like peaches and cherries, as well as berries, causing the fruits to turn brown and shrivel up. They complete their life cycle by overwintering in mummified fruits and plant debris, then producing spores in spring to infect new growth.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other plant pathogens, Monilinia fungi specifically target flowers and fruits rather than leaves or stems. They create distinctive brown, rotted areas on infected fruits and can cause entire blossoms to wilt and die during spring blooming periods.
children.funFact: The New England species Monilinia vaccinii-corymbosi has a sneaky strategy - it can actually manipulate blueberry plants to produce fake flowers that look normal but are actually made of fungal tissue designed to spread spores!

children.description: The Sclerotiniaceae are a family of fungi that are primarily plant pathogens, causing diseases in a wide variety of crops and wild plants. These fungi are characterized by their ability to produce hard, dark survival structures called sclerotia that help them persist through unfavorable conditions. They typically cause soft rots and blights on their host plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: What sets this family apart is their production of distinctive sclerotia - compact masses of hardened fungal tissue that look like small black seeds or pellets. These structures allow the fungi to survive harsh winters and drought conditions that would kill other fungi.
children.funFact: The notorious gray mold fungus Botrytis is actually prized by winemakers when it infects grapes, creating 'noble rot' that concentrates sugars to produce expensive dessert wines like Sauternes.

children.name: Mitrulaceae
Mitrula
children.description: Mitrula is a genus of small, distinctive fungi that produce club-shaped or spoon-shaped fruiting bodies rising from wet ground or decaying plant material. These fungi are commonly known as swamp beacons due to their bright colors and preference for marshy, wetland habitats. All three New England species share this characteristic wetland lifestyle and similar overall appearance.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Mitrula fungi are easily recognized by their simple, club-like or spatula-shaped caps that lack the typical mushroom stem-and-cap structure. Unlike many other small fungi, they have smooth, often brightly colored surfaces and consistently grow in very wet conditions.
children.funFact: Despite their name 'swamp beacon,' these fungi don't actually glow - they got this nickname because their bright yellow, orange, or white colors make them stand out like little beacons against the dark, muddy backgrounds of their wetland homes.

children.description: Mitrulaceae is a small family of tiny, distinctive fungi that produce delicate, club-shaped or spoon-shaped fruiting bodies. These fascinating organisms typically grow from decomposing organic matter in wet environments like swamps, bogs, and stream edges. They play an important role in breaking down dead plant material in New England's wetland ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are easily recognized by their bright yellow to orange, paddle-shaped or club-like caps that sit atop slender stalks. Unlike many other small fungi, they have a smooth, waxy appearance and lack gills or pores.
children.funFact: Despite their tiny size (often less than an inch tall), these fungi are among the first to appear in spring, sometimes pushing up through snow and ice in wetland areas.

children.name: Gelatinodiscaceae
Ascocoryne
children.description: Ascocoryne is a genus of distinctive cup fungi that form colorful, gelatinous discs on rotting wood. These fungi get their common name from their jelly-like texture and circular, cup-shaped appearance that can range from purple to pinkish or brownish colors.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other cup fungi, Ascocoryne species have a uniquely soft, rubbery texture that feels almost like gelatin. They also have a distinctive ability to change form between their sexual and asexual reproductive stages.
children.funFact: Purple Jellydisc can actually exist in two completely different forms - the familiar colorful cups we usually see, and a less conspicuous white, branching form that produces different types of spores.

children.name: Neobulgaria
children.description: Neobulgaria is a small genus of jelly fungi that forms distinctive disc-shaped fruiting bodies on dead hardwood trees. These fungi are saprophytes, meaning they feed on decaying organic matter and help break down fallen logs and branches in the forest.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their smooth, translucent, disc-like appearance that resembles jelly or gelatin when fresh. Unlike many other jelly fungi, Neobulgaria species specifically favor beech and other hardwood substrates.
children.funFact: The Beech Jelly-disc can actually survive freezing temperatures and will rehydrate and continue growing when conditions improve, making it one of the few fungi you might spot fruiting during winter thaws.

children.description: Gelatinodiscaceae is a small family of jelly-like fungi that produce distinctive cup-shaped or disc-shaped fruiting bodies with a soft, gelatinous texture. These fungi are saprophytes that break down dead wood, particularly hardwood branches and logs. They typically appear as colorful, rubbery masses that can range from purple to pink to pale colors.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their unique gelatinous, bouncy texture combined with cup or disc-shaped fruiting bodies that contain asci (spore-bearing structures). Unlike other jelly fungi, they produce their spores in organized cup-like structures rather than spreading them across irregular surfaces.
children.funFact: Some species in this family can actually change color when handled or bruised, shifting from deep purple to bright pink or pale yellow as their tissues are damaged.

children.name: Drepanopezizaceae
Diplocarpon
children.description: Diplocarpon is a genus of plant pathogenic fungi that specialize in causing leaf spot diseases on plants in the rose family. These fungi create distinctive dark spots on leaves that can eventually cause the leaves to yellow and drop off, weakening their host plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other leaf spot fungi, Diplocarpon species produce their spores in distinctive shield-shaped structures called acervuli that appear as dark, slightly raised spots on infected leaves.
children.funFact: Rose black spot caused by Diplocarpon rosae is one of the most well-known plant diseases among gardeners, often appearing after periods of wet weather when water sits on rose leaves for extended periods.

children.name: Blumeriella
children.description: Blumeriella is a small genus of fungi that causes plant diseases, particularly affecting trees in the cherry family. These microscopic organisms are plant pathogens that create distinctive leaf spot diseases on their host plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other leaf spot fungi, Blumeriella produces characteristic small, reddish-brown spots with distinct yellow halos on infected leaves, and causes premature leaf drop in affected trees.
children.funFact: The single New England species, Blumeriella jaapii, is responsible for cherry leaf spot disease and can cause cherry trees to lose most of their leaves by midsummer, weakening the tree's ability to produce fruit.

children.description: Drepanopezizaceae is a family of small fungi that are primarily plant pathogens, meaning they cause diseases in plants. These fungi typically produce tiny, cup-shaped or disc-like fruiting bodies and are known for attacking the leaves and stems of various plants, particularly trees and shrubs.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their small, often dark-colored apothecia (cup-shaped structures) and their parasitic lifestyle on living plant tissues. They differ from related fungi by their specific combination of microscopic features and their tendency to cause distinct leaf spot diseases.
children.funFact: Some species in this family, like those in the genus Diplocarpon, are responsible for the common black spot disease that gardeners often see on rose leaves, causing the characteristic dark spots that eventually lead to leaf yellowing and drop.

children.name: Cordieritidaceae
Diplocarpa
children.description: Diplocarpa is a small genus of cup fungi that forms distinctive, small fruiting bodies on decaying wood and plant material. These fungi are saprophytes, meaning they help decompose organic matter and recycle nutrients back into forest ecosystems. They're part of the larger group of ascomycete fungi that produce their spores in tiny sac-like structures.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Diplocarpa are characterized by their cup-shaped or disc-like fruiting bodies and their preference for growing on woody substrates. They can be distinguished from similar cup fungi by their specific microscopic features and spore characteristics.
children.funFact: Despite being a small genus with only two species found in New England, Diplocarpa fungi play an important role as nature's recyclers, helping to break down fallen branches and dead wood into soil nutrients.

children.name: Skyttea
children.description: Skyttea is a genus of tiny marine fungi that live as parasites on red algae in coastal waters. These microscopic organisms form small, dark fruiting bodies on their algal hosts and are part of a specialized group of fungi that have adapted to life in saltwater environments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most fungi which live on land, Skyttea species are true marine fungi that can only survive and reproduce in saltwater conditions. They produce distinctive small, black, flask-shaped structures called perithecia directly on the surface of red algae.
children.funFact: Skyttea represents one of the relatively few groups of fungi that have successfully colonized marine environments, making them part of an exclusive club of salt-tolerant fungal species.

children.description: Cordieritidaceae is a small family of fungi that includes some of the most inconspicuous organisms in New England's forests. These tiny fungi typically grow as parasites or symbionts on other fungi, lichens, or plant materials, forming microscopic fruiting bodies that are easily overlooked by casual observers.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their extremely small size and specialized lifestyle of growing on or within other organisms. They produce distinctive spore-bearing structures that can only be properly identified under high magnification.
children.funFact: Despite being so small that most people never notice them, these fungi play important ecological roles by helping to break down and recycle nutrients from dead organic matter in forest ecosystems.

children.name: Cenangiaceae
Chlorencoelia
children.description: Chlorencoelia is a small genus of cup fungi that produces distinctive brownish to olive-colored fruiting bodies. These fungi are saprobic, meaning they decompose dead organic matter, particularly wood and plant debris in forest environments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their cup-shaped fruiting bodies with olive to brownish coloration, which helps distinguish them from other cup fungi that may be brighter or differently colored.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'cup fungi,' the fruiting bodies of Chlorencoelia species can actually twist and contort into various shapes as they mature, giving them a more irregular appearance than a typical cup.

children.name: Encoelia
children.description: Encoelia is a small genus of cup fungi that produce distinctive shallow, disc-shaped fruiting bodies. These fungi are saprophytes that help decompose dead wood, particularly from deciduous trees like hazel and other hardwoods.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Encoelia fungi are recognized by their brownish, cup-shaped fruiting bodies that often have a slightly fuzzy or scaly outer surface, distinguishing them from the smoother cups of many related genera.
children.funFact: The spring hazelcup earned its name because it typically appears in early spring on dead hazel branches, making it one of the first cup fungi you might spot after winter.

children.description: The Cenangiaceae are a family of small, cup-shaped fungi that grow on dead or dying wood, particularly on branches and twigs of trees and shrubs. These fungi are saprobic, meaning they help decompose organic matter and recycle nutrients back into the forest ecosystem. They produce their spores in tiny, disk-like structures that often appear in clusters on bark.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their small, shallow cup or disk-shaped fruiting bodies that typically have a waxy or rubbery texture. Unlike many other cup fungi, they often have a distinctive rim or margin around their spore-producing surface.
children.funFact: Some species in this family can remain dormant on dead wood for years, only producing their visible fruiting bodies when conditions are just right with the perfect combination of moisture and temperature.

children.name: Chlorociboriaceae
Chlorociboria
children.description: Chlorociboria is a small genus of cup fungi known for their distinctive blue-green coloration. These tiny fungi grow on decaying hardwood, creating small cup-shaped fruiting bodies that emerge from wood that has been stained a beautiful turquoise color.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The bright blue-green pigment they produce is unique among New England fungi, staining the wood they colonize with an unmistakable turquoise hue that persists long after the mushrooms themselves have disappeared.
children.funFact: The turquoise-stained wood created by Chlorociboria fungi was so prized during the Renaissance that it was harvested and used as decorative inlay in fine furniture and artwork, known as 'green oak' or 'tunbridge ware.'

children.description: The Chlorociboriaceae family consists of small cup fungi that create one of nature's most striking wood transformations. These fungi are best known for producing brilliant blue-green staining in decaying hardwood, particularly oak and other deciduous trees. While the actual fungal fruiting bodies are tiny and inconspicuous, their dramatic coloring effect on wood makes them easy to identify.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other cup fungi, members of this family produce distinctive blue-green pigments that penetrate deep into wood tissue, creating vivid coloration that persists long after the wood has dried. The small, pale fruiting bodies emerge from this characteristically stained wood.
children.funFact: The blue-green stained wood created by these fungi was historically prized by furniture makers and artisans, who called it 'green oak' and used it for decorative inlays and marquetry work.

children.name: Vibrisseaceae
Vibrissea
children.description: Vibrissea is a small genus of unusual aquatic fungi that look like tiny clubs or paddles growing from submerged wood. These distinctive mushrooms are found in streams, ponds, and other freshwater environments where they decompose fallen branches and logs. They have a unique gelatinous texture and bright colors that help them stand out in their watery habitats.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most mushrooms, Vibrissea species are adapted to live completely underwater or in very wet conditions. They have a characteristic club-like or spatula-shaped fruiting body with a jelly-like consistency that helps them survive in aquatic environments.
children.funFact: These 'water club mushrooms' can remain submerged for months at a time, making them some of the few truly aquatic fungi you might encounter while exploring New England streams and ponds.

children.description: Vibrisseaceae is a small family of unusual fungi that produce tiny, hair-like or club-shaped fruiting bodies. These delicate organisms typically grow on wet, decaying wood in moist environments like stream banks and wetlands. They are saprophytic fungi, meaning they help break down dead organic matter in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their distinctive hair-like or slender club-shaped reproductive structures that emerge from rotting wood. Unlike many other fungi, they have a gelatinous or cartilaginous texture and often appear translucent or brightly colored.
children.funFact: The name 'Vibrissea' comes from the Latin word for whiskers, referring to the hair-like appearance of these tiny fungi that can easily be mistaken for plant hairs or small bristles growing on logs.

children.name: Tricladiaceae
Cudoniella
children.description: Cudoniella is a small genus of cup fungi that produce tiny, pin-like fruiting bodies on dead wood. These delicate fungi are easily overlooked due to their small size, but they play an important role in decomposing fallen branches and twigs in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their distinctive pin-shaped appearance, with a small cup or disc at the top of a slender stalk. Unlike many other cup fungi, Cudoniella species are quite small and have a firm, almost cartilaginous texture.
children.funFact: Despite their tiny size, these 'pin fungi' are actually related to the much larger and more conspicuous morel mushrooms!

children.description: Tricladiaceae is a family of small, cup-shaped fungi that are closely related to morels and other spring mushrooms. These delicate fungi typically grow on decaying wood and organic matter in forest environments. They produce small, gelatinous fruiting bodies that are often overlooked due to their tiny size.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their small, cup or disc-shaped fruiting bodies with a gelatinous or waxy texture. Unlike many other cup fungi, they have a unique spore-bearing surface structure and often appear translucent or semi-transparent.
children.funFact: Despite their tiny size, these fungi play an important role in forest ecosystems by helping to decompose fallen branches and woody debris, recycling nutrients back into the soil.

children.name: Hyaloscyphaceae
Amicodisca
children.description: Amicodisca is a small genus of cup fungi that forms tiny, disc-shaped fruiting bodies on decaying wood. These delicate fungi are part of the larger group of ascomycetes, which produce spores in sac-like structures called asci.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their small, brownish cup-shaped appearance and their preference for growing on rotting hardwood logs and branches.
children.funFact: Amicodisca fungi are so small that they're easily overlooked by casual hikers, but they play an important role in forest ecosystems by helping decompose fallen wood.

children.name: Hyaloscypha
children.description: Hyaloscypha is a genus of tiny cup fungi that form small, translucent, disc-shaped fruiting bodies on decaying wood. These delicate fungi are often less than a few millimeters across and can be easily overlooked due to their small size and pale coloration. They play an important role in breaking down dead wood in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their very small size, hyaline (glass-like or translucent) appearance, and their preference for growing on rotting wood. They typically have smooth, cup-shaped or disc-shaped fruiting bodies that lack the bright colors found in many other small cup fungi.
children.funFact: The name 'Hyaloscypha' literally means 'glass cup' in reference to their translucent, crystal-clear appearance that makes them look like tiny glass dishes scattered on decaying logs.

children.description: The Hyaloscyphaceae are a family of tiny cup fungi that form small, translucent disc-shaped fruiting bodies. These delicate fungi are typically found growing on decaying wood, bark, or plant debris in forest environments. They play an important role as decomposers, breaking down organic matter in woodland ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their small size and hyaline (glass-like, translucent) appearance, which gives the family its name. Their cup-shaped fruiting bodies are typically pale or colorless and often less than a few millimeters across.
children.funFact: Despite their tiny size, these fungi can be remarkably long-lived, with some specimens persisting for months as they slowly break down their wooden substrates.

children.name: Tetracladium
children.description: Tetracladium is a genus of aquatic fungi that live in freshwater environments like streams, rivers, and lakes. These microscopic fungi are important decomposers that break down organic matter in aquatic ecosystems, particularly fallen leaves and other plant material that enters the water.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their distinctive branched spores that typically have four arms or branches, which gives the genus its name (tetra meaning four, and cladium referring to branches).
children.funFact: These tiny fungi play a crucial role as food for aquatic invertebrates, helping transfer nutrients from decaying plant matter up the freshwater food chain.

children.name: Rutstroemiaceae
Rutstroemia
children.description: Rutstroemia is a genus of small cup fungi that form tiny, disc-shaped fruiting bodies on decaying plant material. These delicate fungi are decomposers that help break down dead leaves and other organic matter in forest ecosystems. They typically appear as small brown or yellowish cups, usually less than a few millimeters across.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Rutstroemia fungi are distinguished by their minute size and their preference for growing on specific host plants, with individual species often specialized to particular types of leaves or plant debris.
children.funFact: The oakleaf cup fungus is so specialized that it almost exclusively grows on decaying oak leaves, acting like nature's tiny recycling specialist for oak forests.

children.name: Lanzia
children.description: Lanzia is a genus of small, cup-shaped fungi that typically grow on dead plant material like twigs, stems, and leaves. These tiny decomposers help break down organic matter in forest ecosystems, playing an important role in nutrient cycling.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Lanzia fungi are characterized by their small, disc-like or shallow cup-shaped fruiting bodies that are usually pale colored and found on dead woody plant parts.
children.funFact: Despite their tiny size, Lanzia fungi are expert recyclers that can break down tough plant fibers that many other organisms cannot digest.

children.description: Rutstroemiaceae is a small family of cup fungi that typically grow on dead plant material like twigs, leaves, and stems. These tiny fungi produce small, disc-shaped or cup-shaped fruiting bodies that help decompose organic matter in forest ecosystems. They play an important role as nature's recyclers, breaking down dead plant tissue and returning nutrients to the soil.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their small size and preference for growing directly on dead woody plant parts, rather than on soil or other substrates. Their fruiting bodies are typically less than a few millimeters across and often appear as tiny brown or dark-colored discs.
children.funFact: Despite their tiny size, Rutstroemiaceae fungi are incredibly efficient decomposers that can break down tough plant materials like lignin and cellulose that many other organisms cannot digest.

children.name: Pezizellaceae
Calycina
children.description: Calycina is a genus of small cup fungi that produce tiny, delicate fruiting bodies resembling miniature goblets or fairy cups. These fungi are saprophytes, meaning they decompose dead organic matter like fallen twigs and plant debris in forest environments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Calycina are distinguished by their small, smooth, cup-shaped fruiting bodies that typically measure just a few millimeters across and have bright, often vibrant coloration.
children.funFact: The name 'fairy cups' comes from folklore that suggested these tiny, perfectly formed cups were used by woodland fairies for drinking dewdrops.

children.description: Pezizellaceae is a family of tiny cup fungi that produce small, disc-shaped fruiting bodies typically less than 2mm across. These delicate fungi are often found growing on decaying plant material like twigs, bark, and dead leaves in forest environments. They play an important ecological role as decomposers, breaking down organic matter in woodland ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their extremely small size and smooth, cup-shaped fruiting bodies that lack hairs or other surface ornaments. Unlike many other cup fungi, they typically have very thin, translucent flesh and often appear almost glass-like.
children.funFact: These fungi are so small that many species were completely unknown to science until the development of modern microscopy techniques, and new species are still being discovered regularly by mycologists using magnifying equipment.

children.name: Chlorospleniaceae
Chlorosplenium
children.description: Chlorosplenium is a small genus of cup fungi that creates tiny, bright green disc-shaped fruiting bodies on decaying wood. These distinctive fungi are saprophytes, meaning they help break down dead organic matter in forest ecosystems. They belong to the larger group of cup fungi, which are characterized by their open, bowl-like appearance.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The bright green coloration makes Chlorosplenium easily distinguishable from most other cup fungi, which are typically brown, orange, or other earth tones. Their small size and preference for growing on rotting hardwood logs also help separate them from related species.
children.funFact: The green color in Chlorosplenium fungi comes from a unique pigment that remains vibrant even after the fungus dries out, making these tiny cups surprisingly long-lasting natural decorations on forest floors.

children.description: Chlorospleniaceae is a small family of cup fungi that produces tiny, bright green disc-shaped fruiting bodies on decaying wood. These saprophytic fungi help break down dead plant material in forest ecosystems, playing an important role in nutrient cycling.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are easily recognized by their distinctive bright green color, which is unusual among cup fungi that are typically brown, orange, or other earth tones.
children.funFact: The bright green pigment in these fungi is so distinctive that the genus name Chlorosplenium literally means 'green spleen,' referring to both the color and the somewhat organ-like shape of the fruiting bodies.

children.name: Eustilbum
children.description: Eustilbum is a genus of small, cushion-forming mosses that create dense, golden-green mats on rocks and soil. These tiny plants are part of the broader moss family and play important roles in preventing erosion and creating microhabitats for other small organisms.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are recognized by their distinctive golden-yellow to bright green coloration and their ability to form tight, compact cushions that can withstand harsh conditions.
children.funFact: The name Eustilbum comes from Greek words meaning 'good' and 'glitter,' referring to the shiny, metallic appearance of these mosses when they catch the light.

children.name: Patinellaria
children.description: Patinellaria is a genus of small, cup-shaped fungi that grow on decaying wood in forest environments. These tiny fungal cups are part of the ascomycete group, which means they produce their spores in special sac-like structures called asci.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their small, shallow cup or disc-shaped fruiting bodies that typically have bright or distinctive coloration. They differ from similar cup fungi by their specific microscopic features and their preference for growing on hardwood substrates.
