children.funFact: The name 'Patinellaria' comes from the Latin word 'patina,' referring to the shallow dish-like shape of these tiny fungi, which can be as small as a few millimeters across.

children.name: Bryoglossaceae
Neocudoniella
children.description: Neocudoniella is a small genus of tiny moths in the family Gelechiidae, known as twirler moths. These delicate insects are characterized by their narrow wings and small size, with larvae that typically feed on plant roots or low-growing vegetation.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus can be distinguished from other gelechiid moths by their specific wing patterns and the root-feeding behavior of their caterpillars, as suggested by the species name 'radicella' which refers to roots.
children.funFact: The single New England species, Neocudoniella radicella, is so small and inconspicuous that it's easily overlooked, yet it plays an important role in soil ecosystems where its larvae help decompose organic matter around plant roots.

children.description: Bryoglossaceae is a small family of fungi that includes just a few rare species found in forest environments. These fungi are characterized by their unique spore-producing structures and are part of the broader group of ascomycete fungi. They play important ecological roles as decomposers in woodland ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their distinctive fruiting bodies and specialized spore-bearing structures that differ from other related fungal families. They have unique cellular characteristics that set them apart from similar forest fungi.
children.funFact: This family is so rare and specialized that New England is home to just one species, making any encounter with a Bryoglossaceae fungus a truly special find for nature enthusiasts!

children.name: Ascodichaenaceae
Ascodichaena
children.description: Ascodichaena is a small genus of fungi that forms tiny, dark fruiting bodies on decaying wood and plant material. These microscopic fungi are part of the larger group of sac fungi (ascomycetes) and play an important role in breaking down organic matter in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their small, flask-shaped fruiting bodies (perithecia) that are typically dark-colored and embedded in or sitting on their substrate. They can be distinguished from similar fungi by their specific spore shapes and the structure of their reproductive organs.
children.funFact: Despite being incredibly tiny and easily overlooked, Ascodichaena fungi are essential decomposers that help recycle nutrients back into the soil, making them available for trees and other plants to use.

children.description: Ascodichaenaceae is a small family of fungi that are primarily plant pathogens, meaning they cause diseases in plants. These microscopic fungi are characterized by their unique spore-producing structures and their ability to infect and damage various plant hosts. They belong to a larger group of fungi known as ascomycetes, which produce their spores in special sac-like structures.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their specialized fruiting bodies and the particular way they form their spores within flask-shaped structures. They differ from related fungal families in their specific host relationships and the microscopic details of their reproductive structures.
children.funFact: Despite being a small family with only one species found in New England, Ascodichaenaceae fungi play an important ecological role as plant pathogens, helping to regulate plant populations in forest ecosystems.

children.name: Podophacidium
children.description: Podophacidium is a small genus of fungi that forms tiny, cup-shaped fruiting bodies on decaying plant material. These microscopic fungi are part of the larger group of cup fungi and play an important role in breaking down organic matter in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their very small size and specific habitat preferences, typically growing on dead stems and branches of woody plants.
children.funFact: Despite being so small they're easily overlooked, Podophacidium fungi are actually helping to recycle nutrients back into the soil every time they decompose dead plant material.

children.name: Dermateaceae
Pezicula
children.description: Pezicula is a small genus of fungi that produces tiny, cup-shaped fruiting bodies called apothecia. These microscopic fungi are plant pathogens that typically cause cankers and dieback diseases on woody plants, particularly shrubs and trees.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Pezicula are distinguished by their small, pale-colored cup fungi that emerge directly from infected plant tissue, and their role as specialized plant parasites rather than decomposers.
children.funFact: Despite being tiny and often overlooked, Pezicula fungi can significantly impact forest health by weakening trees and making them more susceptible to other diseases and environmental stresses.

children.description: Dermateaceae is a family of small cup fungi that typically grow as parasites or decomposers on woody plants like trees and shrubs. These fungi produce tiny, disc-shaped fruiting bodies that often emerge from bark or dead wood. They play an important ecological role by breaking down plant material and recycling nutrients back into forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their small, often dark-colored cup-shaped fruiting bodies that typically develop beneath the bark or surface of their host plants before breaking through. Unlike many other cup fungi, they often have a close parasitic or endophytic relationship with living woody plants.
children.funFact: Some Dermateaceae fungi can remain dormant inside healthy tree bark for years, only producing their visible fruiting bodies when the host plant becomes stressed or begins to die.

children.name: Godroniaceae
Ascocalyx
children.description: Ascocalyx is a small genus of marine bryozoans, tiny colonial animals that form encrusting patches on underwater surfaces. These filter-feeding creatures build intricate calcium carbonate structures and live together in colonies where each individual animal occupies its own small chamber.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Ascocalyx is distinguished by its unique cup-shaped or tubular zooids (individual colony members) with distinctive calcium carbonate walls that have a characteristic sculptured appearance.
children.funFact: Despite being animals, bryozoan colonies like Ascocalyx are often mistaken for seaweeds or coral due to their plant-like or rock-like appearance when growing on pier pilings and rocky shores.

children.description: Godroniaceae is a family of fungi that includes parasitic species which cause diseases in trees and shrubs. These fungi typically form small, dark fruiting bodies on infected plant tissue and are known for causing cankers and dieback in their host plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their parasitic lifestyle on woody plants and their production of distinctive cup-shaped or disc-like fruiting structures that emerge from infected bark or twigs.
children.funFact: Some Godroniaceae fungi can remain dormant in plant tissue for years before environmental stress triggers them to become active and cause visible disease symptoms.

children.description: Helotiales is a diverse order of cup fungi that includes both plant parasites and decomposers found throughout New England's forests and gardens. These fungi produce small, cup-shaped or disk-shaped fruiting bodies and play crucial roles as both plant pathogens and recyclers of organic matter. The group includes the familiar powdery mildews that coat leaves with white fungal growth, as well as many tiny decomposer fungi that break down dead plant material.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other cup fungi, members of Helotiales typically have very small fruiting bodies and often form intimate relationships with living plants as parasites or pathogens. They produce their spores in sac-like structures called asci, which forcibly shoot spores into the air when mature.
children.funFact: Some Helotiales fungi, like those in the Chlorociboriaceae family, stain wood a beautiful blue-green color that was historically prized by furniture makers for decorative inlay work called 'Tunbridge ware.'

children.name: Rhytismatales
Rhytismataceae
Rhytisma
children.description: Tar spot fungi are plant pathogens that create distinctive black, tar-like spots on the leaves of trees and shrubs. These fungi spend part of their life cycle living within leaf tissues, forming characteristic dark, crusty patches that look like drops of black tar have been splattered on the foliage.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other leaf spot fungi, tar spot fungi produce thick, shiny black stromata (fungal structures) that are raised above the leaf surface and have a distinctive tar-like appearance. Each species typically specializes on specific host plants, such as maples, willows, or other woody species.
children.funFact: Despite their alarming appearance, tar spot fungi rarely cause serious harm to their host trees - they're more of a cosmetic issue that makes leaves look like they've been splattered with black paint!

children.name: Lophodermium
children.description: Lophodermium is a genus of tiny fungi that specialize in living on and decomposing pine needles. These microscopic organisms create characteristic dark, oval-shaped spots on fallen pine needles, playing an important role in breaking down organic matter in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other needle-dwelling fungi, Lophodermium species form distinctive elongated black fruiting bodies that split open in a characteristic line down the middle to release their spores.
children.funFact: The name 'Lophodermium' literally means 'crested skin,' referring to the ridge-like appearance of these fungi's spore-releasing structures on pine needles.

children.name: Angelina
children.description: Angelina is a genus of tiny freshwater tardigrades, also known as water bears or moss piglets. These microscopic animals are found in moist environments like moss, lichens, and leaf litter where they feed on plant cells and other small organisms.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Angelina can be identified by their distinctive reddish-brown coloration and their characteristic body shape with four pairs of stubby legs ending in claws.
children.funFact: Despite being smaller than the period at the end of this sentence, Angelina tardigrades can survive extreme conditions including complete dehydration by entering a state called cryptobiosis where they essentially pause all life processes.

children.name: Coccomyces
children.description: Coccomyces is a genus of small, disc-shaped fungi that are specialized parasites of other fungi, particularly those that cause plant diseases. These tiny organisms act like nature's fungal police, attacking and feeding on harmful fungi that might otherwise damage trees and other plants. They produce small, dark fruiting bodies that look like tiny black dots on the surface of their fungal hosts.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most fungi that decompose dead material or form partnerships with plants, Coccomyces species are mycoparasites that specifically target and consume other living fungi. Their fruiting bodies are characteristically small and disc-like, often appearing as dark spots directly on the surface of infected host fungi.
children.funFact: Coccomyces fungi are considered beneficial because they naturally control plant diseases by parasitizing the harmful fungi that cause leaf spots, blights, and other plant ailments.

children.name: Macroderma
children.description: Macroderma is a genus of small, delicate moths in the family Oecophoridae. These moths are characterized by their narrow wings and relatively small size, typically found in wooded areas where their larvae feed on decaying organic matter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus can be distinguished from related moths by their distinctive wing patterns and the specific structure of their reproductive organs, which are important for species identification.
children.funFact: The genus name 'Macroderma' literally means 'large skin,' which refers to the relatively broad wing membrane compared to the moth's small body size.

children.description: The Rhytismataceae are a family of fungi that specialize in causing leaf spots and needle blights on trees and shrubs. These fungi create distinctive black, tar-like spots or elongated lesions on their host plants, often becoming quite noticeable in late summer and fall. They are important plant pathogens that can affect the health and appearance of many common New England trees.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family produce characteristic black, often shiny fruiting bodies that develop within or beneath the host plant's tissue, creating the distinctive 'tar spot' appearance. Unlike many other leaf-spotting fungi, their spore-producing structures typically open through distinctive slits or cracks in the blackened tissue.
children.funFact: Tar spot fungi can actually help you identify tree species from a distance - different Rhytismataceae species are highly host-specific, so the distinctive black spots can tell you whether you're looking at a maple, willow, or other particular tree species!

children.name: Cudoniaceae
Cudonia
children.description: Cudonia is a small genus of unusual fungi that produce distinctive mushroom-like fruiting bodies with gelatinous, brain-like caps sitting atop slender stalks. These fascinating fungi are saprophytes, meaning they feed on decaying organic matter in forest soils and leaf litter. They're part of the cup fungi group but have evolved a unique mushroom-like appearance.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike typical mushrooms, Cudonia species have smooth, gelatinous caps that lack gills, pores, or spines underneath. Their caps have a distinctive wrinkled, brain-like surface texture and sit on relatively thin, often colorful stalks.
children.funFact: Despite looking like mushrooms, Cudonia species are actually more closely related to cup fungi and morels, representing an interesting example of convergent evolution in fungal forms.

children.name: Spathulariopsis
children.description: Spathulariopsis is a small genus of club fungi that produces distinctive fan-shaped or spatula-like fruiting bodies. These fungi are saprobes that help decompose dead wood and plant material in forest environments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their flattened, fan-shaped caps that often have a velvety texture, distinguishing them from the more cylindrical club fungi in related genera.
children.funFact: The genus name Spathulariopsis means 'spatula-like,' referring to the flattened, paddle-shaped appearance of these small fungi that can easily be mistaken for tiny wooden spoons in the forest.

children.name: Spathularia
children.description: Spathularia is a small genus of distinctive fungi that produce unusual spoon or spatula-shaped fruiting bodies. These earth tongues create flattened, fan-like structures that emerge from the soil, typically in forested areas during late summer and fall.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other earth tongues that are club-shaped or cylindrical, Spathularia species have distinctly flattened, spatula-shaped caps that are compressed from side to side, giving them their characteristic fan-like appearance.
children.funFact: The genus name 'Spathularia' comes from the Latin word 'spathula,' meaning little spatula, perfectly describing their flattened, kitchen utensil-like shape.

children.description: The Cudoniaceae family consists of distinctive cup fungi that produce club-shaped or spatula-like fruiting bodies rising from the forest floor. These fungi have a unique appearance with a flattened, often wrinkled cap sitting atop a slender stalk, making them look quite different from typical mushrooms. They are saprophytic fungi that help decompose organic matter in woodland environments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other cup fungi that form bowl-shaped structures, members of Cudoniaceae have elevated, spatula-like or club-shaped caps on distinct stalks. Their caps are typically gelatinous or rubbery in texture and often have a wrinkled or convoluted surface.
children.funFact: Some species in this family, particularly those in the genus Spathularia, are sometimes called "fairy fans" because their flattened, paddle-shaped caps resemble tiny fans that woodland fairies might use.

children.description: Rhytismatales is an order of fungi that includes many plant pathogens and decomposers commonly found on trees and shrubs. These fungi are known for forming distinctive black, often tar-like spots or lesions on leaves, bark, and stems of their host plants. Most species in this group are specialized to grow on specific types of woody plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this order typically produce dark, sunken fruiting bodies that break through the surface of plant tissue in a characteristic star-shaped or slit-like pattern. Unlike many other fungi, they often remain dormant through winter and become active again in spring.
children.funFact: The most famous member of this group causes 'tar spot' on maple leaves - those distinctive black patches you see on maple trees in late summer that look like someone splattered tar on the leaves!

children.name: Leotiales
Leotiaceae
Microglossum
children.description: Microglossum is a genus of small, club-shaped fungi commonly known as earthtongues. These unusual fungi produce slender, tongue-like fruiting bodies that emerge from the soil, typically measuring just a few inches tall and often displaying vibrant colors ranging from orange and green to olive and smoky gray.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other small club fungi, Microglossum earthtongues have distinctly flattened or spatula-shaped tops rather than rounded heads. Their colorful, smooth surfaces and preference for growing directly from soil help distinguish them from similar-looking species.
children.funFact: Despite their small size and inconspicuous nature, earthtongues are actually closely related to cup fungi and play important ecological roles as decomposers in forest ecosystems.

children.name: Leotia
children.description: Jelly Babies are small, gelatinous fungi that look like colorful, translucent clubs or irregular blobs rising from the forest floor. These distinctive mushrooms have a rubbery, jelly-like texture and typically grow in small clusters on decaying wood or soil in moist woodland areas. All members of this genus share the characteristic gelatinous appearance that gives them their common name.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other club fungi, Jelly Babies have a distinctly gelatinous, translucent texture that feels rubbery to the touch. Their caps are typically irregularly shaped and often appear somewhat brain-like or folded, rather than having the smooth, uniform appearance of related fungi.
children.funFact: Despite their appetizing name 'Jelly Babies,' these fungi are generally considered inedible due to their tough, rubbery texture and bland taste.

children.name: Thuemenidium
children.description: Thuemenidium is a small genus of earth tongue fungi that produce dark, club-shaped fruiting bodies emerging from the soil. These fungi are part of the larger group of earth tongues, which are characterized by their simple, tongue-like appearance rather than the typical mushroom cap-and-stem structure.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Thuemenidium species are distinguished from other earth tongues by their distinctively dark purple to blackish coloration and their specific microscopic spore characteristics.
children.funFact: Despite their simple appearance, earth tongue fungi like Thuemenidium are actually more closely related to cup fungi than to typical mushrooms, representing an ancient lineage that has maintained this basic club-like form for millions of years.

children.description: The Leotiaceae are a family of small, cup-shaped or club-shaped fungi that typically grow from decaying organic matter in forest soils. These fungi produce their spores in tiny, often colorful fruiting bodies that can be found throughout the growing season on wood, leaves, and other plant debris.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their small, disc-like or club-shaped fruiting bodies and their preference for growing on decaying plant material rather than living hosts.
children.funFact: The appropriately named 'Jelly Babies' (Leotia species) have translucent, gelatinous caps that look remarkably like gummy candy when fresh, making them one of the most distinctive fungi you might encounter on a forest walk.

children.name: Tympanidaceae
Durandiella
children.description: Durandiella is a small genus of parasitic fungi that specialize in attacking woody plants. These microscopic fungi live as pathogens, causing disease symptoms on their host trees and shrubs.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their specific host preferences and unique spore structures that help them infect and spread on woody plant tissues.
children.funFact: The single New England species, Durandiella fraxini, specifically targets ash trees, making it particularly noteworthy given the ongoing threats to ash populations from invasive insects.

children.name: Claussenomyces
children.description: Claussenomyces is a small genus of cup fungi that grows on decaying wood in forest environments. These tiny fungi produce small, cup-shaped fruiting bodies that help decompose fallen logs and branches, playing an important role in forest nutrient cycling.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their small, olive-colored to brownish cup-shaped fruiting bodies and their specific association with decaying hardwood substrates.
children.funFact: Despite being a small and relatively obscure genus, Claussenomyces fungi are efficient wood decomposers that help transform fallen trees back into soil nutrients that living plants can use.

children.description: Tympanidaceae is a small family of fungi that includes species which form tiny, cup-shaped or disc-shaped fruiting bodies on dead wood and plant material. These fungi are part of the larger group of sac fungi and play an important role in decomposing organic matter in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their small, often dark-colored fruiting bodies that have a distinctive cup or disc shape. They can be distinguished from similar fungi by their specific spore characteristics and the way their reproductive structures are arranged.
children.funFact: Despite being tiny and easily overlooked, these fungi are nature's recyclers, quietly breaking down dead wood and helping return nutrients to the forest soil.

children.name: Alatospora
children.description: Alatospora is a genus of aquatic fungi that specializes in living in freshwater environments like streams and rivers. These microscopic fungi are part of the decomposer community, breaking down organic matter in aquatic ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Alatospora fungi produce distinctive spores with wing-like extensions (the name means 'winged spore') that help them disperse through water currents.
children.funFact: These tiny fungi play a crucial role in stream ecosystems by decomposing fallen leaves and other organic debris, making nutrients available to other aquatic organisms.

children.description: Leotiales is an order of small, cup-shaped fungi that are commonly found on decaying plant material throughout New England's forests. These fungi typically produce tiny, colorful fruiting bodies that look like miniature cups or discs, often appearing in clusters on rotting wood, leaves, or other organic matter. They play an important ecological role as decomposers, breaking down dead plant material and recycling nutrients back into the ecosystem.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Leotiales are distinguished by their small, cup-shaped or disc-like fruiting bodies (apothecia) that typically measure just a few millimeters across. Unlike many other cup fungi, they often have smooth, waxy surfaces and tend to be more delicate in structure.
children.funFact: Some species in this order are so small that you need a magnifying glass to fully appreciate their intricate cup shapes and vibrant colors, which can range from bright orange and yellow to deep brown and black.

children.name: Phacidiales
Phacidiaceae
Bulgaria
children.description: Bulgaria is a genus of distinctive cup fungi that forms dark, rubbery fruiting bodies on dead hardwood, particularly oak and beech. These fungi are saprophytes, meaning they decompose dead organic matter and play an important role in forest ecosystems by breaking down fallen logs and branches.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Bulgaria fungi are easily recognized by their distinctive black, leathery cups that have a smooth, shiny interior and often appear almost tar-like when fresh. Unlike many other cup fungi, they maintain their dark coloration and don't fade to lighter colors as they age.
children.funFact: Despite its common name "Poor Man's Licorice," Bulgaria inquinans doesn't taste like licorice at all - the name likely refers to its dark, glossy appearance that might remind someone of black licorice candy.

children.description: Phacidiaceae is a family of fungi that includes species commonly known as tar spot fungi and related groups. These fungi typically form dark, flattened fruiting bodies that develop on dead or dying plant material, especially wood and leaves. They are important decomposers in forest ecosystems, helping break down organic matter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their dark, often tar-like fruiting bodies that are typically flattened and embedded in or sitting directly on their host substrate. Unlike many other fungi, they often appear as dark spots or patches rather than mushroom-like structures.
children.funFact: The name 'Phacidiaceae' comes from the Greek word 'phakos' meaning lentil, referring to the lens-shaped appearance of their fruiting bodies.

children.description: Phacidiales is an order of fungi that primarily live as parasites or decomposers on plant material, especially coniferous trees. These fungi typically form small, dark fruiting bodies that emerge from infected plant tissues, often appearing as tiny black dots or cushions on leaves, needles, or bark.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this order are characterized by their apothecia (cup-shaped fruiting bodies) that often remain closed when young and split open in a distinctive star-like or slit pattern to release spores.
children.funFact: Some Phacidiales fungi can remain dormant in dead plant material for months or even years before producing their spore-releasing structures, waiting for just the right moisture conditions.

children.name: Marthamycetales
Propoliaceae
Propolis
children.description: Propolis is a small genus of green algae that forms crusty, powdery patches on tree bark, rocks, and other surfaces. These tiny organisms are among the most common algae you'll encounter in New England forests, though they're often overlooked due to their simple appearance. They reproduce through spores and can survive in relatively dry conditions compared to many other algae.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Propolis species are distinguished by their powdery, flour-like texture and ability to grow directly on dry surfaces without standing water. Unlike many algae that need aquatic environments, these species have adapted to terrestrial life on bark and stone.
children.funFact: The name 'Propolis' comes from the Greek word meaning 'before the city,' referencing how these algae often form the first layer of growth that other organisms later colonize on bare surfaces.

children.description: Propoliaceae is a small family of green algae that live in freshwater environments like ponds, streams, and wet soil. These microscopic algae are single-celled organisms that can photosynthesize, making their own food from sunlight like plants do. They play an important role in aquatic ecosystems as primary producers at the base of the food web.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their unique cell wall composition and specific chloroplast structure that sets them apart from other green algae families. They typically reproduce through specialized spores and have distinctive cellular arrangements when viewed under a microscope.
children.funFact: Despite being microscopic and often overlooked, these tiny algae can form visible green films on the surface of quiet water bodies, contributing significantly to oxygen production in their aquatic habitats.

children.description: Marthamycetales is a small order of fungi that includes species found in various environments, from soil to decaying organic matter. These fungi are part of the larger group of sac fungi (Ascomycetes) and play important roles in decomposition and nutrient cycling in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this order are characterized by their unique spore-producing structures and specific molecular characteristics that separate them from other fungal orders. They typically form small, often inconspicuous fruiting bodies.
children.funFact: This order is so recently discovered and studied that it contains only one known family, making it one of the smaller and more mysterious branches on the fungal tree of life.

children.name: Thelebolales
Holwayaceae
Holwaya
children.description: Holwaya is a small genus of cup fungi that creates distinctive flask-shaped or cup-shaped fruiting bodies on decaying wood. These tiny fungi are saprophytes, meaning they help decompose dead organic matter and recycle nutrients back into forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Holwaya fungi are recognized by their small, dark-colored cup-shaped structures that develop on rotting hardwood logs and branches, often appearing clustered together in groups.
children.funFact: Despite being microscopic decomposers, Holwaya fungi play an outsized role in forest health by breaking down tough woody materials that many other organisms cannot digest.

children.description: Holwayaceae is a small family of cup fungi that includes just one genus, Holwaya. These fungi produce distinctive cup-shaped fruiting bodies that emerge from dead wood, particularly on decaying hardwood branches and logs.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their pale, translucent cup-shaped structures and their specific habitat preference for dead hardwood material, setting them apart from other cup fungi that may grow on different substrates.
children.funFact: The entire Holwayaceae family contains only about 5 species worldwide, making it one of the smallest families of cup fungi, with New England hosting one of these rare species.

children.description: Thelebolales is a small order of fungi that are primarily decomposers, breaking down organic matter in soil and on various substrates. These microscopic fungi are characterized by their distinctive fruiting bodies called apothecia, which are small, cup-shaped or disc-like structures that contain spores.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this order are distinguished by their unique spore-shooting mechanism and their preference for nutrient-rich substrates like dung or decaying organic matter. Their apothecia are typically small and often have a distinctive opening mechanism for spore release.
children.funFact: Some species in this order can literally shoot their spores several centimeters into the air, using built-up pressure to launch them toward light sources where they're more likely to land on suitable new habitats.

children.name: Medeolariales
Medeolariaceae
Medeolaria
children.description: Medeolaria is a genus of small marine snails that live in shallow coastal waters. These tiny gastropods are part of the diverse world of sea slugs and marine mollusks that crawl along the ocean floor and rocky surfaces.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their small size and specific shell structure that distinguishes them from other marine gastropod genera.
children.funFact: Despite being marine creatures, Medeolaria snails are so small that they often go unnoticed by beachgoers, living their entire lives in the spaces between sand grains and small rocks.

children.description: Medeolariaceae is a small family of flowering plants that includes just one genus found in New England. These are herbaceous perennial plants that grow from underground rhizomes and produce distinctive whorled leaves arranged in tiers up the stem.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their unique leaf arrangement, with leaves appearing in whorls (circles) at specific points along the stem, and their small, inconspicuous flowers that develop into colorful berries.
children.funFact: This family contains only two species worldwide, with one species native to eastern North America and the other found in eastern Asia, representing an ancient plant lineage that once had a much wider distribution.

children.description: Medeolariales is a small order of flowering plants that includes just one family and a handful of species worldwide. These are herbaceous perennial plants that grow from underground rhizomes and are found in woodland environments. They are characterized by their distinctive three-parted flowers and whorled leaves.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this order have unique flowers with parts arranged in threes and leaves that grow in circular whorls around the stem. Their flowers are typically small and inconspicuous compared to many other flowering plants.
children.funFact: New England's single representative of this order is the Indian cucumber-root, whose young shoots were traditionally eaten by Native Americans and taste remarkably like cucumber!

children.name: Hypocreales
Hypocreaceae
Hypomyces
children.description: Hypomyces is a genus of parasitic fungi that live on and attack other mushrooms and fungi. These fungal parasites completely transform their hosts, often changing their color, texture, and shape so dramatically that the original mushroom becomes unrecognizable. They create a new outer layer over their victim, essentially turning one fungus into something that looks entirely different.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most fungi that decompose dead organic matter, Hypomyces species are specialized parasites that exclusively target living mushrooms and other fungi. They form a distinctive coating or crust over their hosts, often with bright colors like orange, yellow, or pink.
children.funFact: The famous 'lobster mushroom' isn't actually a mushroom at all - it's created when Hypomyces lactifluorum parasitizes certain white mushrooms, turning them bright orange-red and giving them a seafood-like flavor that's prized by gourmet cooks.

children.name: Trichoderma
children.description: Trichoderma is a genus of fungi that includes some of nature's most effective decomposers and biological pest controllers. These small, fast-growing fungi are commonly found in soil and on decaying wood, where they break down organic matter and help recycle nutrients back into the ecosystem.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Trichoderma fungi are characterized by their rapid growth rate and ability to produce green spores, often forming cushion-like or bracket-shaped fruiting bodies on their substrates.
children.funFact: Some Trichoderma species are so effective at controlling plant diseases that they're commercially produced and sold as biological pesticides to protect crops from harmful fungi.

children.name: Protocrea
children.description: Protocrea is a small genus of fungi that produces bright, colorful fruiting bodies on decaying wood and plant material. These fungi are part of the larger group of cup fungi and flask fungi, playing an important role in breaking down organic matter in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Protocrea species are characterized by their small, flask-shaped fruiting bodies that are often bright orange, red, or yellow in color. They can be distinguished from related genera by their specific spore characteristics and the way their fruiting bodies develop.
children.funFact: Despite being tiny and easily overlooked, Protocrea fungi are nature's recyclers, helping to decompose dead plant material and return nutrients to the soil for new plant growth.

children.name: Mycogone
children.description: Mycogone is a genus of parasitic fungi that specifically targets and attacks other fungi, particularly mushrooms and other fleshy fungi. These specialized organisms make their living by invading and feeding on their fungal hosts, often causing distinctive changes in the host's appearance and structure.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most fungi that decompose dead organic matter or form partnerships with plants, Mycogone species are obligate parasites that can only survive by attacking living fungi. They produce distinctive spores and often cause their mushroom hosts to become deformed or discolored.
children.funFact: Mycogone rosea is sometimes called the "rosé mold" because it can turn white mushrooms pink or salmon-colored as it parasitizes them, creating an almost beautiful transformation while slowly consuming its host.

children.name: Sphaerostilbella
children.description: Sphaerostilbella is a small genus of fungi that produces tiny, colorful fruiting bodies on decaying wood and plant material. These microscopic fungi are part of the larger group of ascomycetes and play an important role in breaking down organic matter in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their small, spherical to flask-shaped fruiting bodies that are typically bright orange to red in color. They can be distinguished from similar fungi by their specific spore characteristics and their preference for growing on decaying wood.
children.funFact: Despite being tiny and often overlooked, Sphaerostilbella fungi produce some of the most vibrant orange and red colors you can find in the fungal kingdom.

children.description: Hypocreaceae is a diverse family of fungi that includes both helpful allies and sneaky parasites in the fungal world. Many members of this family are decomposers that break down organic matter, while others are parasites that grow on other fungi, and some are beneficial partners that help control plant diseases.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These fungi typically produce their spores in flask-shaped structures called perithecia, often embedded in colorful, cushion-like masses. Many species in this family are notable for their bright colors, ranging from vivid oranges and reds to yellows and greens.
children.funFact: Some Hypomyces species are known as 'lobster mushrooms' because they parasitize other mushrooms and transform them into bright orange, lobster-colored masses that are actually considered a delicacy by foragers.

children.name: Cordycipitaceae
Cordyceps
children.description: Cordyceps are fascinating parasitic fungi that grow on insects and other arthropods, eventually taking over their host's body. These fungi produce distinctive club-shaped or finger-like fruiting bodies that emerge from their unfortunate victims. They're part of nature's cleanup crew, helping to control insect populations while recycling nutrients back into the ecosystem.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most fungi that grow on dead wood or soil, Cordyceps specifically target living insects and spiders as hosts. Their fruiting bodies emerge directly from the host's body, creating an unmistakable sight of colorful fungal structures sprouting from dead insects.
children.funFact: Some Cordyceps species can actually control their host's behavior before killing them, essentially turning insects into 'zombies' that climb to optimal locations for spore dispersal before dying.

children.name: Gibellula
children.description: Gibellula is a fascinating genus of fungi that has evolved to be parasitic on spiders and other arachnids. These tiny fungi infect their spider hosts, eventually sprouting delicate, thread-like structures from the spider's body. They represent a specialized group of entomopathogenic fungi that have adapted specifically to target arachnids rather than insects.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other spider-parasitic fungi, Gibellula produces distinctive thin, hair-like conidiophores that emerge from infected spiders. The fungal structures are typically much more delicate and thread-like compared to the club-shaped or branched fruiting bodies of related genera.
children.funFact: When Gibellula infects a spider, it can actually manipulate the spider's behavior before killing it, sometimes causing the spider to move to a location that's more favorable for the fungus to spread its spores.

children.name: Akanthomyces
children.description: Akanthomyces is a genus of entomopathogenic fungi, meaning they are specialized parasites that infect and kill insects and other arthropods like spiders. These fungi produce spiny or needle-like structures called conidia (spores) that help them spread and infect new hosts. They play an important ecological role as natural pest controllers in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Akanthomyces are distinguished by their characteristic spiny or thorny spore-bearing structures, which is reflected in their name ('akantho' meaning thorn or spine). Unlike many other fungi, they have evolved specifically to parasitize living arthropods rather than decomposing organic matter.
children.funFact: The Moth Urchin Fungus gets its name from its spiky appearance that resembles a sea urchin, and it can actually control the behavior of infected insects, sometimes causing them to climb to high places before death to help spread the fungal spores.

children.name: Engyodontium
children.description: Engyodontium is a genus of microscopic fungi that includes species known for their ability to parasitize insects and spiders. These fungi produce distinctive spores and thread-like structures called hyphae that help them spread and infect their arthropod hosts. They play an important ecological role as natural biological control agents in forest and garden ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Engyodontium are characterized by their specialized ability to infect and kill arthropods, particularly spiders and insects. They produce unique spore structures and have specific adaptations that allow them to penetrate the exoskeletons of their hosts.
children.funFact: The single New England species, Engyodontium aranearum, specifically targets spiders - its species name 'aranearum' literally means 'of spiders' in Latin!

children.name: Beauveria
children.description: Beauveria is a genus of entomopathogenic fungi, meaning they are specialized parasites that infect and kill insects. These fungi produce spores that attach to insect hosts, penetrate their exoskeletons, and eventually consume the insect from the inside out. After killing their host, they often cover the dead insect with a white, powdery coating of new spores.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other fungi that decompose dead organic matter, Beauveria species are active hunters that specifically target living insects. They produce distinctive white, chalky spore masses on their insect victims, giving infected insects a frosted or powdered sugar appearance.
children.funFact: Beauveria bassiana is used as a natural, environmentally-friendly pesticide in agriculture and is so effective that it's sometimes called 'white muscardine disease' when it decimates insect populations in the wild.

children.name: Samsoniella
children.description: Samsoniella is a genus of tiny parasitic fungi that lives inside the bodies of insects, particularly moth larvae. These microscopic organisms are part of a specialized group of fungi that have evolved to survive and reproduce within their insect hosts.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other parasitic fungi, Samsoniella species are highly host-specific and have developed unique adaptations to live exclusively within the internal tissues of their particular insect hosts.
children.funFact: The genus Samsoniella was named after the biblical strongman Samson, perhaps referencing how these tiny fungi can overpower much larger insect hosts despite their microscopic size.

children.name: Amphichorda
children.description: Amphichorda is a genus of marine worms that live in shallow coastal waters, burrowing in sandy or muddy sediments. These small, elongated creatures are hemichordates, meaning they possess some primitive characteristics that are thought to bridge the gap between invertebrates and vertebrates. They feed by filtering organic particles and plankton from the water around their burrows.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Amphichorda can be distinguished from other hemichordates by their small size and simple body structure, lacking the complex branching gill slits found in their relatives. They have a more streamlined, worm-like appearance compared to the acorn worms in the same phylum.
children.funFact: Despite being tiny marine worms, Amphichorda and other hemichordates are actually more closely related to humans than they are to most other worm groups, sharing a common evolutionary ancestor with all vertebrates.

children.description: Cordycipitaceae is a fascinating family of fungi that specialize in parasitizing insects and other small invertebrates. These fungi infect their hosts while they're still alive, eventually taking over their bodies and producing spore-bearing structures that emerge from the dead host. They play an important ecological role as natural pest controllers in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike typical mushroom-forming fungi, members of this family are obligate parasites that require living hosts to complete their life cycle. They produce distinctive club-shaped or branched fruiting bodies that grow directly out of their insect victims.
children.funFact: Some Cordyceps species can actually manipulate their insect host's behavior before killing them, causing infected ants to climb to high perches where the fungus can better disperse its spores - earning them the nickname 'zombie fungi.'

children.name: Ophiocordycipitaceae
Tolypocladium
children.description: Tolypocladium is a fascinating genus of fungi that includes both underground truffle-like species and above-ground club-shaped mushrooms. These fungi are parasitic, meaning they get their nutrients by attacking and consuming other organisms, particularly underground fungi and insects. Despite their different appearances, all members of this genus share similar microscopic features and genetic characteristics.
children.distinguishingFeatures: What sets Tolypocladium apart from other fungi is their unique dual lifestyle - some species form underground truffle-like fruiting bodies while others produce distinctive club or drumstick-shaped mushrooms above ground. They're also distinguished by their parasitic nature, specifically targeting other fungi and arthropods.
children.funFact: One species in this genus, Tolypocladium inflatum, is the source of cyclosporine, a crucial immunosuppressive drug that has made organ transplants much more successful by preventing the body from rejecting donated organs.

children.name: Ophiocordyceps
children.description: Ophiocordyceps is a fascinating genus of parasitic fungi that specialize in infecting insects and other arthropods. These fungi grow inside their host's body, eventually killing it and producing distinctive club-shaped or elongated fruiting bodies that emerge from the dead insect. They play an important ecological role by helping control insect populations in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other fungi that decompose dead organic matter, Ophiocordyceps species are active parasites that must infect living insects to complete their life cycle. Their fruiting bodies typically emerge dramatically from specific parts of the host's body, often the head or joints.
children.funFact: Some Ophiocordyceps species can actually manipulate their host's behavior before killing them, causing infected ants to climb to elevated positions where the fungus can better spread its spores - earning them the nickname 'zombie fungi.'

children.name: Paraisaria
children.description: Paraisaria is a genus of parasitic fungi that grows on other fungi, particularly targeting certain species of club fungi. These tiny organisms are part of a specialized group that has evolved to live entirely off their fungal hosts. In New England, this genus is represented by a single species that can be found in forested areas where its host fungi occur.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most fungi that decompose organic matter or form partnerships with plants, Paraisaria species are obligate parasites that specifically attack other fungi. They produce small, often inconspicuous fruiting bodies that emerge directly from their infected host.
children.funFact: Paraisaria fungi are so specialized that they can only survive by parasitizing specific types of fungi, making them some of nature's most particular 'picky eaters' in the fungal world.

children.description: The Ophiocordycipitaceae are a fascinating family of fungi that specialize in parasitizing insects and other arthropods. These fungi infect their hosts from the inside, eventually killing them and producing spore-bearing structures that emerge from the host's body. They play an important ecological role as natural pest controllers in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most fungi that decompose dead organic matter, members of this family are active parasites that specifically target living insects, spiders, and other small invertebrates. Their fruiting bodies typically emerge directly from their host's corpse in distinctive club-like or elongated shapes.
children.funFact: Some species in this family can actually manipulate their host's behavior before killing them, causing infected insects to climb to elevated positions where the fungus can better disperse its spores - earning them the nickname 'zombie fungi.'

children.name: Nectriaceae
Neonectria
children.description: Neonectria is a genus of parasitic fungi that specialize in causing canker diseases on trees and woody plants. These fungi attack the bark and underlying tissues of their host trees, creating sunken, diseased areas called cankers that can weaken or kill branches and entire trees.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Neonectria fungi produce distinctive bright red or orange fruiting bodies (perithecia) that emerge from infected bark. Unlike many other tree pathogens, they create characteristic sunken cankers with swollen edges around the infection site.
children.funFact: The Beech Bark Canker Fungus works in partnership with a tiny scale insect - the insect creates wounds in the bark that allow the fungus to enter and establish infection, making this a classic example of a biological tag-team attack on trees.

children.name: Nectria
children.description: Nectria is a genus of small fungi that primarily live as parasites on trees and woody plants. These fungi are known for producing bright-colored, tiny flask-shaped fruiting bodies that emerge from infected bark and wood.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Nectria fungi are recognized by their small, brightly colored perithecia (fruiting bodies) that are typically red, orange, or pink and have a distinctive flask-like shape with a tiny opening at the top.
children.funFact: The Coral Spot fungus gets its name from its brilliant orange-red fruiting bodies that look like tiny coral beads scattered across dead branches and bark.

children.name: Fusicolla
children.description: Fusicolla is a genus of fungi that includes species commonly known as slime molds, though they're actually more closely related to other fungal groups. These organisms typically form bright, colorful masses that can appear suddenly on decaying organic matter like rotting logs, leaf litter, or mulch. They play an important role in forest ecosystems by helping to break down dead plant material.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Fusicolla species are distinguished by their ability to form distinctive, often brightly colored fruiting bodies that can change shape and move slowly across their substrate. Unlike true slime molds, they maintain a more fungal-like structure throughout their lifecycle.
children.funFact: Despite its unappetizing common name 'deer vomit,' Fusicolla merismoides gets this nickname from its resemblance to regurgitated material, but it's actually a fascinating organism that can appear overnight and completely disappear within days.

children.name: Pseudocosmospora
children.description: Pseudocosmospora is a genus of microscopic fungi that live as parasites or decomposers, often found growing on dead plant material or other fungi. These tiny organisms produce colorful spores in flask-shaped structures and play important roles in breaking down organic matter in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their distinctive spore-producing structures called perithecia and their often bright-colored, multi-celled spores that help distinguish them from similar fungal groups.
children.funFact: Despite being microscopic, Pseudocosmospora fungi can produce remarkably vibrant orange, red, or yellow spores that are visible under a microscope, making them some of the most colorful members of the fungal kingdom.

children.name: Calonectria
children.description: Calonectria is a genus of microscopic fungi that are primarily plant pathogens, meaning they cause diseases in plants. These fungi produce distinctive spores and often create serious problems for agricultural crops, ornamental plants, and forest trees. They thrive in warm, humid conditions and can spread rapidly through infected plant material.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Calonectria fungi are identified by their unique spore structures called conidia, which are typically cylindrical or boat-shaped and produced in flask-like structures. They differ from related fungal genera by their specific spore dimensions and the way their reproductive structures are arranged.
children.funFact: The boxwood blight fungus in this genus was first discovered in the UK in the 1990s but has since spread globally, causing devastating losses to historic boxwood gardens and landscapes that took centuries to establish.

children.name: Dialonectria
children.description: Dialonectria is a genus of tiny fungi that are parasites of other fungi, specifically targeting certain types of flask fungi called perithecia. These microscopic organisms live by attacking and consuming their fungal hosts, making them examples of mycoparasites - fungi that parasitize other fungi.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Dialonectria fungi are distinguished by their specialized lifestyle as obligate parasites of perithecial fungi, and they produce distinctive spores with multiple cells separated by cross-walls.
children.funFact: These fungi are like the vampires of the fungal world - they can only survive by feeding on other fungi and cannot live independently!

children.description: The Nectriaceae are a family of small fungi that typically produce bright orange, red, or pink fruiting bodies that look like tiny cushions or spheres on wood, bark, and other organic matter. These fungi are commonly found decomposing dead wood and plant material, playing an important role in forest nutrient cycling. Many species in this family can also act as plant pathogens, causing cankers and other diseases in trees and shrubs.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are easily recognized by their vibrant orange to red coloration and their small, often clustered fruiting bodies that feel somewhat gelatinous when fresh. Unlike many other wood-decomposing fungi, they typically produce their spores in flask-shaped structures called perithecia rather than on gills or pores.
children.funFact: Some Nectriaceae species are so closely associated with specific tree species that finding them can help identify what type of wood they're growing on, even when the original tree is long dead and decomposed.

children.name: Bionectriaceae
Nectriopsis
children.description: Nectriopsis is a small genus of parasitic fungi that specialize in attacking other fungi, particularly those that cause plant diseases. These tiny but mighty organisms act as natural biological control agents, helping to keep harmful plant pathogens in check throughout New England's forests and natural areas.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many fungi that decompose dead material or form partnerships with plants, Nectriopsis species are specialized mycoparasites that directly attack and consume other living fungi. They produce distinctive small, colorful fruiting bodies that often appear directly on top of their fungal hosts.
children.funFact: These fungi are essentially the 'fungi police' of the forest ecosystem - they help protect plants by hunting down and destroying disease-causing fungi that would otherwise harm trees and other vegetation.

children.name: Hydropisphaera
children.description: Hydropisphaera is a genus of aquatic fungi that live in freshwater environments like streams, ponds, and lakes. These microscopic organisms are part of the complex web of decomposers that break down organic matter in aquatic ecosystems. They play an important role in nutrient cycling in New England's freshwater habitats.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their spherical spore-bearing structures (perithecia) that are specifically adapted to aquatic environments. Unlike many terrestrial fungi, they have evolved specialized mechanisms to release and disperse their spores in water.
children.funFact: The name Hydropisphaera literally means 'water pea sphere,' referring to their small, round, pea-like reproductive structures that float in freshwater.

children.name: Periantria
children.description: Periantria is a genus of microscopic fungi that are parasitic on other fungi, specifically targeting liverworts (small, flat plants that grow in moist areas). These tiny organisms are part of a specialized group that has evolved to live exclusively on their fungal hosts. They represent one of nature's examples of a parasite that attacks another parasite.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Periantria fungi are distinguished by their extremely specialized lifestyle as obligate parasites of other fungi that grow on liverworts. They form distinctive small, dark fruiting bodies that emerge directly from their fungal hosts.
children.funFact: Periantria frullaniae is so specialized that it only attacks one specific type of fungus that grows on leafy liverworts, making it a parasite of a parasite - a biological relationship called hyperparasitism.

children.description: Bionectriaceae is a family of microscopic fungi that typically form small, colorful fruiting bodies called perithecia. These fungi are often found growing on decaying wood, plant debris, or other organic matter in forest environments. They play an important role in decomposition and nutrient cycling in woodland ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their flask-shaped perithecia that are often brightly colored in shades of red, orange, or yellow. Unlike some related fungi, they typically have smooth spore surfaces and produce their spores in sac-like structures called asci.
children.funFact: Some species in this family can appear almost jewel-like when viewed under magnification, earning them nicknames like 'coral fungi' due to their vibrant colors that stand out against dark, rotting wood.

children.name: Clavicipitaceae
Claviceps
children.description: Ergots are parasitic fungi that infect the seeds of grasses and sedges, replacing the normal grain with dark, elongated fungal structures called sclerotia. These sclerotia contain potent alkaloid compounds that can be toxic to humans and animals if consumed. The fungi complete their life cycle by producing spore-bearing structures that emerge from the sclerotia.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other seed-infecting fungi, ergots completely replace the host seed with a hard, dark sclerotium that contains powerful psychoactive and toxic alkaloids. These sclerotia are much larger and darker than the original seeds they replace.
children.funFact: Ergot alkaloids from rye ergot may have played a role in the Salem witch trials, as consuming ergot-contaminated rye bread can cause hallucinations, convulsions, and other symptoms that were attributed to witchcraft in the 1600s.

children.name: Epichloe
children.description: Epichloe is a genus of fungi that live as endophytes inside grass plants, forming intimate relationships with their hosts. These fungi grow within the tissues of grasses without causing visible disease symptoms, and can actually provide benefits to their host plants like increased resistance to insects and drought.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other fungal parasites, Epichloe species form mutually beneficial relationships with grasses rather than harming them. They produce distinctive white, collar-like structures called stromata that wrap around grass stems during their reproductive phase.
children.funFact: The fungus can produce alkaloids that make the infected grass toxic to grazing animals, essentially turning the plant into a chemical fortress that protects both the grass and its fungal partner.

children.description: Clavicipitaceae is a family of fungi that specialize in forming intimate relationships with grasses and other plants. These fungi often live inside plant tissues as endophytes, sometimes helping their host plants while other times causing disease or producing distinctive fungal structures.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their close associations with grasses and their ability to produce potent alkaloid compounds. They form long, club-shaped fruiting bodies (called stromata) that emerge from infected plant parts.
children.funFact: Some species in this family produce ergot alkaloids, which have been used medicinally but can also be highly toxic - ergot poisoning from contaminated grains may have contributed to accusations of witchcraft in colonial New England!

children.name: Tilachlidiaceae
Tilachlidium
children.description: Tilachlidium is a genus of microscopic fungi that lives as a parasite on other fungi, particularly targeting certain molds and fungal spores. These tiny organisms are part of the complex world of fungi that prey on other fungi, playing an important role in controlling fungal populations in nature.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Tilachlidium produces distinctive branched, tree-like structures called conidiophores that bear their spores, giving them a characteristic branching appearance under the microscope that sets them apart from other fungal parasites.
children.funFact: These microscopic fungi are essentially the 'predators' of the fungal world, hunting down and parasitizing other fungi much like a lion hunts gazelles, but all on a scale invisible to the naked eye.

children.name: Volutella
children.description: Volutella is a genus of plant pathogenic fungi that cause leaf spot and blight diseases on various host plants. These fungi produce distinctive spore-bearing structures called acervuli that emerge from infected plant tissues, releasing masses of spores that can spread to healthy plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Volutella fungi are distinguished by their acervuli (small, cushion-like fruiting bodies) that produce both asexual spores and distinctive dark, bristle-like structures called setae that extend above the spore mass.
children.funFact: The single New England species, Volutella pachysandrae, specifically targets pachysandra groundcover and can quickly spread through dense plantings during warm, humid weather.

children.description: Tilachlidiaceae is a small family of fungi that includes species commonly known as conidial fungi, which reproduce through spores called conidia. These microscopic fungi are typically found growing on decaying plant material, dead wood, and other organic matter in forest environments. They play an important role as decomposers, helping to break down dead organic material and recycle nutrients back into the ecosystem.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their unique spore-producing structures and the way their conidia are arranged and released. Unlike many other fungal families, Tilachlidiaceae species often produce their spores in distinctive clusters or arrangements that help mycologists identify them.
children.funFact: Despite being microscopic, these fungi are incredibly efficient recyclers - they can break down complex organic compounds that many other organisms cannot decompose, making them essential cleanup crews in forest ecosystems.

children.name: Illosporiopsis
children.description: Illosporiopsis is a small genus of parasitic fungi that live on other fungi, making them what scientists call mycoparasites. These tiny organisms attach themselves to their fungal hosts and feed off them, playing a unique role in the complex web of fungal interactions in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other parasitic fungi, Illosporiopsis species specifically target other fungi as their hosts rather than plants or animals. They produce distinctive spore-bearing structures that help scientists identify them under a microscope.
children.funFact: Illosporiopsis christiansenii was named after mycologist Mads Peter Christiansen, and like many mycoparasitic fungi, it may actually help control populations of plant pathogenic fungi in nature.

children.name: Polycephalomycetaceae
Polycephalomyces
children.description: Polycephalomyces is a genus of parasitic fungi that specifically targets scale insects, acting as a natural pest control agent in forest ecosystems. These tiny fungi infect their hosts and eventually produce distinctive fruiting bodies that emerge from the infected insects. They play an important ecological role by helping to regulate scale insect populations in New England's forests.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other entomopathogenic fungi, Polycephalomyces produces multiple club-shaped fruiting structures (called synnemata) that emerge from a single infected host insect. The species P. tomentosus is characterized by its fuzzy, cotton-like appearance on the surface of infected scale insects.
children.funFact: This fungus essentially turns its scale insect host into a 'zombie' - the infected insect remains attached to tree bark while the fungus grows inside it and eventually bursts through the insect's body to release spores.

children.description: Polycephalomycetaceae is a small family of parasitic fungi that specialize in attacking other fungi, particularly those that live on insects. These tiny fungal parasites are part of a fascinating world where fungi prey on other fungi, creating complex relationships in forest ecosystems. They represent one of nature's examples of biological control, where one organism naturally keeps another in check.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their ability to parasitize other fungi rather than directly attacking plants or animals. They produce specialized structures that allow them to penetrate and consume their fungal hosts.
children.funFact: These fungi are essentially the 'fungi that eat fungi' - they're like microscopic predators in the fungal world, helping to maintain balance among different fungal species in forest communities.

children.name: Stachybotryaceae
Myrothecium
children.description: Myrothecium is a genus of fungi that are commonly found as decomposers in soil and on decaying plant material. These microscopic fungi play an important role in breaking down organic matter and recycling nutrients back into the ecosystem. They produce distinctive spores in dark, cushion-like structures that help scientists identify them.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Myrothecium fungi are recognized by their dark green to black spore masses (sporodochia) that form on the surface of their host material, often surrounded by a white or pale margin.
children.funFact: Some species of Myrothecium produce potent natural compounds that have been studied for their potential use as biological pesticides and antibiotics.

children.description: Stachybotryaceae is a family of microscopic fungi that includes some species commonly known as "black mold." These fungi are decomposers that break down organic matter, particularly cellulose-rich materials like wood, paper, and plant debris. They produce dark-colored spores and can be found in damp environments both indoors and outdoors.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their dark, typically black or dark green spores that are produced in slimy masses rather than dry, powdery clusters. They have a distinctive wet, sticky appearance when sporulating.
children.funFact: Some species in this family, particularly Stachybotrys chartarum, are notorious for producing mycotoxins and are often called "toxic black mold," though they play important ecological roles as decomposers in nature.

children.name: Emericellopsis
children.description: Emericellopsis is a small genus of microscopic fungi that live as decomposers, breaking down organic matter in soil and dung. These tiny fungi produce distinctive flask-shaped reproductive structures called perithecia that help scientists identify them under a microscope.
children.distinguishingFeatures: This genus is distinguished by its unique combination of dark, flask-shaped fruiting bodies and specific spore characteristics that set it apart from other soil-dwelling fungi.
children.funFact: Despite being incredibly small and often overlooked, Emericellopsis fungi play an important role in recycling nutrients from animal waste back into the ecosystem.

children.name: Trichothecium
children.description: Trichothecium is a genus of fungi that commonly grows as a saprophyte, feeding on dead organic matter. These fungi are most recognizable for their distinctive pink to salmon-colored spores that form fluffy, cotton-like masses on decaying plant material.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other mold fungi, Trichothecium produces characteristically bright pink to rose-colored spore masses that develop on branching conidiophores (spore-bearing structures).
children.funFact: Trichothecium roseum is often called 'pink mold' and while it looks harmless, it can produce mycotoxins that make stored fruits and vegetables unsafe to eat.

children.description: Hypocreales is a diverse order of fungi that includes many species with colorful, often bright orange, red, or yellow fruiting bodies called perithecia. These fungi are found in a wide variety of habitats and lifestyles, from decomposers breaking down dead wood and plant material to parasites that attack insects, other fungi, and even plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this order typically produce their spores in flask-shaped structures called perithecia, which are often embedded in colorful, fleshy tissue called a stroma. Unlike many other fungal groups, Hypocreales species frequently display vibrant colors and have a wide range of ecological roles.
children.funFact: This order includes the famous "zombie ant" fungi (Ophiocordyceps species) that take control of insect behavior, forcing ants to climb to optimal locations before killing them and sprouting fruiting bodies from their heads.

children.name: Xylariales
Xylariaceae
Xylaria
children.description: Xylaria is a genus of wood-decomposing fungi that create distinctive club-shaped or finger-like fruiting bodies, often appearing black or dark brown with white interiors. These saprophytic fungi play a crucial role in forest ecosystems by breaking down dead wood and fallen branches. Most species in this genus produce their spores in tiny flask-shaped structures called perithecia embedded in the surface of their fruiting bodies.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Xylaria fungi are easily recognized by their characteristic upright, club-like or branched fruiting bodies that are typically black on the outside with white flesh inside. Unlike many other wood-decomposing fungi, they produce hard, often brittle structures rather than soft, fleshy mushrooms.
children.funFact: The common names for Xylaria species often reference their eerie appearance - 'dead man's fingers' and 'dead moll's fingers' reflect how these dark, finger-like fungi can look quite spooky emerging from rotting logs in the forest!

children.name: Kretzschmaria
children.description: Kretzschmaria is a genus of wood-decomposing fungi that form distinctive black, crusty fruiting bodies on dead hardwood trees and stumps. These fungi are important decomposers in forest ecosystems, breaking down dead wood and recycling nutrients back into the soil. They typically appear as dark, carbonaceous masses that can persist for months or even years on their host trees.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their hard, brittle, coal-black fruiting bodies that form a crust-like layer on wood surfaces. Unlike many other wood-decay fungi, Kretzschmaria species produce their spores in tiny flask-shaped chambers embedded within the black crust.
children.funFact: The most common species, Brittle Cinder, gets its name because the black fruiting body is so brittle it crumbles like charcoal when touched, yet it's actually alive and actively producing spores.

children.name: Rosellinia
children.description: Rosellinia is a genus of small, dark fungi that grow as parasites or decomposers on wood and plant material. These fungi produce tiny, black, flask-shaped structures called perithecia that contain their spores. They play an important role in breaking down dead organic matter in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Rosellinia fungi are characterized by their black, carbonaceous (coal-like) perithecia that are often embedded in or sitting on a dark, felt-like mat of fungal tissue. This dark, crusty appearance helps distinguish them from other wood-decomposing fungi.
children.funFact: Some Rosellinia species can cause serious plant diseases, including a devastating root rot that affects fruit trees and ornamental plants, earning them the nickname 'dematophora root rot' fungi.

children.name: Nemania
children.description: Nemania is a genus of small, dark fungi that form crusty, coal-black patches on dead wood. These saprophytic fungi help decompose fallen branches and logs in New England's forests, playing an important role in nutrient cycling. They produce their spores in tiny flask-shaped chambers embedded within their dark, carbonaceous fruiting bodies.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Nemania fungi are distinguished by their hard, black, crusty appearance that resembles charcoal or burnt wood on decaying logs. Unlike many other wood-decomposing fungi, they form thin, flat crusts rather than shelf-like brackets or mushroom shapes.
children.funFact: The name 'Nemania' comes from the Greek word 'nema' meaning thread, referring to the thread-like spores these fungi produce within their charcoal-like fruiting bodies.

children.name: Entoleuca
children.description: Entoleuca is a genus of fungi that includes species commonly known as hypoxylon canker fungi. These fungi are parasites that infect and damage hardwood trees, particularly beech and other deciduous species. They form distinctive black, crusty growths on the bark and wood of infected trees.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Entoleuca fungi are characterized by their hard, black, coal-like fruiting bodies (stromata) that emerge from infected tree bark. Unlike many other tree fungi, they create a distinctive canker that can girdle and kill branches or entire trees.
children.funFact: The name 'Entoleuca' literally means 'inside white,' referring to the white tissue that can be found beneath the black exterior of the fungal fruiting bodies.

children.name: Pyrenomyxa
children.description: Pyrenomyxa is a genus of slime molds that forms small, dark fruiting bodies on decaying wood. These organisms spend most of their life as a slimy mass that creeps along surfaces, feeding on bacteria and organic matter before transforming into spore-producing structures.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their small, black, pear-shaped fruiting bodies that develop directly from the plasmodium without forming a stalk.
children.funFact: Despite looking like tiny fungi, Pyrenomyxa slime molds are more closely related to amoebas and can actually move around to hunt for food during their feeding stage.

children.description: Xylariaceae is a family of wood-decomposing fungi that includes some of the most recognizable mushrooms found on dead trees and logs. These fungi are nature's recyclers, breaking down tough woody material and returning nutrients to the forest ecosystem. Most members produce distinctive dark-colored fruiting bodies that emerge directly from decaying wood.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their hard, often club-shaped or finger-like fruiting bodies with tiny flask-shaped chambers (perithecia) embedded in their surface. Unlike many other wood-decomposing fungi, they typically have very dark, almost black exterior surfaces.
children.funFact: The famous "Dead Man's Fingers" mushroom (Xylaria polymorpha) gets its spooky name because its dark, finger-like projections emerging from rotting stumps can look startlingly like decomposing hands reaching up from the ground.

children.name: Hypoxylaceae
Hypoxylon
children.description: Hypoxylon is a genus of wood-decay fungi commonly known as woodwarts. These fungi form distinctive hard, crusty growths on dead or dying hardwood trees, appearing as dark, bumpy masses that emerge from the bark surface. They play an important ecological role as decomposers, breaking down dead wood and recycling nutrients back into the forest ecosystem.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Woodwarts are easily recognized by their characteristic hard, warty appearance and dark coloration, typically black or dark brown. Unlike many other wood fungi, they form distinctive flask-shaped structures called perithecia embedded in their crusty surface.
