children.funFact: The spores of Hypoxylon fungi are shot out of tiny pores in the crusty surface with such force that they can travel several inches through the air to find new host trees.

children.name: Annulohypoxylon
children.description: Annulohypoxylon is a genus of hard, woody fungi that grow as crusty, blackened masses on dead hardwood trees and branches. These fungi are saprophytes, meaning they help decompose dead wood by breaking down cellulose and lignin. They form distinctive charcoal-like structures called stromata that can persist for years on their host trees.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are recognized by their hard, carbonaceous (charcoal-like) black exterior and their flask-shaped reproductive structures (perithecia) embedded within the stroma. Unlike many other wood-decomposing fungi, they form very hard, persistent fruiting bodies rather than soft mushrooms or bracket fungi.
children.funFact: One species in this genus, Annulohypoxylon thouarsianum (Cramp Balls), was historically used as tinder for starting fires because of its ability to smolder slowly and hold an ember for long periods.

children.name: Jackrogersella
children.description: Jackrogersella is a genus of small, hard fungi that form dark, crusty patches on dead hardwood trees and branches. These fungi are saprophytes, meaning they help break down dead wood and return nutrients to the forest ecosystem. They produce their spores in tiny flask-shaped structures embedded within their dark, carbonaceous fruiting bodies.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their hard, black, crusty appearance and their preference for growing on specific hardwood hosts. Unlike many other wood-decay fungi, they form relatively flat, shield-like structures that are firmly attached to the wood surface.
children.funFact: Despite their small size and inconspicuous appearance, these 'woodwarts' are actually performing important ecological work as nature's recyclers, slowly breaking down fallen branches and helping create rich forest soil.

children.name: Daldinia
children.description: Daldinia is a genus of hard, charcoal-like fungi that form distinctive black, crusty masses on dead hardwood trees. These fungi are saprophytes, meaning they help decompose dead wood and return nutrients to the forest ecosystem. They're often called 'carbon balls' or 'cramp balls' due to their blackened, rounded appearance.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other wood-decay fungi, Daldinia species form very hard, coal-black fruiting bodies with a distinctive layered interior that shows concentric rings when cut open, similar to tree rings.
children.funFact: King Alfred's Cakes got their common name because the blackened, crusty fungi supposedly resemble the burnt cakes that the medieval English king famously let burn while hiding from Viking invaders.

children.name: Thuemenella
children.description: Thuemenella is a small genus of fungi that includes species found growing on decaying wood and plant materials. These microscopic fungi are part of the larger group of ascomycetes, which are characterized by producing spores in specialized sac-like structures. They play an important role in forest ecosystems by helping to break down dead organic matter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Thuemenella are distinguished by their unique cube-shaped spores, which is quite unusual among fungi. This distinctive spore shape helps scientists identify them under a microscope.
children.funFact: The name Thuemenella honors Felix von Thümen, a 19th-century Austrian botanist and mycologist who made significant contributions to our understanding of fungal diversity.

children.description: The Hypoxylaceae are a family of wood-decaying fungi that create distinctive hard, crusty fruiting bodies on dead or dying hardwood trees. These fungi are saprophytes, meaning they break down dead organic matter and play an important role in forest decomposition. Their fruiting bodies often appear as dark, charcoal-like bumps or cushions on bark and exposed wood.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other wood-decay fungi, Hypoxylaceae produce very hard, carbonaceous (charcoal-like) fruiting bodies with tiny flask-shaped chambers called perithecia embedded within them. The spores are typically dark-colored and released through small pores on the surface.
children.funFact: Some species in this family, particularly in the genus Daldinia, are known as 'King Alfred's cakes' because their round, blackened fruiting bodies were historically used as tinder to start fires.

children.name: Diatrypaceae
Diatrype
children.description: Diatrype is a genus of fungi that creates distinctive crusty patches on dead hardwood trees and branches. These fungi appear as dark, bumpy surfaces with tiny pores where spores are released, and they play an important role in decomposing fallen logs and branches in New England's forests.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Diatrype fungi are recognized by their black, crusty appearance that forms raised patches on wood, with numerous small bumps (perithecia) containing tiny pores for spore release. Unlike many other wood-decomposing fungi, they create a distinctly tar-like or crusty texture on the wood surface.
children.funFact: Despite their somewhat ominous 'tarcrust' common name, these fungi are actually beneficial forest recyclers that help break down dead wood and return nutrients to the soil.

children.name: Paraeutypella
children.description: Paraeutypella is a genus of small fungi that grow as parasites and decomposers on woody plants. These microscopic fungi form tiny, dark fruiting bodies that emerge from the bark and wood of their host trees and shrubs.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their small, flask-shaped fruiting structures (perithecia) that are partially embedded in the host tissue. They differ from related fungi by their specific spore characteristics and the way their fruiting bodies develop within the bark.
children.funFact: One species in this genus, Paraeutypella vitis, specifically targets grapevines and can cause a disease called eutypa dieback, making it both ecologically important as a decomposer and economically significant to vineyard owners.

children.name: Eutypella
children.description: Eutypella is a genus of fungi that live as parasites and decomposers on woody plants, particularly hardwood trees. These fungi form small, dark, flask-shaped fruiting bodies called perithecia that are embedded in the bark or wood of their host trees. They play an important ecological role by breaking down dead wood and recycling nutrients back into the forest ecosystem.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Eutypella fungi are distinguished by their perithecia being arranged in clusters and surrounded by a blackened area of bark called a stroma. Their spores are typically colorless and elongated, helping to identify them from other wood-dwelling fungi.
children.funFact: Some Eutypella species can cause canker diseases in living trees, creating sunken, dead areas of bark that help weaken branches and eventually lead to natural pruning in the forest.

children.name: Eutypa
children.description: Eutypa is a genus of fungi that forms hard, crust-like growths on dead wood and bark. These fungi are decomposers that help break down woody material in forest ecosystems, often appearing as dark, bumpy patches on fallen logs and branches.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Eutypa species are characterized by their flask-shaped fruiting structures (perithecia) that are embedded in a hard, black crust on the wood surface. The spores are released through tiny pores that give the surface a dotted appearance.
children.funFact: Some Eutypa species can cause serious diseases in grapevines and fruit trees, making them both important decomposers in nature and significant agricultural pests.

children.name: Peroneutypa
children.description: Peroneutypa is a genus of fungi that belongs to the group of wood-inhabiting microorganisms. These fungi are typically found growing on dead or decaying wood, where they play an important role in breaking down woody plant material in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their unique spore-producing structures and their specific association with woody substrates. They can be distinguished from related fungi by their particular fruiting body characteristics and spore morphology.
children.funFact: Like many wood-decomposing fungi, Peroneutypa species are nature's recyclers, helping to return nutrients from fallen trees and branches back to the forest soil.

children.description: Diatrypaceae is a family of fungi that specialize in decomposing dead hardwood trees and branches. These fungi are important recyclers in forest ecosystems, breaking down woody material and returning nutrients to the soil. Most species in this family produce their spores in small, dark, flask-shaped structures that are embedded in the bark or wood of their host trees.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their characteristic black, dot-like fruiting bodies (perithecia) that often appear in clusters on dead bark. Unlike many other wood-decay fungi, they typically don't form large, visible mushrooms but instead create tiny openings in the bark where spores are released.
children.funFact: Some species in this family can cause a disease called "eutypa dieback" in grapevines, making them both beneficial decomposers in wild forests and occasional agricultural pests in vineyards.

children.name: Graphostromataceae
Biscogniauxia
children.description: Biscogniauxia is a genus of fungal pathogens that primarily attack hardwood trees, causing diseases known as hypoxylon cankers. These fungi typically infect stressed or weakened trees, forming distinctive black, crusty fruiting bodies on the bark that contain tiny spores. They are considered opportunistic pathogens that often strike during periods of drought or other environmental stress.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Biscogniauxia are distinguished by their hard, black, coal-like fruiting structures (stromata) that form flat patches on tree bark. Unlike many other wood-decay fungi, they create a distinctive white rot pattern and often leave a characteristic bleached appearance on affected wood.
children.funFact: The black, crusty growths produced by Biscogniauxia fungi were historically used as a source of natural charcoal ink and drawing materials by artists and scribes.

children.name: Camillea
children.description: Camillea is a small genus of fungi that includes just two species found in New England. These fungi are part of the larger group of sac fungi and play important ecological roles in forest ecosystems as decomposers.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Camillea can be identified by their distinctive fruiting bodies and spore characteristics that separate them from other closely related fungal genera.
children.funFact: Despite being a tiny genus with only two New England species, Camillea represents an ancient lineage of fungi that has been quietly recycling nutrients in our forests for millions of years.

children.name: Graphostroma
children.description: Graphostroma is a genus of fungi that forms dark, crusty growths on dead hardwood trees and branches. These fungi are decomposers that help break down woody material in forest ecosystems. They produce their spores in tiny flask-shaped structures embedded within the dark, carbonaceous crust.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Graphostroma is distinguished by its distinctive black, charcoal-like crusty appearance on wood surfaces and its unique spore-producing structures that are arranged in a specific pattern within the fungal crust.
children.funFact: The name Graphostroma literally means 'writing layer' because the dark fungal crusts can resemble charcoal writing or drawings on the surface of dead wood.

children.description: Graphostromataceae is a family of fungi that includes species commonly known as charcoal fungi or carbon balls. These fungi are typically found growing on dead or dying hardwood trees, where they form distinctive black, crusty structures that can look like charcoal or burnt wood. They play an important role as decomposers in forest ecosystems, breaking down woody plant material.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their hard, black, carbonaceous fruiting bodies that often form layers or crusts on wood surfaces. Unlike many other wood-decay fungi, they produce their spores in tiny flask-shaped structures embedded within the black crust.
children.funFact: Some species in this family, particularly in the genus Biscogniauxia, can actually weaken trees while they're still alive, acting as both parasites and decomposers throughout their lifecycle.

children.name: Lopadostomataceae
Whalleya
children.description: Whalleya is a small genus of crustose lichens that form thin, crust-like patches on rock surfaces. These lichens are characterized by their small, pale-colored fruiting bodies called apothecia that sit embedded in the lichen's surface.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Whalleya lichens can be distinguished from other crustose lichens by their distinctive apothecial structure and the specific way their spores are arranged within the fruiting bodies.
children.funFact: The genus Whalleya was named relatively recently in lichen taxonomy, reflecting ongoing discoveries in the complex world of these symbiotic organisms that are part fungus and part algae.

children.name: Creosphaeria
children.description: Creosphaeria is a small genus of fungi that are parasites of plants, causing canker diseases on woody hosts. These fungi produce their spores in small, dark, flask-shaped structures called perithecia that are embedded in the bark of infected trees.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their dark perithecia with long necks and their specific association with certain tree hosts, particularly causing distinctive canker symptoms.
children.funFact: Creosphaeria sassafras is highly host-specific, almost exclusively infecting sassafras trees and playing a role in the natural population dynamics of these aromatic native trees.

children.description: Lopadostomataceae is a small family of fungi that live as parasites or decomposers on woody plants. These microscopic fungi form tiny, dark fruiting bodies that are embedded in the bark or wood of their host trees and shrubs.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their flask-shaped fruiting structures (perithecia) that are completely immersed in the host plant tissue, with only small openings visible at the surface.
children.funFact: Despite being microscopic, these fungi play an important role in forest ecosystems by helping to break down dead wood and return nutrients to the soil.

children.description: Xylariales are a diverse order of fungi that are masters of decomposition, primarily breaking down dead wood and plant material. Most species in this group produce hard, dark fruiting bodies that look like tiny black bumps, clubs, or cushions growing on rotting logs and branches. They play a crucial role in forest ecosystems by recycling nutrients from dead trees back into the soil.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These fungi are characterized by their typically black, carbonaceous (charcoal-like) fruiting bodies called perithecia or stromata, which often feel hard to the touch. Unlike many other wood-decomposing fungi, they usually produce their spores in flask-shaped structures embedded within these dark, crusty surfaces.
children.funFact: Some Xylariales species, like those in the genus Xylaria, are called 'dead man's fingers' because their club-shaped fruiting bodies emerging from rotting wood look eerily like skeletal fingers reaching up from the forest floor.

children.name: Diaporthales
Gnomoniaceae
Ophiognomonia
children.description: Ophiognomonia is a genus of fungi that are specialized plant pathogens, meaning they cause diseases in trees and other plants. These microscopic organisms are particularly known for attacking walnut family trees, where they cause serious canker diseases and leaf spots that can weaken or even kill their hosts.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their ability to form characteristic cankers (sunken, diseased areas) on tree bark and their production of distinctive spores within tiny, flask-shaped structures called perithecia.
children.funFact: The butternut canker fungus in this genus is so devastating that it has caused widespread decline of native butternut trees across North America, making healthy butternuts increasingly rare in New England forests.

children.name: Apiognomonia
children.description: Apiognomonia is a genus of fungi that causes anthracnose diseases in deciduous trees. These microscopic organisms live as pathogens on tree leaves and twigs, creating dark spots, leaf browning, and premature leaf drop. They are particularly common on oak and sycamore trees in New England forests.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other leaf spot fungi, Apiognomonia species produce their spores in tiny flask-shaped structures called perithecia that are embedded in the leaf tissue. They also have a specific two-stage life cycle that overwinters in fallen leaves and twigs.
children.funFact: Apiognomonia fungi are actually helping recycle nutrients in the forest - while they may make trees look unhealthy in spring, they rarely cause serious long-term damage and play an important role in breaking down fallen leaves.

children.name: Discula
children.description: Discula is a genus of plant pathogenic fungi that cause anthracnose diseases in trees and shrubs. These fungi create dark, sunken lesions on leaves, stems, and sometimes branches of their host plants. They are particularly problematic for woodland trees like maples and dogwoods in New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Discula species are distinguished by their ability to produce spores in flask-shaped structures called acervuli that break through the surface of infected plant tissue. Unlike many other plant pathogens, they can survive harsh winters and remain active in cool, wet spring conditions.
children.funFact: The dogwood anthracnose fungus (Discula destructiva) was first discovered in the 1970s and has since caused significant decline in native dogwood populations throughout eastern North America, making it one of the most ecologically impactful fungal introductions of recent decades.

children.description: Gnomoniaceae is a family of microscopic fungi that are primarily plant pathogens, meaning they cause diseases in trees and other plants. These fungi typically live inside plant tissues and produce their spores in small, flask-shaped structures called perithecia that often appear as tiny black dots on infected plant material. Most species in this family are specialized to infect specific types of host plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other fungal families, Gnomoniaceae members are characterized by their distinctive perithecial fruiting bodies that are often embedded in plant tissue and have a unique beak-like opening called an ostiole. Their spores are typically colorless and elongated, often with multiple cells.
children.funFact: Some species in this family, like those in the genus Ophiognomonia, are responsible for major tree diseases including oak wilt and anthracnose, which can cause significant leaf spotting and branch dieback in forest ecosystems.

children.name: Cryphonectriaceae
Endothia
children.description: Endothia is a genus of fungi that causes canker diseases in trees, particularly affecting the bark and cambium layer. These parasitic fungi create distinctive cankers (dead areas of bark) that can weaken or kill their host trees. They belong to the larger group of ascomycete fungi and play an important ecological role as both pathogens and decomposers.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Endothia fungi are characterized by their ability to form orange to reddish-brown fruiting bodies that emerge from tree bark cankers. Unlike many other canker-causing fungi, they produce their spores in flask-shaped structures called perithecia that are embedded in a stroma (cushion-like fungal tissue).
children.funFact: While the chestnut blight fungus was once classified in Endothia, it has since been moved to the genus Cryphonectria, leaving New England with just one native Endothia species that primarily affects oak trees.

children.name: Aurantioporthe
children.description: Aurantioporthe is a genus of plant pathogenic fungi that causes canker diseases in woody plants. These microscopic organisms infect the bark and wood of trees and shrubs, creating diseased areas that can weaken or kill branches and entire plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: This genus is distinguished by producing orange to reddish-brown fruiting bodies (perithecia) embedded in the bark of infected host plants, which give it its name meaning 'orange door.'
children.funFact: The dogwood golden canker fungus was only recently recognized as a separate genus in 2006, having previously been classified under a different fungal group as scientists better understood its unique characteristics.

children.name: Cryphonectria
children.description: Cryphonectria is a genus of fungi that are plant parasites, causing serious diseases in trees by attacking their bark and wood. These fungi produce distinctive orange or reddish-orange fruiting bodies that emerge from infected bark, and they spread through spores that can travel on wind, insects, or human activity.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their ability to cause canker diseases in trees, creating sunken, dead areas of bark that often have bright orange fungal structures protruding from them. They are particularly aggressive pathogens that can quickly kill healthy trees.
children.funFact: Cryphonectria parasitica, the chestnut blight fungus, was accidentally introduced to North America around 1904 and wiped out nearly 4 billion American chestnut trees within 50 years, transforming entire forest ecosystems across the eastern United States.

children.description: The Cryphonectriaceae are a family of fungi that specialize in causing canker diseases on trees and woody plants. These fungi create sunken, dead areas in bark and wood, often girdling branches or entire trees and causing significant damage to forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their ability to form characteristic cankers on woody hosts, along with their distinctive fruiting bodies that develop within the diseased bark tissue.
children.funFact: This family includes Cryphonectria parasitica, the fungus responsible for chestnut blight, which devastated American chestnut forests in the early 1900s and transformed the entire eastern North American landscape.

children.name: Tubakiaceae
Tubakia
children.description: Tubakia is a genus of plant pathogenic fungi that causes leaf spot diseases on various trees and shrubs. These microscopic fungi form small, dark spots on leaves and can cause premature leaf drop when infections are severe.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Tubakia fungi produce distinctive spores called conidia that are multi-celled and olive-brown in color, often forming in clusters on infected plant tissue.
children.funFact: Despite being plant pathogens, Tubakia fungi rarely kill their host trees and instead have co-evolved to live symbiotically with them for thousands of years.

children.description: Tubakiaceae is a small family of fungi that are plant pathogens, meaning they cause diseases in trees and other plants. These microscopic fungi produce distinctive spores and are known for creating leaf spots and other symptoms on their host plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their unique spore-producing structures and their specific parasitic relationship with plants, particularly causing foliar diseases.
children.funFact: Despite being plant pathogens, Tubakiaceae fungi play an important ecological role by helping to regulate plant populations and contributing to nutrient cycling in forest ecosystems.

children.name: Diaporthaceae
Diaporthe
children.description: Diaporthe is a genus of plant pathogenic fungi that cause diseases in trees, shrubs, and other plants. These fungi are known for creating cankers, blights, and dieback symptoms on their host plants. They produce distinctive spores in flask-shaped structures embedded in the plant tissue.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Diaporthe fungi are distinguished by their characteristic black, flask-shaped fruiting bodies (perithecia) that emerge from infected plant tissue and their two different types of spores produced at different times.
children.funFact: Some Diaporthe species can remain dormant in plant tissue for years before causing visible disease symptoms, making them particularly challenging for plant pathologists to detect and manage.

children.description: The Diaporthaceae are a family of fungi that live as plant pathogens, causing cankers, dieback, and other diseases in trees and shrubs. These fungi produce their spores in distinctive flask-shaped structures called perithecia that are embedded in the bark or wood of their host plants. They play an important ecological role as decomposers, though some species can cause significant damage to agricultural crops and forest trees.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their dark, flask-shaped fruiting bodies (perithecia) that have long necks extending through the bark surface. Their spores are typically colorless and elongated, often with multiple cells separated by cross-walls.
children.funFact: Some Diaporthe species are actually beneficial, living peacefully inside plants as endophytes and helping protect their hosts from more harmful pathogens.

children.name: Sydowiellaceae
Stegophora
children.description: Stegophora is a small genus of fungi that includes plant pathogens causing leaf spot diseases. These microscopic fungi develop within plant tissues and produce characteristic dark spots on the leaves of their host plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Stegophora fungi are distinguished by their specific host relationships and the way they produce spores within flask-shaped structures called pycnidia embedded in leaf tissue.
children.funFact: The single New England species, Stegophora ulmea, specifically targets elm trees and creates the distinctive black spots that give the disease its common name.

children.description: Sydowiellaceae is a small family of microscopic fungi that includes species living in aquatic environments, particularly freshwater habitats. These fungi are characterized by their unique spore-producing structures and are part of the diverse world of ascomycete fungi that help decompose organic matter in watery ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their specialized reproductive structures called ascomata, which have distinctive characteristics that set them apart from other aquatic fungi families. They typically produce dark-colored, flask-shaped fruiting bodies.
children.funFact: Despite being microscopic, these aquatic fungi play an important role in breaking down submerged plant material and wood in freshwater streams and ponds, acting as nature's tiny recyclers in aquatic ecosystems.

children.description: Diaporthales is an order of fungi that are primarily plant pathogens, meaning they cause diseases in trees and other plants. These microscopic fungi typically live within plant tissues and produce small, flask-shaped fruiting bodies that emerge through the bark or stems of their hosts. Most species in this group are specialized to infect specific types of plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other plant-pathogenic fungi, Diaporthales species typically produce their spores in distinctive flask-shaped structures called perithecia that have a narrow neck or opening. They also tend to cause cankers, wilts, and dieback diseases rather than leaf spots or surface infections.
children.funFact: The infamous chestnut blight fungus that nearly wiped out American chestnut trees in the early 1900s belongs to this order, fundamentally changing New England's forests forever.

children.name: Glomerellales
Glomerellaceae
Colletotrichum
children.description: Colletotrichum is a genus of fungi that are notorious plant pathogens, causing a disease called anthracnose in a wide variety of plants. These microscopic fungi attack leaves, stems, fruits, and other plant parts, creating distinctive dark spots, lesions, and cankers that can seriously damage or kill their host plants. They're found worldwide and can infect everything from trees and shrubs to crops and houseplants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other plant pathogenic fungi, Colletotrichum species produce characteristic curved, sickle-shaped spores called conidia. They also form unique structures called acervuli - small, cushion-like fruiting bodies that break through the plant tissue to release their spores.
children.funFact: Some Colletotrichum species have a sneaky strategy called 'latent infection' - they can live quietly inside healthy plant tissue for months or even years before suddenly becoming active and causing disease when the plant becomes stressed.

children.description: Glomerellaceae is a family of fungi that are primarily known as plant pathogens, causing diseases in crops, trees, and other plants. These fungi are particularly notorious for causing anthracnose, a type of plant disease that creates dark, sunken spots on leaves, stems, and fruits.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family produce distinctive spores in flask-shaped structures and often have both sexual and asexual reproductive stages. They typically form dark, cushion-like fruiting bodies that break through plant tissue.
children.funFact: Some species in this family can switch between being harmful pathogens and helpful endophytes living peacefully inside plants, depending on environmental conditions and the plant's health status.

children.description: Glomerellales is an order of plant-pathogenic fungi that cause serious diseases in crops and wild plants. These fungi are particularly notorious for causing anthracnose diseases, which create dark, sunken lesions on leaves, stems, and fruits of infected plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other plant pathogens, Glomerellales fungi produce distinctive spores in flask-shaped structures and can survive both as parasites on living plants and as decomposers on dead plant material.
children.funFact: Some species in this order can actually switch between being harmful plant pathogens and beneficial endophytes living peacefully inside plant tissues, depending on environmental conditions.

children.name: Sordariales
Lasiosphaeriaceae
Lasiosphaeria
children.description: Lasiosphaeria is a genus of small fungi that grow on decaying wood, particularly hardwood logs and branches. These fungi form tiny, dark, flask-shaped structures called perithecia that are covered in distinctive woolly or hairy projections, giving them their characteristic fuzzy appearance.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The woolly or hairy coating on their fruiting bodies sets Lasiosphaeria apart from other wood-dwelling fungi, which typically have smooth surfaces. This fuzzy texture is created by dense clusters of dark, thread-like hairs called setae.
children.funFact: The name Lasiosphaeria literally means 'hairy sphere' in Greek, perfectly describing these tiny fungi that look like miniature fuzzy balls dotting the surface of rotting logs.

children.name: Cercophora
children.description: Cercophora is a genus of small, dark-colored fungi that specialize in decomposing organic matter, particularly dung and decaying plant material. These tiny fungi produce flask-shaped fruiting bodies called perithecia that contain their spores. They play an important role in nutrient cycling by breaking down waste materials in forest and field ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Cercophora fungi are distinguished by their dark, carbonaceous (coal-like) perithecia and their preference for growing on dung or heavily decomposed organic matter. Their spores are typically dark-colored and have distinctive shapes that help identify different species.
children.funFact: Despite being microscopic decomposers, Cercophora fungi are incredibly efficient recyclers - they can break down some of the toughest organic compounds that other organisms can't digest, making nutrients available again for plants and other life forms.

children.description: Lasiosphaeriaceae is a family of small fungi that decompose organic matter, particularly wood and plant debris. These fungi produce tiny, dark, flask-shaped fruiting bodies called perithecia that contain their spores. They play an important ecological role as decomposers in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their dark, hairy or bristly perithecia that often have distinctive openings at the top. The presence of these hair-like structures (called setae) on their fruiting bodies helps distinguish them from other similar fungal families.
children.funFact: Despite their tiny size, these fungi are nature's recycling experts, breaking down tough plant materials like cellulose and lignin that many other organisms cannot digest.

children.name: Podosporaceae
Podospora
children.description: Podospora is a genus of microscopic fungi that specialize in decomposing dung and other organic matter rich in cellulose. These fungi are coprophilous, meaning they have evolved specifically to thrive on animal droppings where they play an important role in breaking down waste and recycling nutrients back into the ecosystem.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Podospora fungi are characterized by their dark, flask-shaped reproductive structures called perithecia and their distinctive spores that often have tail-like appendages. Unlike many other dung fungi, Podospora species typically have a specific preference for herbivore dung and produce spores with unique ornamentations.
children.funFact: Podospora fungi have been used extensively in genetic research because they have a unique mating system and easily observable spore development, making them perfect laboratory subjects for studying fungal reproduction and inheritance patterns.

children.description: Podosporaceae is a small family of fungi that are specialized decomposers, particularly skilled at breaking down dung and other organic matter rich in cellulose. These fungi produce distinctive flask-shaped fruiting bodies called perithecia that contain their spores. They play an important ecological role as recyclers in nature, helping return nutrients to the soil.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their dark-colored perithecia with long necks and their preference for growing on dung or heavily decomposed plant material. Their spores are typically large, dark, and often have gelatinous appendages that help them stick to and disperse via animals.
children.funFact: Some Podosporaceae fungi have evolved a fascinating relationship with herbivorous animals - their spores must actually pass through an animal's digestive system to germinate properly, making them true partners in the recycling process!

children.name: Schizotheciaceae
Pseudoechria
children.description: Pseudoechria is a small genus of moths in the family Geometridae, commonly known as geometer moths or inchworms. These moths are characterized by their delicate wings and the caterpillars' distinctive looping movement as they crawl. Like other geometers, they hold their wings horizontally when at rest.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Pseudoechria moths can be identified by their specific wing patterns and the curved neck structure that gives the species its name 'curvicolla,' meaning 'curved neck.'
children.funFact: The caterpillars of Pseudoechria moths move by arching their bodies into loops, which is why geometer moths are also called 'inchworms' or 'loopers.'

children.description: Schizotheciaceae is a small family of fungi that includes species which form distinctive fruiting bodies. These fungi are part of the larger group of ascomycetes, or sac fungi, which produce their spores in specialized sac-like structures called asci.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their unique spore-bearing structures that have a particular way of opening or splitting to release spores. They differ from other fungal families in their specific fruiting body architecture and spore release mechanisms.
children.funFact: This family is so rare and specialized that New England is home to just one species, making any discovery of Schizotheciaceae fungi a truly special find for nature explorers!

children.description: Sordariales are a diverse order of fungi that typically produce their spores in flask-shaped structures called perithecia, which have a small opening at the top. These fungi are commonly found growing on decaying organic matter like dead wood, dung, and plant debris, where they play important roles as decomposers in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Sordariales are characterized by their dark-colored perithecia that often have a distinctive neck-like opening, and they typically produce dark spores arranged in a specific pattern within sac-like structures called asci.
children.funFact: Many Sordariales fungi are specialists that have evolved to grow exclusively on specific types of dung from particular animals, making them excellent indicators of which creatures have been in an area.

children.name: Chaetosphaeriales
Helminthosphaeriaceae
Helminthosphaeria
children.description: Helminthosphaeria is a small genus of fungi that are parasites of other fungi, specifically targeting club fungi and coral fungi. These tiny organisms form dark, flask-shaped fruiting bodies that emerge from their fungal hosts. They represent an interesting example of fungi that have evolved to live on and derive nutrients from other fungi rather than decomposing plant material.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most fungi that decompose dead organic matter, Helminthosphaeria species are obligate parasites that specifically attack living club fungi and coral fungi. Their small, dark perithecia (fruiting bodies) with long necks are distinctive and help distinguish them from other fungal parasites.
children.funFact: These fungi are essentially 'fungal vampires' - they are among the relatively few fungi that have evolved to parasitize other fungi rather than plants or animals.

children.name: Hilberina
children.description: Hilberina is a genus of tiny amoeboid protists that live in freshwater environments, particularly in sphagnum moss and other wetland habitats. These microscopic single-celled organisms move and feed by extending flexible projections called pseudopodia, which they use to engulf bacteria and other small organic particles.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Hilberina are distinguished by their characteristic cell shape and the specific way their pseudopodia branch and move. They have a distinctive nucleated cell structure that sets them apart from other amoeboid protists in similar habitats.
children.funFact: Despite being invisible to the naked eye, Hilberina sphagni plays an important role in sphagnum bog ecosystems by helping to cycle nutrients and control bacterial populations in these unique wetland environments.

children.description: The Helminthosphaeriaceae are a small family of fungi that form tiny, dark, flask-shaped fruiting bodies called perithecia. These fungi are typically found growing on decaying wood, where they help break down dead plant material as part of the natural decomposition process.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their distinctive long-necked perithecia that often have a worm-like or thread-like appearance, which is reflected in their name 'Helminthosphaeria' meaning 'worm sphere.'
children.funFact: Despite being a widespread family of wood-decomposing fungi, only two species from this entire family have been documented in New England, making them relatively uncommon finds for local mycologists.

children.name: Chaetosphaeriaceae
Paragaeumannomyces
children.description: Paragaeumannomyces is a small genus of microscopic fungi that lives as a parasite on other fungi, particularly targeting species in the Geopora group. These tiny organisms represent a fascinating example of fungi that have evolved to feed on their fungal relatives rather than decomposing plant matter or forming partnerships with plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most fungi that decompose organic matter or form beneficial relationships with plants, members of this genus are specialized parasites that attack and consume other fungi. They can be identified by their unique spore structures and their exclusive lifestyle of parasitizing members of the Geopora fungal group.
children.funFact: This genus represents one of nature's examples of 'fungus eat fungus' - they're essentially the fungal equivalent of a parasite that has become so specialized it can only survive by attacking one specific group of related fungi.

children.description: Chaetosphaeriaceae is a family of tiny fungi that live as decomposers, breaking down dead plant material in forests and other natural environments. These microscopic fungi produce their spores inside small, flask-shaped structures that are often dark-colored and have distinctive bristle-like hairs or projections.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their small, dark fruiting bodies (perithecia) that typically have hair-like appendages or bristles extending from their surface, giving them a fuzzy appearance under magnification.
children.funFact: Despite being microscopic, these fungi play a crucial role as nature's recyclers, helping to break down tough plant fibers and return nutrients to the soil for new plant growth.

children.description: Chaetosphaeriales is an order of tiny fungi that live as decomposers, breaking down dead plant material in forests and other natural habitats. These microscopic fungi produce their spores in small, flask-shaped structures that are often dark-colored and may have bristle-like hairs or projections.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this order are characterized by their distinctive spore-producing structures (perithecia) that typically have dark walls and often feature hair-like appendages or bristles, giving them their name which refers to these chaeta or bristles.
children.funFact: Despite being microscopic, these fungi play a crucial role as nature's recyclers, helping to break down tough plant fibers and returning nutrients to the soil for other organisms to use.

children.name: Ophiostomatales
Ophiostomataceae
Ophiostoma
children.description: Ophiostoma is a genus of fungi that are closely associated with bark beetles and cause serious diseases in trees. These fungi typically live in the wood and bark of trees, where they can block the tree's water transport system and ultimately kill their host.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other wood-inhabiting fungi, Ophiostoma species are primarily spread by insects, especially bark beetles, rather than by wind-dispersed spores. They produce distinctive flask-shaped reproductive structures called perithecia.
children.funFact: The most famous member of this genus caused one of the most devastating tree diseases in North American history - Dutch elm disease wiped out millions of American elm trees in the 20th century, forever changing the landscape of many cities and towns.

children.name: Sporothrix
children.description: Sporothrix is a genus of microscopic fungi that are commonly found living on decaying wood and other organic matter. These tiny organisms play an important role in breaking down dead plant material in forest ecosystems. Most species in this group are harmless decomposers that help recycle nutrients back into the soil.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Sporothrix fungi are characterized by their unique spore-producing structures and their ability to grow in both yeast-like and filamentous forms depending on environmental conditions. They produce distinctive oval-shaped spores that help identify them under a microscope.
children.funFact: While most Sporothrix species are harmless environmental fungi, some tropical species can cause a skin infection called sporotrichosis, which is sometimes called 'rose gardener's disease' because it often affects people who work with thorny plants.

children.description: Ophiostomataceae is a family of microscopic fungi that are closely associated with beetles and other insects. These fungi typically live in the tunnels and galleries that bark beetles create in trees, forming beneficial partnerships where the beetles help spread the fungi to new host trees.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family produce distinctive flask-shaped fruiting bodies with long necks that help disperse their spores. They are particularly well-adapted to the oxygen-poor environment inside beetle galleries in tree bark.
children.funFact: Some species in this family can actually change the chemistry of tree wood, making it more nutritious for their beetle partners' larvae to eat.

children.description: Ophiostomatales is an order of fungi that includes species closely associated with bark beetles and other wood-boring insects. These fungi often have specialized fruiting structures that help them disperse their spores via their insect partners. Many members of this group are found in or on dead and dying trees.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These fungi are characterized by their unique flask-shaped fruiting bodies with long necks that extend spores outward, making it easy for insects to pick them up and transport them to new locations.
children.funFact: Some species in this order can cause serious tree diseases like Dutch elm disease, which is spread by elm bark beetles and has devastated elm populations across North America.

children.name: Amphisphaeriales
Sporocadaceae
Pestalotiopsis
children.description: Pestalotiopsis is a genus of fungi that primarily acts as plant pathogens, causing diseases in trees and other woody plants. These microscopic organisms produce distinctive spores with multiple cells and hair-like appendages that help them spread and infect their hosts.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their unique five-celled spores (conidia) that have thread-like appendages on both ends, giving them a distinctive appearance under the microscope.
children.funFact: Some species of Pestalotiopsis have been discovered living inside plants without causing disease, and remarkably, certain species can actually break down plastic, making them potentially useful for environmental cleanup efforts.

children.description: Sporocadaceae is a family of fungi that includes many plant pathogens and endophytes, meaning they can cause diseases in plants or live inside plant tissues without causing harm. These fungi are commonly found on leaves, stems, and branches of various plants, where they produce distinctive spores in small, dark structures. Most members of this family are microscopic and play important roles in plant ecology.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Sporocadaceae are characterized by their unique spore-producing structures called conidiomata, which contain spores with multiple cells separated by cross-walls and often have thread-like appendages at both ends.
children.funFact: Some species in this family can act as both friend and foe to plants - they may live peacefully inside healthy plant tissues as endophytes, but switch to becoming disease-causing pathogens when the plant becomes stressed.

children.name: Amphisphaeriaceae
Microdochium
children.description: Microdochium is a genus of microscopic fungi that are plant pathogens, meaning they cause diseases in plants. These fungi are particularly known for attacking grasses and other plants, often during cool, moist conditions. They produce small, colorful fruiting bodies that help them spread their spores.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Microdochium are distinguished by their ability to cause disease symptoms even at very low temperatures, including under snow cover. They produce distinctive pink to orange colored spore masses that make them easily recognizable among plant pathogenic fungi.
children.funFact: Pink Snow Mold gets its name because it can actually grow and cause plant damage while completely covered by snow, emerging in spring as distinctive pink patches on previously snow-covered lawns and grasslands.

children.description: Amphisphaeriaceae is a family of fungi that includes species commonly found growing on decaying wood and plant material. These fungi play an important role as decomposers in forest ecosystems, breaking down dead organic matter and recycling nutrients back into the soil.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family typically produce dark, flask-shaped fruiting bodies called perithecia that are partially or completely buried in their host material. Their spores are usually elongated and divided into multiple cells.
children.funFact: Some species in this family can switch between different lifestyles, acting as harmless decomposers on dead plant material but occasionally becoming mild pathogens on living plants when conditions are right.

children.description: Amphisphaeriales is an order of fungi that includes species living as parasites or decomposers on woody plants. These fungi typically form small, dark fruiting bodies embedded in or growing on bark, branches, and twigs of trees and shrubs.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this order are characterized by their flask-shaped fruiting structures (perithecia) that are often partially buried in plant tissue. They produce spores through specialized openings at the top of these structures.
children.funFact: Many fungi in this order are excellent recyclers, helping break down dead wood and bark while some species can also act as plant pathogens, playing important dual roles in forest ecosystems.

children.name: Phyllachorales
Phyllachoraceae
Phyllachora
children.description: Phyllachora is a genus of plant parasitic fungi that create distinctive black, tar-like spots on the leaves and stems of grasses and other plants. These fungi are part of a group called ascomycetes and form small, hard fruiting bodies that appear as dark patches embedded in the plant tissue. They're specialized pathogens that have co-evolved with their grass hosts over millions of years.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other leaf spot fungi, Phyllachora species form their spore-producing structures completely embedded within the host plant tissue, creating characteristic black, shield-like spots that are flush with the leaf surface. The fruiting bodies are also notably hard and carbonaceous compared to other similar fungi.
children.funFact: These fungi are so host-specific that each Phyllachora species typically infects only one type of grass, making them excellent indicators of plant biodiversity in grassland ecosystems.

children.description: Phyllachoraceae is a family of plant parasitic fungi that create distinctive black spots or patches on the leaves of their host plants. These fungi are biotrophic, meaning they keep their host plants alive while feeding on them, forming specialized structures that penetrate plant tissues. They are commonly found on grasses and other monocot plants throughout temperate regions.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family produce characteristic black, shiny, tar-like spots called stromata that are embedded directly in the leaf tissue of their hosts. Unlike many other leaf-spotting fungi, their fruiting bodies are completely immersed in the plant tissue rather than emerging from the surface.
children.funFact: The black spots created by Phyllachoraceae fungi are so distinctive that they're sometimes called 'tar spots,' and despite looking like disease damage, the infected plants often continue to grow and reproduce normally.

children.description: Phyllachorales is an order of plant parasitic fungi that create distinctive black, tar-like spots on the leaves of their host plants. These fungi are biotrophic, meaning they keep their host plants alive while slowly extracting nutrients from living plant tissue. They form specialized structures called perithecia embedded within dark, shield-like stromata that appear as black patches on leaf surfaces.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other plant pathogenic fungi, members of Phyllachorales form characteristic black, shiny, tar-spot-like lesions that are firmly embedded in the leaf tissue rather than growing on the surface. Their perithecia are completely immersed within thick, dark stromatic tissue that creates a distinctive appearance.
children.funFact: The black tar spots created by these fungi on maple and other tree leaves are so distinctive that they're commonly called 'tar spot disease,' even though they rarely cause serious harm to healthy trees.

children.name: Boliniales
Boliniaceae
Camarops
children.description: Camarops is a genus of wood-dwelling fungi that creates distinctive flask-shaped fruiting bodies embedded in decaying hardwood. These fungi are saprophytes, meaning they break down dead organic matter and play an important role in forest decomposition cycles.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Camarops fungi are recognized by their unique fruiting structures called perithecia, which are flask-shaped chambers that contain spores and are typically arranged in clusters within the wood substrate.
children.funFact: The common name 'dog's nose fungus' comes from the resemblance of the fungus's dark, clustered fruiting bodies to a dog's wet nose when they emerge from the wood surface.

children.description: Boliniaceae is a small family of fungi that forms hard, woody structures on dead hardwood trees. These fungi are saprobic decomposers, meaning they break down dead organic matter and play an important role in forest nutrient cycling.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family produce distinctive black, carbonaceous fruiting bodies that are embedded in or erupting from the bark of dead trees, with a unique flask-shaped internal structure.
children.funFact: The single New England species in this family, Camarops petersii, creates fruiting bodies so hard and dark that they were once mistaken for charcoal by early mycologists.

children.description: Boliniales is a small order of marine ctenophores, commonly known as comb jellies. These translucent, gelatinous animals drift through ocean waters and are characterized by eight rows of cilia (called comb rows) that create rainbow-like light patterns as they beat rhythmically for propulsion.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Boliniales are distinguished from other comb jellies by their unique body structure and the specific arrangement of their feeding apparatus and sensory organs.
children.funFact: Despite their delicate, almost ethereal appearance, comb jellies in this order are actually efficient predators that can consume prey nearly as large as themselves!

children.name: Coronophorales
Bertiaceae
Bertia
children.description: Bertia is a small genus of fungi that includes species commonly known as wood mulberries due to their distinctive appearance. These fungi are characterized by their dark, rounded fruiting bodies that emerge from decaying wood and have a bumpy, mulberry-like surface texture.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Bertia species are distinguished by their black, spherical to oval fruiting bodies (perithecia) that are clustered together and embedded in a dark, cushion-like structure called a stroma.
children.funFact: The Wood Mulberry fungus gets its common name because its clustered black fruiting bodies remarkably resemble tiny mulberries growing on dead wood.

children.description: Bertiaceae is a small family of fungi that produces tiny, flask-shaped structures called perithecia embedded in plant tissues. These microscopic fungi are decomposers that help break down dead wood and plant material in forest environments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their small, dark perithecia that are typically immersed in the host substrate, with only the neck protruding slightly above the surface.
children.funFact: Despite being microscopic, Bertiaceae fungi play an important role in forest ecosystems by helping to recycle nutrients from dead wood back into the soil.

children.description: Coronophorales is a small order of fungi that includes species which form tiny, flask-shaped structures called perithecia to house their spores. These fungi are typically found growing on dead wood, bark, or other plant material where they help decompose organic matter. They reproduce by releasing spores from their distinctive bottle-shaped fruiting bodies.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this order are characterized by their small, dark perithecia that often have a distinctive neck or beak-like opening at the top. Unlike many related fungi, they typically have a simple pore rather than a more complex opening structure.
children.funFact: Despite being a tiny and often overlooked group, Coronophorales fungi play an important ecological role as some of the first decomposers to colonize freshly fallen branches and bark.

children.name: Thyridiaceae
Thyronectroidea
children.description: Thyronectroidea is a genus of marine sea slugs known as nudibranchs, which are shell-less gastropod mollusks that live in ocean waters. These soft-bodied creatures are characterized by their elongated bodies and distinctive feeding habits. They are part of the diverse world of sea slugs that crawl along the seafloor and other marine surfaces.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus can be identified by their specific body shape and coloration patterns, particularly the golden or yellowish markings that give the species its name 'chrysogramma' (meaning 'golden writing').
children.funFact: The name 'chrysogramma' literally translates to 'golden writing' in Greek, referring to the beautiful golden markings that appear to be painted across the animal's body like decorative script.

children.description: Thyridiaceae is a small family of moths known as picture-winged leaf moths. These delicate moths are characterized by their translucent or semi-transparent wing patches that create distinctive window-like patterns, giving them their common name.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most other moth families, Thyridiaceae have clear, glass-like patches or windows in their wings that lack scales, creating a unique stained-glass appearance.
children.funFact: The clear wing patches of these moths serve as a form of camouflage, breaking up their outline and making them harder for predators to spot when they're resting on leaves.

children.name: Annulatascales
Annulatascaceae
Submersisphaeria
children.description: Submersisphaeria is a genus of aquatic fungi that lives submerged in freshwater environments. These microscopic fungi are specialized for life underwater, where they break down organic matter and play important roles in aquatic ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most fungi that live on land or in soil, Submersisphaeria species are fully adapted to underwater life and produce spores that can survive and disperse in aquatic environments.
children.funFact: These underwater fungi can survive completely submerged for their entire life cycle, making them some of the few fungi that never need to come up for air!

children.description: Annulatascaceae is a small family of aquatic fungi that live in freshwater and marine environments. These microscopic fungi are specialized for life underwater, where they decompose organic matter and play important ecological roles in aquatic ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their unique spore-producing structures called asci, which have distinctive ring-like formations (annuli) that help distinguish them from other aquatic fungi families.
children.funFact: Despite being fungi, members of Annulatascaceae have adapted so well to aquatic life that they can complete their entire life cycle underwater, unlike most fungi that require air for reproduction.

children.description: Annulatascales is a small order of fungi that includes species forming tiny, flask-shaped fruiting bodies called perithecia. These fungi are typically found growing on decaying wood and plant material, where they help break down organic matter in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this order are characterized by their distinctive ring-like structures (annuli) around the opening of their fruiting bodies, which gives the group its name.
children.funFact: This order is so rare and specialized that only one species has been found in all of New England, making it one of the most uncommon fungal groups in the region.

children.name: Pezizales
Pyronemataceae
Scutellinia
children.description: Eyelash cups are small, cup-shaped fungi that get their charming name from the dark, hair-like bristles that fringe their edges, resembling tiny eyelashes. These colorful little fungi are typically bright orange, red, or yellow and grow directly on decaying wood, soil, or organic matter. They're saprophytic decomposers that help break down dead plant material in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The distinctive dark bristles or hairs around the rim of their cup-shaped fruiting bodies make eyelash cups easily recognizable and separate them from other small cup fungi. Their vibrant colors and fuzzy margins create a unique appearance that's hard to mistake.
children.funFact: Despite being tiny (usually less than an inch across), eyelash cups can shoot their spores up to 4 inches into the air when conditions are just right, creating invisible puffs of reproductive material.

children.name: Aleuria
children.description: Aleuria is a small genus of cup fungi that produces bright orange, bowl-shaped fruiting bodies that grow directly from the ground. These eye-catching fungi are saprophytes, meaning they decompose organic matter in soil and leaf litter to obtain nutrients.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Aleuria are distinguished by their vibrant orange color and distinctive cup or bowl shape that opens wide at maturity, unlike many other cup fungi that remain more closed or have different colors.
children.funFact: The orange peel fungus gets its common name because it looks remarkably like discarded orange peels scattered on the forest floor, making it one of the most recognizable fungi for beginning naturalists.

children.name: Anthracobia
children.description: Anthracobia is a small genus of cup fungi that specializes in growing on burned wood and charcoal. These tiny fungi are part of nature's cleanup crew, helping to break down fire-damaged organic matter in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their preference for charred substrates and their small, cup-shaped fruiting bodies that often have distinctive eyelash-like hairs around the rim.
children.funFact: These fungi are so specialized for burned habitats that they're often called 'fire fungi' and may remain dormant in soil for years until a fire creates the perfect conditions for them to fruit.

children.name: Byssonectria
children.description: Byssonectria is a small genus of fungi that produces tiny, colorful cup-shaped fruiting bodies that emerge from decaying wood and plant material. These delicate fungi are part of the larger group of cup fungi and play an important role in breaking down organic matter in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their small, bright orange to reddish cup-shaped structures and their fuzzy, hair-like exterior surface that gives them a distinctly woolly appearance.
children.funFact: The name 'Byssonectria' comes from the Greek word 'byssos' meaning fine flax or cotton, referring to the cottony hairs that cover the outside of these tiny fungal cups.

children.name: Humaria
children.description: Humaria is a genus of cup fungi that produces small, bowl-shaped fruiting bodies that emerge from the soil or decaying organic matter. These fungi are saprophytes, meaning they feed on dead plant material and help decompose organic matter in forest ecosystems. They are part of the larger group of ascomycete fungi that release their spores from sac-like structures.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Humaria fungi are distinguished by their distinctive cup or saucer shape and their characteristic brown, hairy exterior surface contrasting with a smooth, lighter-colored interior spore-bearing surface.
children.funFact: Despite their small size, Humaria fungi can shoot their spores up to several centimeters into the air in tiny puffs that are sometimes visible as little dust clouds on calm days.

children.name: Sowerbyella
children.description: Sowerbyella is a small genus of cup fungi that creates distinctive orange, cup-shaped fruiting bodies. These fungi are saprobes, meaning they get their nutrients by decomposing dead organic matter in the soil and leaf litter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their bright orange coloration and cup-like shape with a distinctive stalk or stem, setting them apart from other cup fungi that typically lack stalks.
children.funFact: The genus is named after James Sowerby, an 18th-century English naturalist and botanical illustrator who created some of the most beautiful fungal illustrations of his time.

children.name: Pyronema
children.description: Pyronema is a genus of small cup fungi that produces bright orange to red, bowl-shaped fruiting bodies. These tiny fungi are commonly found growing on burnt soil, charcoal, and fire sites, where they help decompose organic matter in post-fire environments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Pyronema fungi are distinguished by their vibrant orange-red coloration and their strong preference for growing on burned substrates, earning them the common name 'fire fungi.'
children.funFact: These fungi are pyrophilous, meaning they are literally 'fire-loving' and often appear in large numbers after forest fires, helping to restore nutrients to the soil.

children.name: Genea
children.description: Genea is a genus of underground fungi that form truffle-like fruiting bodies beneath the soil surface. These fungi form partnerships with tree roots, helping trees absorb nutrients from the soil in exchange for sugars from the tree.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other truffle genera, Genea species have distinctively hairy or bristly surfaces on their fruiting bodies, which is where the name 'hispidula' (meaning 'slightly hairy') comes from.
children.funFact: These underground fungi can only be found by carefully digging in the soil near their host trees, making them much less conspicuous than the mushrooms we typically see above ground.

children.name: Sphaerosporium
children.description: Sphaerosporium is a genus of microscopic fungi that specializes in decomposing wood and other plant materials. These tiny organisms play an important role in forest ecosystems by breaking down dead organic matter and recycling nutrients back into the soil.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their spherical spores (hence the name 'Sphaerosporium' meaning 'sphere spore') and their preference for colonizing woody substrates like fallen logs and branches.
children.funFact: Despite being invisible to the naked eye, Sphaerosporium fungi are incredibly efficient recyclers that can break down tough woody materials that many other decomposers cannot handle.

children.name: Miladina
children.description: Miladina is a genus of small cup fungi that creates tiny, brownish fruiting bodies on decaying organic matter. These fungi are saprophytes, meaning they break down dead plant material and help recycle nutrients back into the forest ecosystem.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Miladina fungi are distinguished by their small, cup-shaped fruiting bodies that are typically brown to yellowish-brown in color and grow directly on decomposing wood or plant debris.
children.funFact: Despite being quite small and often overlooked, Miladina fungi play a crucial role as nature's recyclers, breaking down tough plant materials that many other organisms cannot decompose.

children.description: The Pyronemataceae are a diverse family of cup fungi that produce their spores in small, bowl or cup-shaped structures called apothecia. These fungi are commonly found growing on soil, burned areas, dung, or decaying organic matter throughout New England's forests and fields. Many species in this family are quite small and may be overlooked, but they play important roles as decomposers in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their cup-shaped fruiting bodies that open to expose the spore-producing surface. Unlike some other cup fungi, many Pyronemataceae species have distinctive features like colorful cups, hairy edges, or specific habitat preferences that help with identification.
children.funFact: Some species in this family, particularly in the genus Pyronema, are known as 'fire fungi' because they have a remarkable ability to appear in large numbers on recently burned soil, taking advantage of the changed soil chemistry after fires.

children.name: Pezizaceae
Peziza
children.description: Cup fungi in the genus Peziza are distinctive mushrooms that form bowl or cup-shaped fruiting bodies instead of the typical cap-and-stem structure. These fungi grow directly from the ground or decaying organic matter, creating shallow to deep cups that can range from tiny to several inches across. They're saprophytic fungi, meaning they help decompose dead plant material and enrich the soil.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other cup fungi, Peziza species typically have smooth, fleshy cups without hairs or fuzzy surfaces, and they're usually brown, gray, or earth-toned rather than brightly colored. Their cups are often quite large compared to other cup fungi families.
children.funFact: The Home Cup (Peziza domiciliana) gets its name because it often appears in houses, growing on damp plaster, concrete floors, or potting soil - making it one of the few wild mushrooms you might find fruiting indoors!

children.name: Chromelosporiopsis
children.description: Chromelosporiopsis is a small genus of fungi that forms colorful, powder-like spore masses on decaying wood and plant material. These tiny decomposers help break down organic matter in forest ecosystems, often appearing as dusty patches in shades of blue, pink, or other distinctive colors.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their brightly colored spore masses and their specific spore structure when viewed under a microscope. The vivid pigmentation of their spores helps distinguish them from many other wood-inhabiting fungi.
children.funFact: The genus name Chromelosporiopsis literally means 'colorful spore-like,' perfectly describing these fungi's most striking characteristic - their brilliantly pigmented spores that can paint decaying wood in unexpected hues.

children.name: Phylloscypha
children.description: Phylloscypha is a small genus of cup fungi that grows on decaying leaves and plant debris in forest environments. These tiny fungi form small, brownish cup-shaped fruiting bodies that help decompose organic matter on the forest floor.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their small size, brown coloration, and specific preference for growing on dead leaves rather than wood or other substrates.
children.funFact: Despite their tiny size, these cup fungi play an important role as nature's recyclers, breaking down fallen leaves and returning nutrients to the soil.

children.name: Pachyella
children.description: Pachyella is a small genus of cup fungi that produce distinctive disk-shaped fruiting bodies. These fungi are saprophytes, meaning they obtain nutrients by decomposing organic matter in the soil and leaf litter of forest floors.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Pachyella fungi are recognized by their copper-colored, disk-like caps that sit directly on the ground without stems, resembling scattered pennies on the forest floor.
children.funFact: The Copper Penny Fungus gets its common name from its striking resemblance to old copper coins, making it one of the most aptly named fungi in New England forests.

children.name: Geoscypha
children.description: Geoscypha is a small genus of cup fungi that creates tiny, delicate fruiting bodies resembling miniature goblets or fairy cups. These fungi are saprophytic, meaning they feed on decaying organic matter in the soil and leaf litter, playing an important role in forest decomposition.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Geoscypha fungi are distinguished by their small, cup-shaped fruiting bodies that typically measure only a few millimeters across and often display vibrant colors like violet or purple.
children.funFact: The name Geoscypha literally means 'earth cup,' reflecting how these tiny fungi emerge from the soil like miniature chalices scattered across the forest floor.

children.name: Chromelosporium
children.description: Chromelosporium is a genus of microscopic fungi that includes decomposer species found in organic-rich environments. These fungi play an important role in breaking down dead plant material and recycling nutrients back into the ecosystem.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their ability to produce distinctive spores and their preference for acidic, organic substrates like peat and decaying vegetation.
children.funFact: The name Chromelosporium comes from Greek words meaning 'colored spore,' referring to the often yellowish or brownish tinted spores these fungi produce.

children.name: Legaliana
children.description: Legaliana is a small genus of cup fungi that produces distinctive brown, cup-shaped fruiting bodies. These fungi are decomposers that help break down organic matter in forest environments, playing an important role in nutrient cycling.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their smooth, bay-colored (reddish-brown) cups that lack the fuzzy or hairy exterior found in many related cup fungi.
children.funFact: The Bay Cup is one of the few cup fungi that maintains its rich brown coloration even when dried, making it relatively easy to identify in herbarium collections.

children.name: Rugosporella
children.description: Rugosporella is a small genus of fungi that produces distinctive dark-colored fruiting bodies with a wrinkled or rough surface texture. These fungi are typically found growing on decaying wood and other organic matter in forest environments. The genus is characterized by its unique spore-producing structures and surface appearance.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Rugosporella can be identified by their dark, wine-colored to blackish fruiting bodies that have a distinctly wrinkled or rugose surface texture, which gives the genus its name.
children.funFact: The name 'Rugosporella' literally means 'little wrinkled spore,' referring to both the wrinkled surface of the fungus and its microscopic spore characteristics.

children.name: Adelphella
children.description: Adelphella is a small genus of bryozoans, which are tiny colonial marine animals that form encrusting colonies on hard surfaces like rocks, shells, and seaweed. These filter-feeding creatures create delicate, lace-like or sheet-like colonies made up of numerous small boxes called zooids, each housing an individual animal. They play an important role in marine ecosystems by filtering plankton from the water.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Adelphella colonies are distinguished by their characteristic growth pattern and the specific shape and arrangement of their zooids, which help bryozoan experts tell them apart from other encrusting bryozoan genera.
children.funFact: Despite being animals, bryozoan colonies like Adelphella are often mistaken for seaweeds or corals because of their plant-like or coral-like appearance when growing on underwater surfaces.

children.name: Paragalactinia
children.description: Paragalactinia is a small genus of cup fungi that forms distinctive yellowish, cup-shaped fruiting bodies. These saprophytic fungi help decompose organic matter in forest ecosystems, playing an important role in nutrient cycling.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their pale yellow to cream-colored cups and their tendency to develop a yellowing or aging coloration over time, which gives the common species its 'yellowing cup' name.
children.funFact: Despite being called a 'cup' fungus, Paragalactinia succosa actually starts out more disc-shaped when young and only develops its characteristic cup form as it matures.

children.description: The Pezizaceae family includes cup-shaped fungi that grow on soil, wood, or other organic matter. These fungi are decomposers that help break down dead plant material, and they produce their spores in distinctive cup or disc-shaped fruiting bodies. Many species in this family are quite small and can be easily overlooked, though some develop into conspicuous colorful cups.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their cup-shaped or disc-like fruiting bodies that open upward, with spores produced on the inner surface. Unlike many other cup fungi, Pezizaceae species typically have smooth spores and lack the fuzzy or hairy exterior found in related families.
children.funFact: Some members of this family, like the desert truffles, grow completely underground and are prized as food in Mediterranean and Middle Eastern cuisines, where they're traditionally hunted using trained dogs or by following subtle ground cracks.

children.name: Helvellaceae
Helvella
children.description: Elfin Saddles are distinctive cup fungi that produce unusual fruiting bodies with wrinkled, folded, or saddle-shaped caps perched on hollow stems. These fascinating decomposer fungi are commonly found in woodlands, where they break down organic matter in the soil and leaf litter. Their peculiar twisted and contorted forms make them some of the most recognizable fungi in New England forests.
