children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike typical mushrooms with gills or pores, Elfin Saddles have smooth, wrinkled surfaces that fold into saddle-like or cup-like shapes. Their stems are characteristically hollow and often have deep grooves or ribs running along their length.
children.funFact: The genus name Helvella comes from a Latin word meaning 'small pot herb,' though these fungi are not edible and some species can be toxic when consumed raw.

children.description: The Helvellaceae are a family of cup fungi that produce distinctive saddle-shaped or cup-shaped fruiting bodies. These fascinating fungi are saprophytes, meaning they decompose dead organic matter in the soil and help recycle nutrients back into forest ecosystems. Most members of this family fruit in spring and fall, often appearing after rain in wooded areas.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other cup fungi, members of Helvellaceae typically have irregularly folded, saddle-shaped caps rather than simple bowl shapes. Their stems are often hollow and may have distinctive ridges or chambers when cut open.
children.funFact: Some Helvella species, known as elfin saddles, have stems with internal chambers that create intricate patterns when sliced, resembling tiny architectural structures or honeycomb designs.

children.name: Morchellaceae
Morchella
children.description: True morels are distinctive spring mushrooms with honeycomb-like caps full of pits and ridges. These prized edible fungi emerge from the forest floor when soil temperatures warm, often appearing near dead or dying trees. All true morels have hollow stems and caps that are completely attached to the stem at the base.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike false morels and other look-alikes, true morels have completely hollow interiors from stem to cap, and their caps are firmly attached to the stem rather than hanging like a skirt.
children.funFact: Morels have a mysterious relationship with trees and often fruit abundantly in areas affected by forest fires, sometimes appearing in huge numbers the spring after a burn.

children.name: Verpa
children.description: Thimble morels are distinctive spring mushrooms with wrinkled, brain-like caps that sit loosely on hollow white stems like a thimble on a finger. Unlike true morels, their caps are only attached at the very top of the stem, creating a skirt-like appearance around the bottom edge of the cap.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The key feature that separates thimble morels from true morels is that their caps hang freely around the stem like a loose thimble, rather than being fused to the stem throughout.
children.funFact: Thimble morels are sometimes called 'false morels' and while edible when cooked, they're considered less desirable than true morels and can cause stomach upset in some people if not prepared properly.

children.name: Disciotis
children.description: Cup-shaped morels are large, distinctive fungi that form shallow, cup-like fruiting bodies in early spring. Unlike their more famous cousins the true morels, these fungi have smooth, wrinkled surfaces rather than the honeycomb-like pits and ridges of typical morels.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These fungi are distinguished from true morels by their broad, cup-shaped form and their prominently veined, brain-like surface texture without the characteristic honeycomb pattern.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'cup-shaped morels,' these fungi are not actually true morels at all - they belong to a different family entirely and are more closely related to cup fungi!

children.description: Morels and allies are a family of spring-emerging fungi known for their distinctive honeycomb-like caps and hollow stems. These highly prized edible mushrooms typically appear after winter's end when soil temperatures warm, often found in woodlands, burned areas, and near dead or dying trees. They form partnerships with tree roots and help decompose organic matter in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other mushrooms, morels have completely hollow interiors from cap to base, and their caps feature a unique pitted or ridged surface pattern. The cap is also directly attached to the stem rather than hanging free like a typical mushroom.
children.funFact: Morels are so difficult to cultivate commercially that they sell for $15-30 per pound, making them one of the most valuable wild mushrooms and turning springtime morel hunting into a treasured tradition across New England.

children.name: Discinaceae
Gyromitra
children.description: Gyromitra is a genus of distinctive spring mushrooms known for their brain-like, wrinkled caps that are deeply folded and convoluted. These fungi are commonly called false morels because they fruit at the same time as true morels but have a completely different cap structure. They typically grow from the ground in wooded areas, often near decaying wood or in sandy soils.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true morels which have honeycomb-like pitted caps, Gyromitra species have irregularly folded, brain-shaped caps with gyrus-like ridges and valleys. Their caps are also typically reddish-brown to dark brown, contrasting with the hollow, whitish stems.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'false morels,' some Gyromitra species contain gyromitrin, a toxic compound that breaks down into rocket fuel component monomethylhydrazine when cooked, making proper identification crucial for foragers.

children.name: Maublancomyces
children.description: Maublancomyces is a small genus of cup fungi that includes some of the most distinctive and impressive ascomycetes found in New England forests. These fungi produce large, irregularly shaped fruiting bodies that can be quite striking when encountered on the forest floor. They are saprobic organisms, meaning they obtain nutrients by decomposing organic matter in soil and leaf litter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their large, brain-like or irregularly folded fruiting bodies that lack the typical cup shape of many related fungi. Unlike true morels, their caps are not attached to the stem at the base, and their surface texture is more convoluted and less regularly pitted.
children.funFact: The Giant's False Morel (Maublancomyces gigas) can grow to enormous sizes, with some specimens reaching over a foot across and weighing several pounds, making it one of the largest cup fungi in North America.

children.name: Discina
children.description: Discina is a genus of cup fungi that produces distinctive saddle-shaped or ear-shaped fruiting bodies in spring. These unusual mushrooms grow directly from the ground, often appearing wrinkled and folded like crumpled leather. They're commonly called pig's ears due to their resemblance to the floppy ears of a pig.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true morels, Discina species have irregularly folded, saddle-like caps rather than honeycomb-pitted surfaces. Their fruiting bodies are typically reddish-brown to dark brown and attach directly to short, thick stems.
children.funFact: Despite their common name suggesting they're edible like pig's ears, these mushrooms contain toxins and should never be eaten raw, and even cooking may not eliminate all dangerous compounds.

children.name: Paragyromitra
children.description: Paragyromitra is a genus of fungi that produces distinctive saddle-shaped or brain-like fruiting bodies that emerge from the ground in late fall and early winter. These mushrooms have a wrinkled, lobed cap that sits atop a hollow stem, creating their characteristic saddle appearance. They belong to the same family as true morels but fruit much later in the season.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true morels which have honeycomb-like pitted caps, Paragyromitra species have smooth, brain-like wrinkled caps that are saddle-shaped rather than conical. They also fruit in late fall rather than spring like most morels.
children.funFact: Despite being called a 'false morel,' the Saddle-shaped False Morel actually fruits at the opposite end of the year from true morels - appearing after the first frosts when most other mushrooms have finished for the season.

children.name: Neogyromitra
children.description: Neogyromitra is a small genus of cup fungi that produces distinctive brown, wrinkled fruiting bodies in spring. These fungi are closely related to the more well-known Gyromitra (brain fungi) but have their own unique characteristics that set them apart.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike their Gyromitra cousins which have brain-like convoluted caps, Neogyromitra species have more cup-shaped or irregularly folded fruiting bodies with a distinctly brownish coloration.
children.funFact: The genus name Neogyromitra literally means 'new Gyromitra,' reflecting how these fungi were once classified with the brain fungi before scientists discovered they deserved their own separate genus.

children.name: Piscidiscina
children.description: Piscidiscina is a genus containing just one species of small cup fungus found in New England. These tiny fungi grow on decaying wood and have a distinctive whitish, cup-shaped fruiting body that resembles a miniature bowl.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The fishtail cup fungus is recognized by its small, pale cup-shaped structure and its preference for growing on rotting hardwood logs and branches.
children.funFact: Despite its common name 'fishtail cup,' this fungus gets its name from the way its cup edges sometimes split and curl, resembling the shape of a fish's tail fin.

children.name: Pseudorhizina
children.description: Pseudorhizina is a small genus of cup fungi that forms distinctive shallow, bowl-shaped fruiting bodies on decaying wood. These fungi are saprophytes, meaning they break down dead organic matter and play an important role in forest decomposition processes.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Pseudorhizina can be identified by its pale-colored, cup-shaped appearance and the presence of root-like structures (rhizomorphs) at its base that help distinguish it from other similar cup fungi.
children.funFact: The name 'Pseudorhizina' literally means 'false root,' referring to the root-like threads that extend from the base of the fungus but aren't true roots like those found in plants.

children.description: The Discinaceae family consists of cup fungi and brain fungi that produce distinctive fruiting bodies in spring and early summer. These fungi are saprophytes that decompose organic matter in forest soils, particularly favoring areas with rich leaf litter and decaying wood.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their irregular, wrinkled, or brain-like fruiting bodies that often appear cup-shaped or saddle-shaped. Unlike many other cup fungi, they typically have a thick, fleshy texture and lack a clearly defined stem.
children.funFact: Some species in this family, particularly in the genus Gyromitra, contain toxins that make them dangerous to eat despite being considered delicacies in some cultures - they're sometimes called 'false morels' because they can be mistaken for the edible true morels.

children.name: Sarcoscyphaceae
Sarcoscypha
children.description: Elf Cups are small, colorful fungi that form distinctive cup or bowl-shaped fruiting bodies, typically bright red or scarlet in color. These woodland mushrooms are saprophytes, meaning they get their nutrients by decomposing dead organic matter like fallen branches and woody debris. They're among the first fungi to appear in late winter and early spring, often pushing up through snow.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Elf Cups are easily recognized by their vibrant red, cup-shaped appearance and their early seasonal emergence when most other fungi are dormant. Unlike many cup fungi, they have a particularly intense scarlet coloration that makes them stand out dramatically against the brown forest floor.
children.funFact: Elf Cups can actually shoot their spores up to 4 inches into the air using tiny water-powered cannons, creating visible puffs of spores when disturbed on humid days.

children.name: Pithya
children.description: Pithya is a small genus of disc fungi that specializes in growing on coniferous trees and their woody debris. These tiny fungi form small, cup-shaped or disc-like fruiting bodies that emerge from the bark or wood of evergreen trees like junipers and firs.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other disc fungi, Pithya species are specifically adapted to coniferous hosts and tend to have very small, often dark-colored fruiting bodies that can be easily overlooked on tree bark.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'disco' fungi for their disc-like shape, these tiny organisms are actually helping to decompose and recycle nutrients from dead coniferous wood back into the forest ecosystem.

children.name: Microstoma
children.description: Microstoma is a genus of small, cup-shaped fungi that produces some of the most delicate and beautiful mushrooms in the forest. These tiny fungi are saprophytes, meaning they help decompose organic matter like fallen logs and leaf litter. They belong to a group of fungi known for their distinctive cup or disk-like fruiting bodies.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Microstoma fungi are distinguished by their small, bright pink cup-shaped fruiting bodies with distinctive fringed or fuzzy edges. The pink coloration and delicate, hair-like fringe around the cup margin make them unmistakable among other small cup fungi.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'faery cups,' these tiny pink fungi are so small that they're often overlooked by hikers - the cups typically measure less than half an inch across and can easily be mistaken for flower petals or bits of colorful debris.

children.description: Elf Cups and Allies are a family of small, cup-shaped fungi that create bright red, orange, or yellow fruiting bodies that look like tiny colorful bowls scattered on the forest floor. These fungi are saprophytes, meaning they break down dead organic matter like fallen logs, twigs, and leaf litter. Most species in this family fruit during cooler months, often appearing on snow-covered wood in late winter and early spring.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other cup fungi, members of this family typically have bright, vivid colors and smooth, waxy surfaces. Their cup-shaped fruiting bodies are usually stalked rather than sessile, giving them a goblet-like appearance.
children.funFact: Some elf cup species are among the few fungi that actually fruit in winter, with their bright red cups creating stunning splashes of color against snow-covered logs and branches.

children.name: Sarcosomataceae
Galiella
children.description: Galiella is a small genus of cup fungi that produces distinctive rubber-textured fruiting bodies. These fungi are saprophytes, meaning they decompose dead organic matter in forest environments, playing an important role in nutrient cycling.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their unique rubbery, gelatinous texture and cup-shaped fruiting bodies that are typically dark brown to reddish-brown in color with a hairy or fuzzy outer surface.
children.funFact: The hairy rubber cup gets its common name from its distinctive texture - when fresh, it feels remarkably similar to rubber and can be quite bouncy to the touch.

children.name: Urnula
children.description: Urnula is a genus of cup fungi that produces distinctive dark, urn-shaped fruiting bodies that emerge from the ground in spring. These fungi are saprophytes that help decompose organic matter in forest soils, particularly around decaying wood and leaf litter. They belong to a group of ascomycetes known for their cup-like appearance.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Urnula fungi are recognized by their deep, dark brown to black cup-shaped fruiting bodies that resemble small urns or goblets. Unlike many other cup fungi, they have a distinctly thick, leathery texture and often appear almost charcoal-black in color.
children.funFact: Devil's urn gets its dramatic name from its dark, mysterious appearance - the deep black cups were once thought to resemble tiny cauldrons used by supernatural forces.

children.name: Pseudoplectania
children.description: Pseudoplectania is a small genus of cup fungi that produces dark, distinctive fruiting bodies on decaying wood. These fungi are saprophytes, meaning they break down dead organic matter and play an important role in forest ecosystems by recycling nutrients back into the soil.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their dark-colored, cup-shaped fruiting bodies that grow directly from rotting logs and stumps. Unlike many other cup fungi, Pseudoplectania species have a distinctly blackish appearance both inside and outside the cup.
children.funFact: The ebony cup fungus gets its name from its striking jet-black color, making it one of the darkest cup fungi you'll encounter in New England forests.

children.name: Donadinia
children.description: Donadinia is a small genus of cup fungi that produces tiny, disc-shaped fruiting bodies on decaying wood. These delicate fungi are part of the larger group of ascomycetes, which reproduce by forming spores in special sac-like structures.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Donadinia fungi are distinguished by their very small size and their preference for growing on well-rotted hardwood, particularly in moist forest environments.
children.funFact: The single New England species, Donadinia seaveri, was named after mycologist Fred Jay Seaver, who made significant contributions to North American fungal taxonomy in the early 1900s.

children.description: Sarcosomataceae is a family of cup fungi that produce distinctive, often dark-colored fruiting bodies that emerge from the soil or decaying wood. These fungi are saprophytes, meaning they break down dead organic matter and play an important role in forest decomposition. Most members of this family fruit in spring or early summer, making them some of the earlier mushrooms you might encounter during the growing season.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other cup fungi, members of Sarcosomataceae typically have thick, fleshy fruiting bodies with dark exteriors and are often quite large and robust. They also tend to have a more gelatinous or rubbery texture compared to the more brittle cup fungi in related families.
children.funFact: Some species in this family, like those in the genus Urnula, are nicknamed 'devil's urns' because their deep, dark cup-shaped fruiting bodies resemble tiny cauldrons emerging from the forest floor.

children.name: Ascobolaceae
Ascobolus
children.description: Ascobolus is a genus of small cup fungi that specialize in growing on animal dung, particularly from herbivores like horses, cows, and rabbits. These tiny decomposers play an important role in breaking down organic matter and recycling nutrients back into the ecosystem. They produce small, disc-shaped fruiting bodies that release spores to spread to new dung piles.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Ascobolus fungi are distinguished by their small size, cup-shaped appearance, and exclusive habitat on fresh animal dung. Unlike many other cup fungi, they have dark-colored spores and often show a distinctive purple or violet tint when mature.
children.funFact: These fungi have evolved to time their spore release perfectly with the feeding habits of grazing animals - their spores are designed to be eaten and passed through the digestive system to colonize fresh dung piles!

children.name: Saccobolus
children.description: Saccobolus is a genus of tiny cup fungi that grows on animal dung, particularly that of herbivorous mammals like deer, rabbits, and livestock. These microscopic fungi produce small, dark fruiting bodies that look like miniature cups or spheres when mature. They play an important role in breaking down organic matter and recycling nutrients back into the ecosystem.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Saccobolus fungi are distinguished by their unique spore-shooting mechanism and their specialized habitat preference for fresh animal dung. Unlike many other cup fungi, they have thick-walled, dark spores that are forcibly ejected from the fruiting body.
children.funFact: Despite being invisible to the naked eye, Saccobolus fungi can launch their spores up to several centimeters away from the dung pile, helping them colonize fresh patches of habitat as animals move through the landscape.

children.description: Ascobolaceae is a family of small cup fungi that specialize in growing on dung and other organic matter rich in nutrients. These tiny fungi produce spores in flask-shaped structures called asci, and they play an important role in breaking down animal waste in the environment. Most members of this family are so small they're easily overlooked, typically appearing as tiny dark dots or small cups on their substrate.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other cup fungi, Ascobolaceae members are specifically adapted to grow on dung and have dark, thick-walled spores that can survive harsh conditions. Their spores are often ejected forcefully from the fungus when mature, helping them disperse to new locations.
children.funFact: Some Ascobolaceae fungi can shoot their spores up to several centimeters away with such force that you can actually hear a faint popping sound when many spores are released at once!

children.name: Otideaceae
Otidea
children.description: Otidea is a genus of cup fungi that produce distinctive ear-shaped fruiting bodies, typically appearing in brown, tan, or yellowish colors. These fungi grow on decaying wood and forest debris, where they help break down organic matter as saprophytes. Their cup-like structures often have a split or slit on one side, giving them their characteristic ear-like appearance.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other cup fungi, Otidea species have asymmetrical fruiting bodies that are often split down one side, creating their distinctive ear or rabbit-ear shape. They also tend to be larger and more elongated than typical round cup fungi.
children.funFact: The name 'Otidea' comes from the Greek word 'otis' meaning ear, which perfectly describes their rabbit-ear appearance - in fact, one species is commonly called 'hare's ear' because of this resemblance!

children.description: The Otideaceae family consists of distinctive cup-shaped fungi that look like split or ear-shaped mushrooms. These saprophytic fungi decompose organic matter in forest soils and are typically found growing on the ground among leaf litter and woody debris.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their distinctive split or ear-like cup shape that opens on one side, unlike other cup fungi that are typically round and symmetrical.
children.funFact: These fungi are sometimes called 'rabbit ear fungi' because their split, elongated cups can resemble the ears of a rabbit poking up through the forest floor.

children.name: Rhizinaceae
Rhizina
children.description: Rhizina is a small genus of unusual fungi that forms distinctive flat, crusty fruiting bodies on the ground. These fungi are saprophytes that feed on decaying organic matter in forest soils, particularly in areas that have been disturbed by fire or other disturbances.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are easily recognized by their unique flattened, irregularly-shaped fruiting bodies that lie flat against the soil surface and have a characteristic wrinkled or undulating appearance.
children.funFact: The Doughnut Fungus gets its common name from its tendency to form circular fruiting bodies with a depressed center, resembling a flattened donut lying on the forest floor.

children.name: Psilopezia
children.description: Psilopezia is a small genus of cup fungi that forms tiny, delicate fruiting bodies on decaying wood and plant debris. These microscopic fungi are saprophytes, meaning they help break down dead organic matter and recycle nutrients back into forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their extremely small size and smooth, cup-shaped fruiting bodies that lack the fuzzy or hairy exterior found in many related cup fungi.
children.funFact: Despite their tiny size - often less than a millimeter across - Psilopezia fungi play an important role as nature's recyclers, helping to decompose fallen twigs and leaves on the forest floor.

children.description: The Rhizinaceae are a small family of unusual fungi that produce distinctive cup-shaped or flattened fruiting bodies that emerge from the ground. These fungi are saprobic, meaning they feed on dead organic matter in the soil, particularly decomposing wood and plant debris. They are closely related to morels and truffles but have their own unique characteristics.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family produce flattened, often brain-like or wrinkled fruiting bodies that lie close to the ground, unlike the more upright cup fungi in related families. They also have distinctive root-like structures (rhizomorphs) that extend from the base, giving them their name.
children.funFact: Rhizina species are sometimes called 'doughnut fungus' because their fruiting bodies can develop a characteristic hole in the center as they mature, resembling a flat, brown pastry.

children.name: Pyropyxidaceae
Jafnea
children.description: Jafnea is a small genus of cup fungi that produces distinctive brownish, cup-shaped fruiting bodies that emerge from the soil. These fungi are saprophytes, meaning they help decompose organic matter in forest ecosystems. They belong to the ascomycete group of fungi, which release their spores from specialized sac-like structures.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Jafnea cup fungi are distinguished by their brown coloration and their habit of growing directly from soil rather than on wood or other substrates like many other cup fungi.
children.funFact: Despite being relatively inconspicuous, Jafnea fungi play an important ecological role as decomposers, helping to recycle nutrients back into forest soils.

children.name: Pyropyxis
children.description: Pyropyxis is a small genus of tiny cup fungi that grow on decaying wood and plant material. These microscopic fungi produce small, cup-shaped fruiting bodies that are typically reddish in color and barely visible to the naked eye.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Pyropyxis fungi are distinguished by their extremely small size (usually less than 1mm) and their bright red to orange cup-shaped structures that appear on rotting wood.
children.funFact: Despite being so small that you need a magnifying glass to see them clearly, Pyropyxis fungi play an important role in forest ecosystems by helping to break down dead wood and recycle nutrients back into the soil.

children.description: The Pyropyxidaceae family consists of small, cup-shaped fungi that are fire-loving specialists. These tiny fungi have a remarkable ability to appear in large numbers on burned soil and charcoal, often showing up within months after forest fires or controlled burns.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most cup fungi, members of this family have a strong preference for fire-disturbed habitats and produce their spores in a distinctive manner. Their fruiting bodies are typically very small and have a unique cellular structure that helps them thrive in post-fire environments.
children.funFact: These fungi are so closely associated with fire that they're sometimes called 'phoenix fungi' - they can remain dormant in soil for years until the heat and chemical changes from a fire trigger them to fruit abundantly.

children.name: Caloscyphaceae
Caloscypha
children.description: Caloscypha is a small genus of cup fungi that includes just one species found in New England - the Spring Orange Peel Fungus. These fungi are characterized by their bright orange, cup-shaped fruiting bodies that emerge from the ground in early spring. They belong to a group of fungi that form distinctive bowl or cup-like structures to release their spores.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Caloscypha stands out from other cup fungi by its vibrant orange color and its specific timing of appearing in early spring, often emerging through snow or shortly after snowmelt.
children.funFact: The Spring Orange Peel Fungus is one of the first fungi to appear each year, sometimes fruiting while snow is still on the ground, earning it the nickname 'snowbank orange peel fungus.'

children.description: Caloscyphaceae is a small family of cup fungi that produce distinctive bright orange or yellow cup-shaped fruiting bodies. These fungi are saprophytic, meaning they feed on decaying organic matter, particularly decomposing plant material in forest environments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their vibrant orange to yellow coloration and their cup-shaped ascocarps (fruiting bodies) that typically appear in spring. They can be distinguished from other cup fungi by their specific coloration and seasonal timing.
children.funFact: The single New England species in this family, Caloscypha fulgens, is sometimes called the 'spring orange peel fungus' and often appears shortly after snowmelt, making it one of the first colorful fungi to emerge each year.

children.name: Tarzettaceae
Geopyxis
children.description: Geopyxis is a genus of cup fungi that produces small, bowl-shaped fruiting bodies that emerge from the soil or burned areas. These fungi are saprophytes, meaning they decompose organic matter and help recycle nutrients back into the ecosystem.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Geopyxis fungi are characterized by their cup-shaped appearance and tendency to grow directly from the ground, often appearing after fires or in areas with charred wood and soil.
children.funFact: The Stalked Bonfire Cup gets its name from its habit of appearing in areas where fires have occurred, as the heat and altered soil chemistry create ideal conditions for its growth.

children.description: Tarzettaceae is a small family of cup fungi that produce distinctive shallow, cup-shaped fruiting bodies that emerge from soil or decaying organic matter. These fungi are saprophytes, meaning they obtain nutrients by decomposing dead plant material in forest ecosystems. They typically appear in spring and early summer in woodland habitats.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their bright-colored, shallow cups with smooth or slightly wrinkled surfaces that lack the deep bowl shape of many other cup fungi. The spores are released from the inner surface of these cups when mature.
children.funFact: The genus name Geopyxis literally means 'earth cup,' reflecting how these small fungi emerge directly from the forest floor like tiny colorful bowls scattered across the woodland.

children.name: Wynneaceae
Wynnea
children.description: Wynnea is a small genus of unusual fungi that produce distinctive ear-shaped or spatula-like fruiting bodies emerging from the ground. These fascinating fungi form partnerships with tree roots and are typically found in deciduous forests, particularly near oaks and other hardwood trees.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike typical mushrooms, Wynnea fungi have flattened, ear-like or paddle-shaped fruiting bodies that lack a traditional cap and stem structure. Their unique form and reddish-brown coloration make them easily recognizable among forest fungi.
children.funFact: Wynnea sparassoides is sometimes called the 'morel mimic' because its wrinkled, brownish appearance can fool foragers into thinking they've found an unusual morel mushroom.

children.description: Wynneaceae is a small family of unusual cup fungi that produce distinctive ear-shaped or cup-shaped fruiting bodies. These fungi are saprobic, meaning they decompose dead organic matter in forest environments, particularly fallen logs and woody debris.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their unique ear-like or deeply cup-shaped fruiting bodies that emerge from buried wood or roots, often appearing to grow directly from the forest floor.
children.funFact: The fruiting bodies of Wynnea fungi can emerge dramatically from underground wood sources, sometimes appearing to mysteriously pop up from seemingly bare forest soil.

children.name: Chorioactidaceae
Wolfina
children.description: Wolfina is a small genus of cup fungi that produces distinctive orange to yellowish fruiting bodies. These fungi are saprophytes, meaning they feed on dead organic matter and help decompose fallen logs and woody debris in forest environments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Wolfina fungi are recognized by their bright orange cup-shaped fruiting bodies and their preference for growing on decaying hardwood. They can be distinguished from similar cup fungi by their specific coloration and habitat preferences.
children.funFact: Despite being named after a wolf, Wolfina fungi are actually named after mycologist Frederick Wolf, who made significant contributions to our understanding of cup fungi in the early 20th century.

children.description: Chorioactidaceae is a small family of cup fungi that are among the most unusual and primitive members of the fungal kingdom. These fungi produce distinctive cup-shaped fruiting bodies that emerge from decaying wood, typically appearing as small, dark, leathery structures. They are relatively rare and often overlooked due to their small size and inconspicuous appearance.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their unique spore-bearing structures and primitive cellular characteristics that set them apart from other cup fungi. Their fruiting bodies have a distinctive tough, leathery texture and dark coloration.
children.funFact: Chorioactidaceae fungi are considered evolutionary relics, representing an ancient lineage that has remained virtually unchanged for millions of years, earning them the nickname 'living fossils' among mycologists.

children.name: Coprotaceae
Coprotus
children.description: Coprotus is a small genus of cup fungi that grows exclusively on animal dung, particularly from herbivorous mammals like deer, rabbits, and livestock. These tiny fungi produce small, cup-shaped fruiting bodies that help decompose organic matter in forest and field ecosystems. They play an important ecological role by breaking down nutrient-rich waste materials.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Coprotus fungi are distinguished by their strict preference for growing on fresh animal dung and their small, pale cup-shaped fruiting bodies that are typically less than a centimeter across.
children.funFact: These fungi have evolved specialized spores that can survive passage through an animal's digestive system, allowing them to colonize fresh dung deposits wherever animals roam.

children.description: Coprotaceae is a small family of fungi that are specialized decomposers, playing an important role in breaking down organic matter in forest ecosystems. These fungi are typically found growing on decaying wood, fallen leaves, and other plant debris where they help recycle nutrients back into the soil.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their small, often inconspicuous fruiting bodies and their preference for growing on decomposing organic matter in moist woodland environments.
children.funFact: Despite being small and easily overlooked, Coprotaceae fungi are essential recyclers in New England's forests, helping to transform fallen trees and leaves into rich soil that nourishes new plant growth.

children.description: Pezizales is a diverse order of cup fungi that includes some of the most recognizable mushrooms in New England's forests and fields. These fungi produce their spores in distinctive cup-shaped, saucer-like, or brain-like fruiting bodies that open to the sky. The group includes prized edibles like morels, colorful cup fungi that brighten the forest floor, and even underground desert truffles.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other fungi, Pezizales produce their spores on the upper, exposed surface of their fruiting bodies rather than hidden inside or underneath. Their fruiting bodies are typically cup-shaped, disc-like, or have convoluted surfaces with pits and ridges.
children.funFact: Some members of this order, like the morel mushrooms, are among the most sought-after edible fungi by foragers, while others like the scarlet elf cup create brilliant red splashes of color on decaying wood during winter months.

children.name: Mycosphaerellales
Mycosphaerellaceae
Ramularia
children.description: Ramularia is a genus of plant pathogenic fungi that causes leaf spot diseases on a wide variety of plants throughout New England. These microscopic fungi create small, often circular spots on leaves that can range from white to brown in color, and they reproduce by forming spores on the leaf surface.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Ramularia fungi are distinguished by their simple, colorless spores that form on short, branched structures called conidiophores directly on the leaf surface. Unlike many other leaf spot fungi, they typically produce very pale or white spots with distinct borders.
children.funFact: Some Ramularia species have a Jekyll-and-Hyde existence, producing both an asexual stage (Ramularia) that creates leaf spots and a sexual stage (Mycosphaerella) that forms tiny flask-shaped structures for overwintering.

children.name: Cercospora
children.description: Cercospora is a genus of plant pathogenic fungi that causes leaf spot diseases on a wide variety of plants throughout New England. These microscopic fungi create distinctive dark spots or lesions on leaves, often with lighter centers, and can cause premature leaf drop in infected plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Cercospora species are distinguished by their long, narrow, multi-celled spores (conidia) that are produced on dark, thread-like structures emerging from leaf spots. Unlike many other leaf spot fungi, Cercospora typically creates spots with pale or grayish centers surrounded by darker borders.
children.funFact: Some Cercospora species are so host-specific that they're named after their preferred plant victims - like Cercospora moricola, which specializes in attacking mulberry trees!

children.name: Septoria
children.description: Septoria is a genus of tiny fungi that specialize in creating leaf spots on various plants. These microscopic organisms live as pathogens, causing small, dark spots with lighter centers to appear on the leaves of their host plants. Each species in this genus typically targets specific types of plants, from wildflowers to cultivated crops.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Septoria fungi are distinguished by their characteristic leaf spots that often have dark borders with pale or whitish centers, creating a distinctive 'bull's-eye' appearance. They produce their spores in tiny, flask-shaped structures called pycnidia that are embedded within the leaf spots.
children.funFact: Despite being plant pathogens, Septoria fungi play an important ecological role by helping to recycle nutrients from aging leaves back into the soil, essentially acting as nature's cleanup crew in forest ecosystems.

children.name: Sphaerulina
children.description: Sphaerulina is a genus of microscopic fungi that live as plant pathogens, causing leaf spot diseases on various host plants. These tiny fungi produce small, dark fruiting bodies embedded in plant tissue where they develop spores for reproduction.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Sphaerulina are distinguished by their small, spherical to flask-shaped fruiting bodies (perithecia) that contain asci with spores, and their specific association with creating leaf spots on living plants.
children.funFact: Despite being plant pathogens, Sphaerulina species play an important ecological role by helping to decompose plant material and cycle nutrients back into forest ecosystems.

children.name: Pseudocercospora
children.description: Pseudocercospora is a genus of microscopic fungi that are plant pathogens, meaning they cause diseases in plants. These fungi are particularly known for causing leaf spot diseases, creating small dark or discolored patches on the leaves of their host plants. They reproduce by forming spores that can spread to other plants through wind, water, or contact.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike some other leaf spot fungi, Pseudocercospora species produce their spores on branched structures called conidiophores that emerge through the plant's leaf pores (stomata). Their spores are typically long and narrow with multiple segments, giving them a distinctive appearance under a microscope.
children.funFact: The single New England species, Pseudocercospora kalmiae, specifically targets mountain laurel plants, showing how specialized these tiny fungi can be in choosing their plant hosts.

children.name: Rosisphaerella
children.description: Rosisphaerella is a genus of tiny fungi that specialize in living on rose plants. These microscopic organisms form small, spherical structures on their host plants and belong to a group of fungi known for their simple, rounded fruiting bodies.
children.distinguishingFeatures: This genus is distinguished by its exclusive association with roses and its characteristic spherical, dark-colored fruiting bodies that develop directly on rose stems and leaves.
children.funFact: Despite being named after roses, Rosisphaerella rosicola is so small that you'd need a microscope to see its tiny black spheres dotting the surface of infected rose plants.

children.name: Dothistroma
children.description: Dothistroma is a genus of fungi that causes serious needle diseases in pine trees. These microscopic organisms infect pine needles, creating distinctive symptoms that can severely weaken or kill their host trees.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other plant pathogens, Dothistroma creates characteristic red-brown bands across infected pine needles before the needles turn completely brown and drop off.
children.funFact: Dothistroma needle blight has become one of the most economically damaging forest diseases worldwide, spreading rapidly in recent decades due to climate change and global trade.

children.name: Pruniphilomyces
children.description: Pruniphilomyces is a genus of tiny fungi that specialize in living on dead plant material, particularly woody debris. These microscopic decomposers play an important role in breaking down organic matter in forest ecosystems. They belong to a group of fungi known for their simple, often flask-shaped fruiting bodies.
children.distinguishingFeatures: This genus is characterized by its distinctive spore-releasing structures that open by splitting around the middle, like a tiny lid popping off. The fruiting bodies are typically dark-colored and embedded in the substrate they're growing on.
children.funFact: The name Pruniphilomyces literally means 'plum-loving fungus,' though it actually grows on various types of dead wood rather than being specific to plum trees.

children.description: Mycosphaerellaceae is a large family of fungi that are primarily plant pathogens, causing leaf spots, blights, and other diseases on a wide variety of plants. These microscopic fungi produce their spores in small, flask-shaped structures and are among the most economically important plant disease-causing organisms worldwide. Many species in this family have complex life cycles with multiple spore-producing stages.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their production of ascospores (sexual spores) in small, dark, spherical to flask-shaped fruiting bodies called pseudothecia. They typically cause distinctive leaf spot symptoms with dark borders and often have both sexual and asexual reproductive stages.
children.funFact: Some Mycosphaerellaceae species can cause devastating crop diseases - for example, black sigatoka disease caused by Pseudocercospora fijiensis is one of the most serious threats to banana production globally, requiring frequent fungicide applications to control.

children.name: Schizothyriaceae
Schizothyrium
children.description: Schizothyrium is a genus of tiny fungi that create small, dark spots on plant surfaces, particularly on fruits like apples. These microscopic organisms are commonly called 'flyspeck' fungi because their black, dot-like fruiting bodies resemble tiny fly droppings scattered across leaves and fruit surfaces. They are plant parasites that feed on the waxy coating of their host plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other plant fungi that cause rot or large lesions, Schizothyrium species create very small, superficial black dots that remain on the surface. Their fruiting bodies have a distinctive shield-like or circular shape when viewed under magnification.
children.funFact: Despite their unappealing nickname and appearance, flyspeck fungi are mostly cosmetic problems that don't penetrate deeply into fruits, making affected apples still safe to eat once washed.

children.description: Schizothyriaceae is a family of tiny fungi that create distinctive shield-like or circular fruiting bodies on plant surfaces. These microscopic organisms are often found as dark spots on leaves and stems, where they live as parasites or decomposers of plant material.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are recognized by their characteristic shield-shaped fruiting structures that split open in a star-like pattern to release spores. Unlike many other small fungi, they form these distinctive radially-cracked covers over their spore-producing structures.
children.funFact: Despite being barely visible to the naked eye, these fungi create perfectly geometric patterns when their fruiting bodies crack open, resembling tiny natural compasses on leaf surfaces.

children.description: Mycosphaerellales is an order of fungi that includes many species that live as parasites on plant leaves, causing various leaf spots and blights. These fungi are typically microscopic and produce their spores in tiny, flask-shaped structures embedded in plant tissue. Most members of this group are plant pathogens, meaning they cause diseases in their host plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other fungal orders, Mycosphaerellales species are specialized for living on or within plant leaves, where they form characteristic dark spots or lesions. They produce their reproductive structures (perithecia) immersed in plant tissue rather than on the surface.
children.funFact: Some Mycosphaerellales fungi are responsible for economically important plant diseases, including black sigatoka disease of bananas and various leaf spot diseases of crops and ornamental plants.

children.name: Pleosporales
Anteagloniaceae
Anteaglonium
children.description: Anteaglonium is a small genus of microscopic fungi that live as parasites or decomposers on plant material. These tiny organisms form distinctive dark, rounded fruiting bodies that contain their spores and are typically found on dead or dying plant tissues.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their small, globular fruiting bodies (perithecia) that are typically dark-colored and embedded in plant tissue. They can be distinguished from related fungi by their specific spore characteristics and the way their fruiting bodies are arranged.
children.funFact: Despite being microscopic, these fungi play an important ecological role by helping to break down dead plant material and recycle nutrients back into forest ecosystems.

children.description: Anteagloniaceae is a small family of fungi that live as parasites or decomposers, often found growing on dead plant material or other fungi. These tiny organisms play an important role in breaking down organic matter in forest ecosystems. They produce dark, flask-shaped fruiting bodies that contain their spores.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their distinctive dark, carbonaceous (coal-like) fruiting structures called perithecia. They can be distinguished from related fungi by their specific spore shapes and the way their reproductive structures are arranged.
children.funFact: Despite being microscopic, these fungi are nature's recyclers, helping to break down dead organic matter and return nutrients to the soil for other plants to use.

children.name: Didymellaceae
Platychora
children.description: Platychora is a small genus of tiny flies that belong to the thick-headed fly family. These diminutive insects are parasitoids, meaning their larvae develop inside other insects, eventually killing their hosts. In New England, we have just one species in this genus.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Platychora flies can be distinguished from other thick-headed flies by their flattened appearance and distinctive wing venation patterns. They are among the smaller members of their family.
children.funFact: The single New England species, Platychora ulmi, is associated with elm trees, as suggested by its scientific name 'ulmi' which refers to the elm genus Ulmus.

children.name: Boeremia
children.description: Boeremia is a genus of microscopic fungi that are plant pathogens, meaning they cause diseases in plants. These tiny organisms produce spores and typically infect the leaves and stems of their host plants, creating spots, lesions, or other visible symptoms of disease.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Boeremia fungi are distinguished by their specific spore structures and the way they form fruiting bodies called pycnidia, which are small, flask-shaped containers that release spores.
children.funFact: The single New England species, Boeremia hedericola, specifically targets English ivy, helping to naturally control this invasive plant species.

children.description: Didymellaceae is a family of microscopic fungi that includes plant pathogens and decomposers. These fungi are characterized by their ability to produce small, dark fruiting bodies called pycnidia that contain spores, and they play important roles in breaking down dead plant material in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their production of pycnidia with distinctive spore characteristics, and many species have complex life cycles that can include both sexual and asexual reproductive stages.
children.funFact: Some species in this family are "shape-shifters" that can completely change their appearance and spore-producing structures depending on environmental conditions, making them challenging for scientists to identify and classify.

children.name: Sporormiaceae
Sporormiella
children.description: Sporormiella is a genus of tiny fungi that specializes in breaking down animal dung, particularly from large herbivores like cattle, horses, and deer. These microscopic decomposers play a crucial role in recycling nutrients back into the ecosystem. They produce distinctive spores that can survive for thousands of years in soil and sediment layers.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Sporormiella fungi are distinguished by their unique four-celled spores that have a characteristic shape and dark coloration. Unlike many other dung-dwelling fungi, they are specifically adapted to colonize the fresh droppings of large herbivorous mammals.
children.funFact: Scientists use fossilized Sporormiella spores as a 'fungal clock' to track when large mammals went extinct in different regions - when megafauna like mammoths disappeared, so did these specialized dung fungi!

children.description: Sporormiaceae is a family of microscopic fungi that are specialists at decomposing animal dung, particularly from herbivorous mammals like deer, rabbits, and livestock. These tiny fungi play an important ecological role by breaking down nutrient-rich waste materials and recycling them back into the ecosystem. They produce their spores within small, dark, flask-shaped structures that develop on or within the dung.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their highly specialized habitat preference for animal dung and their distinctive spores, which are typically dark-colored and often have multiple cells separated by cross-walls. Their spore-producing structures are usually embedded within the dung substrate rather than growing on top of it.
children.funFact: These fungi are so closely tied to specific animal hosts that scientists can actually identify what type of animal created a pile of dung by examining which Sporormiaceae species are growing on it!

children.name: Dothidotthiaceae
Wilsonomyces
children.description: Wilsonomyces is a small genus of plant pathogenic fungi that causes serious diseases in stone fruit trees like cherries, peaches, and plums. These fungi are particularly known for creating the distinctive 'shot hole' symptoms where infected leaf tissue dies and falls out, leaving behind perfectly round holes as if the leaves were peppered with buckshot.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other plant pathogens, Wilsonomyces creates very characteristic circular holes in leaves after the infected tissue drops out, giving it the distinctive 'shot hole' appearance that makes it easy to identify in the field.
children.funFact: The genus was named relatively recently in honor of mycologist Eileen Eileen Wilson, who made significant contributions to understanding plant pathogenic fungi in the mid-20th century.

children.description: Dothidotthiaceae is a small family of fungi that includes species that typically grow as parasites or pathogens on plants. These fungi are part of the larger group of sac fungi and produce their spores in specialized structures. They are often found causing leaf spots or other diseases on their host plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their specific spore-producing structures and their particular relationship with plant hosts. They have unique cellular arrangements that help distinguish them from other related fungal families.
children.funFact: This family is so specialized that in all of New England, only one species from the genus Wilsonomyces represents this entire fungal family.

children.name: Homostegia
children.description: Homostegia is a genus of tiny bryozoans, which are colonial aquatic animals that live in interconnected chambers and filter-feed on microscopic particles from the water. These creatures build delicate, lace-like or encrusting colonies that can be found attached to rocks, shells, and other hard surfaces in marine environments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Homostegia are characterized by their distinctive box-shaped zooids (individual colony members) with uniform wall structure, which gives the genus its name meaning 'same roof.'
children.funFact: Despite being animals, bryozoan colonies like Homostegia often get mistaken for seaweeds or coral because of their plant-like or mineral-like appearance when attached to underwater surfaces.

children.name: Didymosphaeriaceae
Paraconiothyrium
children.description: Paraconiothyrium is a genus of microscopic fungi that are plant pathogens, meaning they cause diseases in plants. These fungi are characterized by their ability to form small, dark fruiting bodies called pycnidia that produce spores. They typically infect leaves and other plant tissues, causing various types of leaf spots and blotches.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Paraconiothyrium fungi are distinguished by their pycnidial fruiting bodies with thick, dark walls and their production of single-celled, oval-shaped spores. Unlike some related fungi, they don't form complex spore-bearing structures and typically cause localized leaf lesions rather than systemic plant infections.
children.funFact: The Linden Leaf Blotch fungus creates distinctive brown patches on linden tree leaves that often have a characteristic yellow border, making infected trees easy to spot from a distance during late summer.

children.description: Didymosphaeriaceae is a family of fungi that includes both plant pathogens and decomposers found in soil and on plant material. These microscopic fungi are characterized by their dark-colored, flask-shaped fruiting bodies that contain spores. They play important roles in breaking down organic matter in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their distinctive two-celled spores and dark, thick-walled fruiting structures called pseudothecia. Their spores typically have a septum (dividing wall) that creates two distinct chambers.
children.funFact: Some species in this family can survive in extreme environments and have been found growing on everything from tree bark to building materials, showcasing their remarkable adaptability.

children.name: Mycoporaceae
Mycoporum
children.description: Mycoporum is a genus of lichens that form crusty, patch-like growths on various surfaces. These organisms are actually partnerships between fungi and algae, working together to survive in challenging environments where neither could live alone.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their distinctive reproductive structures and the specific way their fungal and algal partners are arranged within the lichen body.
children.funFact: Like all lichens, Mycoporum species are incredibly slow-growing organisms that can live for decades or even centuries, making them some of nature's most patient colonizers of bare rock and other harsh surfaces.

children.description: Mycoporaceae is a small family of crustose lichens that form thin, crusty patches on tree bark and other surfaces. These lichens have a unique relationship between fungi and algae, working together to create organisms that can survive in harsh conditions where neither partner could live alone.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their distinctive flask-shaped fruiting bodies (perithecia) that are embedded in the lichen thallus, and they typically have simple, single-celled spores.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'crustose' lichens because they form crusty patches, these organisms are actually two different life forms living as one - the fungal partner provides structure and protection while the algal partner produces food through photosynthesis.

children.name: Phaeosphaeriaceae
Ampelomyces
children.description: Ampelomyces is a genus of tiny parasitic fungi that specialize in attacking powdery mildew fungi. These microscopic organisms live inside the cells and structures of powdery mildews, essentially acting as parasites of parasites. They play an important role as natural biological control agents in forest and garden ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most fungi that decompose dead material or form partnerships with plants, Ampelomyces species are hyperparasites that specifically target and consume living powdery mildew fungi. They produce distinctive dark, flask-shaped fruiting bodies called pycnidia within their powdery mildew hosts.
children.funFact: Ampelomyces quisqualis is sometimes called the 'mildew slayer' and has been commercially developed as a biological fungicide to help gardeners and farmers control powdery mildew diseases naturally.

children.description: Phaeosphaeriaceae is a family of microscopic fungi that includes many plant pathogens and decomposers. These fungi typically produce dark-colored spores and form small, flask-shaped fruiting bodies called perithecia. Most members of this family live as parasites on plants or help break down dead plant material.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their dark, multi-celled spores and small, embedded fruiting bodies that often appear as tiny black dots on infected plant tissues.
children.funFact: The genus Ampelomyces, found in this family, is unusual because it's a fungus that parasitizes other fungi - specifically powdery mildew fungi that attack plants, making it a natural biological control agent.

children.name: Pleosporaceae
Alternaria
children.description: Alternaria is a genus of common fungi that are found everywhere in the environment, from soil to plants to indoor air. These fungi are known for producing dark-colored spores and often appear as black or brown fuzzy growth on decaying plant material. Many species in this genus are plant pathogens that cause leaf spots, blights, and other diseases in crops and wild plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Alternaria fungi produce distinctive dark, multi-celled spores that have a characteristic chain-like or beaded appearance when viewed under a microscope. Their spores are typically larger and more complex in structure compared to many other common mold fungi.
children.funFact: Alternaria spores are one of the most common outdoor allergens and can travel hundreds of miles through the air, making them a major contributor to seasonal allergies even in areas where the fungi aren't actively growing.

children.description: Pleosporaceae is a large family of fungi that are primarily decomposers, breaking down dead plant material in the environment. Most members of this family are saprophytic, meaning they feed on decaying organic matter, though some species can also be plant pathogens that cause diseases in crops and other plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their dark-colored spores that are typically divided into multiple cells by cross-walls (septate). They produce their spores in flask-shaped structures called pseudothecia, which distinguish them from other fungal families.
children.funFact: The genus Alternaria within this family includes fungi that cause the dark spots you sometimes see on tomatoes and potatoes, but these same fungi also play important roles in composting and soil health.

children.name: Pleomassariaceae
Splanchnonema
children.description: Splanchnonema is a genus of tiny parasitic fungi that live inside the tissues of other fungi, particularly those that grow on wood. These microscopic organisms are pyrenomycetes, meaning they produce their spores in flask-shaped structures called perithecia that are embedded within their host fungi.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike free-living fungi, Splanchnonema species are obligate parasites that can only survive by growing within the tissues of other fungi. Their perithecia are typically immersed in the host's fruiting body and have distinctive neck-like openings.
children.funFact: These fungi are essentially 'fungi that eat fungi' - they represent a specialized lifestyle where one fungus has evolved to parasitize another fungus rather than decomposing dead organic matter like most of their relatives.

children.description: Pleomassariaceae is a family of fungi that includes species which often live as decomposers or plant pathogens. These fungi typically form small, dark fruiting bodies called perithecia that contain their spores, and they play important roles in breaking down organic matter in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their dark-colored, flask-shaped fruiting structures and specific spore characteristics that help mycologists identify them under a microscope.
children.funFact: Some species in this family can switch between being harmless decomposers and aggressive plant pathogens depending on environmental conditions and the health of their host plants.

children.name: Nigrogranaceae
Nigrograna
children.description: Nigrograna is a small genus of fungi that includes species known for producing dark, flask-shaped fruiting bodies called perithecia. These fungi are typically found growing on decaying wood and plant material, where they play an important role in breaking down organic matter in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their dark-colored perithecia and distinctive spore shapes. They can be distinguished from similar fungi by their specific cellular structures and the way their spores are arranged within the fruiting bodies.
children.funFact: The name 'Nigrograna' literally means 'black grain,' referring to the dark, grain-like appearance of their tiny fruiting bodies that dot decaying wood surfaces.

children.description: Nigrogranaceae is a small family of fungi that includes species commonly found on decaying plant material and in soil. These fungi are microscopic decomposers that help break down organic matter in forest ecosystems. They produce dark-colored spores that give the group its name, which refers to their black, granular appearance.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their distinctive dark, thick-walled spores and their ability to grow on a wide variety of decaying organic substrates. They can be distinguished from related fungi by their specific spore shape and the way they form fruiting structures.
children.funFact: Despite being microscopic, these fungi play a crucial role as nature's recyclers, helping to return nutrients from dead plants back to the soil where living plants can use them again.

children.name: Melanommataceae
Phragmotrichum
children.description: Phragmotrichum is a small genus of fungi that belongs to the group known as ascomycetes or sac fungi. These microscopic organisms are characterized by their unique spore-producing structures and play important roles in decomposing organic matter in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their distinctive spore structures called conidia, which have multiple cross-walls (septa) that give them a segmented appearance under microscopic examination.
children.funFact: Despite being microscopic, these fungi are essential recyclers in New England's forests, helping break down dead plant material and return nutrients to the soil for new growth.

children.description: Melanommataceae is a family of tiny fungi that live as parasites or decomposers, often found on dead plant material like twigs and bark. These microscopic organisms play an important role in breaking down organic matter in forest ecosystems. They produce their spores in small, dark, flask-shaped structures called perithecia.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their dark-colored fruiting bodies and unique spore-producing structures that are typically embedded in plant tissue. They can be distinguished from similar fungi by their specific cellular arrangements and spore characteristics visible under microscopic examination.
children.funFact: Despite being incredibly small and often overlooked, these fungi are essential recyclers in New England's forests, helping to return nutrients from dead plant material back to the soil for new growth.

children.name: Leptosphaeriaceae
Leptosphaeria
children.description: Leptosphaeria is a genus of tiny fungi that live as decomposers and plant pathogens, breaking down dead plant material or sometimes causing diseases in living plants. These microscopic fungi produce their spores inside small, dark, flask-shaped structures called perithecia that are embedded in plant tissues. They play important ecological roles in nutrient cycling by helping decompose organic matter in nature.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Leptosphaeria fungi are characterized by their dark perithecia (spore-containing structures) and elongated spores that are divided into multiple cells by cross-walls. Unlike many related fungi, their perithecia are typically immersed in the host plant tissue rather than sitting on the surface.
children.funFact: Some Leptosphaeria species are notorious plant pathogens that cause blackleg disease in crops like canola and cabbage, making them both ecologically important decomposers and economically significant agricultural concerns.

children.description: Leptosphaeriaceae is a family of fungi that includes both plant pathogens and decomposers living on dead plant material. These fungi typically form small, dark, flask-shaped fruiting bodies called perithecia that contain their spores. Many species in this family are found on grasses and other herbaceous plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their dark-colored perithecia with a distinctive neck-like opening called an ostiole. Their spores are typically multi-celled and often have a constricted middle section.
children.funFact: Some Leptosphaeriaceae fungi can switch between being harmless decomposers and aggressive plant pathogens depending on environmental conditions and the health of their host plants.

children.name: Amniculicolaceae
Amniculicola
children.description: Amniculicola is a genus of aquatic fungi that live in freshwater streams and rivers. These microscopic fungi are part of the group known as aquatic hyphomycetes, which specialize in breaking down organic matter like fallen leaves in aquatic environments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their unique spore shapes and their specific adaptation to flowing freshwater habitats, distinguishing them from terrestrial fungi and other aquatic fungal groups.
children.funFact: Despite being microscopic, Amniculicola fungi play a crucial role as nature's recyclers in stream ecosystems, helping to decompose leaf litter and making nutrients available to other aquatic organisms.

children.description: Amniculicolaceae is a small family of freshwater fungi that live in aquatic environments, particularly in streams and other flowing water bodies. These microscopic fungi are part of the diverse world of aquatic decomposers that help break down organic matter in freshwater ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their specialized adaptations for life in flowing freshwater habitats, with unique spore structures that help them survive and disperse in aquatic environments.
children.funFact: Despite being fungi, members of Amniculicolaceae have evolved special mechanisms to thrive in water-rich environments where most fungi would struggle to survive.

children.description: Pleosporales is a large and diverse order of ascomycete fungi that includes many species commonly found decomposing plant material in New England's forests and fields. These fungi typically produce their spores in flask-shaped structures called perithecia, and many species have dark-colored, multi-celled spores. Members of this order play important ecological roles as decomposers, breaking down dead leaves, stems, and other organic matter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: What sets Pleosporales apart from other fungal orders is their characteristic dark, septate (divided) ascospores and their preference for growing on dead or dying plant material. Many species in this order have distinctively blackened fruiting bodies that can be spotted on decaying wood and plant debris.
children.funFact: Some members of Pleosporales are among the most important plant pathogens in agriculture, causing diseases like black spot on roses and various leaf spot diseases on crops, while others are harmless decomposers that help recycle nutrients in forest ecosystems.

children.name: Botryosphaeriales
Phyllostictaceae
Phyllosticta
children.description: Phyllosticta is a genus of microscopic fungi that specialize in causing leaf spot diseases on a wide variety of plants. These fungi create distinctive circular or irregular spots on leaves, often with dark borders and lighter centers that may eventually develop tiny black fruiting bodies visible as small dots.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other leaf spot fungi, Phyllosticta species produce their spores in flask-shaped structures called pycnidia that appear as small black dots on infected leaves. The spots they create often have a characteristic "target" or bullseye appearance with concentric rings.
children.funFact: Some Phyllosticta species are so host-specific that they're named after their preferred plant victims, like Phyllosticta parthenocissi which targets Virginia creeper and Phyllosticta hamamelidis which specializes in witch hazel.

children.description: The Phyllostictaceae are a family of microscopic fungi that specialize in causing leaf spot diseases on plants. These tiny organisms create small, dark spots with lighter centers on the leaves of trees, shrubs, and other plants, often appearing as if someone took a hole punch to the foliage.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other leaf-spotting fungi, members of this family produce their spores in distinctive flask-shaped structures called pycnidia that are embedded within the leaf tissue. The spots they create typically have very characteristic pale centers surrounded by dark borders.
children.funFact: Despite being plant pathogens, Phyllostictaceae fungi are actually helping recycle nutrients in forest ecosystems by breaking down older leaves and preparing them to return essential elements to the soil.

children.name: Botryosphaeriaceae
Botryosphaeria
children.description: Botryosphaeria is a genus of fungi that are primarily plant pathogens, causing various diseases in trees and shrubs. These fungi typically infect woody plants through wounds or natural openings, leading to symptoms like cankers, dieback, and leaf spots. They are commonly found on a wide variety of host plants throughout temperate regions.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Botryosphaeria are characterized by their dark, flask-shaped fruiting bodies (perithecia) that develop beneath the bark or on plant surfaces. They produce distinctive spores that are initially colorless and single-celled, but may become darker and multi-celled as they mature.
children.funFact: Some Botryosphaeria species can remain dormant in healthy plant tissue for years, only causing disease symptoms when the host plant becomes stressed by drought, injury, or other environmental factors.

children.name: Diplodia
children.description: Diplodia is a genus of fungi that includes plant pathogens causing various diseases in trees and shrubs. These fungi are characterized by producing dark, two-celled spores and are known for infecting woody plants, often entering through wounds or stress points in the bark.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Diplodia fungi are distinguished by their characteristic dark, oval-shaped spores that are divided by a wall into two cells. They typically produce their spores in flask-shaped structures called pycnidia that form beneath the bark surface.
children.funFact: The name 'Diplodia' literally means 'double' in Greek, referring to the two-celled structure of their spores that looks like tiny dumbbells under a microscope.

children.description: Botryosphaeriaceae is a family of fungi that are commonly found living on woody plants like trees and shrubs. Most members of this family are plant pathogens that can cause cankers, dieback, and other diseases in their host plants. They typically produce dark-colored spores in flask-shaped structures embedded in the bark or wood.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These fungi are distinguished by their ability to produce both sexual and asexual spores, often switching between different spore types depending on environmental conditions. Their fruiting bodies are typically black and immersed in plant tissue rather than growing on the surface.
children.funFact: Many Botryosphaeriaceae fungi are "endophytes" that can live quietly inside healthy plants for years without causing disease, only becoming aggressive pathogens when the plant becomes stressed by drought, injury, or other factors.

children.description: Botryosphaeriales is an order of fungi that are primarily plant pathogens, meaning they cause diseases in trees and other plants. These fungi are particularly known for causing cankers, dieback, and leaf spots on woody plants like oaks, maples, and fruit trees. They play an important ecological role as decomposers, breaking down dead plant material.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this order are characterized by their dark, flask-shaped fruiting bodies that are embedded in plant tissues. They produce spores in distinctive structures called pycnidia, which appear as small black dots on infected plant surfaces.
children.funFact: Some species in this order can switch between being harmless endophytes (living inside plants without causing harm) and aggressive pathogens, especially when their host plants become stressed by drought or other environmental factors.

children.name: Hysteriales
Hysteriaceae
Hysterium
children.description: Hysterium is a genus of small, dark fungi that grow as saprophytes on dead wood, particularly hardwood trees and shrubs. These fungi produce distinctive black, boat-shaped fruiting bodies called hysteriothecia that split open along a narrow slit to release spores. They play an important role in forest ecosystems by helping decompose woody plant material.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Hysterium fungi are easily recognized by their characteristic black, elongated fruiting bodies that open along a single longitudinal crack, resembling tiny black lips or boat hulls on dead wood surfaces.
children.funFact: The name 'Hysterium' comes from the Greek word meaning 'womb' or 'hysteria,' referring to the way these fungi's fruiting bodies split open dramatically to release their spores.

children.name: Hysterobrevium
children.description: Hysterobrevium is a small genus of parasitic fungi that specifically targets mulberry trees and their relatives. These microscopic fungi live within the tissues of their host plants, causing diseases that can affect the health and growth of mulberry trees.
children.distinguishingFeatures: This genus is distinguished by its highly specialized relationship with mulberry plants and its unique spore-producing structures that develop within the host tissue.
children.funFact: The name 'Hysterobrevium' literally means 'short hysteria,' referring to the distinctive short, slit-like openings through which the fungus releases its spores.

children.name: Purpurepithecium
children.description: Purpurepithecium is a genus of crustose lichens that form thin, crust-like growths on rock surfaces. These lichens are characterized by their distinctive purple-tinged appearance and small, embedded fruiting bodies called apothecia.
children.distinguishingFeatures: This genus is distinguished from other crustose lichens by its purplish coloration and the specific arrangement and structure of its reproductive structures.
children.funFact: The name Purpurepithecium literally means 'purple little barrel,' referring to the color and shape of its tiny fruiting bodies that release spores.

children.description: The Hysteriaceae family consists of small, dark fungi that form distinctive boat-shaped or elongated fruiting bodies called hysterothecia. These decomposer fungi are commonly found growing on dead wood, bark, and plant debris throughout New England's forests. They play an important ecological role by breaking down tough woody materials and returning nutrients to the soil.
