children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are recognized by their characteristic black, elongated fruiting bodies that split open along a narrow slit to release spores, resembling tiny black canoes or lips parting.
children.funFact: The name 'Hysteriaceae' comes from the Greek word 'hystera' meaning 'womb' or 'uterus,' referring to the way these fungi's fruiting bodies open along a slit to release their spores.

children.description: Hysteriales are a group of fungi that form distinctive elongated, boat-shaped fruiting bodies called hysterothecia. These small black structures have a characteristic slit-like opening that runs lengthwise down the middle, resembling tiny lips or a narrow crack. Members of this order are typically found growing on dead wood, bark, or other plant material.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The most distinctive feature of Hysteriales is their elongated, slit-like fruiting bodies that open along a central line, quite different from the round or cup-shaped structures of most other fungi. This boat-like shape with a lengthwise opening is unique among fungal orders.
children.funFact: The name 'Hysteriales' comes from the Greek word 'hystera' meaning 'womb,' referring to the distinctive slit-like opening of their fruiting bodies that resembles certain anatomical structures.

children.name: Abrothallales
Lichenoconiaceae
Abrothallus
children.description: Abrothallus is a genus of tiny parasitic fungi that live exclusively on lichens, forming small dark spots or patches on their host's surface. These specialized fungi have evolved to depend entirely on lichens for their survival, creating a unique parasitic relationship in the lichen world. You'll often find them as small black or dark brown dots scattered across various lichen species.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most fungi that decompose dead material or form partnerships with plants, Abrothallus species are obligate parasites that only grow on living lichens. They form distinctive small, dark fruiting bodies that contrast sharply with their host lichen's typically lighter colors.
children.funFact: Each Abrothallus species is highly specialized and typically parasitizes only one or a few closely related lichen species - for example, Abrothallus usneae specifically targets Usnea lichens, while Abrothallus cetrariae goes after Cetraria lichens.

children.description: Lichenoconiaceae is a specialized family of fungi that live as parasites on lichens, essentially making them parasites of partnerships since lichens themselves are collaborations between fungi and algae. These tiny fungi produce small, dark fruiting bodies on the surface of their lichen hosts, where they obtain nutrients by breaking down the host's tissues.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most fungi that decompose dead material or form beneficial partnerships, members of this family are specifically adapted to parasitize living lichens, often creating distinctive dark spots or lesions on their hosts.
children.funFact: These fungi are essentially 'pirates of partnerships' - they hijack the successful collaboration between fungi and algae in lichens to steal nutrients for themselves.

children.description: Abrothallales is a small order of lichens that are primarily parasitic, meaning they live on and derive nutrients from other lichens rather than photosynthesizing on their own. These tiny organisms form some of the most specialized relationships in the lichen world, often targeting specific host lichen species. They represent an unusual evolutionary strategy where lichens have essentially become parasites of their own kind.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most lichens that form partnerships with algae or cyanobacteria to photosynthesize, members of Abrothallales have evolved to be parasitic on other lichens. This parasitic lifestyle makes them unique among lichen orders and often gives them very small, inconspicuous fruiting bodies.
children.funFact: Some species in this order are so specialized that they can only survive on one particular species of host lichen, making them some of the pickiest eaters in the fungal world.

children.name: Patellariales
Patellariaceae
Patellaria
children.description: Patellaria is a genus of small, dark fungi that form distinctive cup-shaped or disc-shaped fruiting bodies on decaying wood. These saprophytic fungi play an important role in forest ecosystems by breaking down dead organic matter and recycling nutrients back into the soil.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Patellaria are characterized by their small, black, leathery apothecia (cup-shaped structures) that typically measure just a few millimeters across and have a distinctive patella or kneecap-like appearance.
children.funFact: The name Patellaria comes from the Latin word 'patella' meaning kneecap, referring to the rounded, cap-like shape of their fruiting bodies.

children.name: Rhizodiscina
children.description: Rhizodiscina is a genus of distinctive cup fungi that produces large, brown, disc-shaped fruiting bodies that emerge directly from the ground. These fungi form a symbiotic relationship with tree roots, helping trees absorb nutrients from the soil while receiving sugars in return. They are part of the ascomycete group of fungi, which produce their spores in specialized sac-like structures.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other cup fungi that grow on decaying wood or organic matter, Rhizodiscina species emerge directly from soil where they connect to living tree roots. Their large size and deeply wrinkled, brain-like surface texture also set them apart from other ground-dwelling cup fungi.
children.funFact: The name Rhizodiscina literally means "root disc," referring to how these fungi appear to grow directly from tree roots underground, sometimes popping up many feet away from the actual tree trunk.

children.description: The Patellariaceae are a small family of cup fungi that produce dark, disc-shaped fruiting bodies on wood and bark. These saprophytic fungi help decompose dead organic matter in forest ecosystems, particularly on decaying hardwood branches and logs. They're part of the larger group of ascomycete fungi, which reproduce by forming spores in specialized sac-like structures.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their small, dark brown to black disc-shaped fruiting bodies that sit directly on the substrate without stalks. Unlike many other cup fungi, they have a distinctive leathery or waxy texture and often appear almost tar-like when fresh.
children.funFact: Despite their small size and inconspicuous appearance, these fungi play an important role as some of the first decomposers to colonize freshly fallen branches, helping to break down tough woody tissues.

children.description: Patellariales is an order of small, disc-shaped fungi that form dark, button-like fruiting bodies on dead wood and plant material. These tiny decomposers help break down organic matter in forests, playing an important role in nutrient cycling. They are often overlooked due to their small size, typically measuring just a few millimeters across.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this order are characterized by their distinctive dark, flat, disc-shaped fruiting bodies (apothecia) that sit directly on the substrate without stalks. Their spores are typically colorless and elongated, and they lack the bright colors found in many other small cup fungi.
children.funFact: Despite being tiny and inconspicuous, some Patellariales species are among the most persistent fungi in nature, with their tough, dark fruiting bodies able to survive harsh weather conditions for months or even years.

children.name: Venturiales
Venturiaceae
Apiosporina
children.description: Apiosporina is a genus of parasitic fungi that infects woody plants, particularly trees in the cherry family. These fungi live inside their host plants and cause distinctive disease symptoms by disrupting normal plant growth.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other plant pathogens, Apiosporina fungi cause dramatic swelling and black, warty growths on branches and twigs that are easily visible from a distance.
children.funFact: The black knot fungus can completely girdle and kill branches, creating the distinctive 'witches' broom' effect where dense clusters of twigs grow around the infection site.

children.name: Venturia
children.description: Venturia is a genus of plant pathogenic fungi that causes scab diseases on trees and shrubs in the rose family. These microscopic fungi create dark, scaly lesions on leaves and fruits, giving infected areas a characteristic rough, scabby appearance. They are specialized parasites that have evolved to infect specific host plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Venturia fungi are distinguished by their ability to cause distinctive dark, velvety spots that develop into scaly patches on plant surfaces. Unlike many other plant fungi, they primarily infect the surface tissues rather than penetrating deep into plant structures.
children.funFact: Apple scab fungi can survive winter by hiding in fallen leaves on the ground, then launch millions of spores into the air during spring rains to reinfect apple trees - making leaf cleanup an important disease prevention strategy for orchards.

children.description: The Venturiaceae are a family of fungi that specialize in causing plant diseases, particularly affecting the leaves and fruits of trees and shrubs. These microscopic organisms create dark, scab-like spots on their host plants and are most commonly found living as parasites on members of the rose family.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other plant-parasitic fungi, Venturiaceae species form distinctive dark, velvety patches on plant surfaces and have a unique two-stage lifecycle with both sexual and asexual reproductive phases.
children.funFact: Apple scab, caused by a Venturia species, is one of the most economically important diseases affecting apple orchards worldwide, and can reduce fruit yields by up to 70% in untreated trees.

children.description: Venturiales is a small order of fungi that are primarily plant pathogens, meaning they cause diseases in plants. These fungi are known for forming dark, often black fruiting bodies on infected plant tissues and are particularly notorious for causing scab diseases on fruit trees and other plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this order are characterized by their dark, flask-shaped fruiting structures called pseudothecia that develop beneath the surface of host plant tissues. They produce spores through small openings and typically cause superficial infections that create dark, scabby lesions on leaves and fruits.
children.funFact: The most famous member of this order causes apple scab, a disease so economically important that it drives much of the fungicide spraying in commercial apple orchards worldwide.

children.name: Capnodiales
Capnodiaceae
Scorias
children.description: Scorias is a genus of sooty mold fungi that grows on the sticky honeydew secretions left behind by aphids, scale insects, and other sap-feeding bugs. These black, crusty fungi form dark patches on leaves, branches, and other surfaces where honeydew has accumulated. They don't directly harm plants but can block sunlight from reaching leaf surfaces.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other sooty molds, Scorias species form thick, spongy crusts with a distinctive warty or bumpy texture that can be peeled off surfaces in sheets.
children.funFact: Scorias fungi are nature's cleanup crew, breaking down the sugary honeydew waste that would otherwise coat forest surfaces in a sticky mess.

children.description: Capnodiaceae is a family of fungi commonly known as sooty molds that grow as dark, black coatings on plant surfaces. These fungi don't directly parasitize plants, but instead feed on the sugary honeydew secretions left behind by insects like aphids and scale insects. They form thin, dark crusts that can cover leaves, branches, and other plant parts.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other fungi, sooty molds grow entirely on plant surfaces rather than penetrating into plant tissues. They create characteristic black, soot-like films that can be wiped or washed off the host plant.
children.funFact: Sooty molds act like nature's detective clues - their presence on a plant usually indicates that sap-sucking insects are nearby, even if you can't see the tiny pests themselves!

children.name: Cladosporiaceae
Graphiopsis
children.description: Graphiopsis is a small genus of moths in the family Geometridae, commonly known as geometer moths or inchworms. These moths are characterized by their relatively small size and distinctive wing patterns that help them blend in with their surroundings.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus can be identified by their specific wing coloration and markings, including the characteristic red spotting that gives the Peony Red Spot its common name.
children.funFact: The caterpillars of Graphiopsis moths are "loopers" that move by arching their bodies, since they lack middle prolegs and must bring their back end up to meet their front end with each step.

children.description: Cladosporiaceae is a family of fungi that includes many common molds and plant pathogens. These fungi are characterized by their dark-colored spores and branching chains of spore-producing structures that give them their name (from Greek meaning 'branch-like'). They reproduce by forming chains of oval-shaped conidia (asexual spores) that can be easily dispersed by wind.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their characteristic branching conidiophores (spore-bearing structures) and chains of dark, thick-walled spores. Unlike many other mold families, their spores are typically brown to black in color and form in distinctive branching patterns.
children.funFact: Some Cladosporiaceae species are among the most common airborne fungi, and their spores can be found floating in indoor and outdoor air almost everywhere on Earth!

children.description: Capnodiales is an order of fungi that includes many species known for their dark-colored spores and ability to grow on plant surfaces. These fungi are commonly found living as epiphytes on leaves and other plant parts, where they often form dark, sooty-looking colonies. Many species in this group have adapted to live in close association with plants without causing disease.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Capnodiales are characterized by their dark, thick-walled spores and their tendency to form melanized (darkly pigmented) structures. Unlike many other fungal orders, they often grow superficially on plant surfaces rather than penetrating deep into plant tissues.
children.funFact: Some Capnodiales fungi are known as 'sooty molds' because they create black, soot-like coatings on leaves, often growing on the sticky honeydew secretions left behind by aphids and other insects.

children.name: Tubeufiales
Tubeufiaceae
Berkleasmium
children.description: Berkleasmium is a small genus of microscopic fungi that live as decomposers on dead plant material, particularly fallen leaves and twigs in forest environments. These tiny fungi play an important role in breaking down organic matter and recycling nutrients back into the ecosystem. They belong to a group of fungi known for their dark-colored spores and simple reproductive structures.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Berkleasmium are distinguished by their characteristic dark, clustered spore masses that form on the surface of decaying plant material. Their spores are typically grouped together in small, rounded clusters that can be seen with magnification.
children.funFact: Despite being invisible to the naked eye, Berkleasmium fungi are working around the clock as nature's recyclers, helping transform fallen leaves into rich soil that nourishes New England's forests.

children.description: Tubeufiaceae is a family of microscopic fungi that live as decomposers, breaking down dead plant material in forest environments. These tiny fungi are characterized by their dark-colored, flask-shaped reproductive structures that contain spores. They play an important ecological role by recycling nutrients from fallen leaves and woody debris back into the soil.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their distinctive tube-like or flask-shaped fruiting bodies (perithecia) that are typically dark brown to black in color. Unlike many other fungi, they often have uniquely shaped spores with multiple cells and sometimes thread-like appendages.
children.funFact: Despite being invisible to the naked eye, these fungi are essential forest recyclers that can break down some of the toughest plant compounds, including lignin found in wood.

children.description: Tubeufiales is a small order of fungi that includes species typically found growing on decaying plant material, particularly wood and bark. These fungi are part of the larger group of sac fungi (ascomycetes) and play important roles as decomposers in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this order are characterized by their unique spore-bearing structures and specific molecular signatures that distinguish them from other fungal orders. They typically produce dark-colored fruiting bodies with distinctive spore arrangements.
children.funFact: Despite being a relatively small fungal order with only 2 species found in New England, Tubeufiales fungi are essential recyclers that help break down tough woody materials in forests.

children.name: Gloniales
Gloniaceae
Cenococcum
children.description: Cenococcum is a genus containing a single, remarkably widespread fungus that forms beneficial partnerships with tree roots. This fungus creates ectomycorrhizal relationships, wrapping around root tips and helping trees absorb water and nutrients from the soil in exchange for sugars from the tree.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Cenococcum forms distinctive black, hard sclerotia (survival structures) in the soil and produces characteristic dark, thick-walled mycorrhizal root tips that are easily recognized in the field.
children.funFact: Cenococcum geophilum may be the most widely distributed fungus on Earth, found on every continent except Antarctica and able to partner with hundreds of different tree species.

children.name: Glonium
children.description: Glonium is a genus of small fungi that live on dead wood, appearing as tiny black structures scattered across the surface of decaying branches and logs. These fungi are part of a group called ascomycetes, which produce their spores in special sac-like structures. They play an important role in forest ecosystems by helping to decompose fallen wood.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Glonium are characterized by their small, dark, oval to elongated fruiting bodies that sit directly on the wood surface without stalks. Their spores are released through narrow slits or openings in the black surface.
children.funFact: The name 'Glonium' comes from a Greek word meaning 'little point,' referring to the tiny, dot-like appearance of these fungi on dead wood.

children.description: The Gloniaceae are a small family of fungi that includes some fascinating species with very different lifestyles. This group contains both decomposer fungi that break down dead wood and plant material, as well as beneficial mycorrhizal fungi that form partnerships with tree roots.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their dark-colored fruiting bodies that often form elongated, slit-like openings when mature. They typically have thick-walled spores that are well-adapted to survive in harsh conditions.
children.funFact: One member of this family, Cenococcum, forms some of the most widespread mycorrhizal partnerships on Earth, helping trees absorb nutrients while creating distinctive black root tips that are easily recognizable to forest ecologists.

children.description: Gloniales is a small order of fungi that includes species commonly found growing on dead wood and plant debris. These fungi are characterized by their distinctive elongated, slit-like fruiting bodies that appear as dark lines or cracks on the surface of their host material. They play an important role in decomposing woody material in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this order are easily recognized by their unique linear fruiting structures that look like thin, dark slits or grooves running along dead wood surfaces. Unlike many other wood-decomposing fungi, they don't form mushrooms or bracket-like structures.
children.funFact: The name 'Gloniales' comes from the Greek word meaning 'socket' or 'cavity,' referring to their characteristic slit-like appearance that resembles narrow openings in the wood.

children.name: Trypetheliales
Trypetheliaceae
Viridothelium
children.description: Viridothelium is a genus of crustose lichens that form thin, crusty patches on tree bark and other surfaces. These lichens are characterized by their greenish coloration and distinctive blister-like reproductive structures called perithecia that emerge from the lichen surface.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their bright green to yellowish-green thallus and prominent, raised, dark perithecia that give them a distinctly speckled or bumpy appearance on bark surfaces.
children.funFact: The name Viridothelium literally means 'green nipple' in Latin, referring to the characteristic green color and the nipple-like appearance of the raised reproductive structures.

children.description: Trypetheliaceae is a family of tropical and subtropical lichens that form crusty growths on tree bark and other surfaces. These lichens have a unique relationship with algae, working together to create colorful patches that can range from green to gray. They're typically found in warm, humid environments where they slowly grow and spread across their host surfaces.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their distinctive flask-shaped fruiting bodies (perithecia) that are embedded in the lichen's crusty surface. Unlike many other lichen families, they often have brightly colored spores and tend to form thick, warty crusts.
children.funFact: Some Trypetheliaceae lichens can live for hundreds of years, slowly expanding their crusty territories just millimeters per year while serving as tiny ecosystems that provide shelter for microscopic animals.

children.description: Trypetheliales is an order of crustose lichens that form thin, crusty patches on tree bark and rocks in tropical and subtropical regions. These lichens have a unique relationship between fungi and algae, creating colorful growths that can appear as flat, scaly crusts on their host surfaces. They are particularly well-adapted to warm, humid environments and play important roles in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this order are characterized by their distinctive flask-shaped reproductive structures called perithecia that are embedded in the lichen thallus. Unlike many other lichen groups, they typically have very thin, smooth crusts that closely adhere to their substrate.
children.funFact: Some Trypetheliales lichens can live for hundreds of years, slowly growing outward in circular patterns that scientists can use like tree rings to study climate history and environmental changes over time.

children.name: Monoblastiales
Monoblastiaceae
Acrocordia
children.description: Acrocordia is a genus of crustose lichens that form thin, crusty patches on rock surfaces. These lichens create a symbiotic partnership between fungi and algae, appearing as grayish or whitish crusts that seem to be painted directly onto stone substrates.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Acrocordia lichens are characterized by their distinctive flask-shaped fruiting bodies (perithecia) that are embedded in the crusty thallus, giving the surface a bumpy, warty appearance.
children.funFact: The single New England species, Acrocordia cavata, gets its species name from the Latin word for 'hollow' because its fruiting bodies have deep, cave-like openings at their tips.

children.description: Monoblastiaceae is a small family of crustose lichens that form thin, often inconspicuous crusts on rock surfaces. These lichens are characterized by their simple structure and tiny, immersed fruiting bodies that barely peek above the surface of their crusty thallus.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their extremely reduced, crustose growth form and their perithecia (flask-shaped fruiting bodies) that are completely or nearly completely embedded within the lichen thallus.
children.funFact: Despite their tiny size and humble appearance, Monoblastiaceae lichens can live for decades on bare rock faces, slowly dissolving minerals from the stone to create soil for future plant communities.

children.description: Monoblastiales is a small order of crustose lichens that form thin, often inconspicuous crusts on rock surfaces. These lichens are characterized by their simple structure and tiny, dark fruiting bodies called perithecia that are embedded in the lichen thallus.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this order are distinguished by having perithecia (flask-shaped fruiting structures) that are completely immersed in the lichen body, with only small openings visible at the surface.
children.funFact: Despite being one of the smallest orders of lichens with very few species worldwide, Monoblastiales represents an ancient lineage that has survived for millions of years by specializing in harsh rock environments.

children.name: Clavariopsis
children.description: Clavariopsis is a small genus of aquatic fungi that grows in freshwater environments like streams, ponds, and wetlands. These fungi are quite unusual because they live underwater or in very wet conditions, unlike most fungi that prefer drier habitats. They play an important role in breaking down organic matter in aquatic ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: What sets Clavariopsis apart from other fungi is their aquatic lifestyle and their club-shaped or coral-like fruiting bodies that can survive being submerged underwater for extended periods.
children.funFact: Clavariopsis aquatica is one of the few fungi that can actually complete its entire life cycle while completely submerged in water, making it a true aquatic fungus rather than just water-tolerant.

children.name: Catinellales
Catinellaceae
Catinella
children.description: Catinella is a small genus of tiny land snails that are among the smallest gastropods found in New England. These microscopic mollusks are so small they're often overlooked, typically measuring just a few millimeters across.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their extremely small size and translucent, amber-colored shells that have a distinctive saucer-like or shallow cup shape.
children.funFact: These snails are so tiny that you could fit dozens of them on a single fingernail, making them some of the smallest land snails in North America.

children.description: Catinellaceae is a small family of tiny freshwater snails that live in shallow water and wet areas. These microscopic gastropods are among the smallest snails in North America, with shells typically measuring less than 2 millimeters across.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their extremely small size and their preference for temporary pools, ditches, and other ephemeral aquatic habitats rather than permanent water bodies.
children.funFact: These snails are so small that they can actually survive being completely dried out for extended periods, reactivating when water returns to their habitat.

children.description: Catinellales is a small order of fungi that includes species forming tiny, cup-shaped or disc-like fruiting bodies. These fungi are typically found growing on decaying organic matter like rotting wood, plant debris, or soil rich in decomposing materials. They play an important role as decomposers in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this order are characterized by their small, often colorless or pale fruiting bodies that lack a stem and sit directly on their substrate. They differ from similar cup fungi by their unique spore-producing structures and genetic characteristics.
children.funFact: Despite being an entire fungal order, Catinellales is represented by just a single rare species in all of New England, making any encounter with these tiny fungi quite special for nature explorers.

children.name: Hysterographium
children.description: Hysterographium is a small genus of fungi that produces distinctive elongated, boat-shaped fruiting bodies on decaying wood. These saprophytic fungi help break down dead plant material in forest ecosystems, playing an important role in nutrient cycling.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their narrow, slit-like openings (hysterothecia) that contain spores, giving them a unique linear appearance unlike the round or cup-shaped fruiting bodies of many other fungi.
children.funFact: The genus name Hysterographium literally means 'writing hysteria,' referring to the way these fungi's long, dark fruiting bodies can look like mysterious script written across the surface of rotting logs.

children.name: Myriangiales
Elsinoaceae
Elsinoe
children.description: Elsinoe is a genus of plant pathogenic fungi that causes diseases known as anthracnose and scab on various woody plants. These fungi are microscopic organisms that infect leaves, stems, and fruits, creating distinctive spots, lesions, or scab-like growths on their host plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other plant pathogens, Elsinoe species create raised, warty, or scab-like lesions rather than simple spots or blights. They are specialized parasites that typically infect specific host plant families.
children.funFact: The single New England species, Elsinoe corni, specifically targets dogwood trees and can cause dramatic purple-spotted lesions on dogwood leaves that some people mistake for a beneficial autumn color change.

children.description: The Elsinoaceae family consists of plant pathogenic fungi that cause scab diseases on various crops and wild plants. These fungi create rough, raised spots or lesions on leaves, fruits, and stems of their host plants. They are specialized parasites that have evolved to live specifically on plant surfaces.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their ability to form distinctive scab-like lesions on plant surfaces, unlike many other plant pathogens that cause wilting or rotting. They produce their spores in small, flask-shaped structures embedded within the scabby growths.
children.funFact: Despite being plant pathogens, Elsinoaceae fungi are actually helping scientists develop new antifungal compounds, as researchers study how these fungi overcome plant defenses to find ways to boost crop immunity.

children.description: Myriangiales is a small order of fungi that includes plant pathogens causing diseases like scab and anthracnose. These fungi typically form dark, crusty lesions on leaves, fruits, and stems of their host plants. They are microscopic organisms that reproduce through spores and can cause significant damage to crops and ornamental plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this order are characterized by their ability to form distinctive scab-like symptoms on plant surfaces, creating raised, corky lesions that are often darker than the surrounding healthy tissue.
children.funFact: Despite having only one species found in New England, fungi in this order are responsible for some economically important plant diseases worldwide, including citrus scab that affects orange and grapefruit crops.

children.name: Eurotiales
Aspergillaceae
Penicillium
children.description: Penicillium is a genus of microscopic fungi that are among the most common molds found in our environment. These fungi are master decomposers, breaking down organic matter and recycling nutrients back into the ecosystem. They reproduce by producing chains of tiny spores that give them their characteristic fuzzy, often blue-green appearance.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Penicillium species are identified by their unique brush-like spore-producing structures called penicilli, which look like tiny paintbrushes under a microscope. Unlike many other molds, they typically produce distinctive blue-green colors and have a velvety texture.
children.funFact: The famous antibiotic penicillin was discovered from a Penicillium mold in 1928, revolutionizing medicine and saving millions of lives worldwide.

children.name: Aspergillus
children.description: Aspergillus is a genus of common molds that grow as fuzzy, powdery patches on decaying organic matter like fallen leaves, rotting wood, and compost. These fungi reproduce by releasing tiny spores into the air, which is how they spread to new locations. You'll often spot them as dark or colorful fuzzy growths on decomposing materials in forests and gardens.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Aspergillus molds are identified by their distinctive spore-producing structures that look like tiny brushes or brooms under a microscope. Unlike many other molds, they often produce characteristically colored spores that give them their common names, like the dark spores of Black Mold.
children.funFact: Some Aspergillus species are actually beneficial to humans - they're used to ferment soybeans into soy sauce and to produce citric acid for soft drinks and candies!

children.description: The Aspergillaceae family includes some of the most common molds found in homes, soil, and decaying organic matter throughout New England. These microscopic fungi are master decomposers, breaking down dead plant and animal material and recycling nutrients back into the ecosystem. They reproduce by forming chains of tiny spores that can travel through the air, which is why you might find them growing on old bread or in damp basements.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their distinctive spore-bearing structures that look like tiny brushes or aspergillums (the tool used to sprinkle holy water) under a microscope. Their spores are produced in long chains at the tips of specialized branching structures, rather than in enclosed sacs like many other fungi.
children.funFact: The Penicillium genus in this family gave us penicillin, one of the world's first antibiotics, discovered when Alexander Fleming noticed that a Penicillium mold had killed bacteria in his laboratory dish in 1928.

children.name: Elaphomycetaceae
Elaphomyces
children.description: Elaphomyces is a genus of underground fungi that produce hard, round fruiting bodies called false truffles. These fungi form important partnerships with tree roots, helping forests stay healthy by exchanging nutrients with their plant partners. Unlike true truffles, these false truffles have a distinctive warty or bumpy outer surface and are not typically eaten by humans.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their tough, warty exterior surface and their completely underground lifestyle. They differ from true truffles by having a much harder, more durable outer shell and a powdery spore mass inside when mature.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'false truffles,' these fungi are actually more closely related to cup fungi than to true truffles, and their spores can remain viable in the soil for many years!

children.description: Elaphomycetaceae is a family of underground fungi that produce truffle-like fruiting bodies beneath the soil surface. These fungi form important partnerships with tree roots, helping forests exchange nutrients while remaining mostly hidden from view. They are sometimes called 'deer truffles' because wildlife often dig them up to eat.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other underground fungi, members of this family have thick, warty outer walls on their fruiting bodies and produce spores in a powdery mass inside. Their fruiting bodies are typically hard and round, resembling small potatoes.
children.funFact: These 'deer truffles' are so important to forest ecosystems that some mammals have evolved specialized abilities to detect their scent underground and will dig through soil and snow to reach them.

children.description: The Eurotiales are an order of fungi that includes the familiar green and blue molds you might spot growing on old bread, citrus fruits, or in damp corners of your home. These fungi are expert decomposers that break down organic matter and play important roles in both natural ecosystems and human activities. Many species in this group reproduce by forming colorful spores that give them their characteristic green, blue, or blue-green appearance.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other molds, members of Eurotiales typically produce their spores in distinctive flask-shaped or spherical structures. The spores are often arranged in chains or clusters, creating the powdery, colored surfaces that make these molds so recognizable.
children.funFact: Some species in this order are used to make valuable medicines like penicillin, while others are essential for producing fermented foods like soy sauce and miso!

children.name: Mycocaliciales
Sphinctrinaceae
Phaeocalicium
children.description: Phaeocalicium is a small genus of tiny, pin-like fungi that grow on dead wood and other fungi. These minuscule organisms produce dark, slender stalks topped with small spore-bearing structures, giving them their whimsical common name of 'pins' or 'needles.'
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other small wood-dwelling fungi, Phaeocalicium species have distinctively dark, thread-like stalks (called stipes) that are often less than a millimeter tall but clearly visible to the naked eye.
children.funFact: Despite their tiny size, these 'fairy pins' can live for many years on the same piece of rotting wood, slowly releasing spores from their pin-head tops.

children.name: Mycocalicium
children.description: Stickpins are tiny fungi that look like miniature pins stuck into dead wood. They have thin, dark stalks topped with small, round heads that contain spores, making them resemble old-fashioned hat pins or thumbtacks.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other small fungi, stickpins have a very distinctive pin-like appearance with their slender black stalks and round spore-bearing heads. They are found exclusively on decaying wood, particularly dead coniferous trees.
children.funFact: These microscopic fungi are so small that you might need a magnifying glass to spot them, but they play an important role in breaking down dead wood in New England's forests.

children.name: Sphinctrina
children.description: Sphinctrina is a genus of tiny, specialized lichens that form small, dark, cone-shaped structures on tree bark. These unusual lichens are parasitic or semi-parasitic on other lichens, getting some of their nutrients by growing on or within their host species rather than photosynthesizing entirely on their own.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike typical crusty or leafy lichens, Sphinctrina forms distinctive small, blackish, pin-like or cone-shaped fruiting bodies that look almost like tiny mushrooms. These structures are much smaller than a pencil eraser and have a characteristic turbinate (top-shaped) appearance.
children.funFact: Despite being lichens themselves, Sphinctrina species are essentially "lichen pirates" that steal nutrients from other lichens, making them some of the most unusual members of the lichen world.

children.name: Stenocybe
children.description: Stenocybe is a small genus of tiny fungi that grow as parasites on lichens, particularly those found on tree bark. These microscopic fungi produce distinctive pin-like fruiting bodies that stick up from their lichen hosts like miniature pins or needles.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their extremely narrow, elongated fruiting bodies that resemble tiny black pins protruding from lichen surfaces. Unlike many other fungi, they are obligate parasites that cannot survive without their specific lichen hosts.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'stickpin' fungi, these organisms are so small that you'd need a magnifying glass to see their pin-like structures, which are typically less than 2 millimeters tall!

children.description: Sphinctrinaceae is a family of tiny fungi that produce distinctive pin-like or club-shaped fruiting bodies, often appearing as miniature black pins sticking up from surfaces. These fungi are commonly found growing on other fungi, dead wood, or organic matter in forest environments. They are part of the larger group of fungi that includes cup fungi and morels.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their characteristic pin-like or stalked fruiting bodies that are typically dark-colored and very small, usually less than 2mm tall. Unlike many other small fungi, they have a distinctive narrow stalk topped with a rounded or flattened head containing spores.
children.funFact: Some species in this family are parasitic on other fungi, literally growing on and feeding off their fungal hosts rather than decomposing wood or other organic matter directly.

children.description: Mycocaliciales are an order of tiny, specialized fungi that form distinctive pin-like or club-shaped fruiting bodies. These microscopic fungi are often found growing on decaying wood, bark, or other organic matter in forest environments. They produce their spores in small, dark structures that look like tiny pins stuck into their substrate.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this order are characterized by their minute, stalked fruiting bodies with dark, powdery spore masses at the tips. Unlike many other fungi, they often have a very reduced, almost invisible vegetative body and focus their energy on producing these characteristic pin-like spore-bearing structures.
children.funFact: These fungi are so small that their fruiting bodies are often less than 2 millimeters tall, making them easily overlooked despite being relatively common in New England forests.

children.name: Verrucariales
Verrucariaceae
Dermatocarpon
children.description: Silverskin lichens are unique composite organisms made up of a fungus and algae living together in partnership. These lichens form distinctive leathery, shield-like growths that are typically brown to gray in color and have a somewhat silvery or metallic appearance on their surface. They're commonly found growing on rocks, especially in moist environments near streams and in shaded areas.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other lichens that form crusty patches or branching structures, silverskin lichens create thick, leathery sheets that can be peeled away from rocks like flexible skin. Their fruiting bodies are embedded within the lichen tissue rather than sitting on top, giving them a smooth, unmarked appearance.
children.funFact: These lichens can actually curl up and become dormant during dry periods, then quickly rehydrate and resume photosynthesis when moisture returns, making them masters of survival in fluctuating conditions.

children.name: Hydropunctaria
children.description: Hydropunctaria is a genus of rock-dwelling lichens that form thin, crusty patches on coastal rocks and stones. These hardy lichens are specially adapted to life in harsh marine environments where they endure constant exposure to salt spray and crashing waves. They create dark, warty surfaces that blend seamlessly with wet rocky shores.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most lichens, Hydropunctaria species thrive in the splash zone of rocky coastlines where few other organisms can survive the extreme saltwater exposure. Their thick, black crusts with distinctive warty bumps make them easily recognizable on wave-splashed rocks.
children.funFact: Hydropunctaria lichens are so well-adapted to marine conditions that they actually require regular salt spray to thrive and will decline if moved away from coastal environments.

children.name: Normandina
children.description: Normandina is a small genus of lichens that contains just one species found in New England - the charming Elf Ears lichen. These lichens form small, leaf-like structures that grow on tree bark and have a distinctive appearance that sets them apart from other lichen groups. They are part of the diverse world of lichens, which are partnerships between fungi and algae.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Normandina lichens are easily recognized by their small, rounded, ear-like lobes that give them their common name of Elf Ears. Unlike many other lichens, they have a distinctive bluish-gray color and a unique surface texture.
children.funFact: The Elf Ears lichen gets its whimsical name from its small, rounded lobes that really do look like tiny fairy ears attached to tree bark!

children.description: The Verrucariaceae family represents a diverse group of lichens that have adapted to live in some of the most challenging environments. These hardy organisms are commonly found growing on rocks, soil, and even in aquatic habitats where many other lichens cannot survive. They form symbiotic partnerships between fungi and algae, creating tough, often dark-colored crusts or leaf-like structures.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their distinctive reproductive structures called perithecia - small, flask-shaped chambers that are often embedded in the lichen body. Unlike many other lichen families, Verrucariaceae lichens frequently have very thick, protective outer layers that help them withstand extreme conditions.
children.funFact: Some Verrucariaceae lichens can actually live underwater, making them among the few lichens that have successfully colonized aquatic environments!

children.description: Verrucariales is an order of crustose lichens that form thin, crusty patches tightly attached to rock surfaces, tree bark, and other substrates. These lichens are among the most inconspicuous members of the lichen world, often appearing as little more than colored stains or rough patches on their host surfaces. They play important ecological roles by slowly breaking down rock and contributing to soil formation over geological time scales.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this order are characterized by their perithecia - small, flask-shaped reproductive structures that are typically sunken into the lichen thallus rather than sitting on top of it. This gives them a distinctive appearance with tiny black dots or pits scattered across their crusty surface.
children.funFact: Some Verrucariales lichens can survive in extremely harsh environments, including underwater on rocks in streams and lakes, making them among the most aquatic of all lichen groups.

children.name: Onygenales
Onygenaceae
Ophidiomyces
children.description: Ophidiomyces is a genus of fungi that specifically infects snakes, causing a serious condition known as Snake Fungal Disease. These microscopic fungi attack the skin and underlying tissues of snakes, creating characteristic lesions and scabs that can severely impact the health of infected reptiles.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other skin-infecting fungi, Ophidiomyces species have evolved to specifically target snakes as hosts. They produce unique spore structures and enzymes that allow them to penetrate and digest snake skin tissue.
children.funFact: Snake Fungal Disease caused by Ophidiomyces was only scientifically described in 2013, making it one of the most recently discovered major wildlife diseases affecting North American reptiles.

children.name: Onygena
children.description: Onygena is a small genus of fungi that specializes in decomposing keratin-rich materials like horns, hooves, hair, and feathers. These unusual saprophytic fungi play an important ecological role by breaking down tough protein materials that most other decomposers cannot digest. They produce small, club-shaped fruiting bodies that emerge from their protein-rich substrates.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most fungi that decompose plant matter, Onygena species are highly specialized to break down keratin and other animal proteins. Their small, distinctive club or ball-shaped fruiting bodies growing directly from horns, hooves, or similar materials make them easily recognizable.
children.funFact: The horn stalkball gets its name from its preference for growing on old animal horns and antlers, where it can take several years to fully develop its tiny fruiting bodies.

children.name: Chrysosporium
children.description: Chrysosporium is a genus of soil-dwelling fungi that break down organic matter like dead plant material and keratin-rich substances. These microscopic fungi play an important role as decomposers in forest ecosystems, helping to recycle nutrients back into the soil. They produce distinctive spores that help scientists identify different species.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Chrysosporium fungi are characterized by their ability to grow at relatively high temperatures and their production of single-celled, thick-walled spores called aleurioconidia. Unlike many related fungi, they typically don't form complex fruiting bodies visible to the naked eye.
children.funFact: Some Chrysosporium species are specialized at breaking down keratin, the tough protein found in hair, feathers, and animal hooves, making them nature's recyclers of these otherwise hard-to-decompose materials.

children.description: Onygenaceae is a family of fungi that includes species with very specialized feeding habits, particularly those that break down keratin - the protein found in hair, feathers, nails, and skin. These fungi play important ecological roles as decomposers, helping to recycle organic materials that would otherwise be difficult to break down. Many species in this family have evolved to live in specific microhabitats where keratin-rich materials accumulate.
children.distinguishingFeatures: What sets Onygenaceae apart from other fungal families is their remarkable ability to digest keratin and other tough proteins that most organisms cannot break down. They often produce specialized enzymes and have unique spore structures adapted to their protein-rich environments.
children.funFact: Some members of this family, like Onygena, specifically grow on old animal horns, hooves, and feathers, earning them the nickname 'horn fungi' for their ability to thrive on these tough, protein-packed materials that few other organisms can digest.

children.description: Onygenales is an order of fungi that includes species with a particular talent for breaking down keratin, the tough protein found in hair, feathers, nails, and horns. These fungi play important ecological roles as decomposers, helping to recycle organic matter that would otherwise be difficult to break down. Many species in this group have adapted to live in soil or on organic debris.
children.distinguishingFeatures: What sets Onygenales apart is their specialized ability to produce keratinase enzymes that can digest keratin-rich materials like hair and feathers. Unlike many other fungi, they have evolved specific biochemical tools to tackle these particularly tough proteins.
children.funFact: Some members of Onygenales are so specialized at digesting hair and nails that they're used in forensic investigations to help determine how long organic evidence has been in the environment!

children.name: Chaetothyriales
Epibryaceae
Epibryon
children.description: Epibryon is a genus of tiny parasitic fungi that specifically target liverworts, particularly those in the genus Plagiochila. These microscopic organisms live on the surface of their liverwort hosts, forming small, dark structures that can be seen with careful observation.
children.distinguishingFeatures: This genus is distinguished by its highly specialized parasitic relationship with liverworts and its extremely small size, making it one of the most host-specific fungal groups in New England.
children.funFact: Epibryon fungi are so specialized that they can only survive on specific species of liverworts, making them completely dependent on their bryophyte hosts for survival.

children.description: Epibryaceae is a small family of mosses that includes some of the most distinctive and unusual bryophytes in New England. These mosses are known for their unique growth patterns and specialized adaptations to their particular habitats.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their characteristic leaf arrangement and specialized reproductive structures that set them apart from other moss families.
children.funFact: With only one species found in New England, the Epibryaceae family represents one of the region's rarest moss groups, making any encounter with these tiny plants a special botanical discovery.

children.name: Herpotrichiellaceae
Fonsecaea
children.description: Fonsecaea is a genus of dark-pigmented fungi that are primarily found in soil and decaying organic matter. These microscopic fungi are known for their ability to cause infections in humans and animals, particularly a skin condition called chromoblastomycosis.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Fonsecaea fungi are characterized by their dark brown to black pigmentation and their ability to reproduce through multiple types of spore formation, including budding yeast-like cells and branching fungal threads.
children.funFact: Despite being potentially harmful to humans, Fonsecaea fungi play an important ecological role as decomposers, helping to break down dead plant material in forest soils.

children.description: Herpotrichiellaceae is a family of dark-colored fungi that are often found in soil, on decaying plant material, and sometimes associated with plants or animals. These fungi are characterized by their dark pigmentation and ability to grow in various environments, from natural habitats to indoor spaces.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their dark, melanin-rich cell walls that give them a blackish or brownish appearance, and their ability to produce multiple types of spore-bearing structures.
children.funFact: Some species in this family can cause infections in humans and animals, but they also play important ecological roles as decomposers in forest ecosystems.

children.description: Chaetothyriales is an order of fungi that includes many species with dark-colored cell walls, often appearing black or brown. These fungi are commonly found growing on plant surfaces, in soil, or in other natural environments where they play important roles in decomposition and nutrient cycling.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this order are characterized by their melanized (darkly pigmented) cell walls and their ability to produce specialized reproductive structures. Many species in this group are particularly well-adapted to harsh environmental conditions.
children.funFact: Some fungi in this order can actually help plants by forming beneficial relationships with their roots, while others are skilled at breaking down tough organic materials like dead leaves and wood.

children.name: Coryneliales
Coryneliaceae
Caliciopsis
children.description: Caliciopsis is a genus of small fungi that are plant pathogens, meaning they cause diseases in trees and other plants. These microscopic organisms produce tiny, dark fruiting bodies that look like little black dots on the bark and stems of infected plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Caliciopsis fungi are distinguished by their minute, flask-shaped fruiting bodies called perithecia that emerge directly from infected plant tissue. Unlike many other plant pathogenic fungi, they typically cause cankers and dieback symptoms on woody plants.
children.funFact: Despite being so small they're barely visible to the naked eye, Caliciopsis fungi can cause significant damage to forest trees, with some species being major concerns for pine plantation management.

children.description: Coryneliaceae is a small family of fungi that includes species known for forming tiny, flask-shaped fruiting bodies on the bark and wood of trees. These fungi are part of the larger group of ascomycetes, or sac fungi, which produce their spores in specialized sac-like structures. Members of this family are typically found as parasites or decomposers on woody plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: This family is characterized by their distinctive perithecia (flask-shaped fruiting bodies) that have long, projecting necks through which spores are released. Unlike many related fungi, they often have a close association with bark and cambium tissues of living or recently dead trees.
children.funFact: The single New England species in this family, Caliciopsis, is known to cause canker diseases in trees, creating sunken, discolored areas on bark that can eventually girdle and kill branches.

children.description: Coryneliales is a small order of fungi that includes species which form dark, flask-shaped structures called perithecia on plant material. These fungi are typically found growing on dead or decaying plant tissues, where they play a role in decomposition. The order contains only one family, Coryneliaceae, making it one of the smaller groups in the fungal tree of life.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this order are characterized by their distinctive perithecial fruiting bodies that have a unique opening mechanism and specific spore arrangements. They differ from related fungi in their particular combination of structural features and their preference for specific plant substrates.
children.funFact: With only one species found in New England, Coryneliales represents one of the rarest fungal orders in the region, making any encounter with these tiny decomposers quite special for nature enthusiasts.

children.name: Pyrenulales
Pyrenulaceae
Pyrenula
children.description: Rash lichens are small, crusty lichens that form thin patches on tree bark and rock surfaces. They get their common name from their appearance, which can resemble a skin rash with small, dark bumps scattered across a pale surface. These lichens are composite organisms made up of fungi and algae working together.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Rash lichens are distinguished by their tiny, flask-shaped reproductive structures called perithecia that appear as dark dots embedded in the lichen's surface. Unlike many other crusty lichens, they have a smooth to slightly bumpy texture rather than being powdery or scaly.
children.funFact: The single New England species, Easter Pox Lichen, gets its unusual name from its bumpy appearance that early naturalists thought resembled smallpox marks, and it was often noticed around Easter time when people spent more time outdoors examining tree bark.

children.description: Pyrenulaceae is a family of crustose lichens that form thin, crusty patches on tree bark and other surfaces. These lichens have a symbiotic relationship between fungi and algae, creating colorful growths that often appear as flat, spreading crusts with tiny black dots (fruiting bodies) scattered across their surface.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their flask-shaped fruiting bodies (perithecia) that are embedded in the lichen thallus, appearing as small black dots on the surface. Unlike many other lichen families, their reproductive structures are completely enclosed rather than cup-shaped or open.
children.funFact: These lichens are excellent air quality indicators - they're sensitive to pollution and their presence suggests clean air in the environment.

children.description: Pyrenulales is an order of crustose lichens that form thin, often inconspicuous crusts on tree bark and other surfaces. These lichens are characterized by their small, flask-shaped reproductive structures called perithecia that are embedded in the lichen thallus. They are typically found in tropical and subtropical regions, though some species extend into temperate areas.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this order are distinguished by their perithecia (flask-shaped fruiting bodies) that are completely immersed in the thallus, unlike many other lichen groups that have exposed or raised fruiting structures.
children.funFact: Despite being primarily tropical lichens, Pyrenulales represents one of the most species-rich orders of lichens worldwide, with over 2,000 described species globally, though only one has been documented in New England's cooler climate.

children.name: Sclerococcales
Dactylosporaceae
Sclerococcum
children.description: Sclerococcum is a genus of tiny parasitic fungi that specifically target lichens, growing on and within their host organisms. These microscopic fungi are part of a specialized group that has evolved to live exclusively on lichens, forming small black fruiting bodies that can be seen with magnification.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike free-living fungi, Sclerococcum species are obligate parasites that can only survive by attacking lichen hosts. They produce distinctive dark, rounded fruiting structures that emerge from infected lichen tissues.
children.funFact: These fungi are so specialized that they often target specific lichen species, making them important indicators of lichen diversity and health in forest ecosystems.

children.description: The Dactylosporaceae is a small family of fungi that are specialized parasites, meaning they live on and get their nutrients from other organisms. These tiny fungi are particularly known for targeting lichens, forming small dark spots or growths on their hosts. They represent a unique ecological niche where fungi parasitize the fungal partners within lichen communities.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their parasitic lifestyle specifically targeting lichens, and they produce characteristic dark, small fruiting bodies called perithecia. Unlike free-living fungi, they are obligate parasites that cannot survive without their lichen hosts.
children.funFact: These fungi are essentially 'parasites of parasites' since lichens themselves are partnerships between fungi and algae, making Dactylosporaceae a fascinating example of nature's complex web of dependencies.

children.description: Sclerococcales is a small order of crustose lichens that form thin, crusty patches on rock surfaces. These lichens have a unique fruiting structure called a mazaedium, which produces powdery masses of spores that look like tiny black dots scattered across the lichen surface.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this order are distinguished by their mazaedia - specialized spore-producing structures that create distinctive powdery, sooty masses of dark spores on the lichen surface.
children.funFact: The spores produced in their mazaedia are released as a powdery dust, giving some species in this group common names like 'powder lichen' due to their dusty appearance.

children.name: Geoglossales
Geoglossaceae
Trichoglossum
children.description: Hairy Earth Tongues are small, dark fungi that get their name from their distinctive tongue-like shape and fuzzy, hair-covered surface. These unusual fungi emerge from the soil in late summer and fall, standing upright like tiny black clubs or flattened tongues poking up from the forest floor. They belong to a group of fungi called earth tongues that are found in woodlands and grassy areas throughout New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike smooth earth tongues, members of Trichoglossum are covered in distinctive dark hairs or bristles that give them a fuzzy appearance when viewed up close. Their flattened, tongue-like fruiting bodies are typically darker and more irregularly shaped than other earth tongue genera.
children.funFact: Despite their small size and inconspicuous appearance, Hairy Earth Tongues play an important ecological role as decomposers, helping to break down organic matter in the soil and cycle nutrients back into forest ecosystems.

children.name: Geoglossum
children.description: Earth tongues are small, dark fungi that look remarkably like tiny black or brown tongues poking up from the ground. These simple-looking mushrooms have a club-shaped or tongue-like fruiting body that stands upright, typically growing just 1-4 inches tall in grassy areas, lawns, and forest clearings.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most mushrooms, earth tongues lack a distinct cap and stem structure, instead forming a simple, smooth, tongue-shaped body. Their dark coloration and characteristic shape make them easily recognizable among the grass where they commonly grow.
children.funFact: Earth tongues are considered indicator species for high-quality grassland habitats, and finding them often signals that an area has healthy, undisturbed soil with low nutrient levels.

children.name: Hemileucoglossum
children.description: Hemileucoglossum is a small genus of earth tongue fungi that produces distinctive club-shaped fruiting bodies emerging from the soil. These fascinating fungi are saprophytes, meaning they break down dead organic matter in forest soils and contribute to nutrient cycling in woodland ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their pale, tongue-like fruiting bodies with a distinctive pitted or honeycomb-like surface texture. Unlike many other earth tongues, Hemileucoglossum species have a whitish to pale cream coloration rather than darker hues.
children.funFact: The name Hemileucoglossum literally means 'half-white tongue,' referring to the pale coloration and tongue-like shape of these mysterious little fungi that peek up from the forest floor.

children.description: The Geoglossaceae family contains small, unusual fungi that look remarkably like dark tongues poking up from the ground. These earth tongues produce club-shaped or tongue-like fruiting bodies that are typically black, brown, or dark-colored and grow directly from soil or decaying organic matter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other fungi, earth tongues have a simple, elongated shape without a distinct cap and stem structure. Their smooth to slightly textured surfaces and dark coloration make them easy to distinguish from other small club fungi.
children.funFact: Despite their tongue-like appearance, these fungi are actually more closely related to cup fungi than to mushrooms, and some species in this family are among the rarest fungi in the world.

children.description: Geoglossales is an order of unusual fungi known as earth tongues, characterized by their distinctive club-shaped or tongue-like fruiting bodies that emerge from the ground. These small but fascinating fungi typically have dark, often black or brown, smooth surfaces and grow directly from soil or decaying organic matter in woodlands and grasslands.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most mushrooms with caps and stems, earth tongues have simple, elongated fruiting bodies that look like tiny clubs or flattened tongues sticking up from the earth. Their spores are produced on the outer surface of these structures rather than on gills or in pores underneath a cap.
children.funFact: Some earth tongue species are among the world's rarest fungi, with certain species being so uncommon that finding them is considered a significant mycological discovery.

children.name: Coniocybales
Coniocybaceae
Chaenotheca
children.description: Stubble lichens are tiny, specialized lichens that look like miniature pins or matchsticks growing on tree bark. They get their common name from their appearance - short stalks topped with powdery, spore-producing heads that resemble stubble on a face. These lichens are typically found on the bark of older trees, especially in mature forests.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike crusty or leafy lichens, stubble lichens have distinctive pin-like fruiting bodies called mazaedia that release powdery masses of spores. The stalked structure with a powdery head makes them instantly recognizable among New England's lichen diversity.
children.funFact: Despite being tiny (often less than 2mm tall), stubble lichens can live for decades and serve as indicators of old-growth forest conditions, making them valuable to ecologists studying forest health.

children.name: Chaenotricha
children.description: Chaenotricha is a genus of small, bristly flies in the thick-headed fly family (Conopidae). These flies are parasitic, with their larvae developing inside other insects, particularly bees and wasps. They have distinctive bristled bodies and large, prominent heads typical of their family.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Chaenotricha flies can be distinguished from other thick-headed flies by their particularly dense bristles covering the body and their relatively small size. They have a more compact build compared to other conopid flies.
children.funFact: Female Chaenotricha flies intercept flying bees and wasps in mid-air to inject their eggs directly into the host's body, making them aerial pirates of the insect world.

children.description: Coniocybaceae is a small family of crustose lichens that includes the distinctive stubble lichens. These lichens are characterized by their tiny, pin-like fruiting structures that stick up from crusty patches on tree bark, resembling miniature stubble or pins. They form symbiotic partnerships between fungi and algae, creating these unique spore-producing structures called mazaedia.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other lichen families, Coniocybaceae produce their spores in powdery masses within cup-like or cylindrical structures that protrude upward from the lichen surface. These pin-like fruiting bodies make them easily recognizable among the crustose lichens.
children.funFact: The spores of stubble lichens are released as a dry, powdery mass rather than being shot out individually, and they can often be seen as tiny dark clouds when the fruiting structures are disturbed.

children.description: Coniocybales is an order of small, inconspicuous lichens that typically form tiny pin-like or club-shaped structures on tree bark and wood. These lichens are often overlooked due to their small size, but they play important roles in forest ecosystems as pioneers on dead wood and bark surfaces.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this order are characterized by their distinctive pin-cushion or stalked fruiting bodies that look like tiny pins or matchsticks protruding from their substrate. Unlike many other lichens, they often have a very reduced or nearly absent visible thallus (main body).
children.funFact: Despite their tiny size, some species in this order can live for decades on the same piece of bark, slowly growing and reproducing while helping to break down dead wood in the forest.

children.name: Candelariales
Candelariaceae
Candelariella
children.description: Goldspeck lichens are small, crusty lichens that form bright yellow or yellow-green patches on rocks, concrete, and tree bark. These hardy organisms are actually partnerships between fungi and algae, working together to survive in harsh conditions where few other life forms can thrive. They get their name from their distinctive golden, speckled appearance that makes them easy to spot against dark surfaces.
children.distinguishingFeatures: What sets goldspeck lichens apart is their vibrant yellow color and granular, crusty texture that looks like scattered golden dust or tiny beads. Unlike leafy or branching lichens, these form flat, crusty coatings that seem almost painted onto their surface.
children.funFact: Goldspeck lichens are excellent air quality indicators - they're sensitive to pollution, so finding healthy populations suggests clean air in the area.

children.name: Candelaria
children.description: Candleflame lichens are small, crusty lichens that form bright yellow or yellow-green patches on tree bark and rocks. They get their name from their vibrant golden color that can seem to glow like tiny flames, especially when wet. These lichens are composite organisms made up of fungi and algae living together in a mutually beneficial partnership.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Their brilliant yellow to yellow-green color sets them apart from most other crusty lichens, which are typically gray, white, or brown. The edges of their patches often have tiny, finger-like projections that can help distinguish between the two New England species.
children.funFact: Candleflame lichens can actually appear to change color throughout the day - they look more vibrant and flame-like when moist from dew or rain, but fade to a duller yellow when dry.

children.description: The Candelariaceae family includes small, crusty lichens that typically display bright yellow or greenish-yellow colors. These lichens form thin, often powdery-looking crusts on rocks, bark, and other surfaces, and are commonly found in both urban and natural environments throughout New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their consistently yellow to yellow-green coloration and their crustose growth form that often appears granular or powdery rather than smooth.
children.funFact: Goldspeck lichens in this family are among the most pollution-tolerant lichens, which is why they're often some of the few lichen species you'll find thriving on city sidewalks and building walls.

children.description: Candelariales is a small order of crusty lichens that form bright yellow or yellowish-green patches on rocks, tree bark, and other surfaces. These lichens are particularly common in sunny, exposed locations where they can often be spotted as colorful crusts growing directly on their substrate.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this order are distinguished by their vibrant yellow pigments and crustose growth form, along with their preference for well-lit habitats. They typically have simple, disk-shaped fruiting bodies that lack the complex structures found in many other lichen groups.
children.funFact: The name 'Candelariales' comes from the Latin word for candle, referring to the bright, candle-flame yellow color that makes these lichens easy to spot even from a distance.

children.name: Sareales
Zythiaceae
Zythia
children.description: Zythia is a small genus of fungi that are commonly found living on and decomposing resinous materials from coniferous trees. These microscopic fungi are saprophytes, meaning they obtain nutrients by breaking down dead organic matter, particularly the sticky resins that ooze from pine, spruce, and other evergreen trees.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Zythia fungi are distinguished by their specialized ability to grow on tree resins and their unique spore-producing structures that develop within the hardened resin substrate.
children.funFact: Zythia resinae can actually help break down old resin deposits on tree bark, essentially acting as nature's cleanup crew for the sticky messes that conifers leave behind.

children.name: Sarea
children.description: Sarea is a genus of unusual fungi that forms small, dark, cup-shaped or disk-like fruiting bodies on decaying coniferous wood. These tiny fungi are part of the larger group of cup fungi, but they have a distinctive blackish appearance and grow specifically on rotting pine, spruce, and other evergreen trees.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other cup fungi that are brightly colored, Sarea species are characteristically dark brown to black and have a unique preference for coniferous substrates. They also have a distinctive spore structure that helps distinguish them from similar-looking dark cup fungi.
children.funFact: Despite being so small that they're easily overlooked, Sarea fungi play an important role in breaking down the tough lignin in conifer wood, helping to recycle nutrients back into forest ecosystems.

children.description: Zythiaceae is a small family of fungi that includes species which form tiny, dark fruiting bodies on wood and bark. These fungi are saprotrophs, meaning they feed on dead organic matter and help decompose fallen logs and branches in forest ecosystems. Most members of this family are quite small and inconspicuous, requiring a hand lens or microscope to observe their detailed structures.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Zythiaceae are characterized by their small, dark, flask-shaped or disc-shaped fruiting bodies that develop on woody substrates. They can be distinguished from similar fungi by their specific spore characteristics and the way their reproductive structures are organized.
children.funFact: Despite being tiny and easily overlooked, Zythiaceae fungi play an important role as nature's recyclers, breaking down tough woody materials that many other organisms cannot digest.

children.description: Sareales is a small order of fungi that includes some rather obscure species found growing on decaying wood and plant material. These fungi are typically tiny and easily overlooked, forming small, dark-colored fruiting bodies that help decompose organic matter in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Sareales are characterized by their simple, often flask-shaped or disc-like fruiting structures that release spores through small openings. They differ from many other fungi by their particular combination of cellular structures and genetic features that place them in their own distinct evolutionary lineage.
children.funFact: Despite being such a small and inconspicuous group, Sareales fungi play an important role as nature's recyclers, quietly breaking down dead plant material and returning nutrients to the soil.

children.name: Lichinales
Lichinaceae
Ephebe
children.description: Ephebe is a small genus of aquatic lichens that grow on rocks in and near streams, rivers, and other freshwater environments. These unusual lichens form dark, hair-like or thread-like structures that can look almost like wet moss or algae when submerged in water.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most lichens that grow on dry surfaces, Ephebe species are adapted to live in constantly wet or periodically submerged conditions, forming distinctive dark, stringy growths on waterside rocks.
children.funFact: Ephebe lichens can survive being completely underwater for extended periods, making them one of the few lichen groups that have successfully colonized aquatic habitats.

children.description: Lichinaceae is a small family of lichens that form dark, gelatinous crusts or thread-like growths on rocks and soil in wet environments. These lichens have a unique partnership with cyanobacteria (blue-green algae) as their photosynthetic partner, rather than the green algae found in most other lichens. They typically grow in places that are frequently wet, such as stream beds, waterfalls, and moist rock faces.
