children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most lichens that partner with green algae, Lichinaceae lichens exclusively team up with cyanobacteria. This gives them a distinctive dark, often blackish appearance and a gelatinous, almost jelly-like texture when wet.
children.funFact: When dry, these lichens can look like dark, brittle crusts that seem almost dead, but they dramatically transform when wet, swelling up into soft, gelatinous masses that actively photosynthesize.

children.description: Lichinales is a small order of lichens that are specially adapted to extreme environments, particularly hot deserts and rocky areas. These lichens have a unique partnership between fungi and cyanobacteria (blue-green algae) rather than the green algae found in most other lichens. They form dark, crusty growths that can survive in some of the harshest conditions on Earth.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most lichens that partner with green algae, Lichinales exclusively partner with cyanobacteria as their photosynthetic partner. They typically form dark, gelatinous crusts when wet and become hard and brittle when dry.
children.funFact: These remarkable lichens can survive in desert temperatures exceeding 150°F (65°C) and can go dormant for years during drought, instantly reviving when water becomes available.

children.name: Arthoniales
Chrysotrichaceae
Chrysothrix
children.description: Gold dust lichens are a group of crustose lichens that form powdery, dusty patches on tree bark and rock surfaces. They get their common name from their characteristic bright yellow or greenish-yellow granular appearance that looks like metallic dust sprinkled on surfaces. These lichens lack the typical cup or branching structures found in many other lichen groups.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other crustose lichens, gold dust lichens have a distinctly powdery, granular texture and bright yellow coloration. They rarely produce the disc-like fruiting bodies (apothecia) that are common in related lichen genera.
children.funFact: The bright yellow color comes from a pigment called vulpinic acid, which may help protect the lichen from harmful UV radiation while living on exposed bark and rock surfaces.

children.description: Chrysotrichaceae is a family of crustose lichens that form powdery, dust-like crusts on tree bark and rock surfaces. These lichens are characterized by their bright yellow to greenish-yellow coloration, which comes from specialized pigments that help them photosynthesize efficiently in low-light forest conditions.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are easily recognized by their distinctive powdery, granular texture that can literally be rubbed off with a finger, unlike the more firmly attached crusts of most other lichen families.
children.funFact: The name 'Chrysotrichaceae' comes from Greek words meaning 'golden hair,' referring to the fine, powdery appearance that resembles golden dust sprinkled on surfaces.

children.name: Arthoniaceae
children.commonName: Christmas lichens, comma lichens, and allies

children.name: Arthonia
children.description: Comma Lichens are a small group of crustose lichens that form thin, often inconspicuous patches on tree bark. These lichens are characterized by their distinctive fruiting bodies that appear as tiny dark lines, dashes, or comma-shaped marks scattered across their surface. They're commonly found growing on the smooth bark of various trees throughout New England's forests.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The comma-shaped or linear fruiting bodies (apothecia) that look like tiny punctuation marks on the lichen surface are the key identifying feature that separates this genus from other crustose lichens.
children.funFact: The genus name 'Arthonia' comes from the Greek word meaning 'joint' or 'articulation,' referring to the segmented appearance of their distinctive comma and dash-like fruiting structures.

children.description: The Arthoniaceae family includes small, often inconspicuous lichens that form thin crusts on tree bark and other surfaces. These lichens are characterized by their distinctive fruiting bodies, which can appear as comma-shaped or star-like structures scattered across the lichen's surface. They are commonly found on the bark of deciduous and coniferous trees throughout New England's forests.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their unique spore-producing structures called lirellae, which are elongated and often curved like commas or arranged in star-like patterns. Unlike many other lichen families, their fruiting bodies typically lack a prominent rim or border.
children.funFact: Some species in this family get their "Christmas lichen" nickname because their star-shaped fruiting bodies can resemble tiny festive decorations scattered across tree bark.

children.name: Roccellaceae
Lecanactis
children.description: Lecanactis is a small genus of crusty lichens that form thin, often inconspicuous patches on tree bark. These lichens are made up of a fungus and algae living together in partnership, creating a unique organism that can photosynthesize while having the structural support of fungal tissue.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Lecanactis lichens are characterized by their small, dark, disk-like fruiting bodies (apothecia) that sit embedded in or on top of a thin, crusty thallus. They typically grow on the bark of coniferous trees and have a preference for older, established wood surfaces.
children.funFact: The single New England species, Old-wood Lichen, gets its name from its preference for growing on the bark of old-growth or mature coniferous trees, making it an indicator of forest age and stability.

children.description: Roccellaceae is a family of crustose lichens that form thin, often grayish crusts on rock surfaces and tree bark. These lichens are made up of fungal partners living symbiotically with algae, creating composite organisms that can survive in harsh coastal and rocky environments. They are particularly well-adapted to areas with salt spray and exposed conditions.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their unique reproductive structures called lirellae - elongated, slit-like openings that release spores. Unlike many other lichen families, they often have a distinctly cracked or areolate surface pattern.
children.funFact: Some species in the Roccellaceae family were historically harvested to produce a purple dye called orchil, which was highly valued for coloring textiles before synthetic dyes were invented.

children.name: Lecanographaceae
Plectocarpon
children.description: Plectocarpon is a small genus of lichenicolous fungi, meaning they are specialized fungi that live on other lichens rather than forming lichens themselves. These tiny parasitic or parasymbiotic organisms have adapted to live specifically on the surfaces or within the tissues of their lichen hosts, creating a unique three-way relationship between the fungus, its host lichen, and the host's algal partner.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike typical lichen-forming fungi, Plectocarpon species are obligate parasites that cannot survive without their lichen hosts. They form small, dark, flask-shaped fruiting bodies called perithecia that are embedded in or sit on top of their host lichens.
children.funFact: These fungi represent a fascinating example of a 'parasite of a symbiosis' - they've evolved to exploit the already complex partnership between fungi and algae that makes up lichens, creating an even more intricate biological relationship.

children.description: Lecanographaceae is a small family of crustose lichens that form thin, crust-like growths on tree bark and rock surfaces. These lichens have a unique fruiting body structure with distinctive black, elongated or branched marks that look almost like writing or scratches on the surface.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their characteristic lirellae - elongated, narrow fruiting bodies that appear as dark lines or scribbly marks on the lichen surface, often resembling ancient writing or hieroglyphs.
children.funFact: The name 'Lecanographaceae' literally means 'writing on a dish,' referring to the script-like appearance of their fruiting bodies that early botanists thought looked like mysterious writing on the lichen's surface.

children.name: Opegraphaceae
Cresponea
children.description: Cresponea is a small genus of crustose lichens that form thin, crusty patches on tree bark and rock surfaces. These lichens create a symbiotic partnership between fungi and algae, working together to survive in harsh environments where neither could live alone.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Cresponea lichens are recognized by their distinctive bright yellow-green to olive-green coloration and their ability to produce unique chemical compounds that can be detected through spot tests.
children.funFact: Like tiny chemical factories, Cresponea lichens produce their own sunscreen compounds that give them their characteristic greenish color while protecting them from harmful UV radiation.

children.description: Opegraphaceae is a family of crustose lichens that form thin, crusty patches on tree bark and other surfaces. These lichens are known for their distinctive elongated, slit-like reproductive structures called lirellae that often look like tiny black lines or dashes on the lichen surface.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their characteristic lirellae - narrow, elongated fruiting bodies that appear as dark, slit-like openings rather than the round or cup-shaped structures found in many other lichen families.
children.funFact: The name 'Opegraphaceae' comes from Greek words meaning 'opening' and 'writing,' referring to how the dark lirellae can resemble mysterious script written across tree bark.

children.description: Arthoniales is an order of lichens that includes some of the most distinctive crustose lichens found growing on tree bark and rocks in New England. These lichens are characterized by their simple, often inconspicuous growth forms and their unique reproductive structures called lirellae - elongated, slit-like openings that release spores.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this order are distinguished by their lirellae (elongated, often comma-shaped or linear spore-bearing structures) rather than the round, disc-like structures found in many other lichen groups. Many species in this order also have a distinctly crustose (crust-like) growth form that appears almost painted onto their substrate.
children.funFact: The comma lichens in this group get their common name from their distinctive comma-shaped reproductive structures that look like tiny punctuation marks scattered across tree bark.

children.name: Lichenostigmatales
Phaeococcomycetaceae
Lichenostigma
children.description: Lichenostigma is a genus of tiny parasitic fungi that live exclusively on lichens, feeding off their host without killing them. These microscopic organisms form small, dark spots or patches on the surface of various lichen species. They represent a specialized group of fungi that have evolved to exploit the unique biology of lichens.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most fungi, Lichenostigma species are obligate parasites that can only survive on living lichens, forming characteristic dark, pinpoint fruiting bodies on their host's surface. They differ from other lichen-associated fungi by being true parasites rather than beneficial partners.
children.funFact: Despite being parasites, Lichenostigma fungi are so small and cause so little damage that their lichen hosts can live with them for years, creating a long-term parasitic relationship that's more like having permanent tiny houseguests.

children.description: Phaeococcomycetaceae is a small family of fungi that are specialized parasites living on lichens. These tiny organisms make their living by growing on and feeding off other fungi that are part of lichen partnerships. They represent a fascinating example of fungi that have evolved to exploit the complex relationships in lichen communities.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their parasitic lifestyle specifically targeting lichens, rather than living freely or forming their own partnerships with algae. They produce dark-colored, simple fruiting bodies that are much smaller than typical lichen structures.
children.funFact: These fungi are essentially 'pirates' of the lichen world - they steal nutrients from the cooperative partnership between fungi and algae that makes up a lichen, without contributing anything beneficial in return.

children.description: Lichenostigmatales is a small order of fungi that are specialized parasites living on lichens. These tiny fungi form dark, often black spots or patches on the surface of their lichen hosts, where they feed on the lichen's tissues.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most other fungi, members of this order are highly specialized to parasitize lichens specifically, forming characteristic dark pigmented fruiting bodies on their hosts. They have a unique lifestyle as obligate parasites that cannot survive without their lichen partners.
children.funFact: These fungi are so small and specialized that they were often overlooked by scientists until relatively recently, when modern microscopy revealed their complex relationships with lichen communities.

children.name: Orbiliales
Arthrobotryaceae
Orbilia
children.description: Orbilia is a genus of tiny cup fungi that create small, disc-shaped fruiting bodies typically less than 2mm across. These delicate fungi are commonly found growing on decaying wood, bark, and plant debris in moist forest environments throughout New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other small cup fungi, Orbilia species are characterized by their smooth, waxy appearance and often bright colors ranging from yellow to orange-red. They also have distinctive spores and specialized cells that help identify different species.
children.funFact: Some Orbilia species are carnivorous, using sticky traps and explosive spores to capture and digest tiny soil animals like nematodes and rotifers.

children.description: Arthrobotryaceae is a fascinating family of fungi that includes some of nature's most remarkable predators - carnivorous fungi that actively hunt and capture microscopic prey like nematodes (roundworms). These fungi produce specialized trapping structures such as sticky nets, lassos, or explosive spores to catch their victims. Most members of this family live in soil or on decaying organic matter where they encounter their prey.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike typical decomposer fungi, members of Arthrobotryaceae have evolved sophisticated predatory mechanisms including adhesive traps, constricting rings, and harpoon-like structures to capture living animals. This carnivorous lifestyle sets them apart from their close relatives that rely solely on breaking down dead organic matter.
children.funFact: Some fungi in this family can form constricting rings that snap shut around nematodes in less than a tenth of a second - faster than a Venus flytrap!

children.description: Orbiliales is an order of small, cup-shaped fungi that includes some of nature's most fascinating predators. These tiny fungi produce delicate, disc-like fruiting bodies that are often translucent or brightly colored, and many species have developed remarkable abilities to capture and consume microscopic animals like nematodes and other small organisms.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most other fungi that decompose dead material, many members of Orbiliales are active predators that use specialized traps, sticky networks, or explosive spores to catch living prey. Their fruiting bodies are typically small, smooth, and cup or disc-shaped with a distinctive gelatinous texture.
children.funFact: Some Orbiliales fungi are like microscopic hunters - they form tiny lassos, sticky traps, or even shoot explosive spores to capture unsuspecting nematode worms, earning them the nickname 'carnivorous fungi.'

children.name: Laboulbeniales
Laboulbeniaceae
Hesperomyces
children.description: Hesperomyces is a genus of tiny parasitic fungi that live exclusively on insects, particularly beetles and other arthropods. These microscopic organisms attach themselves to their hosts and feed off them without killing them, forming a specialized parasitic relationship.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most fungi that grow in soil or on dead organic matter, Hesperomyces species are obligate parasites that can only survive while attached to living insects. They produce distinctive flask-shaped reproductive structures called perithecia directly on their host's body.
children.funFact: The single New England species, Hesperomyces harmoniae, was discovered living on invasive Asian lady beetles and is so small that hundreds could fit on a single beetle's wing cover!

children.description: Laboulbeniaceae are tiny parasitic fungi that live exclusively on the bodies of insects and other small arthropods. These microscopic organisms attach themselves to their hosts and grow as small, flask-shaped structures that are barely visible to the naked eye. Unlike many parasites, they don't seem to harm their hosts significantly and instead form a relatively peaceful relationship.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other fungi, members of Laboulbeniaceae don't produce typical spores and instead reproduce through specialized structures that cement directly onto their arthropod hosts. They're also unique in being obligate ectoparasites, meaning they can only survive on the outside surface of living arthropods.
children.funFact: These tiny fungi are so host-specific that scientists can often identify what type of insect they're looking at just by examining the species of Laboulbeniaceae growing on it!

children.description: Laboulbeniales are microscopic fungi that live as parasites on insects and other small arthropods. These tiny organisms attach themselves to the outside of their hosts' bodies, where they form small, flask-shaped structures that are barely visible to the naked eye. Unlike many parasites, they don't usually harm their hosts significantly.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These fungi are unique because they grow directly on the external surface of living insects, forming distinctive tiny fruiting bodies that look like miniature bottles or flasks. They reproduce through specialized structures that release spores to infect new insect hosts.
children.funFact: Some species of Laboulbeniales are so specialized that they only grow on specific body parts of particular insect species - for example, only on the left wing covers of certain beetles!

children.name: Pyrenocollema
children.description: Pyrenocollema is a genus of crustose lichens that form thin, dark crusts on rocks and other surfaces. These lichens are characterized by their small, flask-shaped reproductive structures called perithecia that are embedded in the lichen body. They represent a partnership between fungi and algae, working together to colonize harsh environments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Pyrenocollema lichens are distinguished by their black perithecia (spore-producing structures) that appear as tiny dark dots scattered across the lichen surface. Unlike many other crustose lichens, they lack the disk-shaped reproductive structures called apothecia.
children.funFact: The single New England species, Pyrenocollema halodytes, is specially adapted to coastal environments and can tolerate regular exposure to salt spray, making it one of the few lichens that thrives in marine-influenced habitats.

children.name: Taphrinales
Taphrinaceae
Taphrina
Taphrina robinsoniana
children.commonName: Eastern American alder tongue gall fungus

children.name: Taphrina robinsoniana
children.commonName: Eastern American alder tongue gall fungus

children.description: Leaf curl fungi are plant parasites that cause distinctive curling, puckering, and blistering of leaves on trees and shrubs. These fungi create swollen, distorted growths on their host plants, often giving leaves a wrinkled or bubble-like appearance. They primarily infect deciduous trees like oaks, birches, poplars, and fruit trees during cool, wet spring weather.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other plant fungi that form mushrooms or molds, leaf curl fungi live entirely within plant tissues and reproduce by budding like yeasts. They create their spores directly on the surface of the deformed plant parts they cause.
children.funFact: The dramatic leaf curling and blistering caused by these fungi is actually the plant's own tissue growing abnormally in response to the fungal infection, not the fungus itself.

children.description: The Taphrinaceae are a family of fungi that specialize in causing distinctive plant diseases, most notably the curling and puckering of leaves on trees and shrubs. These fungi are parasites that live inside plant tissues, causing leaves to become thickened, distorted, and often reddish or yellowish in color. They commonly affect fruit trees like peaches, plums, and cherries, as well as various native trees.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other plant pathogenic fungi, Taphrinaceae members grow directly within the plant's cells and produce their spores on the surface of the distorted leaves without forming typical mushroom-like structures. They create very characteristic symptoms that make infected plants easy to identify from a distance.
children.funFact: Despite causing dramatic-looking leaf curl diseases that can make trees appear severely damaged, most Taphrinaceae infections are actually not fatal to their host plants and the trees typically recover and produce normal leaves the following year.

children.description: Taphrinales are a unique group of fungi that specialize in parasitizing plants, particularly trees and shrubs. Unlike many other plant parasitic fungi, members of this order live inside plant tissues and cause distinctive swellings, puckering, or unusual growths on leaves, fruits, and branches. They have a simple life cycle and reproduce by forming spores directly on the infected plant surfaces.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These fungi are distinguished by their ability to cause characteristic plant deformities like leaf curl, witches' brooms, and fruit bladders without forming typical mushroom-like structures. They reproduce through simple budding yeasts rather than complex spore-bearing structures.
children.funFact: One common member causes the bizarre "plum pockets" - hollow, bladder-like growths that replace normal plums and other stone fruits, creating swollen, empty sacs instead of juicy fruit!

children.name: Neolectales
Neolectaceae
Neolecta
children.description: Neolecta is a small genus of unusual fungi that produce bright yellow to orange, tongue-like or club-shaped fruiting bodies that emerge from the ground or decaying wood. These distinctive fungi have a waxy, smooth surface and can grow up to several inches tall, often appearing in small clusters during late summer and fall.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most other club fungi, Neolecta species have a unique cellular structure and genetic makeup that places them in their own separate branch of the fungal tree of life. Their bright yellow-orange coloration and waxy texture help distinguish them from similar-looking earth tongues and coral fungi.
children.funFact: Despite looking like simple club fungi, genetic studies revealed that Neolecta represents one of the most ancient lineages of fungi, with evolutionary roots stretching back hundreds of millions of years.

children.description: Neolectaceae is a small family of unique fungi that bridge the gap between yeasts and more complex cup fungi. These fascinating organisms can exist as single-celled yeasts or form small, colorful fruiting bodies that look like tiny bright orange or yellow cups or clubs emerging from decaying wood.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike typical cup fungi, members of this family can switch between a yeast-like growth form and producing small, brightly colored fruiting bodies. They are among the most primitive of the cup fungi, representing an evolutionary link to simpler fungal forms.
children.funFact: These fungi are so unusual that scientists originally thought they were yeasts until they discovered they could also produce tiny fruiting bodies, leading to a complete reclassification of their evolutionary position.

children.description: Neolectales is a small order of unusual fungi that form distinctive cup-shaped fruiting bodies. These fungi are characterized by their bright orange to reddish coloration and their preference for growing on decaying coniferous wood, particularly in cooler, mountainous regions.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other cup fungi, members of Neolectales have a unique combination of molecular characteristics and produce spores in a distinctive way that sets them apart from similar-looking species in other fungal groups.
children.funFact: Despite their small size and limited distribution, Neolectales represent one of the most ancient lineages of cup fungi, providing scientists with important clues about early fungal evolution.

children.name: Culicidospora
children.description: Culicidospora is a genus of microscopic parasitic organisms that specifically infect mosquitoes and other aquatic insects. These tiny parasites live inside their host's cells and can significantly impact mosquito populations in wetland environments. They are part of a larger group of single-celled parasites that have co-evolved with their insect hosts over millions of years.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other parasites, Culicidospora species are highly specialized to infect only mosquitoes and closely related flies. They form distinctive spores that can survive in aquatic environments even when their hosts are not present.
children.funFact: These microscopic parasites can actually help control mosquito populations naturally, making them unlikely allies in reducing pest insects around ponds and marshes.

children.name: Arthrosporium
children.description: Arthrosporium is a small genus of fungi that produces distinctive spores with cross-walls or segments. These microscopic organisms are part of the diverse world of fungi that help decompose organic matter in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their segmented spores (called arthroconidia) that break apart at the joints to spread and reproduce.
children.funFact: The name Arthrosporium literally means 'jointed spore' in Greek, referring to the segmented appearance of their reproductive structures.

children.name: Anthina
children.description: Anthina is a small genus of sea anemones that are part of the larger group of cnidarians, animals with stinging cells. These marine creatures are sessile, meaning they attach themselves to hard surfaces on the ocean floor and feed by capturing small prey with their tentacles.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Anthina are characterized by their relatively simple body structure and their ability to retract completely when disturbed. They typically have fewer tentacles than many other sea anemone genera and often display vibrant coloration.
children.funFact: Despite being animals, sea anemones like those in Anthina can reproduce both sexually and asexually, sometimes splitting themselves in half to create identical clones.

children.name: Vouauxiella
children.description: Vouauxiella is a genus of tiny parasitic fungi that live exclusively on lichens, acting as specialized hitchhikers on these composite organisms. These microscopic fungi are so small and inconspicuous that they often go unnoticed, forming minute black dots or spots on their lichen hosts.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike free-living fungi, Vouauxiella species are obligate parasites that can only survive by feeding on lichens. They produce characteristic tiny, dark fruiting bodies that appear as pinpoint-sized black specks on the surface of their host lichens.
children.funFact: These fungi are so specialized that they've evolved to parasitize organisms that are themselves a partnership between fungi and algae, making them parasites of a symbiosis!

children.name: Amblyosporium
children.description: Amblyosporium is a small genus of fungi that produces distinctive spores with unique characteristics. These microscopic organisms are part of the larger fungal kingdom and play roles in decomposition and nutrient cycling in natural environments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their specific spore structure and morphology that sets them apart from other fungal genera. The spores have particular shapes and arrangements that are diagnostic for identification.
children.funFact: The genus name 'Amblyosporium' literally means 'blunt spore,' referring to the rounded or obtuse shape of their reproductive structures.

children.name: Hyalotrochophora
children.description: Hyalotrochophora is a genus of microscopic marine animals that belong to the diverse group of invertebrates. These tiny creatures are part of the broader community of marine microorganisms that play important roles in ocean ecosystems. They are characterized by their transparent bodies and specialized feeding structures.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their glass-like transparency and unique wheel-shaped feeding apparatus that helps them capture food particles from the water.
children.funFact: Despite being incredibly small and transparent, these organisms are skilled filter feeders that help keep marine waters clean by consuming bacteria and other microscopic particles.

children.name: Miricatena
children.description: Miricatena is a genus of small orb weaver spiders that build circular webs to catch their prey. These spiders are part of the larger orb weaver family and are known for their intricate web-building abilities.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Miricatena spiders can be distinguished from other orb weavers by their specific body proportions and web architecture patterns, though they require close examination to identify definitively.
children.funFact: The single New England species, Miricatena prunicola, was likely named 'prunicola' because it's often found associated with prunus trees like wild cherries and plums.

children.name: Entomophthorales
Entomophthoraceae
Entomophaga
children.description: Entomophaga is a genus of specialized fungi that are natural enemies of insects, living as parasites that eventually kill their hosts. These fungi infect insects by growing inside their bodies, consuming them from within, and then producing spores that can spread to other insects. They play an important role in controlling insect populations in natural ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other insect-parasitic fungi, Entomophaga species typically cause their infected hosts to climb to elevated positions before death, helping the fungus spread its spores more effectively. They also produce distinctive resting spores that can survive harsh winter conditions.
children.funFact: Entomophaga maimaiga was intentionally introduced from Asia to North America in the early 1900s to help control destructive gypsy moth caterpillars, and it has become one of the most effective natural controls of this forest pest.

children.name: Furia
children.description: Furia is a genus of very small, parasitic wasps that belong to the family Mymaridae, also known as fairyflies. These tiny insects are among the smallest known insects in the world, with some species measuring less than 0.2 millimeters in length. They develop as parasites inside the eggs of other insects, particularly other small wasps and flies.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Furia wasps can be distinguished from other fairyfly genera by their extremely reduced wing venation and unique antenna structure. They have particularly short, stubby antennae compared to most other members of their family.
children.funFact: Despite being called fairyflies, these wasps are so incredibly tiny that they could easily walk through the eye of a needle, and some species are smaller than single-celled organisms like paramecia!

children.name: Arthrophaga
children.description: Arthrophaga is a genus of tiny predatory mites that specialize in hunting other small arthropods like springtails and other mites. These microscopic arachnids are active hunters that roam through soil and leaf litter in search of their prey. They play an important role as predators in the complex ecosystem found in forest floor communities.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other soil mites that feed on dead organic matter or fungi, Arthrophaga mites are active predators with strong chelicerae (mouthparts) adapted for capturing and consuming live prey.
children.funFact: Despite being smaller than a pinhead, these fierce little predators can take down prey as large as themselves, making them the apex predators of their microscopic world.

children.name: Entomophthora
children.description: Entomophthora is a genus of specialized fungi that are parasites of insects, particularly flies. These fungi infect their hosts from the inside, eventually killing them and using their bodies as a platform to spread spores to new victims. They represent one of nature's most effective biological control agents for pest insects.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other insect-parasitic fungi, Entomophthora species actively shoot their spores away from the host's body with remarkable force and precision. They also create distinctive white halos of spores around their dead insect hosts.
children.funFact: Entomophthora muscae can actually control the behavior of infected flies, forcing them to climb to high places and extend their wings before death, positioning them perfectly to spread spores to other flies below - earning it the nickname 'zombie fly fungus.'

children.name: Eryniopsis
children.description: Eryniopsis is a small genus of entomopathogenic fungi, meaning they are specialized parasites that infect and kill insects. These microscopic fungi play an important role in natural pest control by helping to regulate insect populations in forest and garden ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Eryniopsis are distinguished from other entomopathogenic fungi by their specific infection patterns and the unique spore structures they produce on infected host insects.
children.funFact: The single New England species, Eryniopsis lampyridarum, specifically targets fireflies and their larvae, making it a specialist hunter of these beloved bioluminescent beetles.

children.name: Erynia
children.description: Erynia is a genus of entomopathogenic fungi that specialize in infecting and killing insects. These microscopic fungi act as natural pest controllers, invading the bodies of their insect hosts and eventually consuming them from the inside out. They play an important ecological role by helping to regulate insect populations in forest and field environments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Erynia fungi are distinguished by their ability to produce specialized spores that actively shoot out from infected insect hosts to spread the infection to nearby insects. Unlike many other fungal pathogens, they can forcibly discharge their spores over considerable distances.
children.funFact: When Erynia fungi kill their insect hosts, they often manipulate the insect's behavior before death, causing infected insects to climb to high positions where the fungus can better spread its spores to other potential victims below.

children.description: The Entomophthoraceae are a family of fungi that specialize in infecting and killing insects and other arthropods. These microscopic predators launch spores that penetrate their host's body, eventually consuming the insect from the inside out and producing new spores to continue the cycle.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other fungi, members of this family are obligate parasites that can only survive by infecting living insects. They produce distinctive spores that are actively shot from the infected host's body to spread to new victims.
children.funFact: Some species in this family can actually control their insect host's behavior, making infected flies climb to high places before death so the fungal spores can disperse more effectively - creating 'zombie' insects!

children.description: Insect Destroyers are a specialized group of fungi that have evolved to be parasites of insects and other small arthropods. These fungi actively infect living insects, eventually killing their hosts and using their bodies as a source of nutrition. They play an important ecological role as natural pest controllers in many ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most fungi that decompose dead organic matter, Entomophthorales are obligate parasites that must infect living insects to complete their life cycle. They produce specialized spores that are forcibly ejected to infect new insect hosts.
children.funFact: Some species in this group can actually control their insect host's behavior, causing infected flies to climb to high places before death, which helps the fungus spread its spores more effectively - creating real-life 'zombie insects'!

children.name: Mucorales
Pilobolaceae
Pilobolus
children.description: Pilobolus is a genus of tiny fungi that grows exclusively on the dung of herbivorous animals like cows, horses, and deer. These microscopic fungi are specialized decomposers that help break down nutrients in animal waste and return them to the soil ecosystem.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other dung fungi, Pilobolus species have a unique crystal-filled structure that acts like a lens to focus sunlight, helping them aim their spores toward bright areas where grazing animals are likely to be found.
children.funFact: Pilobolus fungi are nature's sharpshooters - they can launch their spore-filled capsules up to 8 feet away with incredible accuracy, aiming toward light to increase the chances that grazing animals will eat the spores and spread them to new dung piles!

children.description: The Pilobolaceae are a family of tiny fungi that specialize in growing on animal dung, particularly from herbivores like horses and cows. These microscopic fungi are commonly known as 'dung cannons' or 'hat throwers' because of their remarkable ability to explosively launch their spores great distances.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are unique among fungi for their explosive spore dispersal mechanism, using specialized structures that can shoot spore-containing capsules up to 8 feet away with incredible accuracy.
children.funFact: Pilobolus fungi can aim their spore cannons toward light with pinpoint precision, ensuring their spores land on fresh grass where they'll be eaten by grazing animals and eventually deposited in new dung piles to continue their life cycle.

children.name: Syzygitaceae
Syzygites
children.description: Syzygites is a genus of fungi that belongs to the group known as zygomycetes, which are characterized by their unique sexual reproduction method. These fungi typically grow as fuzzy molds and play important roles as decomposers in forest ecosystems. They help break down organic matter like fallen leaves and dead plant material.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Syzygites fungi are distinguished by their specialized reproductive structures called zygospores, which form when two fungal filaments fuse together. They also produce distinctive spore-bearing structures that look like tiny clubs or pins under magnification.
children.funFact: When Syzygites fungi reproduce sexually, they create thick-walled spores that can survive harsh winter conditions and remain dormant for months before sprouting into new fungal growth in spring.

children.description: Syzygitaceae is a small family of fungi that are specialized parasites of other fungi. These microscopic organisms attack and feed on various types of mold and fungal growth, making them important natural controllers in fungal ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most fungi that decompose organic matter or form partnerships with plants, members of Syzygitaceae are obligate parasites that specifically target other fungi as their hosts.
children.funFact: These tiny fungal parasites help keep other fungal populations in check, acting like nature's own biological pest control system in the microscopic world.

children.name: Rhizopodaceae
Rhizopus
children.description: Rhizopus is a genus of fast-growing fungi that are commonly found decomposing organic matter like bread, fruits, and vegetables. These molds spread rapidly by sending out thread-like structures called stolons that run along surfaces, creating new colonies wherever they touch down. They play an important role in nature by breaking down dead plant material and recycling nutrients back into the ecosystem.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Rhizopus molds are distinguished by their black, pin-head-like spore structures (sporangia) and their characteristic stolons that create a network of fuzzy growth across surfaces. Unlike many other molds, they produce root-like structures called rhizoids that anchor directly into their food source.
children.funFact: Black bread mold can complete its entire life cycle from spore to spore in just a few days under ideal conditions, making it one of the fastest-reproducing organisms on Earth.

children.description: Rhizopodaceae is a family of fast-growing fungi commonly known as pin molds or bread molds. These fungi are characterized by their cottony, white to grayish appearance and their ability to quickly colonize organic matter like fruits, vegetables, and bread.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family produce distinctive sporangia (spore-bearing structures) that look like tiny black pinheads on stalks, giving them their 'pin mold' nickname. They also form extensive networks of root-like structures called rhizoids that anchor them to their food source.
children.funFact: Rhizopus species can grow so rapidly that they can completely cover a piece of bread in just a few days under the right conditions of warmth and moisture.

children.name: Phycomycetaceae
Spinellus
children.description: Spinellus is a genus of parasitic fungi that specifically attacks other fungi, particularly mushrooms and other molds. These tiny parasites grow on their fungal hosts, forming delicate, thread-like structures topped with small spore-bearing heads. They represent a fascinating example of fungi preying on other fungi in nature.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most fungi that decompose organic matter or form partnerships with plants, Spinellus species are obligate parasites that can only survive by attacking other fungi. They produce distinctive pin-like fruiting structures with spherical heads containing their spores.
children.funFact: Bonnet mold earned its common name because its tiny spherical spore heads look like miniature bonnets sitting atop slender stalks when viewed under magnification.

children.description: Phycomycetaceae is a small family of fungi that are parasites of other fungi, particularly targeting mushrooms and molds. These microscopic organisms live by attacking and feeding on their fungal hosts, creating a unique ecological niche as fungal parasites.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their specialized lifestyle as obligate parasites of other fungi, and they produce distinctive spore-bearing structures that emerge from their hosts.
children.funFact: These fungi are essentially the vampires of the fungal world - they survive entirely by parasitizing other fungi, making them some of nature's most specialized predators.

children.name: Mucoraceae
Dicranophora
children.description: Dicranophora is a genus of slime molds that forms distinctive branching, fork-like fruiting bodies when reproducing. These organisms spend most of their lives as mobile, blob-like plasmodia that crawl through decaying organic matter, feeding on bacteria and other microorganisms.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are recognized by their characteristic Y-shaped or dichotomously branched sporangia (spore-bearing structures) that give the group its name, which literally means 'fork-bearer.'
children.funFact: Despite being called 'molds,' these organisms are not actually fungi but belong to a completely different kingdom and can actively move and hunt for food like tiny, brainless animals.

children.description: The Mucoraceae are a family of fungi commonly known as pin molds that produce fuzzy, cotton-like growths on decaying organic matter. These fast-growing molds are among the most common decomposers you'll encounter, often appearing as white or grayish fuzzy patches on old bread, fruits, and other organic materials.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other molds, Mucoraceae produce their spores in round, dark structures called sporangia that sit atop tall, unbranched stalks, giving them a distinctive pin-like appearance when viewed up close.
children.funFact: Some members of this family can grow so rapidly that they can completely cover a piece of bread in just a few days under the right conditions!

children.description: Pin molds are a group of fungi that produce distinctive upright stalks topped with round spore cases, resembling tiny pins or lollipops. These fast-growing molds are commonly found on decaying organic matter like fallen logs, animal dung, and rich soil where they help break down dead material. They reproduce by shooting spores from their pin-like structures, often creating fuzzy patches of growth.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other mold groups, pin molds have simple, non-segmented fungal threads and produce their spores in distinctive spherical cases held up on tall, straight stalks. Their spore-bearing structures lack the complex branching patterns seen in many other mold families.
children.funFact: Some pin molds can literally shoot their spores several feet through the air - the dung-loving species Pilobolus can launch spores up to 6 feet away to land on fresh grass that animals will eat, ensuring the cycle continues!

children.name: Endogonales
Endogonaceae
Endogone
children.description: Endogone is a genus of microscopic fungi that forms special partnerships with plant roots, helping them absorb nutrients from the soil. These fungi produce small, round spore-containing structures that develop underground, making them difficult to spot without careful searching. They belong to an ancient group of fungi that has been forming these beneficial relationships with plants for hundreds of millions of years.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other mycorrhizal fungi, Endogone produces distinctive spherical fruiting bodies that contain spores arranged in a unique pattern. These structures are typically found buried in soil rather than growing on the surface like mushrooms.
children.funFact: Endogone fungi are considered living fossils - they represent one of the most ancient types of fungi on Earth and may have been among the first to help early land plants colonize terrestrial environments over 400 million years ago.

children.description: The Endogonaceae are a family of ancient fungi that form beneficial partnerships with plant roots, helping them absorb nutrients from the soil. These fungi are among the earliest known to form mycorrhizal relationships, a partnership that has been crucial for plant life on land for hundreds of millions of years.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other mycorrhizal fungi, Endogonaceae produce thick-walled spores inside the soil and have a very simple internal structure. They form a type of mycorrhiza called arbuscular mycorrhiza, where the fungus creates tiny tree-like structures inside plant root cells.
children.funFact: These fungi are so ancient that they likely helped the very first plants colonize land from water over 400 million years ago, making them some of the most important partners in Earth's history.

children.description: Endogonales are ancient fungi that form partnerships with plant roots, helping them absorb nutrients from soil. These microscopic fungi live underground and produce large, truffle-like spores that can be found buried in forest soil. They represent one of the earliest groups of fungi to evolve the ability to form beneficial relationships with plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other mycorrhizal fungi, Endogonales produce unusually large spores (up to several millimeters across) that develop inside thick-walled structures called sporocarps. Their spores are among the largest produced by any fungi and can often be seen with the naked eye.
children.funFact: Endogonales fungi have been forming partnerships with plants for over 400 million years, making them some of the oldest known mutualistic organisms on Earth and likely crucial to early plant colonization of land.

children.name: Synchytriales
Synchytriaceae
Synchytrium
children.description: False rusts are microscopic fungal parasites that live inside plant cells, causing small galls, warts, or blisters to form on leaves, stems, and other plant parts. Unlike true rusts, these tiny organisms spend their entire life cycle within a single host plant cell, where they reproduce and eventually release spores. They are among the simplest fungi, lacking the complex structures found in most other fungal groups.
children.distinguishingFeatures: False rusts are distinguished from true rusts by their much simpler structure and their ability to complete their entire life cycle within one host cell, rather than requiring multiple host plants or producing complex spore stages.
children.funFact: Despite their name, false rusts are not closely related to true rusts at all - they belong to an entirely different group of primitive fungi and are actually more closely related to water molds than to typical mushroom-forming fungi.

children.description: Synchytriaceae is a family of microscopic fungi that live as parasites inside plant cells, causing various diseases and deformities in their hosts. These tiny organisms are so small they can only be seen with a microscope, yet they can cause dramatic swellings, galls, and other visible changes to the plants they infect. They reproduce by forming swimming spores that can move through water to find new plant hosts.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other plant parasitic fungi, members of Synchytriaceae live entirely within a single host cell and produce motile spores with whip-like tails called flagella. They also lack the thread-like structures (hyphae) that most other fungi use to grow and spread.
children.funFact: Despite being incredibly tiny single-celled organisms, some Synchytriaceae species can cause such dramatic plant deformities that they create witch's broom formations - dense clusters of abnormal growth that look like old-fashioned brooms stuck in trees.

children.description: Synchytriales are microscopic aquatic fungi that live as parasites or decomposers in freshwater and marine environments. These tiny organisms have a simple structure and reproduce by forming swimming spores with whip-like tails called flagella. They play important roles in aquatic ecosystems by breaking down organic matter and cycling nutrients.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most fungi, members of Synchytriales produce motile spores that can swim through water using their flagella. They also have a relatively simple body structure compared to more complex fungi like mushrooms or molds.
children.funFact: These ancient fungi are thought to be among the earliest forms of fungal life on Earth, with some species capable of infecting algae and helping control algal blooms in aquatic systems.

children.name: Monoblepharidales
Monoblepharidaceae
Monoblepharis
children.description: Monoblepharis is a genus of aquatic fungi that live in freshwater environments like ponds, streams, and wetlands. These microscopic organisms are water molds that play important roles in decomposing organic matter in aquatic ecosystems. They reproduce by producing swimming spores that can move through water using whip-like structures.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most other water molds, Monoblepharis produces distinctive male reproductive cells called sperm that can actually swim to reach female structures. This makes them unique among fungi, as most fungal groups don't produce motile male gametes.
children.funFact: Monoblepharis fungi are among the few fungal groups that have separate male and female reproductive structures, making their mating process more similar to plants and animals than to other fungi.

children.description: Monoblepharidaceae is a small family of aquatic fungi that live in freshwater environments like ponds, streams, and soil. These microscopic fungi are unique among their relatives because they produce swimming spores with flagella that help them move through water. They typically grow as branching thread-like structures and play important roles in decomposing organic matter in aquatic ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most other fungi, members of this family produce motile spores that can actually swim using whip-like flagella. They are also distinguished by their specific reproductive structures and their strictly aquatic lifestyle.
children.funFact: Monoblepharidaceae fungi are among the few fungal groups that have retained the ancient ability to produce swimming spores, a feature that most fungi lost millions of years ago as they adapted to life on land.

children.description: Monoblepharidales is a small order of aquatic fungi that live in freshwater environments like ponds, streams, and wet soil. These microscopic fungi are among the most primitive water molds, playing important roles in decomposing organic matter in aquatic ecosystems. They reproduce through swimming spores that help them spread through water.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most other water molds, members of Monoblepharidales produce true gametes (specialized reproductive cells) that look and behave differently from each other, similar to sperm and eggs in animals.
children.funFact: These ancient fungi are considered living fossils, representing one of the earliest evolutionary branches of water molds that have remained virtually unchanged for millions of years.
